In response to the success of far cry 3, I feel it's time I look back and take a more in-depth review of far cry 2. Upon first look, it's a game with a terrible story and many infuriating game mechanics. More specifically, players hate the permanent dependance on malaria medication, the accelerated weapon degradation, the re-populating enemy strongholds and checkpoints, and the unusual fast-travel system. If you find yourself miserable due to all these problems, I understand if you want to un-install. However...
I find a dusty, bloody, and primal charm from the whole game experience. Every issue I listed above is actually a reason as to why I love this game! And for me, it all comes down to immersion in the game's world. For example, the story doesn't grab you like it does in so many GOTYs. Instead of creating some elaborate story for the player to get distracted by, players are sent on small missions that allow them to play the game their own way. Weapon degradation forces you to use foresight and planning to ensure you are at your prime. Malaria also keeps you focused on living day-to-day, and prevents you from being the uber-warrior that so many games make you into. Never-ending enemy spawning keeps you on your toes. The fast-travel-by-bus system allows you to make short leaps around the map, but only in certain areas, forcing you to plan your routes effectively.
Overall, far cry 2 is unapologetically rough. Underneath the seemingly frustrating game features lies highly immersive gameplay. The beautiful and lifelike ambient sounds and stunning visuals are just icing on the bloody, bloody cake.
P.S.: I originally wanted to call FC2 realistic, but I now see it as engrossing, which is much more fun. If you can buy this game at $2.50 on a sale, please give this game a try.

After the success of the fantastic, open-level, tough as nails FPS, Far Cry, designed by Crytek, Ubisoft decided to make a sequel all on their own. But without Crytek's involvement, things got weird. I don't mean "weird" like the same kind of weird as the Xbox and Xbox 360 re-imaginings of Far Cry starring the same protagonist from the original game in an alternate story of the first game, but rather a game that is so vastly different from the original in pretty much every way.
Instead of being in a beautifully green and blue, multi-colored island, you're in the African savannah, and you start jumping in by making the totally unimportant choice of which character to play as, and it really make no difference except for your hand tattoos, outfit you rarely see, and who your friends are, but all that also really makes no difference. It doesn't have to, so that's not really an issue. But there is still an issue at the beginning. The game starts off with you going for a ride to some hotel but when you arrive, you learn you've gotten malaria and the guy who you're there to kill ends up basically laughing at you and supplying you with a macehete and pistol. Now you must escape that civil war that's suddenly happening around your hotel and find out how to not die from malaria. When you finally are given the freedom to explore the map that's been crafted for you by the developers and search for cases with diamonds that can be used to buy weapons and upgrades after completing some missions for the chain of firearms dealers. But really, you can't, because if you wander around for too long, you'll run out of pills and die. Game over.
So you need to go do some resistance missions in exchange for medication. Then you can explore for just a little while longer. Too bad there's really nothing else to do. Even the developers seemed to notice that. So they set enemy checkpoints at places and tried justifying that by giving each checkpoint some gear: health pack, ammo, explosives, or gasoline for molotovs. But it's not so much helpful as it is annoying.
Almost as annoying as having weapons that degrade over time. After use of reloading and firing, your weapons will jam, and eventually explode because apparently guns do that? Again, that's incredibly frustrating.
The game manages to have that level of difficult that the original had without being frustratingly difficult. You feel that sense of mortality but you do feel like you can take on enemies. That's going to be really useful since stealth has been downgraded to be completely awful. Enemies sense you nearby even if you move slowly while crouched, and there's no ability to throw rocks to distract enemies. I've never been to Africa but I'm pretty sure there's some rocks that I can throw.
All of this adds up to a frustrating experience that only really gets a couple things right about Far Cry. Even the Xbox and Xbox 360 Far Cry games felt more entertaining than this and even though the Far Cry "series" hadn't yet really felt like a series that had quite built something yet, it still didn't feel right. Only the ability to drive, shoot, and somewhat sneak felt like Far Cry. That, and the fact that you are still a Far Cry from home.
I remember playing this on my PS3 when it came out and it didn't feel right to me even then. But now that Far Cry seems to have found the right formula, Far Cry 2 seems even more out of place. More out of place than Primal or Blood Dragon. So if you want an experience that is Far Cry at its truest form, then at the time of this post, I recommend Far Cry and Far Cry 3, as they are the series' finest achievements. I certainly hope that Far Cry 5 can join in as one of the series' greater games.

I have played about 17 hours of Watch_Dogs and this is my thoughts on the experience so far.
Likes:
Story - The story has kept me on track to do the main missions instead of going off the rail and spending hours watching people on their laptop webcams. The story is vague enough to keep you enthralled and wanting more.
Accessibility - The game starts you out with the options to get the best weapons out of the gate. If you have the cash, you have the M-108 .50cal sniper rifle.
Profiler - The profiler (your access to the ctOS system to hack stuff) has some of the best little stories for each person.
You can find a 40 year old CEO who makes $350650 a year that "Internet search - Yiff parties" taking a photo of a statue in a park or the police history of a hobo on the street. I’ve taken more screen shots of random NPC's info than epic stuff I’ve exploded or done.
Music - The music you can steal from people is varried and super awesome, from Weezer to Nos. There is a ton of music I've looked into that I have not even aquired yet.
Dislikes:
Driving - All of the driving is kind of a pain in the butt if you are using a keyboard/mouse. Do yourself a favor and NEVER touch your mouse when you are driving something
Weapon/Accessories selection - The wheel of frustration sucks... selecting firearms on accident will make everyone go bat crap crazy and call the cops on you. Is this feature sudo-realisitic? Yes. Is it annoying as all hell? OH HELL YES!
Windowed vs. Full screen - If for some reason you play full screen like I do you will find that WHEN the game crashes, and it will, you will have to reset your display to full screen since windowed is the default display option. Minor dislike but still annoying if you accidently close your gaming laptop and the system goes all crazy on ya.
Over all I really do like this game and have recommended it to 3 people in real life.
My wife hates it since I haven't set down my laptop or IEM's in 3 days.
The story has me hooked by at ACTII right now and I have SO much more to unlock and do. I can not wait to finish this game so I can start on Watch_Dogs 2.

TLDR; Surprisingly deep and fun Connect-3 RPG, but beware devious monetization.
Generous amount of learning, exploration, and fun available for F2P players.
Strategic variance given by the RPG "troops" in a connect-3 was so novel to me that each new strategic pattern felt like a wonderous breakthrough! Changing all the blues to yellows after collecting mana for your troops and synergizing their abilities had a shocking amount of strategic depth! Very impressed with what I expected to be a trivial connect-3 time-waster. This exploration of strategies and variety of game modes and challenges ties so well into the RPG elements and variable play styles it's one of the most addictive games I've ever played. You always want one more run so you get one more thing to try one new tweak to your team. On par with Stardew valley with how addictive "one more day" felt there.
Not much! Recent UI changes removed contrast in the important numbers and generally was a downgrade but the developers are receiving and acting on feedback. I have little doubt it will be a slick and intuitive interface in no time.
This game knows what it is. If you don't think connect 3 is "real" gaming then obviously move on.
Like any F2P game in order to have a reasonable chance at the top levels (guild wars, the progressively more challenging PvP ranks) money or life-abandoning amounts of time are required. This doesn't mean you can't enjoy a little puzzle game with heavy RPG elements for free, it does mean you need to be wary of your natural human desire to continue progressing in the RPG elements will be met with a pay wall. A subtle, masterful piece of psychological manipulation for trapping maximal numbers of whales as the primary monetization strategy. Don't be a whale. Quit when the paywall arrives, or just play happily on until you've sucked all the fun strategies available to f2p players and move on.
Not recommended due to manipulative monetization structure.

So when I initially wrote this review, I did so when the game was nothing but a few days old. Now that time has progressed, and I felt that this game has come a long way, I would like to update this to give possible buyers a better perspective of what they are getting themselves into.
One of my favorite things so far is the uniqueness you find among the buildable armies. Typically in strategy games such as this, you are often handed a few sprities for a variety of nations. This somewhat lessens the visual appeal of the game because how fun would it be when "everyone" looks like a german soldier. In TWG, the visuals are better such as when you play Japan, your troops look unique compared to what they would look like in Korea. They approach this in a cool way and while minor I think it goes a long way.
Next is the micromanaging and complexity. In previous MH games, players were able to research and produce one item per city which could be a soldier, tank, goods, and so forth. But in TGW, players can actually assign individual factories to produce goods, weapons, or tanks while also training your next batch of troops. Research is going on in the background while you focus building a nation or war machine. This expands the possiblities when it comes to determining how your nation will go but can be consuming to the average joe who just wants to build stuff and fight. Players also must also keep in mind the resources in which you must have to keep your factories turning out new stuff and goes into a new system of trading.
Overall, this game is headed in the right direction, and from a gamer whos been gaming for ages, and a long time MH fan, I feel this game can be the next great stepping stone for this company. The AI is getting better, and has at times made me bang my head because it actually out smarted me on several occasions. If you are into strategy and nation building games, TGW is for you.
In my opinion, it brings a new breath of fresh air to a genre i've long loved and has provided something new. Hopefully they continue on the path to success!

Far Cry 2 is a game that you can either absolutely adore, or just plainly despise.
Personally, I love it.
Far Cry 2 was the sequel-out-of-nowhere that had nothing to do with the original in any way save the fact it shared the same name. But Far Cry 2 holds the spirit of the original in many ways. The game is all about innovation- refining the average FPS style game. You're put right in the shoes of any character you choose at the start , and you will guide your silent protagonist through the entire game as if you were really there in the action.
One thing to notice- the absolutely stunning graphics the game's engine can produce. And along with that, the unpredictable world it creates. Time of day and weather, and even fire, are completely dynamic.
Along with narrative and character development that can make you really feel the world around you, and a story that will keep you engaged in the action, and great shooting gameplay with innovations all over it, Far Cry 2 is worth playing.

After hearing The Curse of Nordic Cove say that every word that leaves its mouth is teeming with useful information, I felt that someone needed to write a dissenting opinion. Before I start, however, I should state that to understand what its particularly imprudent form of corporatism has encompassed as a movement and as a system of rule, we have to look at its historical context and development as a form of splenetic politics that first arose in early twentieth-century Europe in response to rapid social upheaval, the devastation of World War I, and the Bolshevik Revolution. Be honest; can you in any way believe The Curse of Nordic :lol: Cove's claim that its wisecracks are Holy Writ? I cannot, mainly because I cannot promise not to be angry at it. I do promise, however, to try to keep my anger under control, to keep it from leading me—as it leads The Curse of Nordic Cove—to force me to undergo “treatment” to cure my “problem”.
Trying to keep The Curse of Nordic Cove from eroticizing relations of dominance and subordination is a sucker's game. No matter how hard we try to stop it, it'll always find some new way to ignore compromise and focus solely on its personal agenda. It is apparent to me that The Curse of Nordic Cove is doing some pretty niddering things. Or, to restate that without meiosis, it will do anything to prevent us from critiquing its crazy, petulant soliloquies. Don't soliloquies that aim to prey on people's fear of political and economic instability deserve—and in some sense, require—abundant critique and evaluation? That's why I propose that we show pluck and optimism when presented with threats and terror, mainly because if you spend much time listening to The Curse of Nordic Cove's trash talk you'll inevitably hear the term “succinylsulphathiazole” thrown around. Usually The Curse of Nordic Cove hurls that word as an epithet, a way of accusing someone of encouraging opportunity, responsibility, and community or of doing something else of which The Curse of Nordic Cove disapproves. More accepted usage of the word, however, is to describe the manner in which it doesn't do us much good to become angry and wave our arms and shout about the evils of The Curse of Nordic Cove's objectives in general terms. If we want other people to agree with us and join forces with us, then we must carve a tunnel of hope through the dark mountain of disappointment.
The Curse of Nordic Cove's responses to my attempts to search for solutions that are more creative and constructive than the typically self-centered ones championed by libidinous, nefarious blockish-types generally involve crying, whining, and wrapping itself in a self-protecting mantle of superiority. That's clear. But there's no shortage of sin in the world today. It's been around since the Garden of Eden and will really persist as long as The Curse of Nordic Cove continues to snatch people off the street and transport them across the world to be tortured. I sometimes see well-meaning people swallow The Curse of Nordic Cove's lie that arrogant skybalds are more deserving of honor than our nation's war heroes. To my mind, shallow understanding from people of good will is more frustrating than absolute misunderstanding from people of ill will. That's why I wish that all decent people realized that even when The Curse of Nordic Cove isn't lying, it's using facts, emphasizing facts, bearing down on facts, sliding off facts, quietly ignoring facts, and, above all, interpreting facts in a way that will enable it to resolve a moral failure with an immoral solution. I may not believe that it's okay for The Curse of Nordic Cove to indulge its every whim and lust without regard for anyone else or for society as a whole, but I doubtlessly do feel that I think I know why so many abominable, manipulative soulless-types concoct labels for people, objects, and behaviors in order to manipulate the public's opinion of them. It's because The Curse of Nordic Cove has whipped them into a blind frenzy by telling them that we'll be moved by some heartfelt words on the glories of privatism. Unfortunately for The Curse of Nordic Cove, the ground truth is that in my observations upon fanaticism, I have expressed no opinion thus far of the mode of its extinguishment or melioration. I will note, however, though I still have nothing to propose, that The Curse of Nordic Cove can get away with lies (e.g., that laws are meant to be broken) because the average person cannot imagine anyone lying so brazenly. Not one person in a hundred will actually check out the facts for himself and discover that The Curse of Nordic Cove is lying.
People often get the impression that disruptive litterbugs and The Curse of Nordic Cove's myrmidons are separate entities. Not so. When one catches cold, the other sneezes. As proof, note that The Curse of Nordic Cove's jeremiads are more than hideous. They fill me with a sense of despair. More than anything else, they make me realize that we must indubitably call for proper disciplinary action against The Curse of Nordic Cove and its serfs. A compossible option is to tell it like it is. If we follow that approach, however, we must bear in mind that if it were up to The Curse of Nordic Cove, we'd all be grazing contentedly in the pasture of revisionism right now. We'd be totally unaware of the fact that if its attempts to promote the lie of egoism have spurred us to lift our nation from the quicksand of injustice to the solid rock of brotherhood, then The Curse of Nordic Cove may have accomplished a useful thing.
I correctly predicted that The Curse of Nordic Cove would expose and neutralize its rivals rather than sit at the same table and negotiate. Alas, I didn't think it'd do that so effectively—or so soon. It may seem at first that there is an implicit assumption here that The Curse of Nordic Cove is behind much of the sociopolitical indoctrination that goes on in many of our classrooms. When we descend to details, however, we see that for some odd reason, it believes that it is always being misrepresented and/or persecuted. Its unasinous spokesmen, who believe likewise, also fail to see that like a verbal magician, The Curse of Nordic Cove knows how to lie without appearing to be lying, how to bury secrets in mountains of garbage-speak. The Curse of Nordic Cove needs to stop living in denial. It needs to wake up and realize that it seems to assume that serfdom and slavery do not represent oppression unless the serfs or the slaves themselves “articulate” that oppression. This is an assumption of the worst kind because it says that condemning its criminal ineptitude is something to be regulated, policed, feared, and controlled. What it means by this, of course, is that it wants free reign to scupper my initiative to rise above the narrow confines of self-existence to the broader concerns of all humanity. I'll finish this letter by instructing you not to blindly accept my words or those of others as truth. Investigate, discriminate, and question everything not proven. I found this game a few days ago on steam by Searching for Pokemon. I was just curious as to what Steam had to offer in the monster taming genre. What I found left me wanting more. You see, during the pokemon craze there were several games that came out looking to capitolize on Pokemon's formula. This game seems to take elements from quitee a few of them. But what I see it mostly inspired by is one of my favorite roguelikes growing up, well before I knew what a roguelike was. Dragon Warrior Monsters.
This game is like a love letter to that style of game, beautiful retro graphics that would not be out of place on the Gameboy Color, wonderfuly aranged midi's that invoke a feeling of adventure, the randomly generated dungeons, which I might add are superior to DWM in that they are not just empty spaces but filled with things to interact with, from resources to gather, to npcs to help and merchents to buy from. Every dungeon has a duty associated with it, generated randomly when you enter, finish the duty and you get a large reward such as a nice haul of resources for building your kingdom, or artifacts or cores to help you summon more monsters and a nice fat wad of experience. I find this helpful for leveling up low level monsters to help them catch up with the rest of the party as you start the game off only able to have one monster in your party (Two after a tutorial battle which comes quickly in the begining) as you level up you can add more monsters to your party up to six.
The method of attaining your monsters has it's own unique spin this time around, instead of befirending wild monsters you use your magic on weakened monsters in the wild to extract their core. I think of this as something like essential salts from some of H.P. Lovecrafts works. Once you have three of the same type of core you can take it to the summoning brazier and along with some resources, (reagents for a evil summoning spell) you burn them there by calling your monster into your realm of existance from whatever dastardly plain they call home.
The thing I really love about this game though is the sheer bredth of it. You can play forever and still get stronger. There is no level cap. So you can level as long as you like. Crazy right? Yeah and things actually scale to your party's level. So if your character is super high level but you are working with a party of level 1 newbie monsters you can still have a decent shot in battle.
Anyway I love this game and I'm only four hours in. If you think this game is something you would enjoy I can tell you that ten dollars is deffinatly worth the price of admition.
A half hour in and I think I'm hooked. Grab this gemn while it's on sale!

I want to love this title, but the experience falters a bit for me.
The graphics are quite beautiful, and unlike most point n click adventures, the environs are 3d, although you still interact in a 2d fashion. You won't buld too large of an inventory, like most modern games (i miss the massive inventories with tons of possibilities!), and most of the puzzles include talking. A lot of talking.
You talk, you look around, you use some items, then you talk some more, look around, then realize the only way to move forward is to talk yet again.  This is a common mechanic in most p&c games, but this game uses it far too often. The voice acting is fine, but unlike, say, a Walking Dead, where the expressions and gesticulations of the characters can actually bring you to tears, these characters are quite stale in their emotes. You will watch a back & forth convo carry on for minutes, with no more animation than a slight swaying or breathing; nothing indicating the feeling of what they are saying. The game really suffers under the weight of this, and I find it hard to move forward knowing that too much of the time I will be listening and not "doing."  Dialogue is mostly skippable, but at the same time I hate to skip through and miss things.
Some of the dialogue is really funny, with lots of WoW style outside references to pop culture-ish RPG staples (and the in-game mmo is hilarious).
Aside from being to reliant on lengthy dialogue, the puzzles are good stuff, except some are a bit too obvious when they give you hints with each item that might be applicable, and when you actually do get stuck, there is no help to be found within the game. Also, I'm not sure I like the fact that most environment items can only be examined once, after that they aren't clickable. So they are too easily excluded, and also, if you miss hearing what they said about them, that's it, you won't hear it again.
Bit odd that in 16/9 there are black lines on the screen, even though cursor moves over them. but in 1680/1050 it just looks like fullscreen. is this true resolution support? no big, but odd. Otherwise, interface, saves and other elements are all good.
All in all, a good game, that gets bogged down in it's heavy reliance on dialogue and it's inexplicable lack of luster in that area.

Playing The Book of Unwritten Tales is like opening a game preserved in a time capsule for the past two decades. This traditional point-and-click adventure originally released in Europe in 2009 harks back to the days when Sierra and LucasArts ruled the world with legendary franchises like King's Quest and Monkey Island. German developer King Art has crafted a lighthearted fantasy grounded in an earthy sense of humor and grown-up story themes and has avoided the impossible, illogical puzzles well known to plague other games in the genre. In short, this is a great achievement in both story and design that should be played by anyone who appreciates an old-school adventure.

The Book of Unwritten Tales is a point-and-click adventure video game created by German developer King Art originally released in 2009 in Germany and translated to English and re-released in 2011.
Despite being originally released in 2009, the graphics still looks very beautiful and hand-drawn with alot of attention to details which makes this a beautiful journey to adventure in. Animations are smooth and fluid and the whole game is just looks very pleasing to the eye. The cutscenes could use some improvements however, as they are lower resolution pre-rendered videos with no option for subtitles even though the game itself supports it.
Music is also very orchestral and professional sounding, with nice little jingles accompanied with sweeping epic symphonies. Voice acting is really very good and each of the voices add alot of substance to the characters.
The story itself is about 14 hours long and is an interesting and light-hearted tale that pokes fun at itself and pays homage to alot of fantasy and RPG stereotypes.
Although there are no in-game hint system, the puzzles are not very difficult and feels just right. There are however some puzzle minigames that may require a little dexterity (Eg: a rhythm based music game)
For younger gamers who have not played the classic old Lucasarts adventure games however, they may not get some of the jokes. For the most part though, the overall plot is easy to understand, entertaining and a clever plot mechanic near the end certainly surprised me. The ending was a little abrupt however, and while the game does end in a cliffhanger, it is still quite satisfying.
Downside, there was a potential game stopping bug relatively early in the game and I was lucky to have had a savegame beforehand. (Protip: Do not press ESC when you are doing the Wheel of Fortune, because if you do, the character animations will just loop and you will not be able to progress further)
Other minor annoyances include not being able to make the character walk faster, and the typical "mouse-over everything on the screen until something is clickable" type of situations. (2nd Protip: Pressing Spacebar will allow you to see ALL the clickable locations on the screen. Be forwarned however that this might make the game a little too easy.) A superb inheritor of the original Chris Taylor classic, Total Annihilation. Keeping true to the original game mechanics which made that game a trend setter, such as queued build orders, continuous economy and resources, and large battlefields where land air and sea units are all necessary, Supreme Commander adds new gameplay mechanics which make the game even more interesting.
One cannot speak of this game's innovation without mentioning the dynamic zoom function. A zoom which allows a player to focus onto the smallest of units and then, with a flick of the scroll wheel, seemlessly zoom out and view the whole map. It get's even better with two monitors, allowing players to have two maps open and controlled simultaneously.
New gameplay elements are introduced via the experimental units. Massive units which bring new combinations and often deadly and resilient firepower. Turtling simply doesn't work when 10 galactic collosii walk through your defensive position. Many of these experimentals constitue, "game enders," which, as the name suggests, typically means you win if you get one built. Units like the 80 kilometer rapid firing nuclear artillery cannon named the Mavor put an element of urgency into your enemies. If you aren't able to attack the enemy and destroy these game enders, you will have little luck winning.
Overall, the game is one of the top strategy games ever made. Add in the player created units and maps, its replayability is great as well. While the game may be dated, it still holds its own against modern strategy games.

"60 Seconds!" is one of many survival-types games, that are currently available on Steam. The biggest problem of this genre is the fact, that these days, each survival game seems like a copy of a previous one. "60 Seconds!" does not have this problem - although not without issues, it manages to stay unique, engaging and addicting.
Gameplay is split into two parts. First one is time limited (60 seconds) and is based on finding the right items, that will help you to survive next few months that your four (or less, depending on your choices) characters will spend in the bunker. Second part is basically text-based, you'll make decisions regarding your items and situations, you will also manage your food and water. It's not only about keeping track of your supplies, so your family has something to eat (that itself isn't easy, but it's definitely doable). Even if they are well fed, they still may fall sick, run away, not come back from expedition or loose their minds.
Admittedly, first part of the game, although very short, is the most engaging. It's dynamic, it requires quick thinking and gathering as much useful stuff as you can. The second part, is much slower and can gets boring, especially if you play it for long and you've seen most of entries in the diary and most of random situations. During my later playthroughs, I was basically skipping most of the text, as there was nothing interesting there for me. Still, there are a lot of ways to win the game and it's really not easy, so you'll probably find yourself coming back to it and trying again.
First of all, there isn't enough content. There simply isn't. Given that it's mostly based around text, I would be happy to see much more random encounters, few new items, that would be able to change the outcome of some events, new ways to win, a lot more crazy situations
. I really hope that there will be more DLCs and/or updates to expand basic gameplay mechanics and ideas.
Second thing is the diary. It suppose to be helpful, but most of the time, it really isn't, especially for new players. Before I read some guide (which I really don't like to do, as I usually find it fun-spoiling), I gave food and water to Ted and his family basically every other day, because each time diary was nagging me, that they are hungry and thirsty. At some point, literally day after I fed everyone and gave them water, I got this dramatic communicate, that one of the character is about to die of thirst.
Other than that - it's fun game. It's not great, but good enough to be engaging, it's challenging, it requires some strategy, although there is a lot of random events, which is fine for me, but can be annoying for people who like to control the outcome of their actions better.
Definitely get it during sale. I like the game a lot, but I would be disappointed, because of lacking content, if I would get it for full price.

My favourite RPG of 2014 and one of my all time favourites, Shadowrun Dragonfall signals the return of isometric RPGs and excellent, uncompromising writing.
Gameplay: Evidently takes many cues from XCOM Enemy Unknown, you have Action Points (AP) which give you a limited number of actions you can do before the character must wait til the next turn. Not nearly as unforgiving as XCOM however, as your party is for the most part more than capable of tanking several shots without issue. Those familiar with the Shadowrun PnP game may also notice certain systems have been brought over, such as wounds which only allow you to heal the most recent attack. The combat system is also based on percentage values, including the melee, so there are probably times where characters will miss 85% shots, but on the other hand, will make 25% when you least expect it which makes for some tense situations provided you don't savescum. There are certain situations where you can utilize special skills such as Charisma in order to bypass a difficult situation, and even avoid fights outright.
Graphics: Overall has a very simple, almost cartoon style theme. Characters have a model and a more detailed portrait to properly draw you into conversations. Environments are well done, and really capture the advanced tech/low life atmosphere of the Cyberpunk genre, as well as the strangeness of magic. Animations are simplistic, most of them you'll see while in combat, though if I had to list a complaint, it's that melee attacks have no weight or sense of speed behind them, and feel very unsatisfying to watch.
Sound: The music is absolutely great, and again, captures the cyberpunk aesthetic with its low key and dark electronica. The tracks that really stand out however are the ones that incoporate different styles to properly the convey your situation. Combat sounds very visceral, with each weapon having a powerful sound to accompany it to make it that much more satisfying when you get a hit on an enemy, though the rifles sound a bit underpowered. There is no voice acting, which I feel is great since it adds to the immersion, and you can decide for yourself the tones, inflections and accents with which the characters speak.
Writing: This is Shadowrun: Dragonfall's biggest strength, and the biggest reason why this is one of my favourtie RPGs ever. The characters are extremely well written, I guarantee you'll end up loving each member of the cast as you go through the story and get to know everyone, seeing them grow and change. Dietrich is a spitting image of a man from a bygone era, a living love letter to punk and an absolute badass that savours the good things in life. Glory is a runaway who turned to desperate measures to escape her past, turning herself into a killing machine, Eiger, a mountain of a woman and a former special forces operator, she gets the job done one way or another, and though you might butt heads at first, there's no one else you'd rather have in a gunfight. And it's not just the main cast that's well done, side characters have their own stories and personalities which offer you insight into not just the world, but also Shadowrun lore. The main story of Dragonfall is guaranteed to capture your attention and will leave you with some tough decisions which the game leaves up to you to decide whether it's good or bad.
I cannot reccomend this game enough, and it's well worth it even at full price. Those of you who tend to look at the the game length to determine value should note that a full playthrough should take around 24 hours of game time, and add to that subsequent playthoughs where you can take different paths. I can't wait for Shadowrun Hong Kong, and what Harebrained Schemes will unveil in the future.

TL;DR : If you love the good old dragonwarrior/quest monster games and Shin Megami Tensei series then get the game!
I played the game for around 50 hours now in total across 2 files and have been moving my save from my phone to PC. Most of my playtime was on my phone.
Siralim is basically an endless RPG game where you inherited a kingdom and you must bolster your kingdom's defences by diving in to random dungeons along with your monsters, recruit monsters and do quests. The game has no level cap and continue on endlessly. Story is basically non-existent so you will be disappointed if your are looking for some interesting plot or even your basic run-of-the-mill fantasy story.
The game takes inspiration from the old Dragon warior/quest monster games. There are around 325 monsters that you can fight and tame in the game. To recruit a monster, you need to extract 3 monster cores fromthat monster then pay some resources to summon that monster. Your monster doesn't have any skills but they will each have unique abilities similar to the creature abilities of pokemon (i.e one monster has a 50% chance of reviving your other knocked out monster whenever it attacks, this creature gains 200% attack from its equipment, etc.). Only your character can learn spells on your limited number of spellbook slots (expandable by spending points). Spells in this game are different, they use Mana and charges. Once you run out of spell charges, that particular spell is gone. Your creature can only equip one artifact. Each artifact can bestow different stat boost and additional abilities. The game allows you to create and level your artifacts and imbue it with different skill for your monsters. The skills are basically passive ones similar to the abilities.
The battle mechanics are similar to the Dragonquest RPGs. Despite the lack of active skills similar to pokemon/demon/monster moves of SMT, Pokemon and DQ/W monsters, the battle is still tactical and you cannot just rofltstomp all your enemies. The wide variety of abilities per monster and team can let you encounter a lot of different threats. The synergy of each monster abilities in the random mobs you encounter would determine the difficulty of the battle. Different combos and synergies exist because of the variety of monster abilities. Balance might be a problem especially when you encounter a mob that would have overpowered monsters. The best part about the game is that there are no tiers like how Smogon classify pokemons. Any monster is viable as long as you can make in synergise with your other monster's abilities.
The game has no breeding or fusion/synthesis mechanics that are found in Pokemon, DW/Q monsters or the Shin Megami Series. The game allows you to make nether and demonic monsters. Nether and Demonic monsters are basically a version of a monster that has super high stats. They take a long time to create and the monsters take a long time to level but they are worth it.
The game is grindy but basically that kind of addictive grindiness you can get in playing those hack n slash lootfest. This is basically the equivalent of those hack n slash lootfest feeling translated in to an RPG. The game has been classified as a roguelike but it is not meant to be played as one. Activating hardcore mode basically gives you that extra challenge of suriving for as long as you can.
At a glance, you might dismiss this game as some other shallow RPG game. The graphics are similar to those good old GBC games and I am amazed at how the devs captured the colour pallet similar to the old games from the GBC. The art-style is nothing compared to any modern AAA game but it is surely appropriate for the type of game and if you are a fan of those old school sprites then you will definitely love it.
Overall, the game is really worth your money, it is super addictive and you can really see that the devs know what are the addictive parts of the dragonwarrior monsters game and put it in one neat little package. The game has endless replayability since it puts disgaea's 9999 level cap to shame with its infinite level cap. I would highly suggest that you try the game on PC or mobile if you have doubts about it.

In simple terms its a monster taming RPG dungeon turn based game with rougue-like aspects and optional perma-death... yeah. Quite addicting may I add if you play these types of games. You also slowly do rituals to make things even more interesting. A lot of people say it is seemingly simplistic (so much so it can be played with one hand lol) but as you get nether eggs that craft modified monsters that are more powerful and take on harder objectives this game becomes much more.

Siralim goes right to the heart of what’s fun in a stat building, dungeon crawling, turn-based roguelike (esk) RPG.  If you like building creature rosters (catching ‘em all), finding and upgrading items, spending stat points, combining unique passive skills for synergistic badassery and purchasing new parts of your castle to unlock more upgrade potential … this game is for you!  There’s no plot to speak of and no super shiny graphics; just the old SNES RPG look and over 325 creatures to find (that’s not a joke either … just over 325 at this time).  The music is appropriate for an olde-timey RPG and the nether creature system lets you make SUPER high powered versions of the monsters you love the most.  I can’t say enough about the game so I’ll leave it at, “this is pure, unadulterated, unmitigated fun!”
In addition to this game being incredibly fun, the developer is the most stunningly dedicated developer I’ve ever seen.  Example: I mistakenly closed the game (click on the X and she’s gone!) and it was at the absolute worst of times.  I had just handed in 20 hours’ worth of lovingly crafted items all for my first big super high powered creature … but I had not been given the creature yet.  When I restarted the game back up I had no creature nor did I have my creature items.  I posted about this on their website and in a few hours (on a Sunday) the developer, Zack, replies to my post and asked me what I lost and then sent me an e-mail with a code to use in game to get it all back.  You read that right, the developer refunded all of the stuff I lost when it was my fault!  They also go to their own Reddit and hunt down errors to fix there!  Check it out the dev finds problems on there and just asks them to post on the forums about it and VOILA!  FIXED!
I give them game a 10 out of 10 for dedicated development & support.  I also give them a 10 out of 10 for being 100%, unfiltered fun.  Get it on your computer (mac or PC) and then get it on your phone while you’re at it; Get It, Play It, Love It!

When I first started playing this game on August 12, 2016, (on another Steam account), I was in awe of the creators' vision. Instead of having an ordinary game of Bejeweled or Candy Crush, the collaborators created a game that incorporated elements from popular games such as World of Warcraft, Hearthstone, and Faeria and made it not only FREE but accessible to ANYONE with an XBOX, computer, or mobile phone.  And that's saying a lot in these days.
A large percent of gaming companies fail to realize that people with physical limitations (like myself) make up a large portion of their clients.  Therefore, many creators/companies either (a) don't "code" a way to make it playable with one-hand or (b) increase the price of an "accessible" game to $50
.  This is why I loved and will continue to support this game.
Gems of War is a game that is both accessible across different gaming platforms and playable for people with the use of one hand or poor motor skills.  The game starts when a player completes a quick tutorial and chooses what species/race he/she wants to be (WoW).   Then the player starts a journey where they fight monsters by matching gems and controlling different aspects (health, weaponry, and mana). After each "victory" the player earn cards that contain special items whether it's weaponry, a traitstone, a new warrior, increased health, et cetera (Hearthstone).
...And while there are many negative reviews for the recent 3.2 UI update, the developers are continuing to "better" this gaming experience.  Therefore, I think you should at least give this game a try.  After all, it is free!

The graphics - at least with TheWorseMod installed - are great. The feeling of driving around Chicago is incredible. The story - though clichéd - hits most of the right buttons for me. And the things you can do in the game are sufficiently varied that you can stave off boredom for a good long while.
This game, in short, could have been awesome.
If the main character had more emotions than a brick. If the driving controls weren't so awful. If street lamps, trash cans and other city "furniture" didn't destroy all immersion by behaving as if they were made of paper. If money, and hence all equipment, weren't so easy to come by as to destroy all sense of achievement. If escaping the police were fun instead of a chore.

As it is, the flaws outweigh the good stuff by a solid margin and I can't really recommend Watch_Dogs. But I'm still looking forward to seeing if its sequel can do better. Because if it manages this, it could be a really, really good game.

In short: pokemon! But I'm a white mage-like queen ruling a kingdom, and my team consists of a minotaur, unicorn (okay, two unicorns), fire bomb-wielding troll, dragon and...a jawa-looking thing riding a cat.
In not so short: I tend to shy away from any game that has "rogue-like" in the description because of permadeath. This game, however, does not have that, and I am so glad I gave it a shot. I'm about 100 hours in, I'm level 119 and I'm not even close to having a fully customized team or home base/castle yet. I can't believe the amount of content and depth there is in this game. The numbers of different types of creatures you can catch, their abilities, your own abilites, skill points, spells, items, quests, dailies, an arena, artifacts that level, enchantments for artifacts, legendary enchantments, hatching stronger creatures with stat multipliers...it is simply astounding, especially for the price.
I also find the game to be challenging. Not to the point where I want to throw my computer at the nearest wall while playing, but definitely to the point where I die every now and then (and resurrect back at my castle) and it doesn't feel like a boring grindfest.
If you like turn-based, fantasy-themed, team-leveling games, and you don't mind the retro graphics (which also, by the way, have an amazing amount of detail and variety), then this game is for you!

Siralim is a polished, shining gem in the high-and-rising pile of retro indie rpgs. It looks simple, but is more sophisticated than most of all the games I have ever played. As a young king, you crawl through dundeons to provide yourself and your kingdom with valuables of any possible kinds. Let it be monsters for your army, riches, powerful artifacts, crafting materials, new citizens, you name it.
Your party is made of creatures you catch in the dungeons and there are several hunderd of kinds to encounter. This makes infinite possibilities how to assemble your squad. Be aware that every creature has unique abilities and just their right combination can be crucial for success. And this is just the tip of an iceberg. You can also equip your crew with artifacts (levelable and enchantable with many possible features), support it with magic (like in HoMaM), or by levelling up your leadership abilities. Still I´m just writing about basics of the game, there is a lot more to discover.
The best thing is - you will never have enough resources for everything. In fact, you will always be pretty far from it. Therefore you always have to choose where to invest and how to play. Will you patiantly work on buffing your castle, or summon newest aquisitions of your bestiary and go berserk with them? From this point of view, Siralim is satisfying as a strategy/management game as well as rpg.
Even with all this stuff, the learning curve is fluent and supported with well made guiding. Player doesn´t get lost, but naturally continue to explore new and new features and options he has. And after all, exploring is what makes Siralim the bottomless well of fun. Almost every visit of dungeon brings something new (I got currently about 30h played and still feel like on the startline). One of things that surprises me continually is AI, which seems to always be able to find a way to exploit my week spots and send my tuned up badass army to void:-P But don´t fear, there is no permadeath - there is no need for it for Siralim to be tough enough to crack.
Originally I thought absence of storyline will bother me, but rich life of Siralim kingdom is awesome story for itself. Elegant slap in the face of genre rivals.

I have to admit, I haven't owned this game for very long, but I spend almost all of my free time playing it. I've just gotten past the tutorial sections because I spent so much time playing my way and just having fun in the maps and leveling up different aspects of the game before more advanced mechanics were added.
Pros:
+ Great retro feel. The graphics really bring me back.
+ Huge variety of monsters that there are innumerable customization options (although some will clearly be better than others)
+ A great "play at your own pace" game. I ventured out on my own away from the suggested tutorials, leveling my creatures and building up my castle.
+ Rewarding "Duties" system that makes you always feel like you're working towards something.
+ Intuitive level/skill tree. Very customizable and easy to understand exactly what each skill does. There are no real skill walls that you must have one to access another. I personally have mine currently geared towards resource-gathering and quest rewards in order to accelerate my castle advancements and team-building.
+ Challenging without the feeling of hopelessness. If you need to grind, you can, or you can just keep starting over.
+ Tons of communication from Zack on the forums.
Cons
- I would love to be able to see more about my enemies, whether it's their skills, HP more specifically than "Complete health," "Lightly bruised, "Somewhat hurt," "Bady wounded" and "Mortally wounded." Sometimes it feels like a guessing game knowing who I should attack. This is particularly frustrating when I run into a new monster, attack it, and suddenly my entire team is suffering from massive debuffs because I had no idea what the monster did.
- Early game Nether creature quests are just too hard. Particularly the return Siralim's monsters back to the country duties. They're nearly impossible until you have at least one decently high level nether monster of your own. That's daunting so early in the game.
- No wiki. A website has been reserved for it, but man would it be nice. There's just so much variety in this game that sometimes you want to look up information for things like team-building. There is an in-game library that houses much of this information, but it is strictly limited to things that your character already knows about.
Overall, I've enjoyed this game an incredible amount. I'm definitely going to keep playing!
Surirpsingly great game. Simple to learn, fun to play, constant resource acquisition and team building, and no frustrating bits after 10+ hours. I'm a fan.

This game is a great one. It brings back memories of the older games i played like pokemon, digimon and dragon warrior monsters- to say the least. Yet, this game does more to stand out. While the story is nothing special, it sets up the reason for your character to do all this in the first place. The game starts with your father, the king, having died recently. With the responsibility of king/queen (Yes, you can choose your gender) placed upon you, it is your duty to help Siralim prosper while everyone at the castle holds the fort. The tutorial itself is hardly a tutorial, more of a guide of what you would likely want to do, since there is actually a lot to do in this game. If everything was unlocked, i feel that it would have been overwhelming and even downright confusing, so i would not recommend removing castle quests. Even when you complete it all and get your first nether creature (max out gems levels, you will need them,) the game does not stop there, it goes on forever! And there is some nice music too. Nothing spectacular, but it is nice to listen at times.
The game is anything but casual. No matter how good your team setup is, there will always be a counter setup- or even spells to smash you back down to reality. Yes, the first couple realms are easy, but the difficulty spikes as you go deeper. I still have yet to pass realm 5, and yet there are people have that gone MUCH deeper. Thankfully, the enemies tend to stay a general level with your group, to keep things fair. So if you want to go for a new team completely- you can do that without worry... Just be sure to open up a new realm when that happens. Otherwise you may wind up in a battle that is meant for your previous team.
There's a lot to do, losts to customize from how you distribute points to your own character to being able to reroll stats on artifacts (weapons for your creatures in this game.) You can even potentially use a creature's turn to cast a spell, which takes up a charge and some mana. Some spells are pretty disasterous for the one having to take it, while others are not quite as bothersome. Heck, there is a realm that is devoted to having spells as items you find all around the place- among other things. And that's another thing i like about this game, each realm offers different drops, making some a priority over others, depending on what you need. Need more cores? (Ways to summon more monsters,) go to a dungeon realm where you can get cores of creatures you unlocked (Yes, you unlock creatures by tiers... 30 tiers in total, no evolution.) Need more of a certain resource? There are realms that tend to have drops of those resources. Not much mind you, but it gives the necessary boost.
Then there are the creatures. I can go on about them, but i will only say this... Each one is unique and offers an ability that can very well work with others to make an awesome combo. And as the ruler of the kingdom, it's up to you to decide how to mix and match those creatures and abilities. As if that's not enough, you can even get legendary crafting materials that allow you to put a creature ability on an artifact, giving even more customizable options for your team with 6 abilities. Then there is the fact that you will eventually be able to build daily stuff. So far, i have two. One is daily realms, where you can go into a daily dungeon and try to clear it days in a row for increased risk and reward. The other is daily power, where you can use the goblet for free once every day- no matter what. It tends to yield some pretty nice stuff that can help. Oh, and the goblet functions as a random reward generator. You put some power into it (amount you put in varies,) and you can get items, stuff and even exclusive creatures.
Then there is a tiny metal bit like in dragon warrior monsters. Only you collect something called exalted emblems, which you eventually give to a guy that will gladly exchange them for some pretty nice stuff- including several unique monsters that can help with farming. One helps farm gems, one helps farm resources, etc. However, there is something called pandemonium tokens that is like taking a gamble. It can give you some pretty good different stuff, but it can also give you some pretty bad stuff- and then there's some that varies on personal opinion. You will have to find out yourself, because i doubt i've seen all it has to offer.
Now, as for the negatives to this game... It can get rather grindy and repetitive at times. If you don't mind that, then there really is not much to complain about this game. If you are someone who wants a more modern graphics though, then i guess that counts as a flaw to this game. Otherwise, if you have a LOT of time to spare and don't mind going in for the long run, then this game is just up your alley!

is great when you're playing the tables, but it's a flawed gem otherwise. I love modern and historic pinball and  while I'm no expert on ball physics I have no issues with anything once I'm in the game. The music is great, effects are spot-on (as far as I can tell) and the graphics are neat. So just an overall cool game, right?
Boy oh boy, did they mess up everything else. The menus are atrocious, both confusing and technically inept. Choose an item and it may give you a chopped-off affirming beep, do nothing, or beep twice. How hard is it to implement this simple sound effect? The mouse cursor is moved to the next dialog box on its own, confusing you further. Choosing a random table does not seem to work for me either. It really is no fun getting to those darn tables.
Another issue I noticed was skipping letters when entering your initials for a highscore. The game sometimes skips to the next (wrong) letter and then jumps to the next space, ending the entry and messing up your name with no way to correct it. Needless to say that's quite infuriating when you manage a good score. Tables bought through the game (instead of Steam) are not recognised by Steam either (unless I'm doing something wrong). On top of that the game forces constant updates on you. Think you're good with your favourite tables? Expect a few big updates throughout the year, so you can play (and hopefully buy) a short demo of the next tables available. No, thank you!
All in all I wouldn't be so livid if this was a forgettable game, but it does emulate real pinball machines quite nicely and I have less interest in Pinball FX' myriads of Star Wars and Marvel tables (as good as they may are). It's a shame they dropped the ball with something comparatively easy as menus, in-game purchases and controls, when the actual game is quite solid. Can't recommend this.

The Book of Unwritten Tales is a fantasy point and click adventure game with pretty much everything you would expect from a fantasy game: gnomes, elves, ogres, dragons, magic, artifacts, you name it.
The story is rather simple: An incredibly powerful artifact must be retrieved before the evil mage Munkus and his fiendish mother get their, uh, tentacles on it, so you - Wilbur Weathervane, a small gnome - head out on your quest to save the world from unthinkable evil. On your journey you cross paths with the wood elf princess Ivo, the treasure hunter Nate and his furry critter pet, who join you and help you on your important mission.
Being a point and click adventure, there's not much to say about the controls. You point at things and then, surprise, click them. Apart from one puzzle, the game can entirely be played with the mouse only, so it's perfect to lay back in your chair and relax.
Since the point and click genre usually doesn't leave much space for weird gameplay experiments, the presentation of the story, the level design and characters are what keep the boat floating, all of which are things that The Book of Unwritten Tales does exceedingly well.
Beautifully designed levels, extremely likeable characters, great voice acting, fitting music, the hilarious dialogues and all the, more or less subtle, side blows at the RPG and fantasy genre make TBoUT clearly stand out from the masses of point and click adventure games.
Puzzle-wise, TBoUT seems to be more aimed at novice and casual point and click players, so the puzzle elements are rather easy and not a huge challenge for experienced P'n'C fans. Personally, I don't mind it at all because it keeps the whole game on a constant feel-good level without ever getting frustrating to the point where you NEED to google for a walkthrough.
From the technical side, the only thing to complain about is the lack of FullHD-support, so you end up with black bars at the left and right of your screen. However, once you've sunken into the game, you hardly ever notice them.
The playthrough took me pretty much exactly 13 hours with quite a bit of trial-and-error, backtracking and so on. The game could probably be beaten in less time, but then again... point and click adventures are made to sit back and relax and not rush through them as fast as possible, right?
If you're new to the point and click genre, The Book of Unwritten Tales is a prime example of what the P'n'C genre is capable of, so it's the perfect game to start with. If you're a P'n'C veteran, you probably already have played the game... and if not, then what are you waiting for?

What an odd and somewhat surreal game. I found it looking through a list of summer sales, the silly looking banner grabbing my attention. When I noticed it was only something like $0.60 I thought, "Why the heck not". Honestly, I got what I paid for - whatever you decide on whether or not to get this at the end of this review, don't pay the $2. That may not sound like much money, but this game is not worth full price.
Anyway, it's.. well, I wouldn't necessarily call it good, but it's oddly kind of zen? The controls are clunky (I used a 360 controller, I wouldn't recommend the keyboard) and often frustraing to handle, and the game basically just throws you in with no explanation. In a modern age spoiled by tutorials, it was an odd feeling flailing about trying to figure out the controls and how to deal with the enemies. The game only takes about 20-30 minutes or so to play (unless you're a completionist like me trying to go the extra miles for achievements) and is a series of waves where you have to defeat the enemies and save other frogs (assuming the enemies don't kill them first). Your health is gauged by how much breath you have, breathing air bubbles or the last gasps of air from enemies. There's no meter for this, instead the frog changes color and starts to spit bloodied bubbles to indicate its slowly drowning. Graphically I personally felt it looked somewhat juvenile, what may have been the point, though the frog sprites in particular weirded me out over the fact it looks like a double amputee missing its front legs. The music I felt was the best part. It's very calming but also eerie. Very good for atmosphere.
Unlike many other reviews I've seen I personally did not find it all that creepy to be honest. The story is vague and completely unexplained. You play a frog, you dive down into the water where you find strange things happening to the other frogs. The enemies turned out completely different  in origin from what I expected from the screenshots and the game leaves you to draw your own conclusions about what happened. The effort for all of this is rewarded with a link to some website I didn't bother visiting. It's kind of eerie and surreal, but not really "creepy". I feel as though it tries very hard to be more artsy than video game, which isn't by any means a bad thing, but as with all art it's something very subjective.
I don't feel as though I've lost out too badly for having only paid 60 cents, but as I said in the beginning, it is NOT worth $2. If you're morbidly curious, wait for a sale

I haven't spent much time playing Don't Sink currently but the time I have spent has not only been a lot of fun but has also shown me just how much potential this game has, not to mention how much care has been placed in creating it.
Essentially Don't Sink is a pixel-graphics pirate game. You sail the seas by selecting which island you want to sail to and along the way random events may occur, you need to take care of your crew's needs, and - of course - you may encounter ships (more than one sometimes, so be prepared!) to attack - or run away from - and board! BUT WAIT! Not only can you do this, but you can also build on islands as well as govern that island's economy, making money 'legitimately' as well as from your pirating ways. Want to do this on more than one island? Sure, you can do that! Want quests given by NPCs? Yep, those are there too. Oh, you want to buy new ships I hear you say? Oh yes, there are more ships to buy as well!
In short, this game is a fun little pirate romp and the feeling of buying a new ship and decimating those ships you come across can't be described! :)
You must, of course, keep in mind that the game is in Early Access and so there are some features not yet implemented in the game. I haven't, for instance, come across a way to fight myself when boarding a ship rather than having the AI do it (though this may be because I just haven't got that far yet!), and some little flourishes/additions like more to do on the islands, more to buy, upgrading of crew and ship weapons, and so on, would all be great updates. BUT, these things absolutely don't detract from the game - it is EA and the developers are constantly (and I mean constantly!) updating it and adding new content, tweaking the GUI, and fixing bugs. So I have high hopes that as the development of this game continues many more fun aspects of the game and even more things to do/customize will be added. But even as the game stands itself it is a lot of fun!
I would definitely recommend this game and think it is worth a try for anyone who loves pirates or fun little adventures. As always, check out any game-play or LPs of the game on YouTube if you want a good idea of the game, its content, and how it plays. But for me, I will definitely be looking forward to how this game develops and enjoy playing it as it does.

I'll do the TL;DR up front:
1) I really wouldn't describe Siralim as "roguelike" in any sense.
2) It's a fantastic game and you should buy it.
So why isn't it roguelike? Permadeath is not the default, and is only for very, very hardcore players, since I've been playing 35 hours and I still feel like I'm at the beginning of my run. There are random dungeons, yes, but they all feel the same. Nothing you find in a dungeon will make it feel or play any differently from the last time you visited that realm. The only loot I've found that really felt like it changed the game was a weapon with a legendary enchant, and that's happened just once in 35 hours.
But none of that should stop you from buying it! Siralim is all about collecting and battling monsters. And there are hundreds of them, each with its own special ability. Battles are old-oldschool turn based, like the original Final Fantasy, but the tremendous variety of monster abilities keeps it from ever becoming boring.  These are not directly triggered by the player (but you have spells that fill that role), rather they are used automatically in certain situations, such as the beginning of combat, beginning of turn, when attacking, when being attacked, when an enemy dies, or even at the end of combat. You can have up to six monsters in your party, and choosing a group that complements each other is key to your success (or failure). For example, my tank mob is able to provoke enemies into attacking it 100% of the time, and I've got a legendary enchantment on its boots that causes any creature attacking it to fall asleep. There must be thousands of combinations other than this basic and obvious (though very effective!) one.
Beyond monsters, there are artifacts to craft and enchant. Each monster can have one artifact equipped, which will improve various stats and sometimes provide an extra ability. For my tank monster I mentioned above, I enchanted his artifact with defense (duh) and speed (so he can use his "provoke" ability before the enemies attack). Every monster ability in the game has a corresponding material (some are very rare) which can be used to enchant an artifact, giving that ability to the monster who wields it. With hundreds of monsters and abilities, the level of customization is ridiculous.
There's even more--some kind of egg thing that you put jewels into, and enchant the jewels, or something, that gives you a "nether monster", a powered-up version of a regular monster. As you can tell, I'm not familiar with this aspect of the game yet. I just opened it up.
Castle upgrades, character perks, the list goes on...the depth of Siralim is astonishing. During all the 35 hours I've played so far, I've felt like I'm constantly discovering and building toward new things. It's a grinding game, but there's just so *much* stuff to grind that it never feels boring.
Verdict: Highest recommendation. Unless you hate all the stuff I described above, you should buy Siralim immediately.

Wow. This game is great. I've bought about 10 games in the last month (from indie to AAA) and not one has held my attention for more than 30 minutes. I just got Siralim and the next thing I know I already have 100 minutes in. I realize that's not a lot of time, but for me, that's substantial for a first sit down. I'll update with more info as I progress.

On the most basic level, it's a game about an endless lust for power. In terms of sheer customization there is no limit to what you can do in this game. I start to get anxious when I realize I may never be able to try out every possible team/legendary artifact combination, because I simply do not have the time! It's a malicious time sucking game that is hard to pull yourself away from. Endlessly playable, and continually rewarding, based around systems that eternally feed into one another. Someone very evil devised this game.

I would say that the game does a respectable job of creating some interesting combat situations for you to consider, however, unless you're pushing your team to it's limits, the combat can devolve into a button mashing grind, which I would consider it's one failing. Total Annihilation grew up, moved out of its parent's house, and then
Seriously, everything I liked about TA is in SupCom in some fashion, but better. SC added features that (at the time) no other RTS had, like the megamap. Now, if your game doesn't have a megamap, don't bother to come to school - the other kids will just laugh and push your face into the dirt. Looking at you,
.
Shields are also a favorite of mine. In TA and other RTSes, when your defenses repel the infidels, they take damage that must be repaired. With shields, as long as the bubble stays up, the shield will regenerate over a relatively short period, and the defenses will keep on keepin' on. There are mods that add super bubbles (shields) that can stop practically anything, which leads to some "battle of Hoth" instances where ground forces must be sent in to take out the shield generator (if you sprint units inside the shield, they can attack things within) before the long-range bombardment destroys everything else.
It is super fun.
The game isn't perfect, though. The one overriding issue, apart from the developer being dead and no official multiplayer list servers, is performance. The game was developed in a time where dual-core PCs were a new thing, and was quite revolutionary in its multithreaded design. The simulation and the rendering pipeline are broken out to two threads, and this helps the game run fast on multicore systems.
Unfortunately, the sim thread could really use being broken down into multiple threads itself. Mid to late game, even though the FPS will still be 100+, units will act slow. They move slow, react slow, missles and cannon shots will move slower. This is the sim thread being overwhelmed by the 2000+ units running about. Since the dev is gone, this will never be fixed, and that's a damn shame since the game is practically the perfect RTS otherwise.

Disclaimer: I received this game for free because I beat the Dev at a game of Checkers so he owed me.
Like many Early Access games, what you have here is a great foundation. However, unlike many Early Access games, this also feels like a pretty unique idea. You can find tastes of other games here and there (Notable examples include the Roguelite Approach to Transportation of Oregon/Organ Trail, the Hunger Management of Survival Games like Minecraft), but Don't Sink manages to be it's own thing despite these. I think it does this by not leaning too heavily on any one of the influences at a time. The result is a pretty interesting take on this style of game. I was also pleased to see that it's decently well-balanced in terms of combat/inventory. At times, it can feel shoddy, specifically between upgrading ships, as you have to adjust to the new Crew Sizes and Food Storages as a result, but those instances are few and far between, and it does enough right for me to be impressed. The combat could probably benefit from more item options and breadth, but it works as is.
I think Management of Hunger/Thirst/Morale stats are handled extremely effectively. As you sail, your stats decrease, and you need to use food supplies to keep these stats up. At first, I was annoyed that I had trouble getting all these stats to line up how I wanted them to. For example, the only way to increase Morale is to consume an item that also fixes Hunger or Thirst, so sometimes I would satiate both Hunger and Thirst, but I would need to waste extra supplies to boost Morale to maximum. But I realized that I started to like it this way. Rather than just stocking up on 3 consistent items (one for each stat), I need to mix and match, and use the best ones in tandem given whatever my stats currently are. It gives a bit of depth to what could've easily otherwise have been an intentory-breaking systme.
My main issues are exactly what you'd expect of an Early Access game: a lot is missing. I know it'll be more fleshed out and complete in the future, but as it is, it's just a little empty. That said, in it's current state, it's established a wonderful basis. I don't think this will be some Early Access game that I dismiss and never return to; you can tell that it's going to have a lot of great stuff in the future, so even if you don't want to buy right now, I do recommend keeping an eye on this game.
Going forward, there are a few things I'd like to see done. While I do think it'd be bad for the game to become
similar to any of its influences, I think it could benefit from borrowing a little more from FTL. Encounters during travel are pretty rare as is, and while I don't want to impede on the game's current balances, I think it'd be cool if finding things at sea happened more frequently. It doesn't have to always be enemy ships, of course; there could be all sorts of neat stuff to encounter, as I find the sailing portions of the game most potentially engaging. Traveling is different enough from FTL that I think increasing the Encounter Rate (whether that be enemies or not) wouldn't make the game feel too much like FTL. But what do I know?
I'd also like to see more Customization. As it is, you can customize your character's appearance and name, but despite every Enemy Ship having a fun and unique name, you're not allowed to name your own, nor the name of the Island City you govern. It'd also be cool if you could customize elements of your ship (from simple things like color if ship to more complex things like the ability to upload an image/logo for your ship's sail? These are just ideas). I'd also like to see the ability to just go for a casual grind in the sea. Presntly, you can only sail between two locations, but sometimes I want to head out to sea and return to the same place I left from. Maybe a "Passive X Day Expedition" option? Again, just ideas.
I have high hopes for this game. It looks very promising even in this early state, and I trust it will continue to improve. Like I said above, even if you don't plan on buying now, I do highly recommend keeping an eye on it. In the meantime, just play FTL while wearing an Eye Patch.
