When it comes to pinball games on Steam, there are really only two contenders to consider: Pinball Arcade and Pinball FX2/FX3. If you want a quick answer on which you should buy, it's Pinball FX, hands down. It's not even a contest. If you want a detailed comparison of the two, read on.
Gameplay: Digital pinball game reviewers love to talk about "physics". Many of them are concerned with how close a digital pinball table emulates the physics on a real life pinball table. I'm more concerned with one thing: Is a digital pinball table fun to play or not? I mean, does it feel satisfying hitting those ramps, knocking those bumpers, landing those skillshots? Do you feel the need to keep chasing a score higher than your last? Pinball FX, by far, is a more satisfying experience than Pinball Arcade. FX just "feels" better. I'm not going to say which feels closer to real-life pinball tables, but I will say that FX keeps me coming back for more. Pinball Arcade is more like that bad restaurant you try once a year hoping it'll be better, but each experience just reminds you of why it'll be another year before you'll be back. The only thing that Pinball Arcade has going for it are the recreations of real-life tables. These licenses for real-life tables have been squandered though. It's sad, and I can't help but wonder what a more capable development team could have done with the opportunity. If you're in it for nostalgia at the expense of a fun experience, go for Pinball Arcade. If you want great gameplay, go for FX.
Graphics: Pinball FX looks fantastic. Everything looks polished, and each table really "pops" on your screen. You can see the attention to detail that has been put into each table. Pinball Arcade, on the other hand, looks... Dull. It's the best way to describe it. Colors are muted, tables look blurry, and everything just visually falls flat. The DX11 update that the developers talked so much about still doesn't bring the game up to anywhere near the standards of FX. FX looks like a shiny new sports car, while Arcade looks like an unpolished turd.
Audio: The audio for FX is great as well. Great music coupled with excellent table sound effects. Now, to be fair to Arcade, they are limited to the audio that the real-life tables have. Many of those are older tables simply aren't going to have the great audio effects and music that can be put into modern PC video games. I get that. What I don't get is why the sounds in this game seem like a kid walked into his local arcade, cassette recorder in hand, recorded the sounds of each table, and the Arcade development team just said, "Yeah, this sounds good enough." It's not good enough. It's not even passable. FX sounds like above-mentioned sports car revving its powerful V12 engine, while Arcade sounds like a muffled fart.

Features: Pinball FX takes real-life pinball and improves on it in many ways. For example, if you're playing a table, you can exit the table which automatically saves your progress, close out the program, and go on about your day. Feel free to come back a day, a week, a month, or whenever later to resume that game. That progress syncs with Steam Cloud, so you can play at multiple locations, picking up right where you left off, wherever you are, regardless of what computer you're using. In a modern game, it's to be expected. The Arcade development team thinks otherwise though. You can be a half hour into a game, go to exit, to be greeted with, "Any unsaved progress will be lost." Since that messages hints at being able to "save" your progress, you may dig through the menus trying to figure out how to do so. Thing is, you can't. Gotta get to work? Tough, call in sick. Taking the wife out on a date? She can wait. House on fire? That's what insurance is for. No save mid-play... Really?
Pinball FX can also take liberties that cannot be taken with real-life tables. For example, animated character integration into the tables, like X-Wings & Tie fighters dogfighting on a Star Wars table, superheroes and villians battling it out on a Marvel table, or Ripley fighting for her life against the Queen on the Aliens table. It's done in a way that is not obnoxious, and adds to the entertainment level of each table. Pinball purists may  disagree, but it adds to the fun-factor tremendously. Pinball Arcade, by its nature, of course can't do any of these while recreating real pinball tables.

Menu: I normally wouldn't mention a game's menu, but when a menu is so bad as to actually interfere with or detract from your gaming experience, I gotta bring it up. Pinball FX2 had a great menu. All tables could be seen and selected from one screen. FX3 took a step down, and isn't quite as good as FX2's, but is still well usable and doesn't get in the way. Pinball Arcade's, however... It's just garbage. With the original menu they had, you'd have to scroll through a long list of all the tables to try to find the one you wanted. And it took a while! They've redesigned it, and it improves on some areas, but it's still pretty horrible. A menu should be an invitation to play a game, not a barrier to it!
BUYER BEWARE: FX2/3 have proper Steam account integration. When you purchase a table, it shows as a purchase in your Steam account, and shows under the DLC tab of the game. That's expected, right? Well, in Pinball Arcade, I made the mistake of purchasing a table-pack through their "ingame" store. However, that purchase is not recognized by Steam in any way, and doesn't show up under any sort of DLC tab. There are multiple posts regarding this issue, and Arcade's developers don't care to address it, or even acknowledge that it's a problem. So what's the problem? In all likelihood, if Pinball Arcade is ever removed from the Steam store for any reason (Pinball Arcade 2 released, company goes out of business, etc.), then your purchases go right along with it. Since, as far as Steam is concerned, no purchase was made. When Pinball FX3 came out, FX2 was yanked of the Steam store. Someone that never purchased FX2 tables won't be able to install it. I'll always be able to reinstall FX2, though, as Steam allows you to reinstall games you've purchased whether it's still on the store or not. Far as I can tell, I won't be able to do that with Arcade. That's a legit concern. The developers will not address this.
Bottom-Line: The bottom-line is... Why didn't you just take my word for it and buy Pinball FX and give Pinball Arcade a pass, as I suggested right from the get-go? Cause then, you'd be playing a finely polished, professionally done, fun to play pinball game that is well deserving of your time and money INSTEAD of reading this mile-long review. Pinball Arcade is none of those things. It is not deserving of your time, let alone your money. Give it a pass and get a proper pinball game.

A rōnin was a title given to a samurai who, upon the death of their master decided to go rogue instead of committing seppuku during the feudal period of Japan.  The other samurais would banish and exclude a rōnin, isolating them from their groups.  In the modern world, the word can be used in comparison to a person who has trouble fitting into certain social groups; always wandering around, searching for a place to be at ease.
Nil-Ninjahstic: Ronin combines the elements of wandering samurai into a platformer.  Essentially a derivative of super meat boy without all the crazy speeding and sliding, you play as an outcast of society, where you’re always picked to do the dirty tasks that no one else wants to do.  As such in this game, you are put through a ‘test’ where everything and everyone tries to kill you.  In order to pass this initiation, players will need to run, jump and slash through 5 chapters of increasingly difficult levels of platforms and their respective level bosses.
Being the third game in the series of Nil-Ninjahtic, the most well done part of the game is the control scheme in relation to character movement.  Blaze Epic has mastered the basic controls for the game throughout 7 games and the result is a smooth and polished feel.  The character does not move to fast and is extremely responsive in terms of fluidity.  Air strafing is done extremely well and allows for predictable pathing and enables speed runs.
The alternative to running past everything would be to slow chip your way through a level.  Blaze Epic has provided the tools necessary to accommodate for this playstyle by incorporating a sword slash function and block.  Block stops most projectiles and melee attacks, while allowing you to strafe in a direction with no real penalty except moving slower and being unable to turn.  However, it comes at the cost of being not able to counterattack, and limits your movement by restricting the use of block while in midair.
Nil-Ninjahtic Ronin might not have the best music around, but it serves its purpose extremely well.  Since there is no auditory feedback from enemies in the game, Nil-Ninjahtic Ronin can afford to play the role of metronome and pace the game for the player.  Entering different areas of the game whether it be in the streets of Japan, or in the locker room of a gym, will change the music to suit the appropriate setting, a feature not usually found in smaller platformer games.
Nil-Ninjahtic: Ronin is a five chapter game with many levels in between.  However, the most obvious flaw is that it only saves at the end of a chapter.  In order to save your progress, one must completely the whole chapter completely.  Since this game’s skill requirements are quite high, players may find it difficult to find the time or even the abilities to make it to the next chapters.  Implementing checkpoint saves between each sub-chapter would allow for greater re-playability and would make the game feel more complete in a sense.
Though the game’s difficulty increases at a reasonable rate, the game gets pretty frustrating in chapter five where the game slowly becomes more of a chore.  I cannot fathom the amount of times I was so close to completing a level only to accidentally run back into the previous screen, resetting all the progress on the current level, or running through the most annoying chainsaw run only to be slashed down by an edge-guarding samurai on the last platform.
Another huge flaw is the fact that the chapters are also too long, with no dialogue in between the smaller sub-chapters.  The small bits of monologue between the chapters feel out of place and only serve to string the game together.  The writing is not that interesting to begin with and by the time you finish a chapter, you will have difficulty remembering what the story was talking about already.
Nil-Ninjahtic: Ronin not only test your skills, but also your patience as seen with its pixel perfect platforming.  Jumping horizontally into a wall will result in your character bouncing off, but jumping vertically into the ceiling will allow your character’s head to clip through it.  I personally found this out after spending a good 15 minutes trying avoid spikes in a tunnel, thinking I would bounce off the ceiling and die to the buzz saw below.
I personally rate this game 7/10 for the really fun gameplay.  Like all good things come in moderation, this game is best enjoyed in short bursts of 1-2 hours, just enough to completely one chapter each time.  This works to keep the game from getting too repetitive, too quickly. Had the game included checkpoints between the sub-levels and had more consistent art, it would have been a solid 8/10.

Nil-Ninjahtic: Ronin brings a nostalgia feel that you would get from classic titles on old portable Nintendo devices, with a simplistic style the game has a cleverly laid out retro level design which reminds gamers of that 80's feel when playing a video game. Blaze Epic created a game that is progressively more challenging as you progress through the game, although difficult to master
where eventually you have to solve puzzles while defeating enemies and doesn't follow the linear game structure making it hard to predict future events. The game has controller support if you want to play the game in a living room environment or if you are used to the feel of a console controller. If you want a short small sized game that would last 2-3 hours of gameplay that is full of action and adventure then this is the game for you. At the low price tag, this game is a steal, even when it is not on sale.

Siralim is the satanic Pokemon experience that your parents warned you about. You take control of a wizard, select one of the five magic schools to specialize in, and summon an ever-expanding team of creatures to traverse a rogue-like RPG full of retro pleasures, but also rife with rage-worthy pitfalls. Your team caps out at 6 creatures, and you lower the health of enemies to capture their cores and resummon your own creature in the comfort of your castle. Despite the obvious allusion that almost everyone will draw to Pokemon, Siralim truly is a game entirely of its own. Will it work its magic on you? Or is it completely unholy? Let’s find out as we take a deeper look at Siralim.
The controls are extremely dialed back, WASD to navigate the world and menus, E to confirm, Q to cancel. This can lead to some wonky moments when trying to sift through multiple screens to get the right piece of equipment onto the right monster, but overall it works well enough. This extremely simple control scheme allows the entire game to be played with the left hand, which is great because my right hand deserves a break. You are able to construct your own equipment to power up your monsters in battle, as well as building construction projects. These construction projects consume the same resources used to summon monsters, however they will let you travel to new realms and meet more powerful creatures to tame as your own.
Finding the correct synergy between hundreds of different creatures is hard, but necessary. Once you reach the 5th level of this infinite dungeon you’re travelling into, enemies will begin to outlevel you in a big way. Creatures need to maximize the usage of their abilities if you hope to see it through. There is an option for permadeath for the extreme masochists out there, or for the maso-curious there is an option to reincarnate a dead creature with a fraction of its former experience. I find this option extremely intrigued by this option, and for most games I end up leaving it on. Dungeons contain plenty of buffs and loot, but you also might find yourself trapped in an event fight before you’re ready. Hence why I usually leave “real” permadeath off.
Siralim is a game with a lot to love, but it also has its fair share of troubles. The sound is troubling, and replayability is hurt by the lack of differences between the magic schools. It is always nice to see how a new combination of creatures will fare in battle, but wizards should get a unique spell or something, not just a power-up to spells from their chosen school. Still, for the low price of $10, lovers of dungeon-crawlers are sure to get their money’s worth. Just restrain yourself from picking the permadeath option, and enjoy collecting them all. Siralim is a quality game, but in my opinion it needs a spot more polish to be truly great. Big thanks to Thylacine Studios for allowing IndieGameBundles to but this game through its paces. We hope to see more extremely soon!

If you have played games like Dragon Warrior Monsters series, Siralim will scratch that itch with hundreds of monsters to get, plus finding the best artifact to equip them with. Don’t know the party limit of the newer Dragon Warrior Monster games, but in this one its 6 monsters on a first person perspective, turn-based battle system. What’s different in this one, however, is that every creature has a unique ability. It’s fun trying to find the best match of monsters before going to a dungeon crawl.
So, if you like monster collecting games, you should give this one a try.

To sum up what everyone else has stated and more, Siralim is a game made with simplistic yet careful design, crafted on a battle system that has been around since the early ages of gaming, and yet still has enough charm and identity to stand tall in a crowd of Steam RPGs and turn based games. Siralim not only won me over with the constant content updates and responses from the developer, but won me over by its community.
While the game itself isn't multiplayer in any way, the community behind Siralim is more than happy to help new users with their builds, team compositions, and other tips. The reason such a community presence is important is due to the fact that Siralim boasts almost unlimited combinations when it comes to artifact creation (items used to buff party members), Nether Eggs (special monsters that have above average stats), and roguelike randomized dungeons with randomized quests.
With only about 6 hours in the game I have barely scratched the surface, but if you're on the fence at all when it comes to purchasing I have no doubt in my mind that if you enjoy games like Dragon Quest Monster and Final Fantasy styled battles you will enjoy everything Siralim has to offer.
EDIT: In my prior review I stated the game was a mobile port. In actuality the game was created on PC first and then ported to Android/Apple devices! Honestly, I would highly recommend purchasing the game for both platforms to support such a dev team.

Siralim is a retro styled monster collection game. It features a large host of monsters the player can "capture" and randomly generated dungeons. The game has no story or ending which could be good or bad depending on what you are looking for in a game.
What makes the game shine is how the party system works. Monster have very few actions they can take in combat, i think the only choices are Attack, Defend, Provoke (taunt), Magic, and run. There are no skills they learn in games like DQM or Pokemon; however, each monster has a unique passive ability that effects combat in different ways. Party building works around getting these abilities to work in synergy to pass more and more difficult levels.
The ability system is further increased by the crafting system. Crafting allows you to add stats and effects to your gear. Each piece of gear can also have one of ANY (i think) creature ability in the game attached to it. This allows for really deep party customization and gives the player alot of room for strategy.
Pros
+Deep party customization with both monster choice and item choice.
+Essentially endless replayability
+Graphics are retro and look fantastic in my opinion.
+Dev(s) still activly working on the game and very vocal with the community.
Cons
-Alot of the crafting materials and consumables tend to not get used. Bloats the inventory a bit and exacerbates a different problem.
-All inventory pages are sorted alphabetically, a few different sort filters would be nice. E.G. type
-Music and sound effects can only be turned on or off, no volume slider.
Could be a pro or con based on personal preferance
*Game can be quite difficult. Alot of rpgs feel pretty mindless, this one is not.
*No real story or ending (I'm fine with this but some might not be)

The year is 2053, shortly after the completion of Shadowrun Returns.  Our story takes place in Berlin with a new protagonist and a new crew already on a job.  I don’t want to reveal much if anything of the story since that is what really draws players to these games, so I will keep story details to myself and only talk briefly about the npc characters and some of the new mechanics that were introduced in this game.
The Team-
So first off, the four person team is once again the standard size team and the merc hiring system has made a lackluster return.  I say this simply because it robs you of story!  The team you originally run with are your constant companions and offer much more to develop the story with their own unique dialogs during missions, which I highly doubt you get by hiring Elf-ears McMagicshoot for a single run.  They still take a cut of the profit after running the main story missions, but you also do not have to pay them up front like other mercs.
Among your rogues gallery of runners, you have Eigar, a Militaristic Troll who is a weapons specialist, Glory, a heavily cyber enhanced field medic (no magic, but always has health kits) and Dietrich the former punk anarchist turned overly risk taking shaman.  There is also a decker you can acquire fairly early in the game, he uses smgs and if the story is played right he has limited rigger abilities.  I do think there is an option to turn him away if you so wish (I don’t recommend that if you aren’t a decker).
Now, one of the greatest things about using these main story npcs is that they implemented a talent tree for each of them.  There are 5 tiers for each character and it seems you get a point after each big milestone in the story.  A cautionary note – once the points are confirmed there are no refunds.  Also each character has two trees, but you are free to mix and match as you see fit but only one point per tier.
Eigar - become a sniper or shotgun specialist.  Since Eigar is a troll, she is naturally pretty tanky, so getting up in their face is a fun option.  She is far from invincible but one of the options in her tree is to get wired reflexes cyberware that let her dodge the first attack against her per turn for 3 turns with a 4 turn cooldown, this is simply amazing for her.  On the other hand, specializing in Sniper will give you things like armor piercing shots and a double tap.  I recommend a mix between the two, making Eigar very diverse for lots of situations.
Glory - buffs to medic capabilities or pistoleer.  Glory has high armor since she is so cyberized and does have a melee mode similar to a street samurai, so choosing a path with her seems like either way would be pretty good.  The pistol she carries takes 0AP to reload, and seems to be very often inaccurate (make sure your shaman is throwing that +15% accuracy buff out from time to time) even from mid distances but and this is a big but, if you do decide to be a pistol specialist, it does do some pretty decent damage late game with the final tier talent.
Dietrich - better buff shaman or mix in some offensive magics.  I loved Dietrich as a character but his trees left me wanting.  Any way you build him, it won’t have that large of an impact on his gameplay.
Mystery Decker - better decking or focus on smgs.  Not much to say about this character except that he only gets three tiers since you get him slightly later in the game.  If you are a decker, you most likely won’t use him over the other team member choices, but if you aren’t you will probably max out his decking talents just to take advantage of environment variables and normal mission decking activities.
Your Character-
Just like the previous game I went with a decker/rifle specialist which made the game an enjoyable play through with the occasional speedbump in the road.  I only had a handful of times when my main character actually died, but I think that’s mostly because I neglected raising my body stat enough early on (I think I ended with body 5 or 6).
Rifles still seem very op simply due to full auto, but it felt like I was reloading more in this game than in Shadowrun Returns.  In addition to the normal assault rifles they have introduced snipers, which are a great option to keep on you as well, so raise that ranged combat stat and get that extra weapon slot to carry both!  If a sniper catches someone out of cover and it’s a crit, it can easily be a one shot kill or chunk them severely.
Decking, just like the last game is a very common thing pretty much everywhere.  I don’t recommend going straight decking right off the bat, so make sure you get more combat stats than decking points initially to have a smooth early game.
I chose Elf as my race for the max cap on Quickness, but it also came with a default point in charisma, just like in the last game etiquette options are everywhere.  In Returns I believe Shadowrunner turned up the most, but this time I think Security was the most common option.  Often times this will simply turn the conversation in your favor but it wasn’t uncommon to just do nothing for you at all.  Hooray RPGS!
Outside of my own character, here are some other things I noticed.  This game seems friendlier towards melee this time around in general (better cyberware and cover options).  In the cyberware shop you can buy wired reflexes pretty early on to supplement your dodge.   If melee isn’t your cup of tea, they introduced a few new variants on the previous games grenades as well as a grenade launcher to play around with.  Magic still seems pretty weak, but there seems to be more of a variety of spells this time around.
Bugs-
I encountered only a few bugs, and only one really broke the game.   Remember folks, save often!
The one that broke it was a scripted encounter that started by some npcs running up to you in a room and then they just stood there looking at me like I was stupid.  Reloaded my last auto-save, tried again and it worked!
There was an issue with the cyberware shop, where I had 1 essence left but I couldn’t equip anymore gear.  Sadly I couldn’t find a workaround for this.
Lastly, but definitely the most annoying there is a combat/movement lag that mostly happens in the matrix (I only had it happen once outside of the matrix).  Sometimes when you end your turn the game will just sit there and think, for 30seconds at a time, trying to figure out what happens next.  This is annoying but not game breaking.
Conclusion-
I thoroughly enjoyed Dragonfall for its excellent story that kept me constantly engaged, powering through and exploring every nook and cranny that was accessible to me.  The improvements on the previous game weren’t anything fantastic and hell I would even call it negligible at best but this seemed like repeat/sequel of an already great game in my book.  I’m good with that.
Completionist game length – 30ish Hours (32 for me and there is a second run most definitely in the future for unexplored options)

Based on the previous games by this programmer/designer (there are multiple programmers/designers at this developer). Does a number things those games do not. There are some minor things I would change, but the purpose of Steam reviews is to let people know that the game works and that it is playable, not to blather on about opinion. Jet Buster is both of these things, whether you like it or dislike it.

Disclaimer: I was part of the beta testing team.
Cute little shoot 'em up with a very good soundtrack and old school graphics. Like all other shmups from Team Grybanser Fox, this featues a good settings menu with all kinds of stuff: Customizable controls (looking at you doujin), Tate, Scanlines, Boss Rush, Stage Select, etc.
The scoring system is very easy to comprehend and fits the uplifting and happy vibe of the game. See the in-game tutorial for details.
The between the bosses and your character (5 selectable "ships" iirc) there is a little banter before the fight which is amusing and doesnt break the fast flow of the game.
Normal mode gives you quite a lot of extends and bombs to achieve a 1CC.
If you manage to sleepwalk though expert mode or absolutely hate the anthro theme, there is Zenodyne R and Zenohell from the same developer. These two have "normal ships", play a bit harder (especially Zenohell) and the theme/soundtrack is more serious.
In summary, Jet Buster is solid shoot 'em up, as was to be expected regarding the track record of the developer.

Dope scoring system (easy to understand, hard to master, based on cumulative ranked medals combinated with two type of command for weapons) for this indie Shmup gem, that's pretty much all you need to know about this game.
It truly shines into being a treat to the players, you will be hypnotized by the simple yet clever gameplay.
Less brutal on starter perspective that others production from the dev team, the normal game mode is really beginner-friendly, and the arcade mode represent a real challenge for Shmup's veteran.
Grybanser Fox games, and more specifically Shmups are always interresting, often talented but also pretty simplistic in term of presentation : this one is trying to change a little bit the team's standarts on this respect.
Art style is a little bit off at moments, if not worse, but otherwise you will not be disapointed for anything : music is great (not to surprising from the Grybanser fox team, see their lovework on Zenodyne R) but right here we got their most polished games in term of details, so that we got some similarities with a gorgeous old game like Rocket Knight Adventures by certain means (destroyed pigs that crashes themself to the ground for instance) : thats not a bad thing at all, believe me.
So don't be fooled by the strange setting nor the cheap presentation, cause underneath their is a solid-as-rock, simplistic yet truly addictive Shoot'em up game that is amongst the best on steam library, and i know what i talking about : consult my gamelist if you doubt me, i'm a Shmup specialist.

When I finished They Breathe, the only thought going through my brain was "why?"
As a lone frog, you disembark from the safety of your log, and begin your descent into the darkness of the lake below you. It doesn't take long to see that They Breathe has set itself out to be incredibly, ineffectually bizarre. Twisted and morbid things begin to float up and attack you, leaving you almost entirely helpless as you frantically attempt to dodge the unnatural abominations, even as you watch your frog brethren die and be consumed around you.
What awaits you at the bottom of the lake only leads to more disturbing places, which when all is said and done seem to leave no one the better. And that includes the player, who for the last thirty minutes has had to participate in a mundane and frustrating race for the scarce bubbles floating to the surface, with the only end reward being the eventually escape from such a weird and mundane game. If there was a deeper meaning here, it stayed hidden beneath the water, as again and again I was left to asking myself "why?", with seemingly no answer to be found.

Pac-Man CE DX+ is one in a long list of ports and updates to the iconic Namco arcade game and ultimately the definitive one to play. What Namco has managed to do is take the original Pac-Man title and inject it with some true adreneline, revitalizing the classic "high score" culture indicative of the 80s/90s arcade scene.
While this edition adheres to the core Pac-Man gameplay (go around a grid getting pellets and objects, avoid ghosts, and use power pellets to devour said ghosts for points), there's a more significant emphasis on speed and risk/reward gameplay. Whereas the original Pac-Man was devided into rounds that ended once the last pellet was taken, the action in Championship Edition is continuous and relentless (think Tetris), nevering throwing you through stages but instead watching to stage proliferate with more enemies and pellets as you grab each wave of pellets and objects.
The aforementioned risk/reward aspect to the gameplay kicks in with the ghosts that give chase to you. While ghosts still spawn in the center and roam out from there much like the original more ghosts are placed stationary across the game field. These inactive ghosts will pursue you once you've come into adjacent contact with them, typically forming up what amounts to a ghost chain. Building ghost chains comes naturally in pursuing pellets and using a power pellet to vanquish your hunters is only natural. The higher the chain you build the better the score hike once you nab a power pellet to devour them en masse, but one must also consider how much aggro they're creating on the play field and how safely they can manuever their way to said super pellets to down that chain. It's this conflict that forms the basis of the adreneline pumping gameplay combined with the game's speed rachetting up as you consume more pellets, objects, and ghost chains.
Visually the game still contains the black and neon vibes of it's original incarnation (though in a much cleaner modern resolution) but other backdrops for the action include a distinctly Lego feel, as well as Dig Dug and Rallxy X themed DLCs among other things. Stage visuals, character visuals, and background tunes are all selectable per board except for cases where you use the DLC themes which use everything related to that DLC together.
Aside from that little quibble and perhaps the insanity of controlling the final speeds at 40-50 (it felt oddly off on my D-Pad for turns at that point) this is an incredibly simple yet very perfect revamp of a classic. Namco didn't take everything about Pac-Man and turn him on his round head. Instead they opted to go back and explore the original concept with mild (yet still somehow extreme) modifications that paid off. Once the speed kicks up and you start having pursuers all across the board, it becomes extremely satisfying once you grab that power pellet and put every last ghost in its place, watching the points bombard your score counter in the process. This is undoubtably the best coat of paint for this 1980 classic.

If you like getting lots of loot, collecting hordes of monsters, wandering pixely mazes, and clearing randomly generated maps, then this is the game for you.  Try out the demo first.  It'll give you a good idea of what's in store, and the Steam version will even seamlessly import your demo game savefile.
Solid, surprisingly deep old-school RPG game.  It starts out simple, with only one dungeon type unlocked and a limited set of enemies.  Then you start rituals.  Rituals to open up more monster tiers, which give you new monsters to fight.  To open up new dungeon types (each of which tends to be high or low on certain resources).  To build facilities for a forge to make new items and an enchanter to put enchantments on them.  To build an arena.  To give you useful items and monsters.  To enchant gems and eggs so you can hatch yourself super powerful monsters.  The complexity adds on and on, always giving you something new to do.
I also like how the challenge scales.  You control it.  Hang out on the low-level dungeons, and you'll always have a nice, easy slaughterfest.  Go further down in search of rarer items and you'll always have a challenge, until your monsters are fighting things high above their own level and tactical use of consumable items, equipped artifacts, compatible monster skills, and a friendly RNG is all that's keeping you alive.  Not to mention, you get to fight some pretty cool monsters with unique abilities right from the start, then summon them to fight for you.  Overall, the whole system feels well-balanced and fun.

My first and only Steam review!
Let me tell you a story. One day I decided to buy Terraria. When I started it up I was disgusted at the graphics and I laughed at any idiot who would be dumb enough to play a modern game with such ugly graphics and simple gameplay. One week later I had clocked in over 50 hours.
What I realized is that GAMEPLAY and not Graphics are what really matter in a game. No one will ever remember a game for its graphics, but for it's gameplay.
Not all indie games are good and I hate when review sites praise games for being artistic, but when they are good we need  to try and give them a chance to see if we like them. Siralim is only $10. I bought it, and once again I found a great game that feautures far more content than many $60 dollar games that we buy year after year. Try it!
I am now going to go in depth on what I believe makes this game so special.
In Siralim, you gather a team of 6 different creatures that follow you around on maps that get progressively harder the more you complete.
The game is extremely similiar to an older game called Dragon Quest Monsters and feels very much like a spiritual succesor.
There are over 300 creatures in the game and they each have a perk that is oftentimes crazy good, like a unicorn that has a 50% chance to ressurect another creature every time they attack.
In addition, their are gear pieces like swords, shields and helmets that also have abilities on them. With other 300 creatures and a vast variety of gear pieces, the various absurd combinations that can be made are staggering.
The game is hard, but It gives you every oppurtunity to come up with your own unique strategy to overcome that challenge level.
The game is stunningly indepth, even though in the beginning it seems fairly simple. The game is constantly throwing new things to do and work towards and new mechanics to try and master. I love always playing and always have something unique/fresh to look foward to.
Lastly, I LOVE the fact that the developer is willing to stick with the game and update it for free. Heck, I would even pay money for substainal updates. We have an oppurtunity here as gamers to help see such a unique game thrive so that more new ideas can be brought to the table as well.
If you have ever played and liked Pokemon, Dragon Quest/Dragon Quest Monsters, Hearthstone, custimizable party RPG's , turned based RPG's like FF1-10, and really any other game that required you to actually think about strategy in order to overcome difficult challenges, then I promise Siralim is for you.

The Battle for Sector 219 is a strategical card game where two players vie for control of a capital city. Utilizing various troop cards, you must maintain supply lines alongside attacking enemy units, all in an effort to advance towards the enemy base while defending your own. The push & pull style of gameplay where any single turn can mean defeat keeps these games short; however, complexity is still very much present. Although The Battle for Sector 219 is really fun and unique, highly desirable game features that are currently absent, along with a lack of depth due to a weak variety of cards keep Sector 219 from being something truly great.
The complete rules for The Battle for Sector 219 can be found
on the developer’s official website. When you start up The Battle for Sector 219 in Steam, the “How to Play” (tutorial) will just present you with a slideshow of that website. It is a very weak introduction to the game, akin to throwing you into the deep end of a pool, but automatic rule enforcement along with highlighted spaces/enemies alleviate the burden. After playing a couple times, everything will make sense and things will start to click. For those that just want a basic idea of the game, I’ll present the bare bones edition below.
A single card sits in the middle of a virtual, dynamic board (no definite boundaries, expands as you place cards). This single card represents the world’s capital. Your base is permanently positioned immediately below that card, and your opponent’s base is mirrored accordingly. Cards are placed on an imaginary grid, adjacent to each other. The goal of the game is to place one of your troop cards onto your opponent’s base spot.
Each troop card will have 3 different stats representing it: supply direction, attack direction, and support direction. The supply direction dictates where that troop can be placed (adjacent to a previously placed card, diagonally, away from other troops, etc.). The attack direction dictates where that troop can attack once placed onto the board. The support direction can be thought of as spaces of continuous suppressing fire provided by that placed unit.
An enemy will be destroyed if a unit attacks (which it can do only when initially placed on the board) while that particular enemy is also under support fire. There are some cards that deviate from this, such as the Artillery, which can automatically destroy an enemy one or two spaces in front of it. 2 Airstrike cards are also provided to each player that can be used to destroy any enemy on any space. Exceptions to all of the above rules and additional complications are presented in the above linked website.
Online multiplayer is supported with a matchmaking system; however, local coop is not. The matchmaking system is automatic (no lobbies or private matches) and asynchronous play can be utilized – make a move, leave, come back and continue. Also, online/solo play has no option to create a custom game: modify time limit, number of rounds, card limits, etc.
For those that are wondering, there also doesn't seem to be much of an online community to play against. To be fair, The Battle for Sector 219 is fairly new so that is to be expected, but due to the lack of depth (explained in the next section), it would have had a hard time maintaining a solid player base anyways, especially without continuous support (additional troop cards, game features, etc.).
The Battle for Sector 219 definitely feels like an Early Access game, or one that is still in its beta build, even though the game is
. I understand that this is the virtualization of a physical tabletop game so there is only so much the developer can do I suppose; however, it doesn't excuse the lack of very basic/QOL features that The Battle for Sector 219 desperately needs. Some of the missing features include:

I can easily see the tabletop version being a blast to play. The game mechanics themselves are very interesting and unique; however, the PC version offers essentially no online play (due to having such a small community - I don't fault them for this), no local coop play, and a very weak solo/AI play. At least with the physical cards, it's possible to modify the decks and play with a buddy. Even so, I still recommend The Battle for Sector 219 to fans of tabletop games,
, because it seems to be a huge pain to purchase the physical copy itself (not available on major online retailers), and the premise behind the gameplay is still enjoyable and worthwhile to try out. If you are on the fence, definitely wait for a sale.

I'm a fan of The Battle for Hill 218. It's a nice, quick, strategic abstract game of supply and conquer. It's traveled with me in my back pocket for the last few years, ready to break out at any time. When it released on iOS, I snagged the pocket version for my phone ASAP.
Now, a pseudo-sequel with a sci-fi theme hits Steam just as I bought a new computer.  The Battle for Sector 219 is a nice digital card game that plays quickly, is functional and slick. If you love quick, thinky, 2-player card games, you'll enjoy The Battle for Sector 219. But, it will require some patience.
There are some interesting quirks with the UI. There's no UNDO button, which can make an accidental click frustrating. When you click on an individual card it is overlapped by the other cards in your hand, obscuring important info when refamiliarizing yourself with the cards. There's also a weird glitch when you WIN against the computer, the game states that you lost, and vice versa. And sadly, there's no tutorial, simply a set of rules to read which can be offputting to new players.
But, for experience players, BfS219 will seem very familiar. The main changes are the unit types which now feature some streamlined abilities that reasonably improve the play experience, removing diagonal considerations which now seems obvious as a negative from the original game. It feels better.
I hope to return to this review again to note that the above concerns were fixed in an update. For now, I recommend the game, but with caution to new players and to reinforce that you'll need to convince friends to buy the game since online players are in short supply.

I've tried a number of the different pinball games available  Steam, and Pinball Arcade is the only one that makes me feel like I'm playing a real, physical table. The only complaint I have about the game does involve the physics modeling: ball speed can differ greatly from table to table, depending on the amount of lighting and animation involved. A fun Pokemon roguelike, with too much to do.  No really, I mean too much.
Pros:
-Tons to do.  Lots of creatures, unique abilities, gambling, ways to buff your creatures, spells... you name it.
-Pretty decent AI to go with all that.
Cons:
-No end goal (that I know of).  There's a tutorial/story that lasts quite a few hours, but after that it's just sandbox.
-Balance issues.
-Repetitive.
-Too much to do.
Even though it looks like I'm stacking the cons, I'd still recommend the game for simple (if you like strategy) fun.  I'm a fan of widely varied abilities, and this game is one of the best I've seen for that.  However, the risk/reward balance is off.  You can make an unbeatable team with some of the earlier creatures.  There's no incentive to go deeper... in fact, you get more powerful rewards faster by just repeating the first few levels.  And until you make a fairly unbeatable team, you'll just be repeating about the first 5 levels anyway.  As for abilities, some low level creatures have some great abilities.  And as soon as you start getting legendary materials, you can just customize them into the most powerful units, anyway.  The AI is decent, but fights get quite repetitive once you've built a team that can take on anything.
With a little more balance adjustment, this game could be even better.  Unfortunately with all the skills built in so closely with the creatures, I don't see a fully balanced game unless a sequel is made.  But as I said, I'd still recommend it as a good simple game with lots of potential.

Give it a little time, and it will be one of the most popular games on steam! <3

Remember Dragon Warrrior/Quest Monsters?
Well here you go.  Along with some other mechanics if you love grinding out levels for equipment, several resources, base upgrades, character perk system, and loot drops.

An addictive monster collecting JRPG with roguelite elements and a ton of items/effects.  Enjoy calm walks through randomly-generated worlds. Collect goodies.  Cry in terror when you realize that your unstoppable monster army has become a victim to YuGiOh levels of special effect chains by monsters that outclass you. Beaten and bruised, get stronger with a deep item creation and monster strategy, as well as some good ol' grinding.
+Lots of Monsters with excellent pixel art
+Monster collection is intuitive and strategic; much less luck based then DWM
+Random world generation and fixed # of battles per level is brilliant
+Easy to play for hours or minutes; excellent save system.
+Each monster has a special effect...eg, a certain dragon can lower an enemy's _max_ health.
+Great music
+6v6 Combat with every monster having different specialties makes for some unique fights.
All in all, I'm very happy. The game feels unique, and there's tons of content as it stands today. It successfully builds upon the DWM formula with what I've found to be a ton of improvements. Great job devs, and I can easily reccommend this to anyone who likes the idea of monster collecting JRPGs.

This game is like the perfect blend between classic Final Fantasy, Dragon Quest Monsters, and NetHack.  Hundreds of monsters, each with their own strengths and weaknesses, tons of randomized dungeons to explore, lots of spells and items to use, and a rather tongue in cheek story about you succeeding your father as king of the land of Siralim and doing whatever it takes to ensure its prosperity.
I especially enjoy the Power Level system, as its a good example of escalating difficulty.  You gain Power as you win battles.  The more Power you have, the stronger the enemies become, but at the same time the rewards and loot you can find also increases.  If you die, you lose a substantial amount of Power that nerfs your loot, but also makes enemies more manageable.
One last thing, the music's pretty good, especially the boss theme, and the pixel graphics are pretty damn crisp and well made.  Give it a try!

This game is definitely in my top 10 games of all time. It's a perfect mix of everything that makes a great game: excellent gameplay, fantastic visuals, a captivating narrative, and a rich game world. All of these elements blended together make for an extremely enjoyable and satisfying playthrough.
The gameplay boils down to leading a group of four characters, of which you can customize to some extent - and yes, your main character has a lot of customisability options, from hairstyle to race and then your skill class - through levels based around the story. I played as an elf decker, allowing me to jack in to the matrix and hack open doors, take control of turrets, and gain visibility of rooms close by through security cameras. Apart from deckers, there are a bunch of different classes to choose from, such as the street samurais, riggers, and mages. There are also plenty of weapons to choose from - pistols, shotguns, sniper rifles, assault rifles, grenades, throwing weapons, spells, summoned spirits, and even drones!
Now to touch on the combat. In a nut-shell, it's XCOM. But further to that, once you're in a mission (that you accept for your team to complete, often assigned by some elitest wanting you to do his dirty work for him in return for a sum of money) you are able to walk around the levels picking up items, looking for clues and advantages, and talking to people. Engage in combat, however, and you see XCOM-styled tactical turn-based strategy take place on your screen. I had no complaints about the combat! In addition to this, your character can gain karma based off of certain actions that you perform, whether it be helping someone out or completing a mission. You then spend your karma points on certain skills, much like most RPGs.
Overall, I only encountered a few minor bugs that hindered my progress, but they were nothing game-breaking. It's possibly not the type of game that you would want to playthrough again, but given the variety in races, classes, and choices to be made throughout the story, you may find yourself wanting to return to the shadows to run for one last time.
This game is a must-have for turn-based strategy fans and RPG fans alike. I highly recommend buying this and playing it through! Enjoy! :D

At first, I wasn't sure about this game. Normally, "text-heavy," "isometic," and "dystopian (constantly depressing)" scare me away. However, this game quickly became addictive and I enjoyed every moment.

A cRPG that mixes fantasy and cyberpunk to create a refreshing new blend! The gameplay is simple, but complex and the flexible stat/spec system allows you to build your character however you like regardless of your class. That said, the essence system is a nice mechanic that discourages and prevents characters from becoming all-powerful mary sues of all trades.
The story was also quite intriguing, and though I was a tad bit apprehensive, being a newcomer to the series and universe, I have not been let down. I -would- appreciate a little more "fantastical" influence in the story and characterization of metahumans, however it is possible this was an intentional design and is an inherent quality of the pen and paper RPG *shrugs* As I said, new to this universe.
On a more somber note, I would like to suggest to HBS to craft longer narratives with more branching arcs/choices and outcomes. It's a pity the linear nature of this game restricts it so that one playthrough is all that is needed to exhume its treasures.
Furthermore, I do feel that a game with such potential for mods ( it includes an editor ) should have more to choose from, and it's a pity the community isn't larger - though what does exist is fantastic. As such, BUY THIS GAME and GET SHADOWRUN HONG KONG to boot, you deserve it and so does HBS.
In summary, the price I picked SR:DF up for (5.09 CND ) was a flat out steal for the experience it has provided, and despite some minor flaws, they have not prevented me from enjoying this game thoroughly and I fully intend to spend my hard earned money subsidizing HBS' well crafted games; nothing like supporting indie studios that operate from the heart!

Dragonfall c'est l'extension de Shadowrun Returns devenue un jeu à part entière. Du coup on est pas vraiment face à une suite. L'histoire est indépendante du premier opus et le moteur graphique est le même. Il y a toutefois quelques améliorations mais pas de quoi casser trois pates à un canard.
On est en présence d'un RPG classique en vue isométrique (un cRPG à la fallout). On gère une équipe de shadowrunner (Sortes de mercenaires undergrounds) des combats au tour par tour. Tout au long du jeu, le joueur se retrouvera face à des choix moraux. Qui influenceront plus au moins la suite de l'histoire. Le tout est admirablement bien écrit et les drames contribuent à dépeindre l'ambiance de cet univers fantasy/cyber punk.

The game will send you to various locations as you piece together puzzles to progress the story. The beautiful visuals are the highlight of the game. This is a quick-playing little strategy game of card positioning.  I don't know if physical copies exist yet, but it's clearly intended to be.
Players have the same deck (different art) and take turns playing 2 cards each.  Cards will destroy an opponent's card if a previously-played card can support it (artillery being an exception here).  The objective is to occupy your opponent's base space on the opposite side of the city card in the center.
You can see from the screenshots that each card has three 3x3 grid diagrams described on them.  The first describes where supply can come from in relation to the card being played.  The center diagram indicates which spaces this card attacks when played, which will ammount to nothing unless the card is supported.  That brings us to the third diagram, which indicates which spaces the card will support after it goes into play (assuming it isn't destroyed by your opponent).  You can only ever occupy your opponent's base space with a card that will be in supply when played.  Read the short manual here:
for exceptions to the rules.
Overall the game is pretty light and there isn't much variety since there's no variation to the player decks.  You either get lucky with the sequence of cards you draw, or you don't.  It does take a little forward thinking to figure out what your best play will be and the shuffle does mean you can't commit to the same strategy every time; however, with a card pool of 26 per player, there's not a whole lot of room for surprises.
I hate to downvote this, but for what it is, it's a decent way to kill ten minutes or so and it's not terribly exciting or even tense.  As a short distraction, it serves its purpose, but there's not much meat on this plate.  If the setting existed, I'd give it a solid neutral - YMMV.
Note: There is a weird bug where losing is counted as a win, and winning is counted as a loss.  Hopefully that gets fixed.

Battle for Sector 219 is a digital version of a fast playing card game. Imagine a 3x3 grid, with an obstacle in the middle. Each turn, you play two cards into that grid. No, it's not Tic Tac Toe, bear with me. Each card represents a supply route, an attack range, and a support fire range. The supply route dictates where you can play, you must keep a supply chain from your side of the base to where you seek to play. If the card has an attack range that overlaps an enemy card when you play, and you have another card's support range overlapping that card, you can attack with that placement, destroying an enemy card. You can only attack along with placing a card.
That is the game. You try to capture the other player's side of the base, and you are jockeying for position. Only two card plays per turn, yes, but these are two incredibly stressful plays where you and your opponent are engaged in a proverbial knife fight in a phone booth, trying to wreck each other's placements and advance as best you can with each play, trying to squeeze every ounce of firepower you can out of these two simple plays. Because, really, you're only three cards from the opponent's base at all times, and it is incredibly easy to forget that if you try to advance up one side and leave the opponent with one card on the table.
The game itself runs fine. Only played AI but the AI is solid. Online play is on offer, in the mobile sense of you make a move and wait for the opponent to sign back in and make a move, which absolutely murders the pace of the game on PC but works just fine for mobile. The rules link just goes to a PDF at the official site. The digital implementation feels a little bare bones, but there is not much to complain about beyond that; you have music, decent thematic animations...
All in all, this is an incredibly smart and challenging card game that can be played in under 5 minutes

Before Alien Rage I'd played both Sniper Ghost Warrior games from CI Games and to be honest I wasn't impressed. Thus, I was a bit sceptical since gameplay videos / trailers for this game were just as promising as they were for their previous products. How wrong I was!
This is about an ongoing battle between humans and an alien species called Vorus. Remember the Unobtainium's significance in Avatar? The equivalent mineral in this game is called Promethium and it is suffice to say that this is a highly efficient source of energy so both races have all the reason to fight for it. As the intro tells us it is the Vorus that started it all and our protagonist, Jack, is the lonely hero who's dropped at a crucial mining facility (where it all started) to destroy it since it has long been taken over by the uglies. During his mission Jack is assisted by 2 people on the radio - this chit-chat often involves jokes that make the game more fun but since the campaign is not long enough this particular part you will not miss / remember.
You shoot first and ask questions later! You reload sometimes but only sometimes as beside the human weapons your assortment also consists of alien arms - with these you can just shoot but it's worth taking a break from time to time as some overheat pretty quickly. You can take 2 weapons with you and you have a 3rd one - your good old pistol - whose ammunition never depletes. No grenades, no mines, nothing - just 3 weapons to wreak havoc! It should also be noted that every weapon has a secondary fire mode - you have to be careful as all use the same ammunition. It should be noted that in the heat of battle using this mode can save your life by turning the tables.
This is a fast-paced, action-heavy FPS game that takes us back to the old days. The game also looks very nice - it is a bit heavy on the blue colour (also it has a bit too much post-processing effects for my taste) but some of the locales look very promising. We go through dozens of corridors and hangars but then at one point we visit the docking bay. Lots of stuff is going on around us - ship arrivals and departures and sometimes the action is so fast and it requires you to pay attention not allowing you to appreciate your surroundings. Then Jack embarks a train and uses its mounted minigun to shoot up the place. The he visits a mothership to end the Vorus presence once and for all.
This game is challenging! Very challenging! As an FPS "veteran" I started it on "hard" difficulty (even the easiest is called "challenging") and I was in for a world of hurt. I restarted several areas numerous times and at one point I had to lower the difficulty level on the go to be able to rid myself of one of the 9 bosses. Naturally, the bosses are tough and in several cases you have to figure out how to beat them (at other times running and gunning perfectly works). Still, while it is difficult the game appreciates the way you kill enemies - all explosive, melee and double kills are recognised (the voice-over shouts are akin to the ones we heard in 1998 during an exciting Unreal Tournament match) and result in scores. These, in time, unlock some perks you can apply to Jack on the go (you cannot activate more than 3 at one time) that slightly help you in the battle.
Similarly to Hard Rest or Shadow Warrior this game puts emphasis on the action and the action only. However, unlike the aforementioned this game will be TOUGH if you give it a chance. Be prepared otherwise you'll be disappointed! Too bad Alien Rage gamers are not active enough to join me for a multiplayer session - I have to take out my disappointment. again, on Jack's favourite Mech bosses, then!

Well, I’m pretty sure that I got this one out of a Humble Bundle deal; something that I am counting myself as thankful for. Alien Rage – Unlimited is an action, FPS from CI Games. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
First on the list is the graphics. Alien Rage offers some pretty nice graphics even on lower settings. I was pleasantly surprised by this (especially considering that I’d never heard of or seen anything about this game up until I installed and played it).
Secondly, the weapon designs are cool. Every weapon I picked up felt, sounded, and looked different. You want automatics? You got it. You want explosives? You got it. Practically every weapon you can find in Alien Rage would be right at home in Quake or Unreal Tournament.
Thirdly, the game itself plays very similar to games like Doom, Quake, and Unreal Tournament. I loved those games back when I was starting to play computer games and that added bit of nostalgia helped me enjoy this game a little more.
The Bad
Games that are hard because they genuinely test your skill are games that I thoroughly enjoy. Games that are hard because your character is overly squishy are games that I do not enjoy. Combine that with recklessly aggressive AI and your bound to have a bad time sooner or later. This was perhaps my biggest gripe about Alien Rage.
The Meh
Something felt inherently off about the dialogue, but I could never quite put my finger on it. Sometimes it felt genuine, other times it felt like they were trying to hard, and still others it felt like a joke was trying to be made, but it fell far short. Whatever it was that was wrong, it rubbed me the wrong way in the most subtle way possible.
You can “jump” in the game, but it is easily the most pathetic jump I have ever seen in all of my days. You might come six inches off the ground at most. Honestly, if this is what you choose to do with your jump feature, I’d just leave it out of the game.
Verdict: Nay
On the whole, Alien Rage feels like a FPS bullet hell and becomes less fun the longer you play. If you can get it for dirt cheap then maybe, just maybe, it would be worth it.

With few exceptions, the core gameplay of every match-3 game is identical or nearly so.  And there's a
of match-3 games out there.  So the way one match-3 truly distinguishes itself from the next is in the extras; graphics and sound, bonuses and powerups, some sort of larger overworld game that encompasses the match-3 levels.
has taken this principle to heart, because it has extra features for
.
At first,
can look like typical mobile F2P whalebait.  You're barely in the door before it tries to sell you packages of resources at ludicrous prices (don't worry, they're just setting an artificially high baseline -- they'll be offering you big discounts soon enough) and then goes into the usual hand-holding tutorial.  No surprises thus far.
Once you've mastered the basic gem-matching gameplay, however, you start to enter the strategic elements of the game.  Like in a CCG, you collect cards from various random-drop sources, and you select four of them to "do battle" with your foes in the gem-matching segments.  One of those cards can represent your own character, and probably should, as your own stats tend to outpace your cards. Tile matches give you like-coloured mana, which powers your cards special abilities, plus they also have attack and defence statistics.
The initial team-building strategy is simple enough -- choose the rarest, most powerful cards you have, try to ensure that they want a mixture of different mana types so you don't waste matches, and avoid pairing cards whose ability removes certain coloured tiles with cards who want that colour of mana.
But then it gets so much deeper.  First are the currencies -- the usual gold (regular) and gems (premium), of course, but also Souls and Runestones which are used to buy enhancements.  You can upgrade the level of a card by spending Souls; upgrade its rarity by sacrificing duplicates; add additional Traits by collecting the appropriate runestones.  More common cards are easier to boost up, so after a while the choice between your ultra-rare dragon and your common-as-dirt goblin won't be so clear-cut as it was initially.
But that's just upgrading cards. When you complete all the quests in a kingdom, you also gain a character class. You can spend resources to buy levels in these classes, which grant different bonuses.  The kingdoms themselves are a sort of upgrade, because you pay gold to unlock them.  Or you can instead use that gold to increase the level of the kingdoms you already have, improving their bonuses and the passive income they generate.  Or join a Guild and donate gold to the guild to help accomplish Tasks, which gives you keys to access rare drops...
There's a lot of different forms of advancement crying out for your resources, is the point, and they're all rewarding in some way or another.
Picking a favourite loadout from the outset and dumping everything into it won't work here, either, thanks to all the synergistic bonuses included.  A kingdom's power level (not to be confused with the kingdom's level, or your level in the character class governed by that kingdom) is raised by acquiring the cards associated with that city and enhancing them.  So resources invested even in that dumb card you never use will still ultimately benefit you, albeit by a more roundabout mechanism.  Similarly, you can gain various team bonuses by combining cards from the same kingdom, and many card and class traits benefit cards of specific types.  On top of all that,
gives a weekly 10% strength bonus to cards of certain types, making it more worthwhile to bring out cards you wouldn't normally use.
In short,
, once you go beyond the core match-3 part, is a massive problem in optimization that is deliberately made unsolvably complex -- unless you pick a particularly narrow definition of what you're considering "optimal," I suppose.  If gaining levels, filling progress bars and upgrading things appeals to you,
can draw you in like a black hole.

First, the actual gameplay: it's...mixed. The developers want you to feel mortal, and indeed death looms, cackling, behind every thief, rat, and resource meter. You must obey the whims of your body and its hunger and fatigue, and of course the inevitable dose of the Sand Plague. The economy isn't out to do you any favors, either, as prices constantly fluctuate as people panic, and you'll be forced to cheat the town's children out of their lifesaving medicine on a regular basis. Unfortunately, not all of the despair is intentional; combat, in particular, is frustrating instead of tense, and the most surefire way of dealing with it is to have each enemy despawn by jumping into a nearby house every time you make eye contact. The other massive blemish framing the game's design is that Pathologic is fundamentally a walking sim with frills, and good *lord* is there a lot of tedious wandering to do. Prospective players should have a high tolerance for trudging.
But Pathologic's juiciest cuts of meat are its narrative and setting. A nightmarish plague descends upon a forgotten village somewhere in a very Slavic Steppe, just as three healers arrive independently of each other to fight it. Every midnight, as the clock strikes twelve, the disease creeps into one district and abandons another, as the looters attack, the civilians cower, and the mimes rehearse a new performance at the Theater. The townspeople worship bulls, malformed humanoids butcher them, and the children have washed their hands of it all and run away to live inside an impossible tower. The characters are overwritten, to be sure - this is a game in which a ten-year-old is liable to know the phrase "piece de resistance" - and yet almost all are compelling and multifaceted. The dawn of every new day can feel like a cruel punishment just as much as a reward, and yet the Town's characters, customs, and history are so eerie, insane, and mesmerizing, I was pulled back in each time.
I could go on for hours, but it's impossible to tame a beast as behemoth and unruly as Pathologic in a few paragraphs. Its graphics are striking but mushy, its plot is an uneven mess, and it remains one of the most haunting and unforgettable games I have ever played. In brief, it is a game about survival, and it isn't just the player in jeopardy: Pathologic asks us what it means for humanity to survive, and what we will leave behind if we don't. If it sinks its talons into you, it will never let go - and I advise you, if you have any interest in narrative games, to let it in.

This is refreshing. If you're tired of playing linear games, games that treat the player like a child, games were you feel like a god, predictable plots, and your usual formulaic stuff then this game will be up your alley. Most horror games will still treat you like a child and keep a steady difficulty curve, give you all the resources you need to survive, and expect you to eventually make it to the end. This game does none of that besides Day 1 offering explanations of mechanics. This game is unpredictable and it will unsettle you. With other "horror" games like Amnesia, Outlast, Silent Hill 2, or Darkwood you know that no matter what happens it will ease you into things and by the end of the game you can replay it knowing all of the tricks, strategies, and exploits you can just about always bail on. Those games give you security in some form one way or another.
This game doesn't.
Pathologic doesn't rely on jump scares or music cues to tell you when to feel scared or unsettled. It never lets you feel comfortable. Ever. You will beat this game several times and still be unsure if you did everything right. You can play with a guide and still feel lost. You'll hear the mechanics and start a plan to survive everything, feeling completely comfortable and prepared, only for everything to immediatly fall apart in your face. You'll be punished for simple mistakes, and when you ask yourself why/how it all failed, you'll know that that's just what happens.
This isn't a fun game or even a great game, but I think everyone should play this. You will not find another game like this. I mean that. I think just that alone is worth buying this.

This game executes turn based tactical combat well, but I'd say the storytelling is its greatest asset.
The combat is pretty standard for what you would expect of a tactical game.  You have a team, and each member can take a couple actions a turn.  Characters have special abilities and different attack types.  There is a fair amount of variety.  Some characters excel at firearms, others at melee combat.  Mages can cast both damaging and buffing spells.  Summoners can call spirits, and riggers can control drones (the two "pet" classes).  Hackers have their own VR combat where they fight IC in a system very similar to meat combat.  The hacker's efforts in VR can grant access to other areas on the map, provide camera feeds, gain information that can be sold for money and other things.  In addition to character design, there are choices to make in combat such as where to take cover, how to flank enemies, etc.  It's a good system.
As I said above, however, the story is what has really sold me on the game.  Between missions, interactions with NPCs shed light on the developing narrative, and the story kept me engaged.  What's more, each of your team members has their own story to tell.  The stories add a great depth to the characters.  These are not just spell/gun machines that follow you around in combat.  They are living, breathing people struggling with their own motivations.  It's very interesting learning what they are.  I'm perhaps halfway through the game, and I already have a strong emotional connection to the characters who's stories I've played through.
I recommend this game.  For those familiar with the original Shadowrun Returns, this is a definite improvement, both in game play and in storytelling.  It is a solid representation of the tactical combat genre, the RPG genre, and the Shadowrun setting.

Siralim is an old fashion NES dungeon crawler, or if you're a PC sort then think back to the Wizardry series. There's a lot to say about this game so let's dig in.
Gameplay: The basics of this game involve you, a sorceror king/queen, but you're no fighter. You must summon creatures to fight your battles (up to 6) in turn based RPG combat. Along the way you'll collect resources to build your castle out and uncover powerful artifacts that give you the edge you need to delve deeper.
The difficulty is steep, but enjoyable because it rewards thinking about your party setup. Each creature has a unique perk such as "reving upon 1st death" or "casts a barrier on party at start of combat," and so a well thought team packs an extra whollop. What will really break the difficulty for you though is how well you use the 3 primary stat systems: Royalty, Artifacts and Nether Creatures.
Royalty is a prestige system where every level the Lord earns it gets to permanent upgrade some facet of the game in its favor. Increased loot, loot quality, +1% to dmg, etc.
Artifacts add heaps of extra abilities onto your creatures. Though they can only equip one at a time, artifacts level up indefinitely and each level lets you add another enchantment.
Nether Creatures are your usual monsters, but on magical steroids you've been injecting it with since it was an egg. These take a lot of effort to build and a lot of time in investment, but a well thought Nether can be 2-5 times as strong as a plain creature of its level.
Graphics: Quirky old fashion sprites.
Sounds: Ho-hum. I turned it off and played ambient dungeon sounds instead.
Length/Story: There is no story. The game is all about diving deeper and deeper and forever upgrading. Think Disgaea without all the pesky "humor."

Developed and published by CIGames, the same company behind Sniper: Ghost Warrior and Lords of the Fallen, comes Alien Rage - Unlimited; a sci-fi FPS title that's packed with non-stop action. Originally released in 2013 for PC, Xbox 360, and Playstation 3, the game has only seen a minor following to date, and it has received mixed reviews that weigh mostly on the negative side.
Let's just go ahead and rip the band-aid off; Alien Rage is a generic shooter when it comes down to the plot line and characters. It only took me about six hours to finish the game, and I couldn't even tell you what their names are, except for the guy you play as... his name is Jack. However, bland story and people aside, Alien Rage is actually an excellent, solid shooter when it comes down to it. Not to mention, it's one of the few sci-fi shooters that is currently available on Steam that doesn't involve some kind of stealth mechanic.
The basics of the plot are as such: Earth colonized on some asteroid to mine an energy substance known as Promethium. An alien species known as the Vorus got word of this, joined the Earth team on the asteroid, and helped mine the energy source. The Vorus realized that they could have the Promethium all to themselves, and turned on the humans, wiping out the miners completely. Jack is sent in to wipe out the scum, and there are a lot of them to stick bullets in to. While you're there, you gather audio logs to fill in the blanks of the story that the very brief and minor cutscenes fail to explain.
Be forewarned, this game is not for those who are not good at shooters or FPS in general; the difficulty, even on the lowest setting, can be maddening at times. There is no sticky cover system like in Gears of War, it's up to you to find something sturdy to hide behind while bullets and plasma bolts are whizzing by your head. At times, it also seems like no matter where you stand, or what you do, the enemies will be hitting you anyway. It's also incredibly easy to be overrun by Vorus, and it's best to maintain your distance at all times.
Speaking of foes, there are enough enemy types that will keep you satisfied kill after kill in Alien Rage. Everything from your standard rifle-wielding hooded Vorus, grunts that will turn invisible and bum rush you, mini-gun powerhouses, to plasma blasting elites. Each nasty alien is a force to be reckoned with, and in large groups they are nearly unstoppable. Luckily, you can use the aid of explosive barrels and secondary weapon fire to make your pest control service go as smooth as possible. There are also 9 bosses to be dealt with across the 14 levels that you will play through, and while they all have a weakness to exploit, they are immensely powerful and your death will come swiftly many times over while facing them.
There are a total of 10 weapons, from a standard assault rifle, shotgun, pistol, rocket launcher, sniper rifle, to alien weaponry such as the plasma gun. Each one has its own unique secondary firing mechanic, most of which result in a large grenade catapulting from your weapon. Using the secondary fire, you can do some sure damage to the highly destructible, and impressive, environment. While many of the areas look similar, it's important to remember that you're in a giant mining facility, although you do venture out onto the asteroid a few times. The whole game has a very cold, surgical, clean feel to it; despite the strewn about blood and guts of the former Earth miners.
For a title released 3 years ago, Alien Rage surprisingly enough looks as if it was released this year. This is of course due to the fact that the game was made in Unreal Engine 3, and it does well in showing off some highly impressive graphical and mechanical technology. The controls feel sturdy, your character feels beefy, and the optimization is near-flawless. I did experience some framerate issues while transitioning between some sections, and when there were large explosions; however, the results were a brief dip into the mid-40's, and then it was back up to 60 FPS in no time. I also wanted to add in here that the soundtrack for this game is filled with some great beats that are sure to keep your blood pumping the entire time.
Well, there you have it. For a generic shooter, as many people have laid claim to in the review sections of many sites and forums, Alien Rage does have its perks. It's a solid game, with great mechanics and gameplay, and it's surprisingly fun despite it's obvious downfalls. It's really a shame that we're lacking so heavily in action based sci-fi FPS titles, and if more games such as this one came along with a better story and more developed characters, it would be a welcome change of pace from the tried-and-true military shooters that have flooded the market. If six hours of gameplay is enough for you to sink $21.99 CAD over, then go for it. Otherwise, hold out for a sale and definitely pick this one up in the $5-10 price range. Don't miss out on this one if you're craving a decent, action packed, sci-fi shooter.
