I'm an addicted pinball player and played pinball since the age of 6 till my age now 48. That's 42 years of playing pinball. So how does Pinball Arcade compare to real pinball? Well of course do not expect miracles. For instance: on a real pinball machine you would be able to carefully nudge the table, while on Pinball Arcade there's only 3 ways of nudging: left, right and up, all without ability to dose the amount, which in most of the cases results in too much, making an escape from the outlane lanes by nudging more a pot of luck than skiil. The tables themselves have been skillfully recreated that's for sure: I do not see any distinction what so ever in gameplay between real physical tables I know very well like High Speed, Funhouse and Fish Tales and the digital equivalent in Pinball Arcade. All in all with the real tables often hard to find, this is certainly a good alternative; it does in no way replace the actual tables themselves, but if you are nostalgic like me and want to relive the feeling of those classic pinball tables, it's well worth your buck.

I will say that the tables that I tested are pretty spot-on with the real-life versions, but the graphics are a bit dated, configuration is limited (camera angle for example), buying tables individually is too expensive compared to other pinball games, and there's no virtual cabinet support.
Awesome Scorechaser game

More and more often I would like to have a ‘neutral option’ when writing a game review on Steam, Pinball Arcade is one of those games.  The game play is relatively straight forward despite some interface annoyances. The physics of the game are extremely realistic, despite some of the designs of the older tables where the ball just goes straight down the middle – maybe these tables were tough back then and actually the physics are pretty accurate!! You do get a trial period on the tables, but personally I feel the DLC is overpriced, but there are a huge range of tables which have been emulated to precise detail.
Overall the developer states that their goal is for ‘Pinball Arcade to become the most realistic and comprehensive pinball game ever created’ and go on to ask for support ‘to preserve these tables and join the indelible part of Americana that is pinball'. Therefore on that basis I will recommend this game as it falls between a ‘yet another pinball game’ and a ‘collection of historic nostalgic tables’ to take some of us back to a time we played these in reality down the local arcade.

As a long-time player, it pains me to leave this review. What this game does right, is fantastic. But what it does wrong, has gone beyond what I call the "rock in my shoe" analogy. Patches break game functionality, while the developer churns out more tables. I have experienced numerous issues with this poorly-coded game. Balls clipping through flippers where two or more balls meet. Balls clipping through table components, or just flying off into the nether. A UI that breaks, making it impossible to navigate any menu which prompts me to force a close. And now, I can't livestream this game on OBS through window capture. All I get is a black screen. And my controller no longer works. It is not my system; I have been able to window capture other games and use my wireless controller on those same games. Every patch released fixes one problem and creates another in the process.
FarSight has a team of bad programmers and I am really close to asking for a full refund of the 5 season packs I currently own. Shame on you, FarSight.

New interface glitches out sometimes. I've noticed that the game will occasionally redirect to its own internal bluescreen errors, relating to a failure to load assets as you browse tables. Launching the game and going directly to the table you want to play seems to work fine.
The older interfaces were better, but its still functional and a great game to play. Very generously includes one of the better pinball tables made, for free, and has secondary table that rotates once a month that lets you play for free as well. Good way to demo a new table beyond the tiny scoring limits.
Note: To make it easier to impulsively buy new tables and content, installing the game grabs every table they've released so far, and not just tables you own. As of the time of this review, that amounted to a 10gb download that decompressed to about 17gb after the first launch. The size may grow as you explore more of the content the game has on offer.

I decided to recommend this game based solely on the gameplay, despite its numerous technical issues. PA does a pretty good job of capturing the feel on playing on a real table. The physics feel much more natural than Pinball FX3’s. You have the option of demoing every available table before buying it.
I do take issue with how the developer, FarSight Studios, supports the game. Often new updates are focused on implementing new DLC to keep the money coming in. It can take years for them to address some bugs, if they're ever fixed at all. Some of the earlier seasons still sport low resolution scans of the tables, making it difficult to read some of the text on the field. There still isn't an in-game option for portrait mode, you have to switch the orientation of your desktop settings in Windows to achieve the desired effect. The game allows you to toggle between DX9 and DX11 rendering, but mode suffers from different sets of bugs. The UI feels like it was designed for a touch interface. Even though the game is listed as having Steam Cloud support, it doesn’t actually backup all of your in-game records and progress.
Pinball Arcade is absolutely worth it if you can wait for the table packs to go on sale.

First of all: The reason i don't have a lot of hours into this game on Steam is because i play it more on my Android.
I've been playing Siralim for about 7-8 Months now, and i can say i love this game. When i didn't have the money to pay, the dev gave me a free copy to try it out. I loved the gesture and decided i'd pay him back by purchasing the Android version the next month and writing this review about the game now it's on steam.
The devs (Thylacine Studios) have put a lot of time and love into this game to ensure users can have lots and lots of hours of fun.
This game has a TON of replay value (Generated quests, no level cap, leveling of weapons and enchanting them, nether creatures, unlocking all the castle upgrades, etc) and a solid  6v6 battle system. There's also a mechanic where you have to extract cores from your enemies, and after 3 cores, you can summon that monsters to fight alongside you! At first glance, the game looks a lot the the old gameboy games Dragon Warrior (or Quest) Monsters, and this is also where the devs got inspired by and tried to build upon. The music is really good, i LOVE the battle theme and sometimes not finish a battle just to listen to it more. There's frequent updates, adding new monsters, realms, weapons, enchantments, buffs and debuffs (There's already a LOT of them) and Minor/Major sigils (a kind of boss battle with a group of very strong monsters). The community over on the website
is also very active, and this is also where you'll find info on special codes and events to help you in the game!
All in all, i really love this game, and can not give it anything else but a positive review. If you like old school rpg's and/or monster management in the slightest, you should try this out.

If I had a love child with all of video game history, it would look like Siralim, and I would treasure it every day.
So, not much difference then.
REALTALK GAME REVIEW:
If Pokemon focused much more on abilities than having the right combination of attacks, and you could have a rugby brawl with all six of them at once, and Ash Ketchum was a kickass sorceror who actually made valuable contributions to his team and leveled up along with them, and the item system was more complicated than the choice between Life Orb/Leftovers/Choice Band, and it all took place in massive randomly-generated dungeons with no level limit, it might look like Siralim.
But it would still be a pale imitation of the real thing.

I've been playing on Android a long time and I felt compelled to come make a note - this game is really *not* like DQM/DWM, and if you're a fan of those games that's actually a great reason to buy it.
I say that because when I first saw Siralim early on, I saw the graphics (which have changed since then!) and the description and immediately though oh awesome, a procedural DQM for my tablet! This was wrong, and while I bought it after the demo end (because the demo was rather short for me), I soon became disappointed. I mean, monsters only have one ability, and you can't breed, so what the heck, right?
I came back to it later, after a few updates (there was a bug that kept crashing my game once I was around lv 18 or something anyway, so that combined with my disappointment made me put it away). I realised that my initial HEY DQM! was really not giving Siralim a fair chance. For one you can't really dominate in Siralim after a few hours like you can start to in DQM. For two, you can't just haphazardly throw things together and just expect them to work (which you can for like, 99% of the DQM content, haha). For three, fifteen levels is like a drop of ♥♥♥♥ in the ocean for this game; I'd never gotten into Nether monsters, I'd not even gotten into artifacts, much less synergizing monster teams ... I'd even considered spells absolutely useless trash, hahaha.
This game is *very* deep, and if you're looking for a quick nostalgia trip or a replacement for DQM/DWM, I think that you may be disappointed initially like I was. It's definitely a fair comparison of inspiration (monsters, randomly generated maps), but honestly while there is a good level of complexity in the old DWM games (I'm not up to date on the very newest releases), I'd have to say Siralim has a lot more depth going for it.
It also takes a lot more time to ramp up actually needing to get into that content, and it's really something that you discover by accident - it doesn't hold your hand, and things like party synergy aren't just told to you. It requires experimentation and really playing around with things to get a good feel for what works together.
Well, that or reading on the community suggestions. I have to say replacing my Minotaur Warrior with a Brim Smith (after a restart, so pretty early team) has definitely increased my win rate. ;p

Very good RPG which does a damn good job immersing you in the Shadowrun setting. Interesting story as well. Definitely a better game than Returns, and being a Kickstarter backer the money spent has been very well worth it.
You get immersed in the story, your nuyen (credits) aren't infinite and you have to carefully upgrade your skills. Spreading your karma (skill points) too wide can gimp your character and it is heavily recommended to focus on 1-2 "combat groups". Combining decking with rifles is doable, but if you also spend points elsewhere you might not get the abilities and hit percentages needed for later. It is thus best to basically focus on two main attributes (Strength, Quickness, Willpower, Intelligence, Charisma) and a subset of combat skills of attribute chosen. One big minus in my opinion though is that Charisma attribute is very useful as high Charisma unlocks some powerful persuasion options throughout the game. While you can easily play without spending points in Charisma, I felt that higher Charisma would have made my playthrough much more enjoyable.
Combat is nice and simple, but it has some flaws. First is that at times you have no idea if an enemy is within line of sight and I often place a character in a position where he logically should have a line of sight, yet he is not which can screw up your tactics. A visual aid of some kind would have been nice. Second, you should be able to enter turn-based/combat mode yourself, as a few times I have managed to sneak up on an enemy and other times you know there are enemies around the corner or behind the door (like after hacking security cameras, revealing their presence). Getting my team in position that way would have been pretty good.
Looting. When you pick up items during runs, you can only add them to your own inventory or send to your stash. An option to give some items to your fellow runners would have been welcome.
Dialogue is for the most part good, with numerous dialogue choices and options. Depending on what skills you have, you can get extra dialogue options too, like higher Biotech can give insight into medical info, whereas Strength can be used to intimidate or Charisma to charm. Charisma also gives etiquette perks which unlocks extra dialogue for certain categories like Shadowrunner, Street, Gangs etc. There are a few dialogue choices where you can use fellow party members to do a task, but too few. You should have been able to use party members' skills in dialogue too if your own character is not able to, like using shaman to resolve magic-related dialogue options if required skills are there.
The missions themselves are pretty good and you usually have different ways to do them. How you do them will not change the story progression, but will have an effect on what rewards you get and how your party members react.
Overall, the game is fun and challenging and the choices you make have some consequences but not gamechanging though. If turn-based RPGs with thought-out dialogue and stories is your thing, Dragonfall is heartily recommended.

Best RPG I've played in a long time, though it hit a snag when I had to replay a later mission THREE times due to a bug with quicksaving. After I came back and beat the rest of the game, I was less angry, but that really killed the momentum.
It was a great experience besides that, with the writing alternating between badass and hilarious, almost always hitting the mark at whatever it was attempting. Not quite up there with Planescape, but very good. You can roleplay many different kinds of characters, and generally no matter what you choose there's unique ways to solve problems or get hidden dialogue. There's some moral choices to make, and unlike the newer Fallout games, they're actually more interesting than a choose-your-own-adventure novel. The endings are pretty dramatically different in their consequences, but all could reasonably be chosen by a "moral" player.
Combat is pretty entertaining, though the AI is dumb sometimes and the game's still a bit too easy on Hard difficulty. The earlier missions were balanced, but I steamrolled the last two. Almost every mission has at least one exciting twist which keeps things interesting, eg your team has to fight security while your hacker character battles another hacker in cyberspace for control of the turrets, etc. You will not be bored.
Although the character archetypes are quite different, customization is sort of impractical beyond picking 2-3 key skills and pumping them for the whole game. Your teammates also manage their own gear and stats, with some limited skill choices on your part. No complaints about that actually, it makes sense and works pretty well. You can hire temporary mercenaries for missions to replace them, but there's absolutely no reason to because it costs money, they're not noticeably better, and you miss out on dialogue. Overall, Dragonfall doesn't have the technical depth of Wizardry, Diablo II, or even Final Fantasy. The main draw of the game is the setting and the various ways you can react to it, not min-maxing.
I beat the game ~100% in about 30 hours, which is pretty decent, but for some reason it still feels short. I wish you could get more small shadowruns, like the Genesis game had, in addition to the handful of long and detailed jobs that make up this one. There's all these systems - the jobs list, the online message board, the character progression - that give the illusion of a big world, but ultimately there's a limited amount of money and stat points in the game, and you don't have that much agency in where you go. At least the modding tools could potentially put the engine to fuller use. As it is, Dragonfall is great, but there's some wasted potential also.
Overall, judging just on the base campaign, Dragonfall is an easy recommendation. My only real hard complaint is those damn bugs. It's important that you be able to trust the game not to break when you do something wrong, or you know, save.

The story has classical thriller elements and surprising moments, which involve you emotionally. It also presents you with very interesting moral dilemma’s, where you have to make choices that have little to do with immediate rewards or missions objective. ( I wonder if they got this concept from DOS…) So you could say that what ever the game lacks in gameplay, it compensates by good story telling. Long story short for a low budget production, this is a great game.

The game is developed by illogica studio, who you might know as developers of another puzzle game - Hitman GO, which was initially released for mobile platforms but recently has made its way to Steam as well.
Subaeria has been out for some time, but I only got around to record it now because of the technical issues it had at the start (some of them remain to this day).
So, this is a rogue-lite action puzzle game.
The target is to clean your gaming debt while evading evil robots who are out to kill you for it.
The catch is - you don’t have any weapons or equipment to fight them.
You have to manipulate those pesky robots into destroying each other.
And to help you with this, you have a personal drone.
You will find various abilities and powerups for him, that are also limited to manipulating robots.
Like say, take over robot control, or stun robot, or make robot go berserk and attack its allies.
So, in the end it comes down to use of the environment and enemies’ abilities against them.
I wish they would invest more into player-environment interaction though - currently the only way to affect the surroundings is - once again - through enemy robots - which is quite limited.
The rooms you have to fight in generally have some boxes and even exploding crates lying around and while you can indeed use enemies to blow them, there’s no way to do that yourself.
I think it would benefit this game a lot if the developers were to provide a way to manipulate the environment as well - not just enemies.
The game is set in a pretty cool dystopian underwater world that has a lot of cyberpunk vibes to it.
The main story is nothing special, but the characters, world and dialogues have quite a lot of personality.
It’s possible to unlock four playable characters, each with their own storyline as far as I understood.
And what’s even more unusual for a rogue-lite game - there are several possible endings for each of them depending on your quest decisions.
The level layouts are randomly generated, but rooms seems to have a limited number of preset layouts.
After several hours of playing the game, I started to recognize quite a lot of repeating rooms.
Same goes for enemy types - there’s not that many of them.
Essentially, there are two types of enemies: slicing enemies that chase you and shooting enemies that shot at you.
Everything else is pretty much combos of those two: static turrets, grenade shooting enemies, slicing and shooting enemies, and so on.
There are several bosses in game that mix this up a bit.
Although I’d found them to take a bit too much time to beat though (or maybe I just suck at it).
There are several things that are currently stopping me from thoroughly enjoying the game.
One is extremely long loading times - it can take up to 2 mins to load into game. And that’s in a rogue-lite game where it’s quite easy to die.
Another one is very unstable framerate and somewhat glitchy lighting effects. Framerate can randomly jump from solid 60 fps to 1 fps in a cutscene and back to 60 after cutscene ends. This happens for no apparent reason.
And the last one is absence of any way to save the game - once you quit mid-game, there’s now way to continue from you last point, you’ll have to start from the very beginning again.
Hopefully all of those will get addressed in one of the upcoming patches.
All in all, it’s a pretty enjoyable little action puzzler for the price. It does requires some more technical polish and maybe some thoughts on more meaningful player-environment interactions.

Subaeria caught my eye just recently when it was first released on Early Access. An action puzzle game where you have to use the enemies against each other and the environment sounded promising and like a unique experience. And the fact that the levels would be procedurally generated made it sounds even better. So is it what I hoped it would be or did it fail to meet my expectations?
The gameplay consists of one simple objective really: move through the labyrinth while destroying the Cleaners, robots that are after you and who will try to attack you because you have no more credits left in your account. It’s a simple story, but it gets the job done and like many other games it doesn’t need a good story in the first place for it to be enjoyable.
Your character will be able to talk to other characters in some of the areas you visit, but none of them have anything particularly helpful to say, although they sometimes do give you a hint about where you need to to go. Problem is, however, that you usually have to head in a certain direction anyway and you’ll most likely get there even without having talked to them.
Each area consists of a square layout, a block if you will, and the entrance and exit will be locked until the Cleaners have been defeated. This usually means you have to trick them into moving through the lasers or by letting them bump into each other. But for this to happen they must be of the opposite color. So a yellow enemy can bump into a yellow fellow without any problems, but let them bump into a red or blue enemy and they’ll both blow up. Same principle goes for the lasers, of course.
You will do all of this with the help of a little drone, who can be used to help defeat enemies. You can let him pick up powerups that can be found throughout the levels. You have two slots, a left and a right one, and if both slots are full then the powerup you pick up will replace one of them (depending on which trigger you pick it up with). Unfortunately it’s very unclear what the powerups exactly do without opening the proper menu. During my playthroughs I just started using them randomly, hoping at least one of them would be helpful. And even then it was hard to see what they would exactly do. Note that the game is still in Early Access, but this is definitely something that needs to be addressed; let it be a small tutorial, (paused) textbox or just a floating name/description above the powerups itself.
The destroyed enemies will usually leave credits for you to pick up that you can sometimes use to upgrade specific skills, but since the labyrinth is randomized this isn’t always possible (in my experience so far). You’ll also be able to find some sort of ‘perks’ from time to time that will give you things like extra health and increased speed (for your drone).
There are multiple endings per character, though, but unfortunately the endings just aren’t terribly interesting. I’m not saying they’re not worthy of your time, but if you’ve finished the game once you probably won’t play it again with that same character, unless you’re absolutely in love with her (/him?).
One other thing I’d like to mention is the camera, which shows everything from the top. But sometimes it’s hard to see where you’re standing or walking and since you can’t rotate the camera this can lead to frustration, since you’ll bump into enemies or lasers regularly. It’s also hard to see depth at times, especially when you have to jump onto boxes to get to higher places.
But despite the frustration it’s still a unique experience. At the moment it needs a lot of work in order for it to be brilliant, though, but then again, it’s still an Early Access game. Who knows what we’ll see in a few months time?
The audio is fine: it feels a little minimalist at the moment, but let’s just assume it’s still a work in progress and more music and effects will be patched in later. No real complaints here.
What isn’t fine is the performance, which is absolutely horrible. It’s not unplayable by any means, but there’s a bit of lag and the framerate fluctuates a lot. Something I did not expect to see in a game like this. Again, it’s a work in progress, but I’ve played tens of Early Access games that were way better optimized than this. It sometimes took over 2 minutes to load a level: that’s just insane.
The graphics themselves are simple. There’s not much style. Every area has a lot of metalic objects laying around and they don’t have any personality. I personally felt like every room was pretty much the same, with (some of) the objects moved to different places. There is a lack of variety in the level design and it’s a shame, because the setting is great (although unexplained) and there’s so much more room for added details and different locales.
I won’t sugarcoat it, but the length right now is just not worth the asking price. A playthrough will take about 1-2 hours, depending on your skill. You can repeat the game as many times as you want, but it won’t show you anything new once you finished it. I’m sure the game will be much longer by the time the final version releases, but right now I would recommend to wait for a sale or at least more content, unless you’re intrigued by the concept and want to experience it all for yourself.
A somewhat unique experience that could’ve benefited from some extra content and more polish. Right now it’s a good demo (not technically, though) that partially shows you what they hope to achieve eventually, but in my opinion it’s not worth the current price. Does that mean the game sucks? No, not at all: it’s just that the price is too high at this very moment.

There really isn't anything else like this game. It's different and fresh, especially considering how long ago it was made... way ahead of its time. It breaks a lot of conventions, sometimes in ways that frustrate people (slow pacing, unclear what to do, etc,) but does so with such confidence that you have to admire it.
The gist of it is that you have twelve days to identify and cure a plague in a weird, backwards town in the middle of nowhere. The town is brilliantly realized, with its own culture and local politics, and you'll come to know it and many of its inhabitants intimately by the end. Everyone has secrets and agendas, Twin Peaks-style, and you'll get caught up in them. Each day, the tension will ratchet up even further as the economy tanks, the looting begins, and worse. The atmosphere is very grim and slightly alien. It's noticeably a product of Russia. There are three "campaigns" as different characters which overlap, and you'll realize that things weren't what you thought in a previous playthrough. The story is legitimately brilliant, not just by video game standards, and it actually benefits from being a game rather than a book. It's not just a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t art experiment like so many walking simulators today - its gameplay has merit too.
Mechanically, Pathologic is a survival game before that was the cool thing to do. You'll always be short on some resource, trying to balance eating, sleeping and getting the day's tasks done. Time goes on no matter what you do, and it's possible to fail main story missions and have important people die. You'll be walking back and forth a lot, which can be tedious, but it's still tense because you're thinking of your next move, glancing at the clock and your physical needs, etc. There's scavenging and looting, combat with other looters and thugs, avoiding infected areas, trading with the creepy kids... Pathologic has a reputation for good story and bad gameplay, but I actually found it decently fun.
If any of this sounds intriguing to you, give it a try. It's a unique experience, to be sure.

I'm very much into pixel horror RPGs, and I've seen people play the original version of Misao.  This 'Definitive Edition' is an updated version that has revamped certain things and changed certain elements of the game in ways that I believe improve the game in some ways and maybe serve a little to its detriment in others.
The old trope of 'dead student sets curse on high school' is pretty well explored across games and anime, and Misao does fall into that cliche category, but at the same time, it has its charms.  It almost makes a joke out of how easy it is to unexpectedly meet your doom in this game - there are over 40 ways to die in Misao, most of them insta-death moments a result of either accidentally or purposely interacting with a trap, and some of them are completely ridiculous!  The death sound followed by the game over screen almost becomes a meme by the end of it...  it becomes a competition, like the Pokemon of deaths...  gotta find em all!  I won't lie though, it becomes infuriating if you're not familiar with all of the traps or you just forget, and then you make some good headway with the plot but then fall victim to a stupid trap and then have to reload way further back...  my advice is to QUICKSAVE ALL THE TIME.  Literally after you do every little thing.  There are so many opportunities to die that it seems almost unavoidable sometimes.  Save like a maniac and watch where you're going, what's around you and what you're touching.  Otherwise you'll be in for a world of hell.
For those that have played the original, there are a few changes that are a bit jarring or confusing.  They changed pretty much the whole layout of the school, so things weren't where I thought they were and I kept getting confused.  If you've never played the original though, you obviously won't have this issue.  Another big change was that in this Definitive Edition, you collect objects that are associated with Misao, whereas the original had you collecting her physical body parts.  I think the change took a little of the horror aspect out of the game, since you're picking up hair ties and jackets, which is a lot less disturbing than finding yourself holding your dead friend's rotting brain in your hands.  It kinda softens the creep factor a bit.  However, another change is the addition of choosing whether the protagonist is male or female, which actually has an effect on the events of the game and grants an additional two endings.  I do like that expansion.
I have one last criticism for Misao, and I feel bad for it, but while games are meant to be challenging, I actually got stuck and had to look up what I was meant to do next because there were so many things to interact with in the game, I couldn't be sure what I was meant to do in what order, and this is coming from someone who already knows the general outline of the game.  Perhaps I was just being stupid and you guys might find it no problem, but I play these kinds of games a lot so I'm usually used to their puzzles, but Misao had me a bit lost at times.  I do have to mention the fact that I believe Misao was the first game ever created by its developer as a test to see what they could make, so with that being said, we can give Misao the benefit of the doubt in that it was not intended as an incredible, polished and perfectly thought out game.  Everyone starts somewhere.
Despite these little drawbacks, what does redeem Misao is the way its plot comes to its end.  There are several endings you can reach, each one exploring one horrible conclusion after another.  If you achieve the 'true' end, you'll then activate an extra option on the main menu which then extends the game by a whole extra scenario that really fills in a lot of lore and goes further into the plot which you thought was over.  It's eye-opening stuff that makes you think, and does give you a satisfied feeling that going through the myriad insta-deaths and confusing puzzles was worth it.  The enjoyment of how the story ends definitely outweighs any of the aforementioned elements you may find annoying.  There are better games in this genre, but I'd still recommend you give Misao a play.  It comes from the same developer that created Mad Father, which is a really good game, so I'd recommend you try both.  Speaking of Mad Father...
I said this in my Mad Father review, so I'll keep it short and spoiler free, but basically...  If you play Mad Father before Misao, you're going to be very surprised and intrigued at some of the things that appear in Misao.  I won't tell you details, but playing Misao will give you extra insights into some of the biggest mysteries that remain unsolved in Mad Father...  there's something strange going on, I tell you.  Play Misao second and you'll know what I mean.

Original review
After thinking for a long time, I decided to review the game.
I played over 1000 hours (950Steam + easily 400+ mobile), level 1050 and playing GW in top brackets (1 to 3)
As many others pointed, this was a funny game before. For a brief explanation, the game is a match3 with some "RPG" details(you fight with cards/troops) also available in PS4, XOne and mobile devices, and this is the main cause of it's downhill. It's not crossplatform based, so there are "3" groups, PC+mobile, PS4 and XOne. As PC user you will never face anyone playing consoles and the same goes the other way.
Not so long before, the game had 2 builds, one for consoles and another for PC-mobile. The PC-mobile version always went a month or so ahead with the updates, which is nothing good or bad for this review. But the biggest issue is that the meta of the game was different in consoles. The algorythm that plays the AI was different.
Ok, so what's the problem? Is that big of an issue? Yes.
Console players were complaining MONTHS about the status of the metagame. Basically 95% of the people use the same setup and the AI will cheat you whatever you do. This didn't happen on PC-mobile. As per the devs, I cannot remember the exact words, was more user "friendly".
Solution? Implement the IA algorythm to consoles? NO, but the opposite.
Result? The game, that was somehow tactical and enjoyable passed away. Now you just need to pray for the AI to let you win. You will win a lot, but when it decides you need to lose, you'll lose.
As soon as that was implemented in PC, players started to ask to return the game to it's original status (don't touch what is working already), but they only "tweaked" the AI and some kind of troops, like exploders or gem creators.
The funniest statement was one saying something like: "We made the game fairer for the AI". So the AI may have fun? What about the loyal players?
Note that the game is F2P but includes transactions. Not microtransactions because the cheapest one is $5.
Good thing is that you can complete your collection playing, but Im just thinking for those that paid. Ok, I paid XXX in transactions for this game, because I liked it. Now I need to play a game that favours the AI heavily in some cases. Not good.
As I said, you still can win, but feels artificial. Doesn't matter you win or lose. It's not rewarding. Before you could say:" Damn, I could turn the game with that other move", or even control the table. Now it's random. Note that the game has a "PVP" mode. The term is on quotes because you always plays the AI. A team created by your opponent, but the AI itself. There is a lot of grinding for resources and that's not bad - it's free - but it's really frustrating when playing the so called Guild Wars.
You can join a Guild and then sign for Guild Wars. Guild Wars is somehow different because it forces you to play with an specific color of troops to maximize your points. At the start, that was nice because the community came up with new setups and original combinations of troops that didn't exist before. Then you return to the AI and just pray to win your Guild War games.
For someone that didn't play, this review will be probably useless until now, but veterans will be very familiar.
Now let's try to be useful for someone that looks for a new game:
Pros
- Free to play. While paying help, it is not mandatory
- Nice for collectioneers, lots of cards to get your hands on
- Different playstyles (when the AI lets you play in peace)
- Constant updates (new small content patches every Monday)
- The community is quite friendly for a F2P game
- You can resume your game in Android-IOS. Nice for traveling in public transport or short breaks.
Cons
- Hard learning curve. Game doesn't explain you anything and you may try to complete the quests. They're nearly impossible in the early game, which forces you to play PVP. Issue? Nobody tells you that - people will, but game not.
- Improving troops may be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ The really good stones takes a lot to get.
- The AI makes completely artificial combinations/cascades. You may be winning and lose in one turn from a single 3Match. It's not only unfair many times but with a poor design as it is very noticeable.
- Translations are bad. They don't have much grammar mistakes but the expressions are somehow...strange. This doesn't affect the gameplay at all
Im probably missing some things but lets resume:
Will I continue to play? Yes, every week there is something new so it will not hurt. But the rythm will be much slower
Do I recommend the game? No, because while the community in the forums give ideas (that the devs sometimes hear), the old status will not return. I don't think a new player may get the same fun (in hours) that we had. Considering how grindy is the game, and unfair on it's gameplay, someone might get addicted but the feeling will stop after 200-300 hours tops.

The recent bad reviews say it all.  Longtime players now hate this once decent and quite promising game.  The developers have abandoned innovation and even the semblance of quality for an unabashed money grab - stupid move for a free game.  The most recent update - 3.1 - has numerous bugs.  New troops are introduced but clearly not play tested and have their stats changed just a few days into their introduction.
You might think a game available on console, mobile and PC is a good thing but it plays differently on each and so skews the advantage to certain players.  The fairly recent move to the Unity engine stripped away most of the interesting graphics from before leaving the new version quite stale and boring to watch.
If all of the above isn’t bad enough, the game cheats.   I can't say this enough. The game cheats and - now and quite often - is buggy adding to more ways the game developers cheat you.
You will see lots of claims to this effect and many who wave it off claiming “recall bias” but I can attest to some serious flaws in the “randomness”.  Even though I most often win, it is frustrating to see the AI ignore clearly good moves and be so dependent on “lucky” gem drops and placements.   Cheating by the AI is a common shortcut made by poor programmers in many games but when it injects itself into player-vs-player action then it is just a turn off.  Combine this with the recent watering down of the reward system and you get a very clear picture of a group of seriously corrupt and amateurish game designers just trying to steal your money.

This is hands down the best RTS game that I have ever played. Large scale battles with thousands of units under the command of 2-8 players (12 on some custom made maps). Many maps ranging from 5 square kilometers, all the way up to 81 square kilometers - just shy of 50 square miles! - and yes, they really do feel that large.
Pros:
Playing alone is great; playing with friends is pure awesomeness.
There are tons of moving parts. If you go up close, you can see all the tank treads spinning, as well as multiple parts of legs making coreographed motions to create movement.
If a unit has more than one weapon, each weapon will by physically present on the unit, and each projectile will appear different.
If there is a unit that has a passive ability, for example shielding, or radar jamming, you will see that there is a physical part on the unit that creates this effect. What's better is that it will even resemble the actual building structures that use the same effects, to a certain degree.
One of my favorite examples of the above is the Cyrbran Tech 2 Tactical Missile Defense structure and the Cybran Tech 3 Siege Assault Bot. The T3 Bot has it's own personal Tactical Missile Defense system, and looking at the left shoulder will show a similar structure on it (in this case a shpere on a pillar). It even functions by shooting a small red laser at Tactical Missiles, returning them to sender!
Up to 8 teams with up to 1,000 units/structures per team, or up to 8,000 in one game, all at the same time. This unit cap can be increased to 2,000 per team and 16,000 in one game with the Lobby Enhancement Mod. Further more, custom made maps can also increase the number of players to a maximum of 12, making the maximum unit/structure count go to a whopping 24,000!
Many units, while similar to one another, can vary so wildyl in combat that they can serve completely different purposes.
One example is the UEF and Cybran battleships. The UEF  battleship's main armaments consist of 3 turrets with 3 cannons per turret. It fires all three cannons per turret at the same time, dealing massive damage. The Cybran battleship's main armaments consist of 2 turrets with 3 cannons per turret. However, it fires only one cannon per turret, resulting in much lower damage, in exchange for much higher rate of fire.
There is still quite a big following playing this game even today. You can find this community on the Forged Alliance Forever (FAF) servers. If I'm not mistaken, downloading the Forged Alliance Forever app will also give you the Sourian AI mod as well as the Lobby Enhancement Mod. Personally, I wouldn't skip these two mods for this game, especially the AI mod if you like to play against computers.
One of my absolute favorite features of FAF is the ability to play the campaign in co-op mode with friends. There are pletny of games being played every day from many players with ranging skill levels. You'll find tournaments and just for fun games alike. You'll also find a nice hand full of custom made maps you can download directly from the Vault in the FAF app.
Cons:
Sometimes they'll get stuck or confused trying to walk around one another, and it can be frustrating, though I find this generally not to be much of an issue.
You are never forced to try harder to win; you can simply just test yourself on how fast you can do it. You can simply take your time to build up your army before advancing to the next checkpoint.
Playing co-op completely changes the experience for me. I guess I just like playing with friends and family.
Older and lower tier CPUs simply cannot handle this game on it's maximum scale. Towards the end of matches, and especially longer ones against the computers, you will notice massive slow down in game play. The Sourian AI mod, while also more fun due to being more of a challenge, alleiviates a lot of this issue when compared to standar AI that was programmed into the game. The standard computers tend to build tons, and tons of units and leave them at the base for long periods of time, resulting in less fun, and more CPU usage which results in slower gameplay.
For example, an older rig I used with an AMD FX-6300 played the game just fine with 7 standard AIs, up until the end of the game where it was practically grinding to a halt. It was unplayably slow; roughly 3-4 real time seconds per game second. Now I'm using an Intel i7 4790k with the 7 Sourian AIs and I can easily play games well past the 2 hour mark with 0 slow down, with some head room to spare.
All in all, this game is an absolute blast to play! One of my favorite games that I own.

It's not often a spiritual sequel lives up to the glory of it's predecessor - Supreme Commander (And this expansion, Forged Alliance), is one of those rare gems.
With it's roots in the masterpiece that was Total Annihilation, Supreme Commander keeps that incredible feel of a glorious RTS with four well-balanced factions, unique units, each with their own checks and balances found among the other factions, mod compatibility, stunning graphics, intuitive but rewarding tech trees, and... The list just goes on.
When you fight in Supreme Commander, anything can happen. You've begun your siege against the enemy and have an array of missile units; but wait, the enemy has tactical missile defenses, rendering your forces useless! Luckily for you, your chosen battlefield was just in range of your navy, who begin pummeling the shore with their artillery... Until their airborne torpedo bombers are on your radar... Did you bring AA cruisers? Or do you have your own air force in waiting?
This is RTS at it's finest. As one who sunk countless hours into Total Annihilation as a child (and as an adult), this is one game that lives up to the greatness of it's origins, and is an absolute steal at $14.99. Give this one a try, you won't regret it.
And if you're into older games, want to try the predecessor to SupCom, with a soundtrack epicly composed by Jeremy Soule (you may know him from Skyrim, Dungeon Siege, or Guild Wars 2 to name a few), check out Total Annihilation.
Convert now, or fall forever! Join The Supreme Commander: Forged Alliance

They Breathe is extremely short, only about half an hour, but that is the perfect amount of time needed for the ideas to be expressed without the simplistic yet engaging gameplay becoming boring. You play a frog in a dark and twisted environment, battling for the small bubbles of oxygen against horrific creatures and also trying to save your fellow frogs from drowning. The game doesn't hold your hand at all and you have to discover how to deal with situations and enemies by observing the world around you, which makes for an interesting experience when gauging how to vanquish foes seeing as there is no combat system, which also makes escaping from enemies frenetic and fairly nerve-wracking. The game has a creepy and foreboding atmosphere coming from both the visual and sound design, and the gradual realisation of what's happening to your frog brethren and your surroundings as you swim deeper and deeper is fairly disturbing. For such a short and cheap game, well worth it.

Look, Far Cry 2 isn't for everyone. BUT, if you're willing to put up with it's few faults (mainly enemies respawning after you clear an area) Far Cry 2 is a gorgeous and immersive single player experience that allows you to 'play it your way' a lot more than most shooters. It also helps if you find it funny when things go sideways on you in the middle of a gunfight.
The best way to approach the game is to try doing stuff you'd do in a real situation - it's pleasantly surprising how often this works. :)
Tips: Learn how to navigate using your map (also, learn the map locations). Stealth works best in the dark of night. You don't have to take every mission you're offered - the story line will adjust itself to your schedule (mostly). Africa is the LAND of FREE CARS, so don't get too attached to your current ride. Always check the wind direction before starting a fire. ;)
Finally, DON'T just follow the roads-- this isn't a corridor shooter!
Also, you can set things on fire. :D

While I pride myself on being a pretty nerdy guy, I had never had any experience with Shadowrun in any of its incarnations. Now that I've played Dragonfall, I'm starting to regret that lack.\
This game is great. Not just for a Kickstarter. But genuinely great. The characters are rich and detailed, the dialogue is tight, the plot epic and the combat is challenging yet fun. In fact, I'd say that while I was playing Dragonfall, I caught myself thinking that I hadn't enjoyed an isometric RPG like this so much since Baldur's Gate 2.
So Shadowrun. For those of you that are unfamiliar, the world of Shadowrun is "fantasy cyberpunk" setting. If you're having trouble processing that, just imagine a usual vanilla fantasy world with humans elves, orks and dwarves. Magic poofs in every corner. Got it in your head? Now give the humans cybernetic implants, hook the elves up with sniper rifles, provide some rocket launchers for the orks and robotic drones for the dwarves. Add a souped up version of the internet (called the Matrix which is true VR you can deck into). Finally dip it all in post apocalyptic dystopia where the governments are mere puppets of the mega corps (which are, of course, run by immortal dragons). Everyone is tagged, tracked and monitored. Just mindless corp slaves. Sounds pretty cool, right? And it is!
You show up in this cavalcade of madness as a "Shdowrunner". See, unlike the rest of society you and those like you aren't owned body and soul by the corps (at least not to the same degree as most of society). That makes you valuable. That's because Megacorps can't go and declare full scale war on each other. It's bad for business. So what do they do? Corporate espionage, sabotage, extraction, data hacking and the occasional assassination. Of course, they can't use their own guys for that, it'd be too incriminating. What they need is a "deniable asset" namely, a Shadowrunner. A person living on the edge of society with no background, no history, no ties and most importantly, no connection to the Corps. Just looking to make a buck in a crappy world.
As Dragonfall begins, you have just hooked up with an old friend of yours in Berlin for a job. From there you'll explore an enclave of other refugees from society call the Kreuzbasar, help your team work through their problems (and they DO have some pretty heavy ones), do what you can to influence the world for good or ill, get caught up in so many conspiracies that you might need a spreadsheet to track them all and might have possibly sacrificed your body (and your humanity) for shiny cyber parts. By the end of the game, you'll have gone through a few plot twists and have had your share of surprises along the way.
Gameplay wise, it could best be described as if you took X-COM crossed it with an old school turn based RPG. Surprisingly enough, it works great. When out of combat, you and your squad are free to roam around the area (no need to take up action points). When enemies are detected you drop into X-COM style combat mode. You have 2 action points that you can use to move, fire weapons, cast spells or use other special abilities. Cover and deployment are vital as the AI will actively seek to flank you and has a fondness for chucking grenades. Some abilities will take up all your action points but are very powerful so you need to use them wisely. Other abilities allow you to fire off more rounds in one go, thus creating a veritable bullet storm, but drains your clip rapidly which forces you to reload more often.
The combat is deeply impacted by the class you choose in Dragonfall. All classes have some amazingly differing and complementary uses. The classes are naturally based around the Shadowrun universe, so if you want to be a frontline fighter you'd be a Street Samurai wielding a variety of guns, close combat weapons or both. Mages are still squishy and useful for buffing, AOE and provide vital support to your frontliners. Riggers use a variety of drones to do their fighting while Deckers slip into the cyber Matrix and can hijack enemy bots, cameras and gun turrets. As you level up you get to spend karma to improve your character. Where you spend karma not only impacts your combat effectiveness, but also what sorts of dialogue and actions you'll have access to. Your team doesn't spend karma but you can choose one of two skills each time they level.
Shadowrun: Dragonfall, has almost everything going for it. A few little quibbles exist, like sometimes your character moving instead of attacking and the lack of minimap. But those are minor and I'd say negligible for what you're getting. Epic story, great setting, memorable characters and really fun combat system all tie together to make this game a real gem. Hare Brained Schemes is currently working on a sequel call Shadowrun: Hong Kong, and if it's anything like Dragonfall, I'm getting it right off the bat.

It's more difficult for me to review good games, I feel, because I feel I have so little to say beyond "it's so good."
So, I'll start by saying a good thing in a negative way that actually means a good thing, but it will be written out as a negative.
This game has ruined my ability to play other pinball video games without seeing how bad they are. When I was a kid I played a ton of "Pinball Illusions." We had the shareware I think, or maybe it was the whole thing it's so hard to remember (that was, like, 20 years ago ya'll), and I remember really enjoying it quite a bit. Recently I found it again on GOG and boy does it not hold up. It wasn't the game I remember. I already knew the physics weren't there because I remember that, but the sounds aren't great, and there wasn't really much to the tables beyond hitting the ball and getting points. There is little to no nuance (unfortunately no pinball game has, or maybe can, replicate some pinball strategies from reality but unlike Pinball Arcade most pinball games have 0 strategy- even table bumps which only seem feasible in this).
The thing about really good pinball, beyond scores that really matter, is that you need to feel like you're accomplishing something. Even if it is in a very short amount of time (which really good pinball does). That moment when you've done everything you need to do to line up the shot to attempt the 1 billion point score in "Bride of Pinbot" is a real accomplishment and feels good when you do it again.
This game not only captures the look of real pinball tables (most of the greatest pinball tables of all time), this game captures the actual feel of a real pinball machine. Maybe not entirely- but as a digital substitute it is truly incredible how much this feels like you're playing the real thing.
I wish it had a few more tables (there are some licensed tables I don't think they'll ever be able to actually get the rights to), but overall I cannot say enough good things about this pinball simulation.
Also, I don't know if this is recent as I only really started noticing it within the last few months, but there are some cool options to turn down the lights in the room the table is in and turn the lights on the table up. They also added some light up pinballs which make it more feasible to play the "dark room" tables and it adds a lot to the game for me as some tables are best in the dark.
I do have some negatives to say here. While they have mostly ironed out all the bugs I care about (I play this in DX11 and other than occasional hiccups after patches, which usually get fixed very quickly, this game runs fine and they never take tables I own away like some other Pinball games that I do not recommend *cough*ZenTrashPinballFXTrash*cough*) I really hate that there is no way to play and see the entire table. When I play a real pinball table one of the things that I love is being able to see the back board while I play (because often tables do things with the back board). They float the score board just above the table in space, except tables where you can see the display right above the table (which is only a few tables) and I really wish I could just see the whole table sometimes because a lot of times so much happens up there, but I also understand why this is not ideal to implement so it really sucks. You also cannot implement the strategy of bumping a pinball tables plunger forward rather than pulling it which is a strategy you can use on a few real life tables but not here. I don't even know if that is possible in a simulation given subtle variances to bumping a plunger like that.
To go on from here would be to just get into Pinball as a hobby (tables that give billions of points easily are bad score board tables) so there just isn't more I can say. This is unequivocally the best pinball simulation around. Anyone who says otherwise is technically wrong (even if they enjoy another one, that doesn't mean that one is better- because it's not).

Pinball Arcade has serious problems as a pinball simulator, even compared to free options available.
First and foremost, the in-game physics are very strange and do not feel like real pinball at all. Flippers launch the ball at unreasonably high speeds across all boards, which trivializes most ramp shots while making closer shots suicide, as the ball loses all control and ricochets everywhere, often resulting in outlane drains. Many hole shots, especially ones where the ball must sink into the hole, are finicky. Furthermore, nudging is unreasonably powerful. Every single nudge has about 2-3 times the strength of a real pinball nudge, and can be done rapid-fire 3-5 times in a row while getting only one tilt warning at first, which would more than likely instantly tilt most real tables. Slam-tilting is borderline- if not outright-impossible. Some tables have even more severe issues. Black Knight 2000 allows you to blast balls outside of the play area and back into the plunger lane just by making a steep left shot, in the general direction of the 2-ball multiball plate. On the same board, some loop shots that would be successful on a real board will randomly hitch on the gate to the right of the W-I-N rollovers. Bride of Pinbot has extremely strange slingshot bumpers with hair-trigger activation on the entire inward surface of each, to the point where attempting a post pass will cause you to lose control of the ball instead, and even slowly rolling over the slingshots has the same effect. Tales of the Arabian Nights, the free board included with the game, has flippers that are not flush with the return lanes despite this being the case on the real board, as well as 99% of real pinball games in general. I have actually launched the ball outside of the board completely several times while playing No Good Gofers normally, and 2-3 times on Black Knight 2000. The physics issues render some boards almost unplayable, make some boards much harder than they should be, and others much easier.
Secondly, the engine's construction is overall very sloppy and is missing an unreasonable amount of basic quality-of-life features that any engine like this should. Bindings are an absolute nightmare, especially on controllers. For instance, attempting to bind the button assigned to "menu confirm" to a gameplay feature will immediately attempt to re-bind the button again, leaving you unable to, say, bind the A button on a 360 controller to anything unless you go and bind the menu confirm button to something else first. Another issue is that the pinball ROM's start button is completely unbindable. Normally not a problem because the start button on the UI will allow you to start a game, but in some games, the start button will not start a new game if activated during the game over prompt, such as on No Good Gofers. Attempting to press start on the UI here will kill the UI, but not start the game, rendering it unplayable without exiting the game from the pause menu, which effectively resets the ROM. Furthermore, I have crashed the entire engine multiple times with an "out of memory error" by simply selecting multiple (10-20) games in the main arcade menu and previewing their splash screens. The complete lack of ability to adjust lighting at all outside of the DirectX 11 version of the game is also unacceptable, leaving most boards effectively fullbright, with a couple of exceptions, making this even more unacceptable. Not to mention the DX11 version has an enormous amount of visual bugs related to important board indicators and lights that cripple gameplay anyway.
Third, the pay model is, quite frankly, completely unreasonable. I wouldn't have a lot of problem with paying $5 for a pinball table if the table and its physics were well-constructed, but that's not even my main issue.
My biggest problem is Pro Mode. Pro Mode costs $5 in addition to the table itself's cost and includes the following: ability to manually adjust the camera to look at the table while not playing the game, ability to access the operator mode in the game's ROM, a meter that shows how close the table is to tilting when nudged, ability to cheat and manually move the ball, and a short list of tips given from actual pinball pros on how to play the game.
For some context, there is no built-in camera control outside of 4 presets for normal play, a lock toggle that stops the camera from chasing the ball, and 3 plunger presets. On most boards, 2 and 3 are the only reasonably playable modes, with 3 resembling a normal pinball view when locked. However, the camera's position and rotation are arbitary on a per-board basis. Notably, Fish Tales is excessively hard to play even with setting 3, because it's still a low-board angle that you would only see if you were a child attempting to play a table without a barstool to prop you up. FT and other boards, such as Medieval Madness, have issues with the board itself being obscured by board elements with no camera angle that gives full visibility. The ability to choose the camera angles manually in any context without requiring paid DLC feels like a given. The fact that you have to modify the game's files in order to do so at all during gameplay is a joke. Especially if you wish to emulate the games on a virtual pinball table, which is much harder than it needs to be with this engine for this reason alone.
Not to mention, it's already slightly questionable to be selling the equivalent of ROM's for an emulator for money when the only part you actually made yourself, the board recreation, is of extremely poor quality. Especially when three of the four manufacturers featured in your game (Williams, Bally, Gottlieb) have been defunct for at least 15 years each, with Stern being the only one that still exists and responsible for only a small handful of the original boards, consisting of well below 10% of all boards in the game. Having the nerve to charge for access to the operator's menu, a normal function of the vast majority of pinball machines, even late 70's boards, if not earlier, is outright scummy.
The disgusting frosting on the sewage cake is that the DLC is not actually DLC at all. Regardless of which tables you own,
with the DLC only being a key that grants unrestricted play to the game. The trial version is the full game with a UI block that instantly ends the game if you score high enough on it, but lets you play again as you please otherwise.
As much as I hate to say it, after thoroughly giving this game a shot, I can't comfortably call it anything more than a scam. There are free, similar pinball games, such as Visual Pinball X, which do their job much better. Better physics simulation, ability to adjust those physics, ability to directly position camera as you please, actual lighting effects (adjustable at that) even on DX9 or DX10, ability to create custom tables, and completely legal if you happen to own the board to the associated ROM, assuming you're playing a classic table remake. Playing a custom table, of course, is 100% legal.
The fact that Farsight has the nerve to not only charge $5 for someone else's content, but also a remake of it that's so shoddy it may as well be a bootleg, as well as charging double for a small handful of basic QoL features or parts of the original ROM itself while structuring the whole thing as the Steam equivalent on-disc DLC anyway, wasting hideous amounts of hard drive space, is quite frankly despicable. If you're a pinball fan or looking to get into pinball, please look elsewhere for your own sake. There are alternatives, free and paid alike, that work much better and don't skimp on engine quality or try and charge you for basic functionality on content that they didn't even create.

Subaeria is an intriguing hybrid of RPG, puzzle game and arena "shooter" - only you don't shoot anything. Instead you happily trick robots into killing themselves on the environment, or each other.
Each region of the game is divided into a map of cubes, with each playthrough of the game shuffling the cubes into a different layout. Each cube is an arena. The doors are sealed, and you have to get rid of all the robots.
The game feels 2D, but does use the third dimension for some platforming action and mini-puzzles where power-ups are hidden in tricky places.
My gameplay video:
The robot killing is mainly stuff like positioning yourself so that when the robot fires its gun, the recoil sends it tumbling into a laser. Or getting in the middle of two buzzsaw robots and watching them plough into each other. It's great fun to achieve these things, especially when you first work it out and put the plan into operation. But sometimes you won't even do anything and discover that a robot has somehow killed itself!
Your droid companion helps you out by storing and deploying the power-ups you find. These include simple stuff such as one-shot healing, and more tactical stuff such as "make the targeted robot go a bit mad and hopefully spin into the nearest laser beam".
There's some plot to follow (not all in place yet in early access), which helps guide you between set points of the story - some cubes act as barriers to progression until you've, say, talked to a person hidden in a different cube.
So far in early access, you'll find the randomly allocated arenas get a bit too familiar as you do more runs, but each environment is lovingly crafted, with funny details everywhere. This is a well-thought-out world they've built here under the sea.
There's only a few types of killer robot in the game - once you know the strategies to kill them, the puzzle aspect is replaced purely by action. A few extra enviromental touches add more puzzle elements - pads that change the colour of lasers to allow you to destroy different robots, for instance - but so far it's not that complex.
It's a fun, absorbing game that's worth following as it goes through early access, but yes, there are a few quibbles. The droid is sometimes ungainly to control (using the right-hand joypad stick) and simply isn't that essential yet - it just slows down your deploying of power-ups rather than adds an extra gameplay dimension. The 3D doesn't play any real part in the puzzles, it's just there to add some tricky jumps for the most part. And the game isn't very well optimised yet, with some slow loading times.
Thanks to Studios Illogika for the preview copy.

The begging of the game was nice where it taught you how the game works, with a nice asthetic look but annoying, although soon after that mission ends the look of the game changes to what you're seeing the the trailers/screenshots, so that's a relief.

Alien Rage is a gory sci-fi FPS that advertises itself as an old school shooter but is far from it due to having a 2 weapon limit, regenerating health, linear level design, and checkpoints. The combat itself is visceral and the graphics are great. However, the enemies all have perfect accuracy and most of them have rocket launchers. The game has a "skill tree" and ridiculously enough, the further you get into the game, the easier it gets. Alien Rage starts off being infuriatingly hard forcing you to constantly hide behind cover praying that the next AOE blast from a rocket launcher wont kill you. By the time you're around 75% through the game, you can run and gun as you please thanks to the upgrades you receive. The game doesn't know whether it wants to be Call of Duty or Serious Sam.
The final upgrade makes your pistol 1 shot everything. Bosses take like 4 shots to go down.
This inverse difficulty is one of the most absurd design choices I've ever come across. If this was tweaked, this game would have been pretty decent.
Alien Rage is also full of bugs that warp you to checkpoints that are ahead of you. So when you respawn, you have the joy of fighting all the enemies you "skipped" as well as all the enemies ahead of you. The AI pretty much bum-rushes you the second they see you so have fun!

A rather good story presents the conflict over promethium, a very rare resource, that involves the humans and an alien race called Vorus. At first, the two races seem to get along and share a giant meteor where promethium was found in abundance, but later the Vorus decide they want it all for themselves. You play as a badass marine that is sent to wipe out the aliens and stop any mining operations on that meteor. Parts of the story are told later on with the help of audio logs that you can find as collectibles and a more sinister plan is unveiled half-way through the game.
Level design is liniar, made up mostly of corridors connecting rooms and larger spaces for the boss encounters. In general, the action takes place inside the meteor's mining facilities and structures, with very rare moments when you go outside and get to admire the great sci-fi scenery. There is a turret ride and another level where you get to shoot things from inside an alien mech. Except for these, you can roam freely between checkpoints without many cut-scenes to bother. I also found some minor bugs, but nothing game-breaking.
Gameplay is very fast because many enemies will rush on your position. Tactical play is not impossible, but most of the time it is a run and gun scenario. Killing aliens is rewarded with points and badges pop-up at the top of the screen for certain actions (double-kill, explosive-kill, etc.). There is also a perk system that will unlock bonuses once you scored enough points. Aliens come in different types, from fast flankers to heavy armour, so you need to adapt and use weapons from both races. Guns feel great as aliens tend to melt under fire. I favored the energy weapons, but there is a weapon suited for every situation. Boss battles are brutal and you can die very fast if you don't stay in cover. Learn the specific mechanic for each boss and strike at the right time to succeed.
A fun little mindless shooter

Absolutely spellbinding despite its flaws! Story, setting, and characters so far are very compelling, the barter economy and survival mechanics are interesting and extremely immersive, and while the graphics are dated, the art and design of the game world have been crafted with a lot of care and attention, and mesh well with the excellent, unusual soundtrack. The overall mood and tone are so good that I feel completely present and immersed in the narrative.
Some words of caution:
Stealth makes no sense. You can fire multiple rounds from a gun while standing right behind someone and they won't react so long as you're holding Crouch. They will if you shoot or stab THEM, but not somebody else right next to them. But 9 times out of 10 someone inside a building will notice you as soon as you enter the front door even if you were sneaking when you entered. I'd assume it was supposed to work that way, were it not for the OCCASIONAL success.
I go back and forth about the combat. It's very difficult and often avoidable, which I like, but the difficulty feels like it's caused by poor mechanics rather than a deliberate design choice. The timing feels off for your punches and knife swings, and guns (the revolver, at least) seem to suffer unreasonable accuracy drop-off across even rather short distances. I fired at someone about 15 feet away with a weapon in almost perfect condition and missed 3 times in a row. They were standing still and I had the reticle carefully trained on their head. I like that this makes fighting more than 1 or 2 people at once next to impossible and incentivizes looking for nonviolent solutions - the player-character is no super soldier, after all. But there are better ways to do it than super-awkward weapon handling.
THAT BEING SAID, the story and worldbuilding are so good that I've been happy to make peace with these shortcomings. Simply save very often to protect yourself from unfair outcomes and janky knife fights.
The game is heavily story-driven, so I will update this review with more complete impressions after I've finished at least one playthrough.

Pathologic is best described as an EXPERIENCE, rather than another game you have played. It has unique characteristics that help you realize that gaming can become something very different than a simple game you play to have fun.
Pathologic is not always fun. It may not be fun for most of it's part. It is undoubtedly tedious, hard, painfull and offers you huge doses of depression. However, it is uniquely realistic, innovative and deeply immersional. It becomes a personal bet, which determined players will decide to take to the very end.
Pathologic is, above all, ART.
You start by chosing one of the two characters of the game (the third becomes available after your first playthrough). Each of the players has it's own, unique walkthrough burdened by the hard choises he has to make. The gameplay is consisted of two different things, survival and unraveling the plot which merge together beautifully, after you get aquainted with the gameplay mechanics. The first slap on your face comes from the very beggining, where you have to get aquainted with the gameplay basics. Equipment, trading, combat, locations, nothing is explained to you. Considering it from a different aspect, this is not bad at all. It is hard but not unfair. You have just arrived in a remote town. As in real life, nothing will be explained to you by a walkthrough. You have to find out how things work on your very own. In real life, no-one will be there to help you out or tell you how things work. You will have to use your brain to find out that it is much easier and cheaper to get some nice things from children (ammo, meds etch), than buying them from the local stores. You have to use your brain and think "What do children like? What kind of things would tempt them into giving me the stuff they have randomly collected o the streets?" The same goes with every other aspect of the game. You have to figure everything on your own, just like in real life. Of course it is hard, and it will definitely be the cause of your early demise in your first playthroughs. Here, I have to warn you about something in order to get the most of this game. DO GET INFECTED by the Plague as early as possible in the game. Only then will you be able to get fully immersed into the universe of this game. Of course, all of the above mentioned things, will be the reason you will give up the game because it's too hard or/and because its not fun. But Pathologic is not always supposed to be fun.
Pathologic is supposed to tire you, make you scream, make you want to give up. You are in a town ravaged by a deadly form of plague and while you are trying to save it, everyone and everything is against you. Time is against you, the townsfolk is against you, the powers that be are against you. In many cases you will make wrong decisions, you will let people die, you will do things that will alter the course of the game and your final choises. In almost all of those cases you will not have the courage to load a previous save to change what you have done wrong. As the game advances, you will get more tired by the constant repetition, the endless walking and the fact that everyday hides new unpleasant surprises. You will get tired because time keeps running out and you have to struggle to complete your daily tasks while keeping yourself alive. As you reach Day 12 when the final resolution is given, you grow tired, all you want is for this nightmare to end.
That's why the game is unique. It is not just another adventure that involves making choises which have consequenses and cannot be taken back, like Life is Strange. It is not another harsh survival game where death is around every corner like The Long Dark. The game makes you wonder: Is it worth it? Is it worth my time? At the same time however, you come to think that you have already gone too far, that you already have invested so much time in it that you want to see it done. It sort of becomes a personal bet, a marathon which you are determined to make it to the end. Pathologic is the very first game that takes an impact on the player's resilience, which helps him to understand all the♥♥♥♥♥♥that the protagonist is going through. No other game has ever done that. We have all experienced games in which the protagonists question everything, that are being lied, are getting tired by their enormous effort, but never have those very feelings been gotten across the players so succesfully like Pathologic.
For a more comprehensive approach on the game, make sure you read this brilliant study on the game by Quintin Smith published on Rock, Paper, Shotgun’ .
