Since recent changes (notably 3.0) it's just no longer fun to play PvP and at end-game, there's (basically) only PvP. Even mid-game you will more than likely be doing 20 to 1 PvP to PvE.
MONEY GRAB
I used to love this game and recommend it to friends, but the most recent changes have me within a hair's breadth of quitting.
[I unfortunately just convinced one of my best friends to join and I hate to leave my guild and my friend in the dust.]
The main reason I haven't quit is because the devs ALWAYS make some kind of adjustment after customer feedback. It often takes 4-8 weeks, but they do it. Most games cannot say the same.
Now, those adjustments are not always full corrections, but at least they take steps.
In this case, it is unfortunately clear that they have drastically reduced the best--by FAR--in game currency (gems) and increased a dependence on other new currencies...which are easiest to purchase with gems.
So they doubled the importance of gems and cut the amount of weekly gems we receive in half. There's effectively no way to get extra gems other than through MICROTRANSACTIONS. (Or macro transactions.)
This team has never done anything like that before. Of course there have always been micro/macro transactions ranging from $5 to $50 but you never had to purchase those to keep up with new releases.
I personally did purchase many of these (I'm VIP 10, which means I spent a LOT on this game) but I never HAD to purchase them.
When you spend money, you get access to VIP chests which are the best chests in the game, forever. This is a great reward for voluntary paying customers...but those chests require gems, which the developers just cut in half.
And on top of that, other things now require gems...so we are probably looking at a 75% reduction in VIP chests.
With the new system it is very clear that they are trying for a money grab that is not optional for players who want to fully experience the game. That was obviously a business/financial/accounting decision (as opposed to a game design/coding one) and I don't see them reversing it, regardless of feedback.
GAMEPLAY
A lot has changed with how the game plays. Now gem cascades and mana earning have increased dramatically.
Generally speaking in this game you could beat the AI opponent 90-100% if you took your time and there was still a 75-90% chance even if you rushed.
In other words, this was a casual (standard) Match 3 game where you could enjoy yourself wasting some time, usually--but not always--winning. There was just enough of a challenge that you felt like you had to pay attention to win, but not CLOSE attention. A perfect phone game. Or something to play on Steam while you watch TV.
Now thanks to the mana explosion, you can lose a match in 2 or 3 turns. This primarily happens in Guild Wars, which is the ONLY time your matches win/loss matters. It's extremely frustrating. It's not fun and it's certainly not casual fun.
Also they've introduced improvements to the AI so now the AI is more competitive.
Overall this has increased the difficulty of matches and reduced the casual enjoyment (if not eliminated it entirely in some cases like Guild Wars).
It also obviously decreased the win rate.
And when you lose, it's not like you lost because you made a strategic mistake. That might be enjoyable, as it is with standard strategy games ranging from Hearthstone to Civilization and even to MOBAs and FPSs.
You lose because SOMETHING RANDOM HAPPENED and things blew up in your face.
I'm not talking about Roguelike emergent story telling randomness, I mean just pure randomness.
I cannot recommend this game.

Now that 3.1 has been out for a few weeks I'd like to provide some updates since my original review did contain a few points of uncertainty.
Dungeons have been adjusted to always drop Diamonds instead of having a 25%/25%/50% chance. The quantity of Diamonds has been adjusted so that you now get 20 per day and 70 on Sundays ("Diamond day" or "Lucky day").
The "Gem bounty" pack that gives Diamonds gives 20 per day and 80 on Sundays.
The amount of time needed to craft a Mythic using the Soulforge has been more accurately figured out.
If you buy the "Gem Bounty" pack for 50 Gems per day, and if your guild can complete rank 11 of each task every week for the Diamond reward, and if you religiously clear the Dungeon every day, you should be able to craft a Mythic troop every 8 weeks.
If you do all the above plus purchase the $5 "Daily Deal" pack, you will be able to craft a Mythic troop every 4 weeks.
If you don't buy the Daily Deal cash pack, and only buy the Gem Bounty on Sundays (where it gives you 80 Gems instead of the usual 20), that time frame increases to 10 weeks, but you gain back an extra 300 Gems per week to put toward VIP chests or anything else you wish to use them for. This amounts to 1200 Gems per month, or half of  VIP pull per month, that you save if you don't buy the daily Gem Bounty.
The publisher has decided to lessen the original Gem nerf and players can now earn 390 per week from the Blue task instead of 140. This is still a net loss of 200 per week from the original 590.
The devs have stated that Gems will not be returning to Legendary tasks because "allowing ungated numbers of Gems into the game harms the economy, especially with more gold freely available in 4X speed".
For the last couple of weeks, players' overall win rates have been dropping and the AI seems luckier than ever. My own personal win rate prior to 3.1 was usually between 89-92%. The week of 9/11/17, I finished with a 72% win rate. The start of the week of 9/18/17, I was at 71% after one day. I have managed to recover to around 85% using a team of event week troops, but changes to the AI behavior are still quite obvious. It's sufficiently broken that there are cases where giving the AI a single turn results in a loss. Getting the AI down to 1-2 troops seems to activate some kind of "AI luck" mechanism and the AI will repeatedly cascade for large amounts of mana.
3.1 broke the "Impervious" trait in two ways - Devour and Mana Burn now go through Impervious and still affect your troop. Krakens are now everywhere in the game. You can still use other anti-Devour traited troops (such as Dwarves with the Fortitude trait), but having a key trait like Impervious be broken in this way has resulted in a significant increase in the number of Kraken teams in both PVP and Guild Wars because a lot of popular invade teams include Impervious specifically.
It was finally posted yesterday that the fix to Impervious "will be released in a mini update within 14 days". This means a potential 5 weeks with a game-altering glitch before a fix will be released.
Still a solid thumbs down. Obvious pay-to-win direction with crafting due to the cash packs offering twice the progress of the Gem packs, and both being required if you want to be able to craft a Mythic per month. Game-wrecking bugs being left in the game far too long. Dawnbringer (a Mythic craft-only weapon) being almost unbeatable in Arenas when it comes up as an AI team.
Since my original review posted, the game's rating on Steam has dropped nearly 20%. It's obvious I'm not the only one who disapproves of the changes.
In conclusion...spend your money on something other than this game.

Three months ago I would have given this game a thumbs up. While I still play daily, and while I would still say it's a fun casual game, I would no longer encourage anyone to spend real money, and therefore need to give it a thumbs down overall.
Gems of War has been on a horrible downward spiral for the last couple months. Other posters have already given plenty of reasons why, but the patch that hit on August 30th pushed the game in a blatant pay-to-win direction.
Jewels and Diamonds were introduced as new currencies along with new a new 3-boss daily dungeon. Diamonds are rarer by an order of magnitude, and there are (currently**) only three ways to get them: a daily pack that costs 50 Gems and gives 20 Diamonds, 100 of that day's Jewel, 400 Shards, 250 Souls, and 4 runic traitstones; a daily pack that costs $4.99 USD and gives 50 Diamonds, 200 of that day's Jewel, 800 Shards, 500 Souls, and 3 Gem keys; and the three daily dungeon battles which have a 25%, 25%, and 50% chance respectively to reward 20 Diamonds for a win. The dungeon battles can only be won once.
**Since there are only six Jewel colors and one color is featured per day, the 7th day will supposedly be Diamond day each week. We haven't had a Diamond day yet so there is no knowledge about whether any Diamonds will be available as a guaranteed reward from the 3 dungeon battles, or how many the player will earn.
Compounding all of this is the fact that the rewards offered by guild tasks and legendary tasks have been reduced by 20% and 16% respectively, and the fact that "some" Gem rewards have been converted to Gem keys instead. The developers will not reveal what "some" means...is it 5%, 10%, 25%, 40%, 60%, or some other value?
It is worth note that as of this posting, no guild has reported receiving Gems from completing a Legendary Task. Previously, receiving a small amount of Gems was a somewhat regular occurrence.
In summary, a new Gem sink was added, Gem income nerfed to a stupid degree, and you're on a slot machine for Diamonds unless you either pay Gems or real money, with the sole exception possibly being the Diamond day each week, and even then, you can only complete the daily dungeon one time.
(Note: Gems are absurdly expensive in the shop. It costs the equivalent of $40 USD to buy enough gems to buy a pack of 50 Gem chests, and $130 USD to buy enough to buy a pack of 50 VIP chests. This is a gacha game; these prices are asinine given that you're not guaranteed to win anything useful from those chests.)
I decided a couple months ago to stop spending money in the game, and this reaffirms my decision. I'm VIP level 6, for reference.
I won't even get started on the other "adjustments" that give the AI ludicrous advantages in PVP. The player can make a single match-3, and the AI will proceed to make multiple matches while peppering the player with skulls. The developers have admitted to "tweaking" the mana gem spawning algorithm, and many players now consider troops that generate mana gems to be largely worthless because they tend to leave the board pre-populated with free turns for the AI. This has improved slightly over the last month, at least in my own experience, but the AI still has a very obvious advantage.
I still find the gameplay itself to be mostly enjoyable, HOWEVER, until some of the massive nerfs are undone or things are implemented to make them more fair to players again, I would not encourage anyone to spend real money on this game.

Despite what several other reviewers have stated, I wouldn’t consider ‘They Breathe’ to be a horror game.  There are some creepy elements that gradually unfold to reveal what’s really happening the deeper you dive.  But honestly, it is more of a game that makes you think.
Unfortunately for me, the “twist” in the game did not come as a surprise as I saw it almost immediately very early on.  However this did not prevent me from enjoying the game in the least bit.  The beauty of ‘They Breathe’ is in the presentation.  The game does not force any kind of a story on you but instead leads you on a journey to discover it for yourself.  There is the obvious discovery at the bottom of the sea, but it still leaves many unanswered questions that are up to each player to interpret for themselves.
The art style is simple and reminiscent of some illustrations you might find in a children’s storybook.  With the content being rather dark, it is both ironic and brilliant.  The soundtrack (consisting mostly of ambient sounds) is effective and the gameplay/controls are top-notch.
I purchased this game for $0.61 on sale.  And although you can beat this game in under 30 minutes, there is some replay value (especially for achievement hunters).  This is a nice little indie title that is well-designed and fun to play.  I would recommend this game for the short, simple experience that it is.

Siralim ties together the best traits of a ton of your favorite RPGs in a modern package. As you get deeper into the game, its complex systems will be revealed. You have a multitude of options from creatures, spells, artifacts, and more from which to customize your own playstyle.
The art and music in Siralim are extremely impressive for a very indie game like this. The game wasn't kickstarted- you can appreciate the effort the developer put in! If you like the boss music from Final Fantasy games, you'll also like it in Siralim.
I can't recommend this game enough- try it! You've probably spent much more on "AAA" titles that you enjoyed much less than you will enjoy Siralim!

An addictive, turn-based rpg that makes me remember the days of my childhood playing a Gameboy Advanced. If I received this game as a child back in 2001 it easily would've been one of my favourite games, competing with pokemon for my gametime on those long car-rides we used to love or hate.
As it stands today, though, the game APPEARS to be too simple. But then you dig deeper, you unlock some more creature tiers, you upgrade the blacksmith a bit more, you find your first nether orb. It then becomes apparent that this game is much deeper than you initially thought, and before you know it you've clocked up over a day of gametime.
You spend your time running through simple, randomly generated levels, to defeat enemies, gather loot, and get resources. The combat itself is simple, you use your creatures attack, defend, and taunt your enemy's creatures, all the while deciding whether you should extract a creature (think of it like throwing a pokeball, kinda), or if the fight goes south, flee.
The levels can be completed in between 5-15 minutes. Where you are then challenged by the choice of whether you should go down to the next level, or head back to your Castle.
The game has a progression system similar to a roguelite. After you head back to your castle you spend the resources you've gathered on new creatures, gear, and castle upgrades. All of this to improve your ability to take on greater challenges.
this game is an iceberg. Deceptively simple and small on the surface but a behemoth once you dive deeper. Well worth the 10 dollars, but if you're still not sure there is a demo available on their website.

Shadowrun: Dragonfall improves in its predecessor in every way. Better story, better writing, better interface, better character and skill progression.
It's like like a well written choose-your-own adventure book, with a slightly simpler X-Com style combat system. Every mission is a new environment to explore, and is filled with a narrative text that let's your imagination build on top of the gloomy magic-tech-future that the game's artists have hand painted.
On top of the rich world, every character has a colorful backstory worth exploring. After a hard fought mission, the first thing I would look forward to was going back to the central town, and talking to my team members and the city citizens to learn more about their characters.
Although not as deep a combat system as X-Com, it scratches all the right itches for giving a rewarding, strategy combat experience. I recommend playing on Hard mode, as Normal mode is more of a casual experience. Whichever you choose, enemies intelligently use cover, toss grenades at bunched up teammates, and use their abilities to maximum effectiveness. I had to restart maybe 2 or 3 fights on Hard-Mode throughout the game, but had so many well won victories to show for my effort, I didn't mind the occasional mulligan.
Shadowrun: Dragonfall is the perfect weekend killer, and will tempt you to come back for a second playthrough, just to see how it all turns out. Highly recommended.

Far Cry 2 is a strange game, containing both soaring heights and unfortunate lows for the series.
The pervasive criticism of Far Cry 2 is the travel system and the respawning outposts - an annoying combination that makes a good portion of the game feel like repetitive, tedious filler. This is a very valid criticism in my opinion.
On the other hand, Far Cry 2 has many unique gameplay elements that are not seen in the later titles, or indeed in other open world shooters on the whole. Features and mechanics such as the buddy system, the enemy AI and dynamic elements that can occur during combat really make this title stand apart from the rest.
Some of these gameplay elements include:
-Alternate ways to complete missions that are significantly different, including new objectives and locations. Your buddy will call you up after you are presented with each story mission and give you the alternate option, should you choose it.
-Your buddy can dynamically rescue you during combat when you lose all your health, or you can revive a mortally wounded buddy during certain missions. If you have no more meds, you can either leave them to bleed out, or use your sidearm to finish them.
-Enemies can be wounded, and will fire their pistols at your from the ground if you don't finish them. They will bleed out eventually. Their allies can also pick them up and carry them to safety, and then patch them up so they can fight again. When a wounded enemy is on the ground, you can use the machete to perform a killing thrust with a unique animation.
-Interactive and responsive world items. Leaves and plants dynamically move when you pass through them, much more than current Far Cry titles. Grenade explosions are much stronger and cause more physics reactions. The first use of fire propagation in the the series. And my favorite - ammo crates can be set off by explosives, spraying live rounds everywhere and randomly killing everyone in the vicinity.
-Dynamic hinderances during combat, such as malaria attacks that require you to take a pill, and weapon jams when you have been using a weapon for too long, or were forced to pick up a shoddy replacement off the ground. Many people complained about these features, but personally I felt they added to the tension and I was never killed because of them.
In addition to all these great systems, I personally think that the general gunplay in Far Cry 2 is by far the best in the series. Weapons have a feeling of weight to them - there is substantial recoil and sway, leading to more challenging gameplay and an authentic feel. The firing sounds and reload animations are also superior to the later games in my opinion. Each gun is more distinct.
Another major benefit of Far Cry 2 is the the atmosphere. The setting and story are relentlessly harsh. There is a darkness in this game that the others never come close to, mostly because they weren't trying to. The difficulty of the game combined with the fact that your character is a hardened mercenary in a war-torn nation creates a sense of desparation and isolation. Your character, whichever one you choose, is an objectively bad person that is killing for money, profiting off the the destruction of a country and its people.
Far Cry 2 is a deeply flawed game, but it also has several redeeming factors that aren't seen in other titles. If you are looking for a gritty, realistic and challenging FPS, this is one of the better options out there.

When I saw this game on Steam I felt it was going to be a nice purchase, but when I saw some reviews and metacritic’s final score, I thought something must be wrong, this game can’t be that bad to get a score of 52, so I bought it on a sale just to be sure I would not spend that much money on a possible bad game… Oh, boy… this game is a mixed bag and it tends to have more cons that pros in the end.
The storyline is straightforward and simple, there are not complicated background stories nor characters and to be honest, its story is not the main protagonist here, it is just bland and lack originality. In the far future Humanity has reached the stars in search of new energies, earth’s natural resources are almost depleted and we need a solution, it happens we found an asteroid full of some new energy called Promethium, but we are not the only ones, another species called Vorus has also reached this asteroid in search of this new energy, so both races start jointly to exploit the mineral, everything was good for a time until the Vorus turn on the human miners and wipe them out. So Jack, our main protagonist, is sent to investigate the situation, kill the Vorus and destroy the facility.
The game is just a linear, first person shooter with zero variation, kill all enemies, go to the next stage, kill all enemies again, find mini-boss or first boss, end stage, next. Most levels look the same, they are mostly a corridor, except for when you reach certain larger areas to find enemies coming from multiple points. According to the game info on Steam, gameplay offers a cover mechanics to help you stand your ground over waves and waves of enemies, though, this apparently does not work or simply doesn’t exist, anyway, the gameplay is difficult, especially on hard and insane difficulties, so be prepare to die many times. Alien Rage has a scoring system, depending on the way you kill your enemies you are rewarded with medals, multi kills and blast master badges, among many others.
Enemies are not that varied, but they are fast and hard to kill at times, or just spawn in multiple waves over and over again, they also tend to blend with the stage’s environment, making it hard to see sometimes, in other occasions, they will just get you from behind or simply flank you, this tends to happen when you are being crowded, enemies also count with spawn options they have scattered all over the place. Weapons are not that varied either, and some of them are just useless or slow to use because you will usually have long distance fights by trying to use the “cover system” to your advantage, fortunately the secondary firing option of some weapons cause a lot damage and give you a break from the multiple enemies waves. Overall, gameplay is monotonous and it doesn’t offer more than what you can see on a gameplay or in-game images. So don’t expect anything out of the ordinary, Alien Rage is a simple, dull FPS.
Alien Rage uses Unreal Engine 3, it looks good in game, flashy and shiny, some aspects of the limited access we have to the level’s environments are detailed, while some others show some muddy graphics, at times we encounter multiple layers of textures not loading properly, as most levels look the same and the lack of variations is patent, there is not much to add here, Unreal Engine shows off at key moments if we consider the amount of explosions that look great, the chaos we can create demonstrate the power of the engine regarding physics.
The in game sounds and effects are decent, not groundbreaking, but they do their job, explosions and weapon effect sound exactly as you may expect from a game like this, nothing new, but they fit the concept here.
As for the voice acting, yeah, they are ok, main protagonist sounds always overly heroic and he tends to sound like a typical pseudo action man, annoying at times, yes, but I guess the voice acting fits the concept as well, the other two main acting voices exist only to give you instructions and deliver a quota of relief, with bad jokes and some sort of internal issue between them, they are just there doing their job with minor help.
Where to begin? Alien Rage is filled with gameplay issues and graphical problems, starting with the mechanics of the game, there is no cover system to begin with, extremely necessary for a game that is relentless with many waves of enemies, AI is totally ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, Vorus just run towards you shooting nonstop waiting to be killed, The main character is very limited in movement, he is slow, big and clunky, sometimes during combat, the same stage is a total mess with explosions, bullets from every direction while you desperately look for a decent cover while trying to see where fire is coming from, multiple enemies that blend with the environment make the gameplay a continuous disaster regarding mechanics, I rather wait in a corner for the enemies to come to me so I can kill them one by one.
Graphical problems are constant here, textures not loading, muddy details, monotonous levels and stages, overly glossy elements invisible walls, of course there are invisible walls, the game is linear as hell, so you have a certain pattern to follow. Usually the textures don’t load properly every time you enter a new level or when you load a last save, showing the engine’s known issues.
Checkpoints are terrible, they constantly let you in the middle of enemy fire, you die, you load last save and again, multiple enemies surround you so you die again unless you act quickly enough to find some corner where to hide and recover or use the “cover system” to save your skin, again, the game has a terrible balance between you and your enemies, it is hard, I understand the crying over the difficulty is not an option, but handicapping you is also a problem when it comes to running or jumping, the latter is nonexistent, why the jumping mechanics are so messed up? I don’t really know, so you better bind the default space bar to another more functional action.
When it comes to boss battles, things are equally terrible, most of them are just bullet sponges that do a lot of damage and the lack of a proper cover system will only give you one option, which is running from one place to another trying to avoid enemy fire or whatever the attack is, they have weak spots so you have chances to beat them, running out of ammo will be always present in those moments, so you better shoot correctly. Some bosses will glitch-out at times, it happened in my play through a couple of times, these battles are not that challenging, but they tend to be monotonous and boring.
Alien Rage is a terrible decent game, it doesn’t offer original ideas or storyline, nor is any character worth remembering, which are not that many anyway, but if you want a challenge, a difficult one that will lead you to rage, this game is for you, other than that, you will be disappointed since the beginning. In my opinion, this game barely makes it to get a thumbs up, but as there is no neutral option between good and bad, I tried to be explicit regarding the bad side of it.

This review is hot off the heels of my second 100% playthrough. I cannot recommend this game enough!
Music: The soundtrack in this game is absolutely incredible. You will definitely remember many of these tunes well after you've finished playing the game. Most of the tunes fit their respective areas quite nicely and don't feel out of place.
Story: Perhaps the weakest point, but by no means terrible. You are basically a panda trying to save his village and the princess. Along the way you will meet many friends with some funny dialogue, but ultimately you don't get any real attachment to the characters. That said, if you follow similar tastes to myself, this point does not bother you so much, and you are really here for the gameplay.
Gameplay: This is the greatest aspect of game. The game follows what most call a Metroidvania style exploration, which because of this game I have grown to love. Movement feels extremely smooth and fast and becomes incredibly fun to master once you learn more skills. Learning how your foes will attack and adjusting your fighting style to the situation feels very rewarding (especially on the hardest difficulty, you can really get a bite taken out of your health if you don't adapt!).
The game allows you to distribute stat points earned from level-ups, making it possible to do multiple runs of the game trying a different primary fighting style. You can go all out offensive, or try to be defensive, or a fine mix of both, it's all up to you! One thing to note is you cannot fill in every skill, so I definitely recommend focusing on a single style of fighting.
There is also a weapon/armor upgrade system based on finding a certain item throughout the world. By collecting enough of this item, you may spend it to upgrade one of your two weapons or your armor. Again, this adds some replayability as you can choose to focus your level ups on damage and then focus your collectable upgrades on armor, or maybe go all out damage on the weapon.
Difficulty: The game presents you with multiple difficulty options, which is fantastic for all types of players. If you want a decently hard game, this game delivers. If you want a nice casual run through the game to explore the mechanics, you can absolutely do that as well and not be so punished for taking a hit.
Almost every run of this game (including my very first run) was done on the hardest difficulty. I absolutely recommend this, as being able to master this game feels so rewarding. Your decisions and quick reflexes make a huge difference in the outcome of your battles, ESPECIALLY the boss battles. These are some of the most intense fights that may make you want to slam your controller to the ground, but ultimately you realize that there is so much you can do to improve your chances next time you attempt. When you finally triumph, it feels so satisfying.
Final thoughts: TL:DR I consider this game to be one of my favorite games of all time, and I abolutely recommend purchasing it. You have no reason not too, just look at this price! $3.00 for one of my favorite games of all time? Heck yes!

In my opinion Pathologic is an amazing game, probably even in my top 5 of all time. That being said, it is definitely a cult classic and almost avant garde in design so it is not for everyone. If you can't handle walking simulator this game is certainly not for you.
You set out as one of three characters in a town infected by a deadly plague that nobody knows how to cure. Pathologic is not a mechanical game but focuses more on the relationships between characters in the town. A lot of time will be spent in the game just reading what people have to say to you, and then reading again between the lines.
One of Pathologic's strongest and most interesting features is the fully fleshed out culture. Once you are a few hours into the game, you will know each of the three families in charge of the town, what family members they have, rules for children in the town, what kind of people can mend your clothes vs your weapons, and so much more. Even trading in the game is different between shopkeepers, guards, and children so you have to know who values what and why.
The survival aspect of Pathologic hangs in a delicate balance all game. In most games you have one health bar, occasionally a game will spice things up and give you two. But Pathologic gives you like five. You can die from being shot, from being infected, from hunger, from sleep deprivation, or from getting a bad reputation and being arrested. I think I covered them all. The point is, decisions in game typically try and play with the balance you try so desperately to keep.
Pathologic makes the player think for themselves in order to be rewarded. The envelopment the game offers is second to none if you are willing to dive in.

I guess after spending over 1,100 hours in this game I ought to say something about it. Gems of War gave me a lot of fun for a long time, while giving me an equal amount of frustration.
When I first started playing, this was pretty much a straight-up match-three with minor RPG elements. It was really fun and intuitive, and the learning curve was pretty forgiving. My spouse also played, and we'd talk about Gems and make Gems-related jokes to each other all the time.
Then came all the never-ending, ever more complex and obtuse new mechanics. I'm by no means opposed to games changing up their systems, but a year after I first picked up this game it had pretty much become an entirely different one. That in and of itself isn't necessarily bad, but the way it happened broke me. Trying to keep up with the rapid fire additions to battle and troop mechanics, and the ridiculous amount of micromanagement that required,
, got so old so fast. Keeping my PvP rank high enough to earn all the glory rewards every week got old, too. Old and harrowing.
I kept up with the near-constant stream of massively game-changing updates for over a year, which was ♥♥♥♥ing exhausting. I finally gave up around the time they nerfed the Centaur's true damage ability, because I was just too damn tired to build yet another team for yet another completely different meta. Maybe it's just me not having the patience anymore for intense micromanagement and building up new teams over and over. I don't know. What I do know is that uninstalling the game from my computer and tablet was a relief.
Sorry, Gems. We had a good run.

This is a pretty weird, and extremely smart, rogue-like. OK... Mixed feelings about this game but mostly negative. The game has great atmosphere and is quite creepy. You want to know what will happen next, but the progress is so painfully slow that I had to eventually abandon the game. You need to do endless walking (how about a teleportation option? that would make things so much easier), using a map that is scarcely labelled, search in trashcans for items to use and trade, and make sure that your level of hunger, disease and other stats do not reach dangerous levels. The progress is divided in "days" and each day you need to do the same routine of searching the same areas in case something new has happened (especially for side quests). When a character has nothing new to say to you, you can respond by saying something like "Sorry to have bothered you" or "Just doing the rounds", which shows that the game expects you to do the same repetitive routine again and again. The combat is ridiculous and the dialogues so cryptic that make no sense. I guess that if you have a huge amount of time to waste, then it is worth trying this game for its atmosphere, but for all other players who value their time, it is not recommended.

The Depths of Tolagal has a forgettable name and is not the prettiest game on te block, but it is surprisingly engaging and well designed. It's almost more of a turn-based-combat-puzzle generator - like Hoplite with which it was rightly compare in RPS article - than a roguelike. The combat turns are divided in a small number of action points, so it's all about planning and positioning. With fast moving enemies it might mean trying to get as many hits in as possible (and maybe knocking them back or putting a shield up, or hiding behind a door - the options are there, and this is where it differs from Hoplite and puzzle games), while battles with slow enemies are more like a war of attrition... unless you make a mistake and allow yourself to be ambushed by some goblins.
Each enemy has a gimmick to keep things fresh: trolls can charge at you if you're in a straight line, cultists are invisible, only leaving a trail of smoke behind them, others have shields that they can raise meaning you have to hack through them. There are hardly any popcorn enemies, and you have to be thinking in almost every battle - except the first couple of levels, which are hard to mess up after you've played through them a couple of times, and can become boring in repeated playthroughs.
The only other criticism I can think of at this point (I've played some more in offline mode, but admittedly not enough yet) is the lack of variety. There are no classes, and so far I've come across a grand total of four different weapons, a shield and a ring of regeneration. Still, the game keeps it fresh by offering different attributes for the items that change the way you use them considerably. Also, there are no character stats and each new level comes with a choice of a passive skill that will also influence the whole run considerably - and there are a lot of them, although you're only given two random ones in each levelup to choose one from.
The game scratches a similar itch to Hoplite, and it does its thing very well. The combat system is well done, and the permutations of different item/skill combinations keep it from going stale quickly, but still I hope the game grows in variety some more.

I really want to recommend this game, but unfortunately I cannot mainly due to the games lack of depth and very short length.  Sure the game is fun enough, and is tough like a roguelike should be, but it is ultimately very unsatisfying when you compare it to the excellent Tales Of Majeyal.  Here are the pros and cons...
Pros:
1.  I enjoyed the games tactical approach to defeating enemies.  The game makes you think when you are in tight spots.
2.  Overall combat is fun.
3.  I thought the music was pretty decent.
Cons:
1.  No classes.  For me this means 0 replayability once the game is completed.
2.  You cannot attack enemies diagonally in melee combat.
3.  When you level up skills/traits are randomly generated.  You could end up having no choice but to chose a skill that is essentially a negative skill.  In my opinion this is a cheap way to make the game more difficult.
4.  The game is too short.  Basically 4 hours to complete the main game.
5.  The price.  I don't mind spending money on a game at all but at this is more expensive than Tales Of Majeyal and has a fraction of the content.
I know that I have mentioned TOME a few times in my review, but I sunk in over 70 hours into that game and have still not completed it yet.  The Depth Of Tolagal is a minor distraction for a few hours, but simply does not have that depth that I am looking for.
So, if you are looking for a more "simplistic" roguelike that you can play for a few hours of fun then I would recommend it...if you want a rich, deep experience look elsewhere.

What it lacks in replayability, it makes up for with a solid tone and a fun experience. Misao: Definitive Edition does nothing to provoke the player with intricate gameplay tricks or groundbreaking premises; its true merit lies within the foundation of good ol' fashioned scares and gory goodness. To some, it's an immediate turn-off, as without any shred of creativity, the game could be just another title to those experienced with the horror genre. For what it's worth, outside the expectations of those who revel in its spooky genre, the game does offer eventful fun for those who aren't too careful about where they travel. Better yet, the game can be completed within an hour, so it'd be a nice atmospheric piece to play for Halloween!
+ A well-performing snack for horror fans
+ Solid atmosphere
+ Intriguing end-game content
- Little to no replayability
- Can be too vague with progression
- Sound effects are too cheesy

A round of applause for the developers here! They succeeded in creating a tough as nails rougelike that challenges you measure ever step and I do mean EVERY step but (for the most part) only punished the clumsy or the uninformed. I have died several times by virtue of approaching a hallway and accidentally alerting an extra orc or two and promptly getting my teeth kicked in. I have come to realization that the tactical aspect of the game is actually a good bit deeper than rpg aspect of it. Level progression unlocks triats as opposed to a solid stat boost across the board. Many of the traits simply open up intersting opportunties which require you to adjust your playstyle in order to gain an advantage. So overall I would say this game is TACTICAL rougelike more than a classic rougelike rpg.
The game is starting to feel a little bland (obviously graphically its retro over modern) in terms of variety. Given a good deal of this has been the difficulty that keeps sending me back to the starting stages and the same enemies. Additionally some of the traits (at least early on) are clearly superiour to the others. In a very difficult game that does not hold your hand but allows you progress consistently if you think and learn from your mistakes (for the next time) this a minor balancing issues. They were kind of enough to allow you play through without the permadeath if you buy the game and decide you'll never get through it with only one life (I may eventually give up and fall into this category myself).
I would recommend this game to just about anyone who likes tactical combat games. Fans of the original X-Com series and Desktop Dungeons (one of my all-time favorites) are going to be disappointed they did not hit add to cart sooner. For anyone else I would say it is worth a go if your intersted in the tactical games.
My current feeling (i'm writing this after only about 10 hours to help out people wavering on buying it or not) on this title is that it has definetly been fun but has not quite driven me to the maniac gaming addict level of worship and adolation I usually bestow to games I wind up putting in my top 50. From a value standpoint I would say its definetly worth the money.

Quick Summary: Fast paced First Person Shooter with regenerating health (so you can charge in like a badass) and semi destructible environments. You can choose to replay chapters as you want in order to get higher scores and unlock “perks” which are passive bonuses such as increased health or damage.
You play a kind of space marine sent in alone to investigate what has happened on the asteroid Deimos, a “promethium” mine. Deimos happens to be the site of first contact with an alien race called the Vorus who are also very interested in the promethium. Everything was going well for a long time, so a sudden Vorus attack caught everyone off guard, and it’s up to you and your 2 teammates (a computer AI and a shuttle pilot) to get to the bottom of it while blasting the hordes of Vorus guarding the mines.
I mentioned that you have teammates on your mission, but they don’t actually help you in the game. Instead they serve as support, telling you which direction to go and giving you someone to talk to/banter with throughout the 8 hour game. There are 3 difficulties to choose from: Challenging, Hard, and Brutal. I chose Hard as my first runthrough, thinking that it was the equivalent of “medium” but I was wrong. Hard mode can be extremely difficult because you have no clear “advantage” over your enemies. They have access to the same guns you do, including the “secondary attack” of each weapon, which most of the time is some kind of underslung grenade/rocket launcher that can kill you in one shot (and they use them A LOT). The first couple of bosses are especially frustrating because they use chainguns that can tear apart whatever you’re taking cover behind (not giving you a chance to regenerate). The later bosses are actually much easier to beat (maybe because I unlocked some decent perks by then).
As for the weapon variety, there’s actually quite a bit to choose from, and they all have a different secondary attack. Personally I found the Vorus guns to be more useful since they don’t need to reload (just cool off once in a while). The player “perks” that I mentioned earlier are unlocked in tiers as you progress through the game, earning as many points as possible with special kill types (headshots, environmental kills, melee streaks, etc). I suspect you earn points faster on Hard difficulty because I unlocked all tiers of perks about halfway through the game. You can only equip 3 at one time though, so I focused on defensive perks. You really don’t have a lot of life on Hard difficulty.
Pros:
+Nice graphics and action packed gameplay. Like Halo or any other modern shooter for that matter, you can pick up just about any gun dropped by fallen enemies and just run/gun through the levels. No need to play it too safe scrounging for ammo or health kits (your health regens automatically).
+The game’s plot is told in “audio logs” that you find throughout the game and adds some nice backstory. The situation on Deimos really isn’t what it seems from first glance.
+There are a number of giant alien bosses to fight with your arsenal of guns.
Cons:
-Multiplayer is dead. It’s not too surprising since this isn’t a very well-known game and there’s no co-op gameplay.
-The Steam achievements are bugged. Some of them refuse to unlock and may require multiple playthroughs. For example, I’ve played through the game twice and haven’t gotten the “find every weapon” achievement even though I’ve unlocked the “kill an enemy with every weapon” achievement pretty early.
Overall, I’d say Alien Rage is closer in gameplay to Bulletstorm than anything else, but without the constant vulgarity, and with much less humor.

Although there are a few strange graphical glitches and one or two spelling errors, I expect these are pretty easy to fix and judging by the active dev involvement in the community hub, I'm sure these kinks will be ironed out very quickly.

There are loads of good tower defense games on steam but this one (and its predecessor, Defense Grid) take the tower defense genre and polish it to a diamond shine.

First one I played alot more than average.   Bought it one different platforms, played through more than once, thought about how to better beat the maps in my off time.
I didn't have any of that with this game, felt like a big let down.  It's close enough to part one, maybe it just didn't "advance the series" enough for me.

Short version: Very bad interface and mechanics.
Long version: DG2's user interface is in several ways inferior to a lot of the free TD games you'll find on places like Kongregate.
Let's start with the cursor lock. DG2's normal view 1) locks your cursor to the center of the screen, moving the play area around it, instead of moving the cursor, and 2) locks that movement to the "field", not letting you mouseover anything but the current board for tooltips or information.
Also there aren't any tooltips.
When you click a tower, then, your cursor is locked to the "Select upgrade" area of the tower. A tower is listed as having Abilities, but these abilities are displayed only as nameless icons outside the upgrade area, so you can't mouseover to see what they do.
There is very little concrete information offered to the player. The Next Wave indicator has only vague outlines hinting at 'small aliens' and 'big aliens'. You can't mouse over the waves for info or tooltips, and you can't mouse over the aliens on the board either.
Tower stats aren't given with any sort of numbers, but with sliding bars of vagueness:
Damage --O----
Rate of fire ---O---
Range -----O-
There's no indication of whether late-wave small aliens have more hit points than early-wave small aliens, or if they're just more numerous.
There's no "Send next wave now" button, either, to take advantage of the various AOE effects one has available.
Go play something like Gemcraft or Monkey Bloons TD instead if you want a good tower defense.

is an action-packed fast-paced FPS. This game went under the radar for me.I bought it recently, and I’m very glad I did.
Despite the corny jokes, thin story and character development, Alien Rage represents a throwback to the roots of first person shooters. It stands on its own and proves that you don’t need a great plot to justify the fact that you’re just shooting aliens in the face.
That said, the story intrigued me at first. In a time where Earth is facing an energy and financial crysis, humankind discovers a resource called Promethium, which is able to produce enormous amounts of energy. Shortly after settling down and beginning mining operations, an alien race appears. Despite the initial cooperation between the two, things go south real fast. Thus, it is your job to make sure that the enemy can’t get their hands on this precious resource. What better way is there to do that than killing and blowing up everything in that forsaken asteroid?
The game is ridiculously hard on maximum difficulty, so only consider playing on it if you’re a masochist or a godlike player. I played on  Hard setting until the very last boss. There I changed to Normal because it was too frustrating after dying many times.
Alien Rage - Unlimited is an hectic and frantic shooter, and it was refreshing. It is one of those games that stands out in an era where most FPS take place in a modern or near future setting. The gunplay is extremely satisfying and you’re able to pick between sticking with human or alien weapons. Despite the fact that what you mostly do is gun down aliens, there are some memorable moments, such as boss fights and when your character starts screaming while you’re unloading a minigun clip. I highly recommend Alien Rage to any fans of first person shooters. It is well worth your time!

The potential is there, but the lackluster experience point system and strong enemies make this game more of a hassle than fun. Oh, and of course the multiplayer is dead.

The definitive version of PAC-MAN, if you like the waka-waka sounding, ghost evading-at-first-till-he-eats-a-pellet yellow fella (thing? being?), you have to play this game. Originally released for PS3 and X360 (as Championship Edition DX) on the 20th anniversary of the classic one, the DX+ version adds various new features.
Stylish visuals (lots of skins to choose for both our protagonist and his adversaries, and awesome color palette), great soundtrack (waka waka doesn't bother you anymore, if it ever did), and a twist to the standard gameplay (with a looong rainbow trail of ghosts following you in addition to the four usual ones) make this game a must-buy to fans of PAC-MAN.
The only con is that every mode has a time limit, which might feel a bit weird to old-school players. But that's a minor problem compared to every plus this game has.
+ Lots of visual flair
+Awesome soundtrack
+Classic gameplay enhanced
-Time limit in every mode
Highly recommended not only to fans, but to people who haven't played PAC-MAN before (are there any, though?) and people who might not like the original.

Its fun but flawed. I came back to this game after watching some Watch Dogs II videos and was really surprised why I never finished it.
About 3 1/2 hours in, I remembered. It's too hard. And not strategically hard, I mean its just ridiculous AI that makes the game broken.
Case 1: I followed a random encounter and waited to intervene until instructed. Upon doing so the suspect pulled out a gun and started shooting. I chased after him and finally caught and tackled him. Upon doing so I realized the cops that were also pursuing may not have been after him afterall but after me. For no reason.
Case 2: There is a mission that you are supposed to drop off fancy cars. The cops immediately swarm you and if by chance you do get away, a helicopter follows you around indefinitely and never stops searching for you. WTF
Case 3: I was walking around doing profiler and accidentally hit one of those steam pipe things that explode. It killed 3 people and a nearby person called the cops. They immediately start chasing after me? Again WTF? Why and how would they blame me for that?? So I tried to escape and ran into water and swam away from shore thinking I could relax there until the heat level goes down. Instead, a helicopter that I can't even see follows me around indefinitely until I finally just quit the game.
I hope they addressed these issues in the next game because it makes this game unplayable. Despite some of the other claims, I really liked the story so far but its a shame I won't be able to experience it because the gameplay is buggy and flawed.
Aforementioned broken cheaty cops, snipers don't seem to ever get distracted even if a device is going off right next to them, the buttons are quite finnicky, the profiler jumps from person to person with no easy way to control it, and there aren't enough safe houses.
Despite all the hubbub about its launch with people trolling and complaining about the graphics, they are truly stellar. Probably the nicest part of the game, you can actually just walk around and take in the sights when flawed AI isn't constantly hounding you for crimes.
If you are used to these games, you should give it a try. If you are like me and a "GTA novice" then I would skip it because this is too hard.

I picked this game up based on what I read saying "scariest game"; because for 61 cents, what the hell right?
You are a frog and somehow you are descending down into an abyss of unfolding mystery. At first I thought to myself, "Cows?! What in the world are cows doing in a place like this?" Then a couple of segments down, I then realize how these "cows" were made. That revelation, to me, was horrific. Mind you, it wasn't scary, but it was indeed disturbingly horrific.
A+ on the story-telling. As you play, if you take notice of the enemies and the background, you start to unravel some clues as to why, what & how. Just a fair warning though, this game is extremely short but for a 61cent trip, it was well worth it.
I love the ambience and the art style very much. It speaks, well... horrors! The game-play is actually a puzzle type where you have to figure out the best way to defeat the enemies (Megaman bosses, anyone?). Nobody tells you what to do and that makes it even better.
I would have liked it even more if it was longer or if there was some kind of new game + or difficulty upgrade somehow. All in all, this game is a short but great diversion. Pick it up if you want to have some frog-cow nightmares! :)

There are only two problems with this game. One is that the game crashed quite regularly, i.e., almost each time I was playing it for some minutes. That was not a big deal because I could simply start it agian, but it was still a bit annoying.

All in all, I would give this title a 78 % rating.

For emulation of real, historical pinball machines, there is no other competitor. This game features loving 1:1 reproduction of dozens of machines - this game is standard if you have any investment in pinball as a hobby. Red and Ted’s Road Show is my favourite!
Another great feature is the rotation of monthly free tables and generous trial play for each table, so that you have plenty of opportunity to try before you buy. Even the standalone game has bountiful entertainment value!
However, this game also has some substantial oversights which are much less work to overcome than it is to make the virtual pinball tables, and because of this, this drives my overall review into "negative".
These oversights include:
* The user interface looks absolutely disgusting.
The UI looks like the same UI you would see on a "100-in-1” games compilation disk that you would find in a dime store in the year 1999. Dark, dank, drab colours and gradients for the sake of gradients. The “ball shaped” icons for each table also look horrific and cluttered. Many UI elements such as the logos and table icons are in inconsistent resolutions – if a graphic design student at a university/college presented that, they would likely fail. The gameplay is great, but the overall experience is like eating a premium steak off of a piece of torn-off pizza box cardboard. The low-fidelity cover of “Pinball Wizard” is also dinky. I would just replace that with some original instrumental composition.
*The prices are too expensive for me to ever consider buying when not on sale.
I appreciate that these are real machines, which by application are robbing pinball manufacturers of revenue (barring whatever they receive from licensing them to this game), but the standard prices for a table pack in Australian currency are $53.33 and $39.49 respectively (which is expected to become even more soon due to a tax on digital goods being implemented by our government!).  Buying every pack is more expensive than buying a Playstation 4 here. The "Pro" features are not worth $10 more also. I’m thinking maybe this game is aimed at older pinball-acquainted demographics who have more disposable income, because these prices will be sure to alienate casual players. Consider including smaller, more entry-level packs (and discounting for already-owned tables).
*No cross-platform purchase functionality.
This would make a purchase so much more worthwhile. I would make a standalone account for The Pinball Arcade on your site and add capability to link it to your steam/google play/PSN/whatever and detect and merge the purchases. You may as well add this feature, because re-buying a table for another platform is not a reasonable ask.
*The graphics and features are inconsistent between platforms.
I have also played the Android version, which has some beautiful bright colours which even complement the retro aesthetic of the tables. Comparatively, the PC version looks dark and washed out, even on a monitor that was similarly-specced to my phone's screen. I had to turn bulb and room brightness up to maximum for it to be more palatable. A global setting for these would be convenient. The Android version also lacks volume control of music and sound individually, so you can’t play your own music in the background without muting all aural feedback.
*Bugs and crashes are a regular occurance.
In both this and the Android version, selecting “recently played” and “random table” resulted in instant crashes, and on the PC version, the music would return after muting it in "Goin’ Nuts".   Many settings don't persist between program closes.
*An option to download tables individually, like on the Android version, would be great for windows tablets to save space (They usually use solid-state drives only).
*No native windows tablet/touch screen support.
I was able to make the screen portrait from graphics options, but after that, I was unable to operate both flippers with touch commands. Please consider including a Portrait/Landscape orientation toggle in options, and touch commands like on the smartphone version. Those were good touch commands!
*Some sound effects don't sound realistic.
The flipper sound effect sounds like a key turning in a lock. Not like pinball flippers in real life, a hearty, mechanical "THUCK!". The tilt sound effect also sounds like pushing a couch and not like a pinball machine. Changing those would make the experience much more authentic!
Overall, the content is spot-on, the free content is generous, but the implementation is sloppy. Please consider fixing, and this will be a 10/10 pinball experience.
Also, please add:
*The Simpsons Pinball Party
*The Lord of the Rings 2003
*Popeye Saves the Planet
*The Wizard of Oz 2013
*More post-millennial machines!

Defense Grid 1+2 are my favorite tower defense games. They offer an incredible array of methods to tactically arrange towers for powerful synergies. I really haven't seen another tower defense game that allows such intricate tower combinations.
New to Defense Grid 2 from DG1 is the ability to acquire tower upgrades from winning missions. These can simply make your towers stronger, or they may add a new effect. At first you'll just be happy to have any upgrade, but later you'll have an assortment to choose from. As you gain tower upgrades, you can replay earlier missions with the new upgrades.
There also alternatives to the orbital laser super weapon. You pick which one to take for each mission. Maybe you'd rather temporarily supercharge a group of your towers. Or maybe you value a temporary boost to resource gain over having a superweapon. For some of them, it's hard to tell how they work without actually trying them out.

The more I play this game, the more I like it.

First, steam has no idea how many hours I have poured into this game.  It will never know, like a second wife, there are large mysteries of your past that are best just not brought up.
Let me say this then: This game has ruined the RTS genre for me.  It's sequel was worse.  the spiritual successor was a different beast that I am less enamored with.
SupCom really allows one to focus on the macro level, rather than all the Miniature that occurs in an RTS.
Want to have a base pumping out units?  Put the factory on repeat.
Want to set up a defensive line?  Put a patrol path at the end of the factory's move order.
Want to speed up the rate of production? Put engineer's on a patrol around it, If you can afford it, they'll assist, or (Cybran and UEF can) build an engineering station.
Ran out of resources in production? Put an engineer in the factory queue, they'll deploy with the army and police up resources (If needed) that they encounter on patrol(This also applies to that base patrol mentioned earlier).
Want unit's to follow a specific path to the defensive line? Give the factory a series of move points to path there then draw a patrol line.
Want to speed up production? Make additional factories and have them assist the existing one.
Want to speed up deployment time? Build, and give air transports the order to assist a factory, they'll lift, ferry, and drop units.
Want to make the air transports follow  a specific path to drop?   They'll follow those move points mentioned earlier.
Want to speed up deployment without air factories?  Build land factories closer to the front-line and tell them to assist the factories further back.
I think the point has been made: This is a game designed with the macro level as the default play level, and the entails 101 little tweaks and convenience features only add to the enjoyment because you won't find yourself wanting to order your troops to "Stop being ^$@*ing Morons!".
I cannot even adequately explain the awesomeness that is: Built for dual monitors(Or Display's, Try the "HOME" key on your keyboard sometime,) Strategic zoom (Think google maps right down to google street view tied to your mouse wheel,) and built for Multi-core-processors(this was much more impressive and unique in 2007).
The take away: The game is damned fine sir/ma'am, and if you play it with friends, you'll give 5 or 6 years have passed before you want to buy another game.

Travel down into the depths of a flooded forest with your frog protagonist, competing with the forest's other inhabitants for the world's most precious resource. The game says this is oxygen- little bubbles of life floating up from the depths- but I think it may be something else entirely.
What is that? Well, this is one of those games where knowing too much about the plot going in may very well make it not worth playing. They Breathe tells its story in twenty to thirty minutes, provides you with no quest markers. No on-screen hud, no explanations, no sonorous narrator lamenting your plight. It trusts you, the player, to find the story, at your own pace. For once this works, because the simple gameplay and single path leaves little room to get lost or distracted.
Despite its short length, They Breathe nevertheless takes its time on its storyline, and obvious care was put into the crafting of this game. Gameplay is simple- you swim around collecting oxygen bubbles, facing one wave after another as you head deeper and deeper. You have access to a dash move and little else. The game doesn't tell you how to take down the predators you face in the forest, but your little frog is tough enough that you have some time to figure it out, and will respawn if you don't quite get it in time.
The graphics are again simple but lovely, colorful enough to catch your eye but still looking like something that has been submerged deep underwater, so not especially bright. The flooded forest doesn't look like a place you would want to spend an afternoon, but it looks the part. The actors onstage are simply but boldly drawn. The design of the land's predators is especially good. This isn't a game for everyone, but everyone should try it to see if it's for them. Because if it's a game for you and you won't play it, you'll miss out on something that will change your attitude towards the video games for good.
If you don't like to read - don't bother playing.
If David Lynch made adaptation of Albert's Camus "Plague" - this would be the game setting. The atmosphere is depressingly heavy and stifling. From the very beginning the game drags you - the player - into the city which bizarre architecture is matched with the society inhabiting it. Quickly enough you'll realize that deadly infectious disease has struck the city and on you lies responsibility to try and stop it...
And you will try - but you won't make it to the third day, because you didn't buy enough food the first day, and you won't afford any of it the second day, because prices rose due to panic of disease outbreak...
And you will try - but you'll be killed by a goon while you are trying to get to safe bed and get some sleep late at night...
And you will try - but you catched the disease trying to loot infected house, hoping to find some food, and now you've run out of antibiotics...
And you will try - but one of the characters you - the person in front of the screen - cared about, was killed by the disease, so you reload save from previous day and play it all over again, hoping there was something you could do to save him/her...
And every time you fail, you'll know exactly why you failed and who did you let down. And you will feel the burden of responsibility on your shoulders slouching over your keyboard. And you will feel guilt, so you'll try again - "maybe one day back in saves will be enough, or maybe two".
Eventually you'll get into the game routine - you'll get around managing your money and inventory. You'll learn that time management is crucial, because time is running fast, you are moving slow, and no event will wait for you to trigger it. You'll learn how to optimise walking routes to make the most out of every day. Only to have your routine shattered by a turn of events you wouldn't expect. Needless to say - beating this game is really rewarding, and it is so in more than a one way.
All of the features above are system-based, not scripted - you have food/water/immunity/health/exhaustion bars which are drained during the gameplay and affected differently by some items. You have inventory, along with clothing and weaponry which have their durability and have to be repaired by certain NPCs. There is also reputation bar that will be affected by your actions. You can kill innocent people and burgle their houses, but it will have an impact on your reputation, and this will affect your other interactions in-game. I'm mentioning this not only because it's implemented, but because you might fall in such a position you'll have to consider doing it.
The plot is incredible, on par with characters. There are enough mysteries and unanswered questions to fill three playthroughs, each from different protagonist's point of view. This review is getting really lenghty, and no matter how long would it be, it won't convey all the love I've got for this game. Playing it is like putting little pieces together of something that turns out to be a mirror. And believe me - you won't like the reflection of yours that this mirror will show you.
But first you'll have to survive some serious beating - from graphics, collision system, and mostly dialogue (not dubbed) based gameplay.
-graphics are ancient - but style and design are excellent
-you can't jump nor run, and the clipping is awful (i.e. you may be stopped by an edge of a sidewalk)
-gunplay exists in the game, and that's the only positive thing you can say about it
-same goes with melee combat system and sneaking
-models are poorly animated and game rather avoids showing key characters moving around in the open
-interaction with NPCs MASSIVELY relies on text dialogues - but they are very well written and sit at the core of the game idea - think of it in Planescape: Torment terms
-the other GIANT part of the game (besides dialogues) is moving around the city - the pace is rather slow, but this gives you time to plot your way through the city wisely, because there is MUCH to do and your time is limited every day; you'll push that 'w' button and you'll feel the same pressure that time running out is exerting on you, but the protagonist won't move any faster
But once you get through those obstacles, and I believe you will, since you've got all the way through my review, you'll be up for a really rewarding and enriching experience.
tl;dr:
+IMMENSELY immersive, great story, unique characters, leaves permanent mark on your mind, painful to play
-PAINFUL to play

One of a kind game. It is a slow-paced adventure game with survival and RPG elements.
The gameplay is focused around quests that advance the story. At the beginning, you just have to visit the various characters of the town and get to know them, but then the game gets a lot more interesting as the various quests start presenting you with choices and also combat gets introduced into the game. Some might argue that the combat system is uninspired, but I think it's just fine for a dialogue-based adventure game. I found the knife vs knife fights against the thugs to be quite fun honestly. Finally, what makes the game truly interesting is the fact that you also have to manage a set of gauges, such as hunger, immunity or exhaustion. This, plus the fact that you have limited supplies and limited time to finish each day's quests, make the gameplay really interesting in my opinion. The graphics and (especially) the dialogues were a lot worse in the non-HD version of the game, so that's a step in the right direction too. Despite the dated graphics however, the atmosphere is amazing.
There are a few things that could have been done better in the game. Even though dodging clouds and looting trash cans is part of the game, there is way too much unnecessary traveling going on (at a slow walking speed). It took me a good 2 hours to beat each in-game day on my first playthrough. Multiply this by 12 (as there are 12 days in each playthrough) and it would pretty much mean that each playthrough is about 24 hours long. Now, there are some differences between each character, but I don't really think it's worth it to spend another 24 hours just so you can experience the same story from a different perspective. The characters interact with each other anyway, so you kinda know what to expect from the Haruspex playthrough once you've beaten the game as the Bachelor. For some people it might be interesting regardless, yet I think one must really have a lot of free time in order to play this game multiple times and not get bored of all the walking around. The other negative is obviously the dialogues, as the game was not really designed for an English speaking playerbase. They did improve the translation quite a bit in this remastered version however.

The game looks like a fusion between the Worms franchise, the turn based system though being eliminated from the ecuation, resulting into a RTS.
You are given an array of offense, defense, economy, utility and most important your ship which will give you an advantage granted if you know how to use it to said advantage.
Offense is made out of laser, cannon, drill, freezing, missile, flamethrower, grenade launcher towers and even nukes! Defense is composed out of shields that can deflect incoming laser or take the damage may it be cannon, freezing or the missile tower, et cetera. Using the shield's perk of deflecting can prove of good use in the case of lasers. Utility has various tools such as the platform, bank, territory balloon, terraforming tower and I recall there being an aerial building that gives a speed boost to the buildings. Economy has mines and can be used on diamond or gold deposits.
Campaign has quite a solid story for the genre, with boss battles and it covers the basics and advanced topics of the game. Competitive is quite a challenge, since it's not balanced at all, you lose your rank way, way too fast and it lacks a player base.
It's a really good game for casual playing, the AI is satisfying in my opinion since ranked is not really optimal for playing.
You can lay all sorts of tactics on the battlefield, but be swift and merciless as every second matters in this game.
The 2D environment is really fascinating, I love the sorta cartoony way all the textures have been designed and how they blend into the gameplay, the campaign's map is a really nice adding as well.
Soundtrack is always a must and will set the game's ambience and in this case it's a good choice along with the sound effects. No complains on this one.
I don't recommend buying the game only for yourself but get the 2 pack so you can play with a friend, multiplayer isn't active so you'll encounter problems in multiplayer. If you have only the possibility and the mood to play only single player, then go for it, you'll face some difficulty from the AI, being able to enjoy the game thoroughly for complete hours.

Don’t be fooled by the looks and childish image of this game, for you will have a nice time due to the amount of fun and secrets it holds.
Super Panda Adventures is one for those games that should be tagged as a “Hidden Gem”, while the story is not that original at all, its value is easily found on the mechanics, gameplay and partly RPG elements, the 2D and immature-like but intelligent design made of this game a total surprise to me.
We play as Fu, a panda, trained to protect a princess, a princess that happens to be abducted by evil robots from outer space and whose evil plans of taking over earth and turn everything into mechanical beings are their final goal. So the young panda facing this threat looks for a way to rescue the princess, save his land and destroy this evil.
The mechanics are quite simple and follow the classic 2D elements of gameplay, but what makes this game rich is the amount of well hidden secrets and powers we can have at hand to advance further in the storyline and into more difficult enemies to beat. During the game we should face a limited number of side quests that will lead us to gain more powers, abilities and weapons. In the beginning we are quite underpowered, but this changes shortly after doing some special side quests, enemies are quite tough to beat and we must level up fast, grinding is key to the mechanics for we must develop the many skills we have.
Also, to add more fun to the gameplay, there are certain relics scattered all over the different levels, these relics will grant you individual abilities that are very helpful to achieve certain tasks, some of them are easy to find, some others are really difficult, adding more hours of gaming.
What was a surprise on this game is the fact that we must come and go over and over again to different locations of the map, a reminder of the old school Zelda games, A Link to the Past to be precise.
It is normal to expect midi elements and 8-bit music, the soundtrack is quite interesting, from high-tempo tunes to slow ones, fitting the atmosphere and aesthetics of the many places we visit.
On the other hand the sounds are very old-school like, many of the sound and effects have this vibe that reminded me of Kirby, Super Mario, Zelda, etc. classic NES and Super NES titles. It also has some sort of Super Meat Boy atmosphere at times.
I must say I encountered not a single bug or glitch and not even a crash, the game runs good, it is stable and smooth. But my complaint goes in the direction of the grinding, it is an important part of the game, enemies are hard to beat when you start, and it becomes easier once you gather enough powers and level up, while the grinding of enemies works this way, it tends to be repetitive and monotonous at times and it is also linked to the fact that every time the same enemies will re-spawn at the same place over and over again, this affected me at times in the beginning, not enough health, not enough manna or shields and many deaths were part of this re-spawning system.
Another aspect that many players complained about is related to the boss fights, in my case I did not have any problems with them, but sometimes I felt that they were really hard to beat on normal difficulty, I learnt that some patches changed some aspects of this, but still, I can’t but feel some sort of drawback at some point. Nothing that serious though.
Finally, my last complaint and maybe the most annoying is related to the many secrets, sometimes there is not a certain way to know if you visited x part of a level because nothing seems to indicate that you were already there, this happened to me many times. The levels tend to reset what you already did before while discovering new zones. I often found myself running around confused thinking or doubting if I already did x thing or not due to the fact that some locations must be visited many times.
Super Panda Adventures is a game that has more pros than cons, evidently. The game highlights the many good things that 2D games have to offer, even more today with all the AAA titles and the masses demanding state-of-the-art graphics and effects, forgetting and proving that simple and classic looking games can deliver the same amount of fun or even more sometimes. I recommend this game to any fan of 2D style that likes games with simple and dumb humor; SPA is a great game that stands out by being original and fun.
I urge the developer to deliver more games like this; you have potential, my friend. I can’t wait for a sequel!

Alien Rage is about as linear a FPS you can get, even including a useless jump ability that makes you wonder why they bothered with the effort to implement it.  There are objective markers leading you from one section to the next, but there really isn't a reason for it because you have no other direction to go. The weapons are few and lackluster.
