Pathologic is a particularly peculiar game. It should be noted that the game is slow, reliant on (text) dialog that is either purposefully written to be esoteric or is a representation of the developers native language (Russian, I believe) not being translated to English particularly well and averse to explanation. If this doesn't sound like your kind of game - it's likely that this is the case.
The storyline of Pathologic, as explained by a charming opening sequence set in a theatre, is that there are three playable characters - all of whom believe that they are the best choice to save a small, 19th century town in Eastern Europe. When the player assumes the role of any of these characters, they will attempt to save as many people in the town as possible from a series of seemingly impossible deaths.
The game doesn't explain anything more than that from the getgo - all additional plot information is inferred through talking to the various characters that populate the town.
The game is old, and it's not particularly aged well. The interfaces are manageable, but often confusing. The graphics are dated, but not offensively poor. The game is absolutely nonlinear - even to the point that it seems directionless initially, but makes up for it in intrigue.
I would not recommend this game if you're looking for something fast paced - but if you're looking to make your own path and try to solve something - this game might be for you.

Watch_Dogs promised a lot and delivered a considerable amount. The premise is very, very overdone but I feel like in this case, I can allow a pass to happen. Criminal does criminal things, other criminals get involved to take out said criminal, criminal's family end up as collateral damage, and criminal is out for revenge and get involved in a conspiracy that left gripped me until the resolution of the story.
This is an open world game with instanced events that build a reputation (with both civilians and police) and fun mini-games inside the game that help break up the monotany that can sometimes happen in both the main storyline and in doing all of the side-events and side-quests. The immersion, which is really important to me, is what gets me the most is the fact that the reality of Watch_Dogs is very close to being reality. So the suspension of belief is very easy and keeps that suspension going without anything that stands out in such a way that disconnects me from the world of the game.
There is an online component that you can participate in along with a mobile phone app (iOS and Android) that allows you to build your reputation and compete against other players in such instances like cops and robbers, stalking, and hide-and-seek. It's very fun but I can't say, as is the case for most games of this nature, that the online component is going to be very active. So while it is fun, I can't really speak for the overall active nature of the community that continues to play Watch_Dogs.
The graphics are fine but be prepared to experience some stuttering if you don't have a higher end PC to push out all of the instances that may be going on at once. There is also a secondary inclusion of DRM via uPlay which has become more and more refined while at the same time less intrusive. You can disable the overlay at any time plus there is exclusive content on uPlay that you get with "points" that are accumulated during normal gameplay achievements. This is pretty standard fare for Ubisoft, so nothing positive or negative to say overall.
I do wish that the control scheme overall was a little more polished for controllers and quite possibly keyboard and mouse. At times, there can be a little bit of sluggishness (which very well might be from the physics engine) when it comes from free running and vehicle movement. It may be improved in a sequel with a more mature engine for this game, but it does leave something to be desired. The interface is well designed and interactions in game are fluid and intuitive, making hacking to driving to doing jobs for cash fluid, intuitive, and has me spending less time in an interface and more time in the environment. This was well received by me and I can't help but feel like wishing other games really worked on this more in order to achieve a more fluid user experience.
At this time, with no DLC explored, I recommend the core game of Watch_Dogs. It is unique, different, and tries something else in an open world genre that feels like we're running out of settings or stories to tell. It has its bugs, but those are always expected when one has a game in a sandbox (just look at Skyrim). All I can truly say, is that having me come back and do a second playthrough is enough for me to recommend it (I don't like games that I can only play once and find no desire to go back and play again).

Watch Dogs (stylized as WATCH_DOGS) is an action-adventure video game developed by Ubisoft Montreal and published by Ubisoft. It was released worldwide on 27 May 2014 for Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 3, PlayStation 4, Xbox 360 and Xbox One, while a Wii U version was released in November 2014. Set within a fictionalized version of Chicago, Illinois, the single-player story follows a hacker and his efforts to seek revenge after the killing of his niece. The open world design lets players freely roam the urban city, suburbs, open countryside, and run-down neighborhoods of Chicago.
The game is played from a third-person perspective and its world is navigated on-foot or by vehicle. Players control Aiden Pearce, a grey hat hacker who can hack into the "ctOS", a centralized operating system which manages the hyper-connected city of Chicago, and formed after the Northeast blackout of 2003 was caused by a hacker. An online multiplayer mode is also provided in the game, allowing up to eight players to engage in both cooperative and competitive gameplay in a recreation of the single-player setting.
Development on the game began in 2009. As part of their research for the open world, the developers conducted field research around Chicago throughout development and captured footage for the design team. Duties were shared between many of Ubisoft's studios worldwide.
Following its announcement in June 2012, Watch Dogs was widely anticipated. At release, it received a polarized reception; praise was particularly directed at the game's hacking elements and mission variety. The game received criticism concerning the discrepancy in graphics quality between marketing and the real game and also concerning the overall gameplay, plot, protagonist, and some technical issues. Watch Dogs was a commercial success, breaking the record for the biggest first day sales of a Ubisoft game, and becoming the biggest launch of a new intellectual property ever in the United Kingdom at the time. As of 1 January 2015, the game has shipped over 10 million copies. It was followed by a sequel, Watch Dogs 2, in November 2016.

There are more 2D RTS and "Artillery" games every year, but I generally don't see one that has brought anything new to either genre. Cannon Brawl has improved upon both. I haven't played much more than an hour but its experience has immediately brought to mind Swords & Soliders, Worms.... while already securing a place for itself in my memory.
The game is quick but that is part of the charm for anyone who doesn't have time for lengthier or more competitive RTS games; the actions-per-minute goals (APM) attached to the early levels are easily attainable and pragmatic. That is, when the game says it expects at least 13 APM, you find yourself nodding in agreement instead of shaking your head in exasperation that anyone could play that fast and not be a professional gamer. There are smart details in user interface as well, with cooldowns being explicitly shown, and previous flight paths of your artillery being logged each time you come back.
$14.99 might be a bit much for some people for the length of game you get - on sale it is an immediate must buy. Regardless, I recommend it in either case.

-Solid Graphics and particle effects, if your system can handle it.
-Fun little story.

Cons -
-Lack of any real DLC campaigns (compared to DG1).

If you like Shadowrun 4th, you'll like this game.  It's not blow-for-blow an exact port of the pen and paper, but it does an excellent job capturing the essence of it.  Most importantly, it's got a great story... one that I actually, absolutely HAD to adapt to the pen and paper game.  While the story does have a lot of the standard Shadowrun cliches (the Johnson betrays you... WHAAAAAT?!) it also pulls you in an unexpected direction more than once.  Do yourself a favor and don't read any spoilers... if you don't read ahead, the story will have you constantly changing and reassessing your theory as to what's "really" going on all the way up to the end (and I mean ALL the way up to the end, even past the climactic battle).
There are a few clunky things about the game that Harebrained Schemes has acknowledged it by endeavoring to fix them in Shadowrun: Hong Kong... most notably that, unless you're in combat, you can't have party members pick up stuff.  That gets supremely frustrating toward the end when you're popping a few med kits every fight, because you can't restock your medic, or anyone else that's been using them, and are likely going to run out of room really quick on your main character.  There are work-arounds, of course... you can start a fight, then run away from it to loot all the medkits... but that's a pain to have to remember to do, and you risk needing a medkit just for starting the fight.  Still, like I said, they've acknowledged that it's a problem, and they're going to fix it in their next game.  It doesn't fix it in THIS game, but at least it's something.
I love this game well enough that I'm going to buy Hong Kong the second it comes out.  It also inspired me to convert Shadowrun to the Legend of the Five Rings rules (because I love the SR setting, but hate the ruleset)... but the rules themselves work pretty well for a computer game... they just get a bit too clunky for the table top, with combats lasting 30 minutes to an hour sometimes.  But... that's the tabletop, not this game... this game is actually really great.

I just put 33 hours into beating this game and now I just want to play again. As other reviewers have mentioned, Dragonfall's story is *fantastic*. The game is very text-heavy, but there isn't really any tedious world-bullding/ lore-heavy reading, it's almost entirely conversational. The game is gorgeous; HBS did a great job building a really vivid cyberpunk world. What I like about the RPG system in this game is that it doesn't feel restrictive at all; you can branch into anything you want. The combat is fun, if sometimes a bit tedious. The main reason I'm inclined to play it again is that there are things I definitely things I missed/decisions that I made which I'd like to revisit. Overall, a fantastic game. with ~30 hours of story, it's easily worth 15 bucks. I got it on sale, but had I known I would enjoy it this much, I would've easily paid full price.

When I started Dragonfall I kind of had the plan to make a non-cyberware based street samurai, but I wound up making a mage who also uses pistols and was quite pleased at how it turned out.  The team you run with is fun, overall, and you get to choose who you bring with you.  That can significantly change how you approach some parts of certain levels.  With one character you can send a drone through air ducts to flank an enemy but wIth another you can hang back, bait the enemy in and snipe them.
I really like how they incorporated the matrix runs for deckers.  In the table-top game it was tedious for four or five players to sit there watching someone do a run becuase a decker could do so many actions in a combat round while jacked in.  In this game the decker gets a couple turns of cyber-combat then the game goes back to the action in the physical world.  I personally thing it was handled really well, and it's fun.  I'd usually try to do the cyber-combat without using any support programs, but sometimes using them just made a decking run way, way easier.
Stats are represented well, and each skill seems to be useful, even etiquettes can sometimes significantly change the way parts of the game turn out.  That and not having the proper etiquette makes you sometimes frown because instead of that additional intelligence of body point you COULD have bought Corporate Etiquette and talked your way around a fight, or tricked someone into letting you bypass a security door.  It's wonderful to have the option.
Combat and cover mechanics are handled fairly well, too.  The stun grenades got annoying at times, but it adds another element to the combat and makes you really watch your positions.  If you spread out just enough you can avoid multiple characters being hit by grenades.  The weapon variety is okay, and you can "lend" weapons to your team-mates on a per-run basis if they have a spare slot.  This was a nice addition and opens up more combat options.  I never felt like I had to give anyone a weapon, though, as each character is competent.  You also get to make choices for the NPCs in your team when they level up, the game doesn't arbitrarily assign their skill choices.
As always, get it on sale if you're not sure but this one is worth the full price, if for nothing else to simply support the Devs. who I think have done a great job bringing Shadowrun up to speed.
Just as much fun as the original Shadow Returns. The new system elements add a nice touch to combat, and the new missions really bring out a lot in the characters.

This is is great return to the PC world for the SR universe. The main campaign is on rails, but the story is still fun and worthwhile. I recommend Dragonfall over this SR:R due to the imrpovement in AI, interface, and a better story (that feels less on rails due to all the RO opportunities, but has more fetch quests). SR:R/Dragonfall was made primarily with touch screens in mind and so it plays a little clunky on the PC. Sometimes you'll run into problems with trying to get your character in a certain position to only have the game think you clicked the next spot over - not a major issue but an annoying one. The mod support is great and increases the games longevity. The mods even allow you to keep playing your same character through community mods or through the campaign again. Originally Dragonfall was DLC for this engine, but has since released in it's own engine. I recommend buying both games, and then placing SR:R module in the dragonfall engine for a better experience. SR:R has more mods than Dragonfall so you might just want to copy Dragonfall's module into the other engine to utilize more mod's.

Awesome cyberpunk setting, amazing story and varied characters. Combat is also surprisingly in-depth and fun. This is an upgrade to Shadowrun Returns in almost every way. The devs have even included a nice mod-kit for the budding modder to make something special.

Using Quicksave too often also makes the game act up (some save files don't load up at all sometimes). My advice is to save often but not to the point of abuse and to save in different slots.
Despite those caveats, this game comes highly recommended!

WAKA WAKA WAKA! PAC-MAN Championship Edition DX+ is an excellent game that has elements from Snake, the original PAC-MAN, and some score attack games. It's fast paced, surprising and all-around a great addition to the PAC-MAN franchise! You start out at a rather slow speed, getting faster the more ghosts and pac-dots you eat. Along with the original ghosts, (Blinky, Pinky, Inky and Clyde) there is a time limit (1 minute, 5 minutes, and 10 minute modes) and  green ghosts that start flashing the colors of the rainbow and start chasing you when you pass by them. The rainbow ghosts all follow the exact path PAC-MAN is following, creating a Snake-like trail behind him. Think you've cleared the maze and won? Think again! clearing one half of the maze will create an item and make that half become darker. Upon collecting the item, the cleared half of the maze will go back to normal, with a new design and the usual green ghosts, pac-dots and power pellets.  As usual, there are the power pellets that power you up and let you eat the ghosts, resulting in you being able to eat the entire trail of ghosts behind you. Some ghosts carry power pellets and bombs (The bombs will come in handy in some situations.) that allow you to keep that score chain going for as long as you can! when ghosts get close to you, the game will become slow-mo, allowing you some time to get away from the ghosts or use a bomb, which moves all ghosts currently chasing you back to their hideout. Oh, and did I mention the visuals and music? No? Ok. The music is epic and fast paced, which adds to the heart racing nature of the game. there are many visuals, ranging from classic arcade PAC-MAN to modern PAC-MAN, and even some that make the game look like the other arcade classics, Dig Dug and Rally X. All-in-all, the game is fun for both people playing since the arcade version came out and newcomers who want an exciting PAC-MAN experience. I reccomend it to anyone who likes PAC-MAN and wants a unique game.

+ Good graphics, art style, and animations
+ Nice campaign and looks like quite a few levels
+ Nice twist and adds something new to the "artillery" games
+ Has multiplayer  (I've only done the solo player campaign, but seems like a great option)
~

~

But if I beat the mission in a certain time, why does it matter how many actions I did or DIDN"T do ?   APM simply measures how "busy" you are; which has nothing to do with how well or effective you played.
~
The placing of the buildings to be built which dangle beneath your airship as if you are transporting them to where they go.  This isn't intuitive for placement selection and is mostly problematic when trying to place "territory expanding sky-balloons" which I kept having to settle for "close enough", yet end up NOT being close enough after all...
~

It's like they couldn't decide which towers to include in the game so they through them all in, or they didn't want to make enough levels to support gradually introducing them.  They should either remove some tower types or create more levels so as to introduce them at a better pace.

Rapid-paced 2D giant robot action across 5 levels each with an enormous boss. 14 weapons for various loadouts and play styles. Full Japanese VA for a straightforward plot featuring a badass lead heroine. This is GUNHOUND EX in a nutshell.
Interested? Take my advice and the game will be a decent experience.
Controls can be remapped in Options and recognizes controllers (my xbox 360 controller worked perfect). Default confirm key is Z.
Do the tutorials. Practice. The controls are complex and physics take some getting used to compared to your typical 2D platformer or run \'n gun.
If default weapons aren\'t working for you, Customize your suit to the Light Frame and farm Tutorial 5 for points until you unlock the weapons you want. Score adds to a total score, which you need to cap at 99 million to unlock everything. But, default guns and Iron Claw are enough to get you through the game just fine. The Claw (and all melee weapons) will block and destroy any enemy bullet, so constant spam of your default gun with Claw auto-attack can help you breeze through things.
It\'s a challenging fun game, but not one you can just immediately jump in and expect to be good at. It\'s difficult, controls do not cater well to KB&M players, and requires a bit of practice. But honestly it\'s worth it.

Off the top of my head, I can't think of a better example of the Steam userbase downrating a game because they're complete garbage at it. I've yet to complete it from beginning to end using one continue, but I've beaten the final boss using keybard controls and the only thing I had a bit of trouble with was locking on to a direction and using secondary fire at the same time; even that, though, becomes easy once you've practiced enough.
Gunhound is a sidescroller with actual physics, and you're controlling a mech that's meant to feel heavy. That's it; that's what the "irredeemable horribleness" of the controls boils down to. As soon as you realize that you're not supposed to play this as if it were Mario or Megaman, it stops being an issue.
Presentation's not amazing, but totally fine. The music's fitting enough and the graphics get the job done. Most of the mechs are made of smaller sprites put together and spun around in a Mode 7-esque way, which can be an issue and feel unnaturally robotic in games featuring organic characters but is totally fine in a mecha-piloting game.
The silly anime story didn't amuse me as much as the one in Astebreed, but it's certainly easier to keep track of what's being said during gameplay given you can actually stop in your tracks in this game. Bonus points for a fairly likable female protagonist.

Mech combat is best presented in 3d, which shows what's in front of the mech.  In this game, you can only see a short distance in front of your mech, so you'll need Ninja Reflexes (get it?) to take out the enemies before they damage you or your escorts.

In Pathologic, you play as one of three amateur and probably rather unqualified medical professionals who is visiting what appears to be an isolated post-WWII Russian factory town. You become trapped in the town when a sudden plague outbreak forces a quarantine, and you end up spending several days making necessary sacrifices so you can hopefully save the town (and yourself) from extinction. At its core, this is an adventure game, but you play it like a first-person shooter. There's a strong survival simulation element, as well. I'll break it down with a few pros and cons.
I haven't played another game quite like Pathologic, and I know I'm going to enjoy finishing it in spite of its old-school flaws. It's tough to go wrong with it at the price it's selling at, as well. Give it a shot!

Pathologic is a quarantine simulation FPS with a bizarre Eurasian setting that’s sure to raise a few eyebrows. The story basically follows one of three characters who end up trapped in a small town due to a mysterious outbreak with no explainable source.
Pathologic combines several gameplay mechanics to keep things challenging for the player. There are survival elements such as health, hunger, and exhaustion, which are managed by fairly obvious means. In addition, you have immunity and infection meters, the first of which is raised by fairly common drugs that will decrease your chance of becoming infected, a status curable only by vary rare drugs. Infection is not a death sentence, however, as you can find many antibiotics and even very dangerous cures to reduce or remove it entirely. Infection will typically occur within quarantined areas by either contact with infected civilians, collision with plague clouds, or bites from plague rats.
Another system of interest are the “bound” NPCs which are initially critical to surviving each day but eventually become expendable beyond a certain point. It’s up to you whether to save them or not. There are additional “bound” that belong to two other characters who can also fall ill or die, potentially effecting your playthrough.
Normally, I’m one for eccentric games, often giving a chance to games that buck the average person due to being too weird or complicated. I lost interest in Pathologic for a different reason: the game is a huge chore.
You will spend FOREVER walking around each day doing all the necessary tasks. This game needed a fast travel system like JFK needed a bulletproof helmet. In fact, some sort of doodle-based system where you draw lines on the main map that “cost” the player time when executed would have been a perfect way to balance the time-based mission mechanic with a convenient movement system. Instead, you spend about 3/4ths of the game just walking between places with the occasional fight or flee moment. Moving through infected areas can also be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥due to the fact that your character will clip onto just about anything, getting you stuck on a street corner or building edge right as you’re trying to slip past a dangerous plague cloud or rat.
Speaking of fighting, the combat system is downright bad. Your bullets are wildly inaccurate at totally feasible real-life distances at certain angles, but totally on the mark when everything is on a flat z-plane. Good luck if you try to do any knife fighting, by the way, your character randomly alternates between a single slash and double slash and you have to guess which one he’s going to do as you charge in.
I gave Pathologic HD a fair effort (I also tried the original version before this review) of about 22 hours of gameplay before finally breaking down and asking myself “what the ♥♥♥♥ am I doing with my free time?” This game had potential and I really liked the story, but the execution is less than lackluster and downright confusing or boring for most of the game. It’s a shame but I can’t find myself recommending this title even though I really wanted to like it.

Holy pogo-sticks, people -- I have just started playing this game but feel it is worth commenting on.
If you care to take the leap keep in mind that the game is going to be experienced in an egine that feels of the era of a well-polished THIEF 1: The Dark Project. This technichal fallback on graphics may be too much for some people to handle, so be warned. That said, I am in awe of what the game seems to be trying to accomplish -- story-wise and in terms of what a game is. I wish there was a run command to or a way to move about the town(s) more quickly, but apparently at least in the beginning it's important for the player to walk. The absolutely mundane crash with the COMPLETELY SURREAL with an odd nonchalance, making me wonder if the whole game is supposed to be a dream, or alternate plane, or who knows.
Sadly, the fact that a million games coming after Pathologic have not seemed to borrow from it. I can already tell aspects of it might sag under it's own weight -- but I'm with-holding judgement until I get a bit farther. Atmospherically and voice-talent wise... as well as the ambitions of the game give me a very strong first impression.
The idea that there is an invisible cat I can only meet in the factory district at night and perhaps only on day 1 intrigues me... and the game suggests that a lot of weird stuff happens at specific times, much of which you are likely to miss. Very strange concept for a game -- progression though the content you are ABLE to witness, as opposed to showing you everything and leaving nothing to the imagination. Life isn't like the latter, so the idea of a game trying to be more like life in a temporal/reality sense is quite impressive. Will update review when I can honestly pass judgement. Right now I'm down the rabbit-hole, but give it a positive benefit of the doubt.

I want to say I recommend this game, but there are too many issues that get in the way of playing it. I'll make it short, I can only recommend this game if you have 4 other friends that are interested in playing it. That's what I do.
The game runs terrible (for some people not all). To be clear, it only likes to render around 8-15fps. This has been the case for me on two computers already. Both met the requirements to easily run this game. I'm running a setup with a Ryzen 1700 with a GTX 1060, there's no way I can't meet the requirements. I've tried various methods to tackle this, still no dice.
- The game runs currently using Python 2.7.6. I have tried replacing this version with 2.7.14 within the files themselves. No change in performance whatsoever.
- I replaced Python 2.7.6 using 3.6.3, game failed to run. Probably due to the differing syntax between 2 and 3, but it was worth a shot.
- Forced 3D settings using Nvidia Control Center, rather than allowing the application itself to control these settings. No change in performance.
- Uninstalling and reinstalling the files. No change in performance.
- Unplugged any HID devices that could've possibly affected the program. Nothing as expected, but it was recommended by a friend.
If I actually find a solution I will edit this review explaining how. There are some Steam forums that currently have a few methods to fix this, none of which have been of use.
EDIT:
Actually got the game to run correctly at 60FPS. I have not touched the files in weeks. Suddenly it has decided to run fine. No idea how but it's running well.
To move on to the actual game itself, it's a blast with friends. The atmosphere, insanity, differing monsters are all fresh and well thought out. Although I will say on some maps, some of the monsters are absolutely useless. EX: Playing as The Fallen on open maps renders him almost unable to actually spawn in to get a single kill. The Phantom is extremely OP. It can simply spawn near survivors within another parallel realm for an inst-kill. His speed makes him even more deadly, especially in tighter maps. Thankfully when hosting a game, you can change characters, maps, and toggle a ton of settings, this is nice.
Also, the game servers are nearly dead. And so is the development. Unless you want to wait in-game or in the lobby for an hour to hope that people will join, you're best off playing something else. Go play Dead by Daylight or The Hidden (Source) if you want a good monster vs. humans horror game. Again, I can only recommend for people that have others to play with.

Sweet lord I cannot recommend this game enough to true lovers of RPGs. This game has given me more hours and more enjoyment than quite a lot of full priced games. The story is absolutely fantastic and there can't be enough praise given to the writing. All the characters are interesting with very few that you meet falling under any obvious cliches. The combat mechanics are mostly the same as in Shadowrun: Returns. Only this time the encounters and combat zones seem to be better designed so the fight sequences are quite fun and tactical (unlike in the last game where tedious was a good description). The matrix sequences are also FAR better than they were in SRR. But again, it's the story, the writing and the world that sucks you in. Right at the end of the game, effectively the epilogue, long after the last achievement has been earnt, and quest has been completed you're presented with a choice that effectively has no tangible outcome to you, the player. Yet, the world has you so invested in your character and the world, you can't help but agonise over the decision. The game ends after making the choice and for days afterwards I was questioning whether I did the right the thing. Such is the quality of the writing in this game.
There's a handful of small bugs but only once was it bad enough for me to forcefully quit the game. Thankfully it resolved after I reloaded my save - others who encountered this particular bug apparently had to reset the level so I'm happy with my experience. No serious negatives that jump out at me. The fact that you can’t heal more than your latest injury using magic is fine, but only once I got used to that. Players of SRR beware, magic is no longer a cure-all. Always keep med-kits. I feel the game doesn’t communicate this change well enough. Or it did and I wasn’t paying attention :/
Two weeks after finishing it, I'm still thinking about how good it was and how sad I was to leave my persona behind when the story ended. If that's not a sign of how good it felt to walk those streets then I don't know what is.

This game is a hidden gem on Steam.
Let me start by saying I'm not a fan of the Steam review system. Quite often you see reviews from people with less than 1 hour in a game and whether positive or negative there's just no way that review is accurate. There's also the possibility of abuse and I think most of us have seen that as well. It's just not a trustworthy way of knowing whether a game has value or not. Playtime versus Price. That's the best way to judge a game imo. As you can see from my hours played this game has that in abundance.
World Boxing Manager is a simple yet addictive, old school feel, text based game. It's not easy to understand when you begin but it's not that difficult to figure out before long. It doesn't have shiny graphics or anything 3D. It's not going to set the world on fire either and I'll admit, I doubted the game when I began playing. For $5 I figured it wouldn't be that good and that carried over into the first couple of hours playtime. I was wrong. It's a really good game and it's certainly worth the price being asked.
If I had one complaint it would be the lack of a tutorial, but that's certainly not enough reason to dislike the game. It has a "Help" page but it's lacking. Other than that the game really doesn't have any glaring flaws. The fight engine is excellent. The training system is good. The matchmaking system is good. The marketing system is excellent. The fight instructions are good and seem to work properly. All in all everything works great for a text based game. The biggest problem is those things aren't explained very well on the Help page. Hopefully Aggroblakh will address this issue but either way, everything functions well once you understand how they work and it makes for a lot of fun.
Anyway, I believe WBM is well worth the small price being asked. For $5 it's a steal. Thanks, and good gaming.

Soviet Monsters: Ekranoplans is a simulation and strategy game developed by Santa's & Co. and published by Merge Games and IV Productions. It was released in July 2016. You, the player, own a historical Russian ekranoplan and you use it to complete missions. The simulation tag is through you controlling your ekranoplan to complete missions whereas the strategy aspect is through hiring crew members, purchasing equipment, and regularly monitoring both.
The idea for the game of owning an ekranoplan, controlling it, and then playing it was a very neat idea on paper, but fails in execution. Its lack of polish and abundance of issues screams unfinished development. For instance, there is no in-game options menu, instead the options menu is displayed prior to launching the game. Furthermore, the max resolution is 1680x1050, which is a big issue because the text within the game goes off the screen. That affects mission briefings because each mission has requirements, for instance, you need five soldiers, two pilots, and so forth, so with the unclear text, you cannot see the full requirements to launch a mission.
My main issue lies in the lack of explanation of informing the player what you need to do, what is the objective, and how do you play the game. For instance, it is unclear on how to operate the ekranoplan, specifically, explanation on buttons such as the one that lifts your ekranoplan. In saying that, the game does feature a tutorial, but it is very basic and mostly unhelpful. To showcase its unfinished state, the game has no save game feature which is a nuisance because missions are lengthy and you cannot leaving unless you want to restart. Furthermore, Soviet Monsters has placeholder filler text such as 'dddd' instead of the names of cargo.
The gameplay within this is not much better at all. The controls are very buggy and unresponsive. Driving the ekranoplan is mostly difficult because the controls have a delayed response, which means it's quite difficult to turn. Not all of the models are difficult, but the majority are. You can enable your ekranoplan to rapidly increase its speed and fly, but it is embarrassing because you are not going far up into the air, you are barely off the water. Finally, with no save games creates a very frustrating experience because if you turn off your ekranoplan prematurely for any reason, it glitches by massively swaying, or alternatively, goes into a rampage which means you cannot control it and essentially you have to restart the mission.
Soviet Monsters has subpar performance. On my PC, the game on average uses 20% of your CPU and 2,000mb of memory, making my PC run loud. This may be an early-release thing, but it's not the worst thing to happen to this game. Loading times for missions are quite lengthy at about thirty seconds, which if you have to frequently restart due to the issues causes frustration. But hey, this game uses unity and the Internet states the engine sucks. In saying all this, I can sustain a solid FPS over 50 for the most part. Overall, the performance in its current state is not that good but it’s a fresh breathe of air considering the issues that plague the game.
The game is not terrible as it seems as it does have some positives. Notably, the game features very nicely designed ekranoplans. It also features a fine looking environment that has quality water and random weather effects. So, each level could either be sunny, snowing, night time, and so forth. These weather effects really do complement the landscape when you complete a mission, however, these weather effects significantly hit FPS by making the game regularly stutter. If a mission is sunny, you can look at the scenery and design of the ekranoplan through various solid camera angles. If a mission is at night time, you cannot see the long distance but you can get some slick graphics that showcase the night environment. There are various ekranoplans and all have different abilities such as accelerating faster, carrying more cargo, higher top speed, and so forth. It's nothing big but it adds some variety to the game. In saying that, it is odd the player has access to the very best ekranoplans  instead of an unlocking system that would have been preferred in this type of game.
Soviet Monsters: Ekranoplans is a very poor game in an unfinished state. It features a profound amount of issues, particularly in the UI and gameplay components. It has a lack of features to help explain and progress in the game such as a very basic tutorial and no save game features. The performance is mediocre as I can manage to have a stable 50FPS, but weather affects dramatically reduce FPS and loading times are long. Soviet Monsters' primary feature is the variety of ekranoplans that are strongly designed and very detailed. I believe early access would have ensured a much more stable release because I was disappointed in my play through of it. At USD$12.74, I cannot recommend this in its current state.
Rating: 3/10
- Very detailed ekranoplans.
- A solid landscape and impressive weather effects.
- A very buggy and unpolished game.
- Lack of features, such as no save game.
- Somewhat un-optimised performance.
- Long loading times.
- Very basic tutorial.

The problem with steam's review system is that it is binary. You either recommend a game or you don't, which leads to hard decisions with games that live in the limbo of mediocrity between the two.
<Pro/con list in the end if you prefer a TL;DR thing>
So, about the game itself.
First of all, you should disregard at least half of my playtime, since I've left the game running while studying and used it as a short break. This is important for what i'm about to say: the main problem with gems of war is that it doesn't have a good endgame content, it eventually gets ultra repetitive and pointless.
"Wait, what? There are several people here with hundreds of hours of playtime!" Yeah, and that is unexplainable for me too.
When I started gow and I saw the blend between card game and rpg I've got really hooked and hyped. There were thousand of things to do, learn and collect and a grinding that could lead you for powerful upgrades so I thought: "I'm gonna love this!" And I was right for a while, I really did love the beginning! It succeeded in making me want to get better and try new things all the time.
But it decays. After 40-50 hours you will have (easily) learned everything you need to know in the game and you will eventually build decks that can win most of the ""pvp"" (huge quotation marks here) matches of the top rank.
And that is where the game dies.
I mean, what is left to do? Sure, you can keep improving super slowly by winning pvp matches and waiting for a new week to get a bunch of guild task rewards, but what's the point? Winning the same pvp matches you already do easier? So there is your endgame: You get even stronger that you already are while you keep trying new decks that are more or less the same thing (I will get to that).
But that isn't all, that are other problems:
The quests -- The quest are boring, uninstersting, painfully long and, again, pointless. Since almost nobody uses the hero in their decks, there is no real reason to keep getting classes. And even if you do want a specific combination with the hero in a certain class, just aim for the one you need.
The AI/gameplay -- The AI is super stupid and easy to fool, I've lost the count of how many games I've won by letting it hit me with skulls while filling my mana, or knowing that it would go for a specific gem match that would help me in the next turn. And I won't even mention the frustrating luck based games, because several people already did.
The pvp -- It isn't a pvp, you will be playing the same stupid AI formerly mentioned while always having the huge advantage of starting the game.
The troops combinations -- You want to win, right? Everyone does. So that is why everyone usess more or less the same things in pvp. You will be facing all the time the same three things: The-class-of-the-week-with-super-upgrades team or the Flux-control-team-that-creates-a-bunch-of-gems-in-order-to-maintan-their-turn-while-attacking-with-some-op-cards and finally the brute-force-deck-that-just-puts-a-bunch-of-op-cards-together-without-any-sinergy-but-it-works-anyway-cause-they-are-really-op.
In the end of the day, GoW isn't a horrible game. It has its goods and it is fun until you master it, but would I recommend it to a friend?
No.

Alien Rage: Unlimited claimed to be the old school shooter that fans had been dying to play since the days of last unreal tournament unfortunately it didn't live up to it's name. The game was critically thrashed by every major reviewer and certainly didn't get the attention it truly deserved and same goes for all the titles developed by City Interactive. However it isn't a bad game, and certainly doesn't deserve  1's, 2's and 0's.
Alien Rage is a very fun and fast paced first person shooter. It looks beautifull, something that we can say for all the games created by CT Interactive. The game relies heavily on running and guning system and you have to make sure you are constantly moving otherwise the enemies will put you down, explosions look sick and pop ups appear every now and then to remind you of your badassery level (UUULTRAA COMBO!, KILLING SPREE!, EXPLOSIVE KILLS, 5 x Explosive KILLS.........u get the idea). It certainly isn't a walk in the park type of experience, the games lowest difficulty is Hard, so u are going to die ''A LOT". Enemy AI is somewhat smart I'll say. They will get behind covers, give suppressing fire, so that the others can get an advantage over you and force you to find cover as soon as possible, the enemy will often try to flank you by cloaking and then stunning you. The gameplay feels solid every gun has a distinct taste to it that makes them unique, each gun is also equipped with a unique alternate firing mode which further adds and expands your alien killing arsenal. The game has a decent amount of guns, the game also introduces new enemy types from time to time to keep things interesting. the boss battles are also somewhat well done, each boss battle requires you to be fast and to be on your toes, if you rely on cover too much you will die, if you don't take cover you will die, so act smart strike at the best time and then move your♥♥♥♥♥away from the enemy and repeat. Some of the boss battles also require you to shoot specific parts of their body  in order to bring them down. The game unlike old school FPS games features your standard ADS and regenerating health, something that everyone complains, but I simply have no issues with it. The game isn't long but has replay value, you can find hidden audio logs, complete some in game challenges to set your score on the leaderboards.
Despite it's best efforts, there are a lot of issues with the game, something I can see that might have played a huge role in earning this game 2's and 3's. There are tonnes of bugs, from occasional crashing to broken level design.....you name it, this game has it......sometimes the doors won't open preventing you from advancing, the bosses become invincible, explosive containers go missing from the level which result in you dying all the time no matter how many headshots you score and all of these issues require a restart. There was this one section where you were on a moving tram with a minigun and you had to stop enemies from killing you untill you reached your destination, but after dying once in the level, I retried but found that the explosive containers had all gone and I literally had to deal with everyone of them individually which resulted in me dying all the time and requiring me to restart the game. The game has weird texture issues and the framerate drops like♥♥♥♥♥♥during intense firefights. The game also has a very poor sense of explosion radius, if an enemy is firing rockets at you and you are standing behind a metal wall, which is thick as F**k, you'll still take the same amount of damage as you would have if it hit you directly to your face,  if an explosion takes palce meters away from your cover u still take tonnes of damage, instantly killing you in the process and in the worst case scenario u end up throwing your controller through the window. This issue makes bossfights feel like pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ The game also has a very weird framerate lock in it's multiplayer part and it just doesn't feel as fast as the main campaign. You character can't jump more than two inches in campaign but can seriously parkour it's way through in the multiplayer. It's issues like this that pulled alien rage back from easily becoming the old school shooter we always wanted.
It has a nice touching story in which it eventually tells the player to go fk themselves because they were expecting one

Pick it up during a sale. It's above average but in no sense deserves 2's. It will keep you engaged in it's explosive combat if you know your way around the multiple game breaking bugs it will thow at you.

THE GOOD
-Shooting feels great. The pistol, in particular, is awesome and a huge amount of fun to use.
-OK weapon variety
-You can move quickly
THE BAD
-Entirely linear. There are a few times when it opens up into slightly larger rooms but they are still just rooms with one entrance and one exit.
-Monotonous visual design, which makes it even more boring. The visual design in a game can sometimes alleviate the boredom brought on by linearity, but here every level looks the same, which makes it worse.
-Frequent bad checkpointing. The game itself isn't as hard as it's cracked up to be. I played it on the easiest difficulty because I had heard the hype about how hard it is, and that was a mistake. I didn't die that much. Most bosses I didn't die at all. (The game wasn't compelling enough for me to give it another playthrough on a higher difficulty.) However, when I did die, I usually re-spawned right back into the middle of a firefight and immediately died again before I was able to get to cover. C'mon developers, checkpoint placing is a really basic thing, how did you screw it up?
-There just isn't enough playstyle variety to make the Bulletstorm-esque style points system interesting. You can get headshots, explosion kills, and kill streaks. That's it. If you're going to make a style points system in your game you have to at least give you more than two basic combat methods.
-Terrible performance. I have an i5-3470, GTX 970, 16GB ram, and a 144Hz monitor. On medium/high settings I can sometimes get 144 FPS solid, but at other times it tanks down to 40 FPS for no apparent reason. Even locked 144 FPS or locked 60 FPS feels pretty bad and stuttery, so it seems like the game has wildly erratic frame times. Games should feel smooth at 60+ FPS and when they don't that's because the game engine blows at regulating frame time varience, which is pretty basic stuff for any competent developer.
Overall it's just got too many problems to recommend. If not for the performance issues, I would recommend it as a sub-$5 buy for FPS fans as it's a decent enough mindless romp, but the performance problems are unpleasant enough to put it solidly in the "don't buy" category.

I...really don't like this game, Firstly, I won't go into the graphics quality, it's an older game and technical limitations wouldn't have let the team make something comparable to today, but a good story, game mechanics, etc can overcome that easily.
You start off listening to three people talk about nothing and then choose to play as someone, you're given a couple paragraphs of backstory and treated to a long scene where the camera goes close up on a dozen different people just standing around not saying anything, it explained nothing and made me feel like I was just wasting time. You are then tossed into a situation that has you investigating stuff(entirely through talking to npcs, for at least an hour), memorizing terminology, and forced dialog that often doesn't make sense(I chose the Bachelor, after hearing that a guy he never met and was skeptical about died, he starts swearing vengeance and being as melodramatic as possible, it was fully over the top), with no investment in the events going on around you.  None of the characters are interesting, and sometimes seem to reply to your questions with something off topic(With one woman, she says she hasn't been feeling well and thinks she may be dying, I said she's probably just tired/exhausted, she immediately agrees that some flowers are in bloom, which I didn't mention at all), almost always with cryptic nonsense and loads of jargon that isn't explained, by the time a character redirected me to another character which redirected me to another character in an unskippable chain of boring useless hard to follow dialog for the 7th time, I just had to stop playing.
There's no tutorial or even just a little pop-up page explaining controls and what you can do, I was told by an early npc that people won't like it if I commit theft, but won't care if I just don't get caught, of the 10 buildings I entered while playing there was only one interactable object, an empty drawer, despite a dozen identical drawers littered around, silver goblets and plates, food, books, and more, I couldn't do a thing with them, so I honestly don't understand what the guy was talking about.
One of the reasons I bought this was the many reviews praising the excellent sound design, I can say with absolute sincerity that the sound is garbage, the song playing while you're wandering around is alright, until it gets to one high point, and it just keeps going up until it's a high pitched screech that literally hurt my ears, I'm not using that figuratively, I had to remove my headphones after the third time I heard that part of the song because it was causing aching pain, the voice acting ranges from uninspired to awkward, with Maria Kain being especially terrible, she sounds like a goth girl forced into reading off a school play. On the note of voice acting, why is there no option for subtitles? The voices often don't match the dialog screen at the bottom, or will take place outside of the dialog, not bothering to include the subtitles seems like an oversight.
Hey, maybe half the stuff that irked me isn't a problem later in the game, but I can tell you that the first hour and a half was enough of a boring slog to keep me from playing any further.

Fatalistic themes, a lingering sense of dread, and quite the long walk.
+The atmosphere is top-notch. You're in an uphill battle, and almost everything in this version works to the benefit of the product.
+Better translation. --While infamous for its creepily pseudo-english start, I much prefer this translation. It conveys the tone and overall theme a bit better, in a digestible format.
+If you enjoy a good book, or can get engrossed in a story, this's for you. The main actors in this 'play' are fleshed out to a pretty insightful extent, reflecting the complexities of the noble (Or 'tribal') classes (Or 'castes') in this foreign, alien setting.
-The game itself suffers from some design flaws from the get-go, unless my drivers and cards are working against me, environmental lighting occasionally flickers violently in the worst possible situation.
-The combat. It would be gloriously brutal if it were more... Streamlined. (Not arguing to be MORE combat-oriented, but flow better.)
-Certain points of the plot need to be explained better to avoid confusion. (Such as when you're Daniil, and suddenly no-one is giving you the option to take their blood sample because you spoke to someone for just a moment.)
I will admit that replaying this game is quite... Hard. You know certain twists are coming, and you know how things work. I bought this remake on steam to see the better translation and what was changed.
Same game, better skin, better writing. I bought this to support the devs, they did great. Looking forward to the remake.

So the world is open, which in my opinion is almost always a plus. However, some would argue that the world is not a vast as some other titles. But when one considers the entire game is spent traveling by foot and time is the most important resource in the game then I think most would agree that the map is a good size for the circumstances. Which leads me to atmosphere. Each area is fairly unique. The industrial district, the warehouses, the centre of town, etc. Each area is recognizable and everything fits into a sort of Gothic Nightmare theme. That being said the graphics are very dated. I'm not the kind to argue that they may or may not be good for the time it was made. They are objectively bad compared to the moderns standard. Not that big deal to me, but it is something worth mentioning.
Then there are the mechanics. The game provides some very interesting mechanics. They change depending on the circumstances, so I'll mention them by the status of a particular district.
If a district is healthy then you have the ability to break into houses and steal from the people inside. The system is very straight forward. You find a cabinet. You steal stuff. Nobody sees you, you leave. If someone sees you they attack you. You move in for a hit, punch, back off, repeat ad infinitum. It get's fairly tedious. Plus if you hit a citizen you lose reputation, which if it gets low enough the people in the streets will attack you and store keepers won't do business with you. If you kill them your reputation is hurt even worse. That being said the act of stealing doesn't affect you reputation and when you break into a house you can walk around the people inside and they don't react at all unless they witness you stealing. How realistic. But outside at night and in the early morning you will run into bandits. They will almost always throw their knife which is almost an inevitable one hit kill unless you bought the right clothes and have full hp. Good thing there is auto save and quick save. Otherwise fighting is the same as with citizens except you take more damage for each hit. You can even the odds by having a knife or scalpel as a weapon, or even a shotgun, revolver, or rifle if you're lucky. Note that all weapons degrade as you use them, which you have to pay to have repaired. Killing a bandit gives good reputation which means you could effectively be the town's worse serial killer and everyone still like you because you murder a few “bad guys” as well.
If you're in an infected district you can give medicine to certain sick people for good reputation or get a hug of death from one of the various roaming infected. Hurt one and loose reputation. Plus sentient clouds of disease will attack you trying to get you infected. And rats will do the same except they will chase you forever, or until you go in a building. Which you shouldn't because in the houses you will be chased by a cloud of disease in a confined space. That being said you can loot the houses still. I guess that's a plus.
The day after a district is infected it will cease to be infected and be perfectly safe, except the streets and houses will be filled with various thugs. But you can loot the houses to your hearts content as long as you have a gun and the ability reflexes to kill the spider bandits inside.
All the time you have to manage your hunger, exhaustion, health, and degree to which you are infected. As a note you can get through the game with out ever being infected. Plus everyday you have tasks to complete or one of your friends will inexplicably fall ill and then you can't get the “good ending”.
Now I'll talk about the learning curve. I can't do it justice. It can be baffling hard for no reason. Like I said before, the towns people can hate you so much they try to murder you in the street. And they will chase you forever unless you go in a building. Not to mention that you might not know what your daily objective is and spend all day wandering around just to fail you're daily task. Eventually you get use to the combat and it is easy to maintain a good reputation, but it is frustrating to get to that point
Finally there is the story. There are three characters you can play as, each with unique abilities and stories that intersect. But after that there isn't really any re-playability. However, they add up to around a seventy five to maybe a hundred hours. I don't really know because I haven't finished the last scenario for one very good reason. The writing. The game is Russian originally and so the English version is a translation. It's not bad per say. But it is boring. I normally like reading, but the writing for this game is more than I can handle. And I'm not sure I understand the whole story even, because it is so difficult to read every single thing said in order to piece together the puzzle of what's happening. What little I understand is very interesting though. It really is. But I constantly have this nagging feeling that I don't get it all.
So in conclusion to a review that is way to long to begin with, no I would not recommend this game. I really like the game and see enormous potential. But I feel it isn't executed well. Yes it is cheap and if you even vaguely want to buy it and experience it for yourself, then do so. Especially if it's on sale. But I can not in good faith recommend it as it really is a niche game for people who can overlook glaring problems in order to see something different from the norm. That being said, there is a “remake” in the works coming out in 2017 and I have a lot of hope from what little of it I've seen.

Admittedly, it is not an easy game to play. It can be hard to know exactly what to do and where to go, there's a lot of walking across the city and it has a narrative-induced time limit. Some might say it has dated visuals (which I personally love). But despite all of this, Pathologic has a magic-realism tale of murder, corruption and disease worthy of classic Russian literature status wrapped in an ambitious, unique first-person adventure.

Pathologic is a strange game to me, mainly due to how much of a game it's not, yet it still kept me engrossed in things.
First off, if you're expecting a game with indepth survival mechanics, dynamic gameplay, or high-paced action, you're looking in the wrong place. Playing this game is fairly agonizing. Movement is slow, combat is shallow and clunky, and the game loves ambushing you with rude spawns. I think the worst bit however is how this game doesn't tell you any of the important♥♥♥♥♥♥ Letters, which tell you where to look for quests and clues, is bound to L yet you are never outright told about this or even hinted to that at all. Along with that, you are only given vague hints about things such as your quest log, status menu, and the weird trade economy that you need to work with in order to survive. From a mechanical standpoint, this game is busted as hell.
That being said, this story is absolutely fascinating and does a great job at weaving together plot, lore and drama together in a dynamic manner. The game revolves around a small town that is struck by a debilitating plague, and its up to three totally different types of "healers" to save this town from the Sand Plague. While this sounds like a very innocuous and tame adventure, the sheer amount of detail IPL puts into Town-Along-the-Gorkhon is fascinating and helps with player immersion to a staggering degree. The game's world has an indepth culture, religion, economy, working-class economy, among many other small things you don't see in games that help the Town-Along-the-Gorkhon feel less like a videogame town and more like a dynamic world. Another great thing about the plot is that one character doesn't see everything; Each character represents both a kind of difficulty modifier but also a different viewpoint of the scenario: For example, Bachelor Dankovsky sees the town as just a mass of people, buildings, & ideals and seeks to find a rational cure for it all; meanwhile Artemy the Haruspex was born in this town, understands its culture and people, and uses this old knowledge to cure the "organism" that is the town itself. Sadly the end-state is roughly the same for all three paths, but its fascinating to see how each viewpoint varies in their approach and standing within the town.
tl;dr, Pathologic classic ver. is the most interesting and agonizing game you will ever play. Its not for everyone, but if you're willing to suffer through the painful entry barrier, you'll find a fascinating story.

Shadowrun is a solid RPG that is good throughout, with rare moments of greatness.
I played through the game on "hard" and think that is what most players will want to set it through. The combat system is a turned based strategy deal, but the tactical aspect isn't anything that is going to give anyone a headache. Keep your guys spaced out to avoid eating grenades, buff your main attackers with the aim bonus and haste and then shoot/punch everyone. The cover based/RNG system for hitting is rather bogus... you can have someone with a shotgun miss four times in a row from two meters away because the guy is kneeling behind a potted plant for instance. But as you go along, you'll figure out who to buff and blaze through most fights without much trouble.
The story meanwhile is good and interesting. The world of Shadowrun is a weird sort of 'Okay let's do everything then' kind of world, with magic, hackers and sorcery. But the story is consistent and rich enough for you to sort of get immersed in the world. It has some issues though...
First:
The game tries to get you to make moral choices, usually involving how merciless you want to be. There are some interesting choices in here, particularly when the game pits your professionalism as a Shadow Runner against your morality (kill this guy in cold blood or botch the job, deliver the cyborg guy with no free will or free him). But that sort of thing leads to a bit of ludonarrative dissonance when on any given job you kill about 100 ordinary security guard dudes. Why's it only a dramatic moral choice when the dialogue box opens? Why doesn't my character ever agonize over whether or not killing Bob the Security Dude is the right thing to do?
I feel that if a game wants to make keeping blood off your hands a major thing, then it should be a part of regular gameplay (a la Deus Ex), rather than just making it so that you are only concerned with NPCs with a name.
Second:
The game maybe presumes that you know more about this universe than someone who is first encountering it now would. There are a bunch of big choices involving dragons in this thing, but I never really had any idea what would be a good choice because my character had never met a Shadowrun dragon and was basically guessing what might be the best thing to do. Perhaps that is 'realistic', but I feel that the game needed to spend more time showing and not telling.
Third:
I hate that there's a four person cap on missions. When you're on a final mission where your team is making a last ditch heroic effort, it makes no sense that the fifth person is chilling in the van.
These quibbles aside, it's a solid game with some truly excellent stories. Glory's side mission in particular was quite fascinating I have to say.
I'll look forward to playing sequels.

This game is relentlessly grim, and I mean "grim" in the sense it's hard to feel good while playing. The whole game sees you pushed around like a dumb animal and no matter who you work for you're as welcome as the plague. The "buddies" are harsh too. There are very few innocents and no sympathies to be won. Everyone dislikes you.  This was a notable thing for me because I questioned many times what the hell was motivating my character to continue on with his task.  Every single person was unpleasant and ready to kill me if not actually pulling the trigger the instant I was even slightly visible.
The game starts out promising with unbelievably pretty visuals and an enormously strong appreciation for the real-ness of the landscape. The open world presentation is extremely compelling and made me want to go out and explore and admire everywhere, but it's nigh impossible to trave0l more than 2 minutes without being harassed by gunfire. There's no avoiding it either because while you can jitty-bop around trying to explore things (river travel is safest) the game requires you to backtrack through all of creation in order to perform certain missions or find the hidden gems needed to upgrade your weapons.  If the game were short or linear this might not be a problem but it ruins the sense of freedom since it kills your desire to go anywhere when the journey is a constant unyielding grind.  You can't even floor it and speed past the patrol stations in the hopes of actually making fast progress to your ultimate destination because inevitably some crazed vehicle will give chase and follow you FAR beyond all reasonable distances, and even if you manage to avoid the patrol stations there's still the chance you'll encounter a random vehicle and be locked into escape mode yet again.  There is satisfaction to be had if you've got a grenade launcher armed vehicle because you can vent your frustrations into the enemy when the umpteenth chase occurs, but really, it happens SO OFTEN that it just becomes tiresome.
Despite that the game does have some rewarding combat shooting, a good driving experience, and a nice treasure hunt mechanic. It's such a pity that the fun to be found is mired in a frustrating slog of irritation.

They Breathe seems almost simple and cute upon initial inspection - it is anything but. The game paints a macabre view of an ecosystem gone awry, and you are tasked (as a frog) to discover its secret. It is a short game, but the atmosphere leaves a lasting impression on the player. From its saccharine looking main screen you may be deceived into thinking that this isn't a horror game, but that soon changes as you delve deep into the pond you are forced to explore. When you realize the true reality of the protagonist's new environment and the enemies you encounter, you are left with a deep seated uneasiness.   There is a bit of replayability with attempting to get achievements, but this game isn't anything more than a well written horror short story. Paying $2 to be left wholly unsettled and unnerved by such a short and simple game is a fair trade.

Story? Nah. Beautiful graphics? Eh. Repetitive? Yeah.
Awesome gameplay? Hard as nails difficulty? Yesss. This game is awesome fun. A little hard to get into, pretty slow to start, but once you gather a few upgrades, you're set. In Far Cry 2, you are not a badass murder machine who roams the lands with impunity. You are a malaria infected loner who prefers to wage gun battles with rusty pistols which explode on short notice while popping pills like candy when the fever strikes.
If taken at face value, the game would be fairly boring. A large varied world with not a lot in it, lots of bad guys to shoot, a few collectibles. What it is, though, is an extremely immersive battle simulator. The AI is great, the gunplay is quite fun, the weapon jams add depth and unpredictability, and the amount of ways you can enter an encampment and ruin the mercenaries' day are many.
When someone watched over my shoulder as I played, he said it was like watching an action movie. It's like that. It's tense, precise, and satisfying, and at higher difficulties, brutally decisive. You won't play it for the story. The characters are two-dimensional, all of them inhabit little huts where they spout exposition and then send you on another kill all the peoples mission. You almost make your own story in the playing of this game. With no HUD and a sprawling savannah, Far Cry 2 will suck you in if you let it.
It's a dangerous world. Bring your machete.

The problem with steam's review system is that it is binary. You either recommend a game or you don't, which leads to hard decisions with games that live in the limbo of mediocrity between the two.
<Pro/con list in the end if you prefer a TL;DR thing>
So, about the game itself.
First of all, you should disregard at least half of my playtime, since I've left the game running while studying and used it as a short break. This is important for what i'm about to say: the main problem with gems of war is that it doesn't have a good endgame content, it eventually gets ultra repetitive and pointless.
"Wait, what? There are several people here with hundreds of hours of playtime!" Yeah, and that is unexplainable for me too.
When I started gow and I saw the blend between card game and rpg I've got really hooked and hyped. There were thousand of things to do, learn and collect and a grinding that could lead you for powerful upgrades so I thought: "I'm gonna love this!" And I was right for a while, I really did love the beginning! It succeeded in making me want to get better and try new things all the time.
But it decays. After 40-50 hours you will have (easily) learned everything you need to know in the game and you will eventually build decks that can win most of the ""pvp"" (huge quotation marks here) matches of the top rank.
And that is where the game dies.
I mean, what is left to do? Sure, you can keep improving super slowly by winning pvp matches and waiting for a new week to get a bunch of guild task rewards, but what's the point? Winning the same pvp matches you already do easier? So there is your endgame: You get even stronger that you already are while you keep trying new decks that are more or less the same thing (I will get to that).
But that isn't all, that are other problems:
The quests -- The quest are boring, uninstersting, painfully long and, again, pointless. Since almost nobody uses the hero in their decks, there is no real reason to keep getting classes. And even if you do want a specific combination with the hero in a certain class, just aim for the one you need.
The AI/gameplay -- The AI is super stupid and easy to fool, I've lost the count of how many games I've won by letting it hit me with skulls while filling my mana, or knowing that it would go for a specific gem match that would help me in the next turn. And I won't even mention the frustrating luck based games, because several people already did.
The pvp -- It isn't a pvp, you will be playing the same stupid AI formerly mentioned while always having the huge advantage of starting the game.
The troops combinations -- You want to win, right? Everyone does. So that is why everyone usess more or less the same things in pvp. You will be facing all the time the same three things: The-class-of-the-week-with-super-upgrades team or the Flux-control-team-that-creates-a-bunch-of-gems-in-order-to-maintan-their-turn-while-attacking-with-some-op-cards and finally the brute-force-deck-that-just-puts-a-bunch-of-op-cards-together-without-any-sinergy-but-it-works-anyway-cause-they-are-really-op.
In the end of the day, GoW isn't a horrible game. It has its goods and it is fun until you master it, but would I recommend it to a friend?
No.
TL;DR PRO/CON LIST:
PROS:
- Not a p2w game. You can obtain everything that is on the store.
- Fun and engaging in the beginning.

- It is easy to master, in my opinion, but the game does reward intelligence.
CONS:

- Same ideas in troop combinations all the time with just different cards.

I loved the original Defense Grid (DG1), spending well over 100 hours in that game.  While not as enjoyable as the first game, I do recommend Defense Grid 2 (DG2).
One of the strangest decisions for DG2 was an attempt to create more of a "story."  The story in DG1 was basically non-existent: Aliens want the cores, kill the aliens.  However, when I played DG1, I never felt that there was a need for more story (is there need for a story in a tower defense game?).  The developers added additional AI characters for DG2, most of which are really annoying, and I think, detract from the quality of the game.
I also prefer the scoring system in DG1 over DG2.  In DG1, you got a slight trickle of resources automatically, which increased with the more overall resources you had.  For every alien you killed you gained more resources, and killing them inside of a command tower netted you additional resources.  There was a definite strategy to this scoring system.  Do I upgrade this tower now, or do I hold off so I can gain more "interest?"  DG2 simply gives you a steady amount of resources, regardless of killing the aliens.  This definitely removes a great deal of tension from the gameplay.
With these complaints aside, I still think this is a solid game that is worth your time.  If you liked DG1, you will probably like DG2.  I would give it a 7.5/10.

I will recommend this game but cautiously. It is fun, it does come with a large selection of tower choices, has controller support, it is local co-op (with controller support) and it does have two parts to it's campaign. It does fall a bit short in keeping the gamer's attention.
Cannon Brawl brings a new sort of game style to the table. Similar to Castle Storm (which is also a good game), Cannon Brawl's purpose is to destroy the opponents castle. Unlike Castle Storm (which has it's own rooms to upgrade weapons), CB doesn't allow you to see into your castle or upgrade a javelin like device to take out your opponent. What you are working with though is a hero (of your choice after completing a bit of the campaign) where each hero have their own special ability (such as one hero heals towers when in proximity). The approach the game has taken towards commanding ones towers is quite admirable.
In fact, it's what probably separates the game from being another boring Castle VS Castle type game. Unlike Castle Storm where you can summon and control your hero, you are ALWAYS in control of your hero. The hero flies through the air to either build new structures or command a tower. Before building anything, the hero needs to grab territory VIA using hot air balloons. When these balloons are placed, the player may build within the vicinity. The balloons also provide extra protection as they can take a hit instead of a bullet or bomb hitting your tower. Gold is the currency used by the game to build new towers on the landscape. To acquire gold (or diamonds), the player must build a gold mine on top of either element. Diamonds may not be available to build on and the player may have to shoot away at the ground to properly expose them. Upon acquiring enough currency, the player may build a tower. These towers (to name a few) come in form of a simple cannon tower, a rocket tower (which shoots out a grouped rocket which then spreads out), a shield tower (to protect from nasty air assaults), a laser/rail gun tower, a bomb tower that launches a walking bomb, and a bank tower that can bribe one of your opponents towers to take it over.
I haven't mentioned all the towers but there are quite a bit to choose from. There is a key combination I found that usually leads me to victory using the gold mines, shields, rocket and laser tower accordingly. Some towers have adverse effects such as using a laser tower against a shield tower. If the laser does fire onto a shield, the shield will rebound the laser in another direction. If you fire in the wrong direction or angle, you can expect a shot going back your way eating away at the ground and dropping your tower from an obscene height leading to destruction. All towers are available for upgrade and make the game even more interesting. I have mentioned that the ground can be blown up as seen in Worms Armageddon. This is a great feature to the game and really makes you think of the locations regarding gun placements.
Visuals are suited to the games cartoon atmosphere. The effects after something blows up or when something hits a shield is visually apparent. The sounds are equally as good as they reflect exactly what you are doing whether it's flying, shooting, or defending. The music is enjoyable and the menus are presented extremely well. If you can find local co-op easily, you know you've got a good interface. Navigating the campaign mode is done on a giant map. There two levels to choose from as you progress : the next mission and puzzle levels. Puzzle levels can be survival to trick shots.
Overall, a good game but not worth it's stated price. Even when it was on sale I was still on the fence. I do enjoy the game and come back to it here and there, but once you've had your fill or have beaten all there is to beat, you may not like it anymore. I definitely enjoyed my time playing it.
