First, let me get this out of the way: NOTHING, EVER, in the computer gaming world will EVER be exactly like a real life analog pinball machine. There is no way to 100% digitize the analog workings of pinball games, EVER.
With that said, this game gives us a very good digital representation of the real life tables. It's not perfect, but it's very close. It's close enough that I don't even notice the difference. There are probably some minor glitches but I haven't personally noticed them. The tables can be expensive though, at $5 per table, or buy the table packs to save some money. You DO, however, get a free table, which to me is still one of my favorite tables to play: The Tales of the Arabian Nights. The tables are a little pricey to purchase, but I understand there are licensing fees I'm sure they're paying, plus the work that goes into each individual table, so I don't complain THAT much about it.
One thing I do like is, before you buy a table, you can play any of the tables you like for free, to see if you will even like that table or not. You just can't play for a high score, but you can see if you will even like the table so you don't have to buy the table blindly.
Another thing that's great here is that for each table, there is a menu option that explains in detail how that particular machine works, what the objectives are, and how to score maximum points on it. It helps to know what you are trying to do on each table, and they outline each objective very well.
I do wish the interface while selecting a table was a little bit better, but it's a minor complaint, as I don't play this game for the interface.
All in all, I definitely like this one, and suggest you give it a try. It's great to play some of my favorite real life tables: Whirlwind, Tales of the Arabian Nights, The Addams Family, Star Trek, etc and have it look and feel a lot like the real thing. I feel like they spent a lot of time on each table to get it to act just like the real life analog tables, or as close as possible. Just be prepared to spend some money if you want to have a high score on your favorite tables.

I admit my expectations may have been high, but the main thing this game has going for it are its graphics and unique surreal Asian / Eastern locales. However, in motion the animations and gameplay can be quite clunky.
The game itself is obviously an homage of sorts to the Souls games, however all of those (and arguably Malebolgia) are more polished than this game. It has some interesting ideas in place, including approaching enemies and NPCs in various stances / states of mind (i.e. Aggressive, Pacifist, etc..) but the game does very little (akin to Dark Souls) to explain any of these subsystems.
Certain moments look awesome, and the game functions for the most part (it is free from bugs etc..) but what is presented becomes plodding and bland. I was hoping to be interested in the locales enough to want to progress through in spite of any less than stellar gameplay, however I have to say for me that is not the case.
Unless this appears at a heavily discounted price, your money would be better spent on a Souls game on sale or perhaps even on the comparable title Malebolgia, although to give the developers of this game some credit, many more people were present on the Souls team. With more time and variation to this game to become more polished it could be awesome, but as-is I will  not be playing it anymore and wouldn't recommend others seek it out.

July update: Welp, it's July now, and Blade & Bones has seen no updates since the last one, nary a peep from the developers since the beginning of March when they responded to a thread in the forums, from what I can tell. It's hard not to assume abandonment at this point, considering the game is at below 50% positive reviews (and still riddled with crippling gameplay issues), and how up-front and transparent the developers used to be. I recommend steering clear until there's some activity, if any, on the developers' side.
One positive though: Steam reviews have been updated so when I edit my review I can indicate I got my copy for free. So, yay, or whatever.
Link to original review for posterity:
January update: I've played some more after the latest update, and I definitely wanted to get some more thoughts out there because I think the game is moving in a good direction. First, however, I want to talk about the devs themselves.
A short time after my original review went up, Coffee Addict Studio contacted me, thanking me for my review and promising that my issues were already in the process of being looked at. This immediately left a good impression upon me. Too many developers nowadays only care about those who say nice things; they want to release their games into an echo chamber where everyone tells them they did a great job. I get it: game development is difficult and everyone hates having people dump on their passion project -- but only listening to praise and ignoring criticism leads to stale, sub-par content. Coffee Addict Studio, on the other hand, is comprised of people who look at a negative review and think "How can we improve on these areas?"
is the attitude the games industry needs more of.
Not only did they keep me informed of the timeline to an update releasing, but after I explained that I'd love to try the update out but had to refund the game due to monetary issues, they even gave me a free key. (I apparently don't have the ability to now indicate that this product was received for free, though, and I didn't want to delete this review to post a new one because I think it's important to save the resultant debates and ratings this one received.)
So, in short, the developers are very kind, stand-up people with great attitudes.
That is why I wish there were more options for reviews than Thumbs Up or Thumbs Down, because...
The latest update (1.2) added several quality-of-life features that the game sorely needed: a little bit more context as to why you're searching for these seven swords (even if the story still doesn't really make sense), a small glint on the player's sword when you're able to swing again (hugely helpful, even if it would make more sense to tighten up the animations and eliminate the downtime in the combat -- but I'll get into that in a bit), and a little bit of information as to various buffs you might acquire, among other things.
These are all solid changes, no doubt about it. Unfortunately, Blade & Bones still needs more work before I can truly recommend it.
To reiterate a point I made in my original review: combat is the most important part of this game, so it's what I'll be focusing on most here. It's the activity the player will spend the most time doing, so it's
to make it satisfying. Blade & Bones 1.2 still isn't quite there yet. It's nice to now have a numerical representation of how much damage I'm doing, and the "followup-glint", as I'll call it, is a nice touch, but is more of a band-aid that somewhat masks the issue rather than solving it.
As I alluded to above, the existence of the "followup-glint" is indicative of an issue. If the animations and timing for followup attacks were more intuitive (or if there was a window, of sorts, in the animation where hitting the attack button again would trigger an attack after the current one) there would be no need for what is essentially a popup saying "You can attack again!"
The issue is that, in combat, it ends up feeling as though your character spends as much time having just attacked and waiting to attack again, as he does actually attacking / moving around. It makes the combat feel incredibly slow and pondering. This issue of "downtime" in the combat extends to when you finish your combo as well -- the Basic style doesn't really suffer from it, but using Miten almost guarantees you'll be hit once or twice. After you finish swinging, there is a period that is
where you simply can't do anything aside from swing again at the right moment. It feels like an eternity of watching your character sit in their followup pose, where you can't move or dodge or
, which is a huge problem -- issues like this cannot exist if you want combat to feel tight and refined.
You might be thinking "Well then, just use Basic, idiot!" Well, the issue with that lies at the other end of the combat cycle:
lead-up animations for either type of attack. Miten suffers from a lesser version of this, but the issue is exemplified with Basic.
So with these issues with both of the early-game Styles, combat essentially becomes a game of strafing forward until the enemy attacks, backing up out of their range (because the backstep dodge goes
), then stepping back in and stunlocking with Basic. It pains me to say it, but it's not very fun. However, without any way of blocking / parrying, it's the only option -- because every type of dodge takes you way too far out of the fight to actually be useful. Dodging in a game like Dark Souls allows you to exploit a vulnerable enemy by attacking from another angle when they've committed to an attack. Dodging in Blade & Bones simply resets the process, because you can't get back in fast enough to attack before they ready back up.
However, there is
issue: occasionally you run into enemies that primarily use quick thrusting attacks. There is no way to beat one of these enemies without taking a hit unless you get extremely lucky and they walk into your (incredibly short) attack range as you swing, despite having far superior range on their thrusts. You cannot side-strafe, because their tracking is perfect; As I said before, dodging doesn't get you anywhere, it merely resets the combat flowchart, and if you dodge past them to end up behind they will simply stab you as you roll by; you cannot hope to wind up and have them blunder into your attack range, because they can hit you from much further away; there is no option to block or parry for some reason; the best option is to tank a hit (and hope they don't do a quick double-thrust, as I've seen) and then stunlock them as best you can.
There is more, but I don't want to sit here and bash this game, and honestly I think right now bringing the combat up to snuff is the most important thing anyway. I have faith in you guys, Coffee Addict Studio. I know the passion is there and that you guys will work on this.

Blade and Bones is a 3rd person combat and metroidvania indie game with some perma-death mechanics thrown into the smoothie.
You assume the role of the last Orin Warrior in Blade and Bones.  As one of 7 godly beings, you defied Niro - the creator of the world Asocrac - and he stole your voices away in return.
You must travel the lands of Blade and Bones to find 7 ancient swords in order to restore your voices that have been lost for 700 years.
You are dumped into the world of Blade and Bones with nothing but your bare fists.  After being treated to some basic button prompt tutorials that teach the gameplay basics such as light and heavy attacks, roles and the use of signs...you bust out of that door filled with light and make your way to the main area of the game.
So you’re in charge of finding the 7 swords to restore the voices to the Orin, so where do you start?  Well...there is absolutely no context whatsoever in Blade and Bones, and thus the game starts off in this strangely obscure.  The tacky, stock green fields and sunburst background stare at you while you contemplate your options.  You’ve got a sword, there are enemies, okay great..we can start fighting stuff right?
The weapon system is a melange of strong and light attacks, rolls, signs and a few other mechanics thrown in.  For the price point, the combat is adequate but I think it could be tidied up a bit so it's more immersive.
Taking damage can be restored with life fragments collected from ancient relics, which is where you can also find additional secret weapons - these relics are often tucked away into hidden corners of the game so there is some incentive to wander off the beaten path.  However, you do want to be on your gaurd because perma-death is ever-present depending on how many lives you have in the tank.  Once it reaches 0, you’ll need to restart the game.
The most interesting, although not original, idea that Blade and Bones presents is the ability to advance time to alter the time of day.  While mildly exciting, the game does claim that many hidden shortcuts and secret passages to forbidden lands that can only be used in a right time of the day, although I haven’t found too many of these myself.
I want to quickly point out that the game performs moderately well, with some usual suspects such as minor frame rate dips and camera clipping, but overall it looks decent.  The sounds are pretty stock, but work well with the design of the game.  The developer has also added music to the game, which I've heard is very good.
So that’s pretty much the game in a nutshell, you’ll be wandering around killing♥♥♥♥♥♥ finding ancient swords and relics, and killing bosses every once in a while.  Personally, i found the experience to be a bit ordinary, although for an indie title you could certainty do much worse than Blade and Bones.
-Overall, the design is unique
-Varied and rich color palette
-Interesting backstory
-Movement feels just right
-Day/Night cycle mechanic
-Combat needs to be more 'weighty' and satisfying
-Developer needs to tidy up the responsiveness when attacking and rolling
-More exposition would be nice to give clarity to what players need to do at the start of the game
-Style system is not necessary and could have been replaced by specific weapon animation variation

This game... this game.... Where do I even begin?
A peculiar, remote steppe town is ravaged by a terrible plague. Three healers in the town strive to save its people and defeat the disease. Simple enough, right?
Wrong. With three totally different perspectives, 12 in game days to survive and solve mysteries, over 70 hours of total gameplay time, the situation is much more complicated than you think. It is not just the epidemic that has more than meets the eye, but the entire situation surrounding it. With each character, you have almost two weeks to experience their part of the story before concluding the tale with one of the toughest choices to ever make in a game.
On the surface, this game is rough, crude, illegible, and utterly alienating. With outdated graphics, mediocre mechanics, seeminly indecipherable dialogue, and the lack of a proper tutorial, this game is really hard to get into. It is not impossible to get past the initial footslog however, and once you do, you not only get used to everything, but start understanding its magnificence. It may take a while, but considering how massive the game is, only a small percentage of gameplay time will pass before you get to the diamond in the rough.
As you cut deeper, you start identifying the game's main puzzle pieces. Your understanding of the world around you begins to form definite chuncks, from what it takes to survive to understanding the lore. Eventually, you start putting things together into a bigger picture. What was once seen as disordered fragments of puzzle pieces becomes the wholesome, organic anatomy that the game truly is.
*Pros:
- Story and lore is rich, thick, and thought provoking.
- Very immersive in making you roleplay as your character, feeling the weight of the crisis on your head, and manipulating your perspective on the world around you.
- Atmosphere fits really well: bleak, strange, and surreal.
*Cons:
- Bare bones mechanics and gameplay is unflavorful and unexciting (if you ignore the story); lots of text and walking around town.
- Survival is tough and the game does not hold your hand.
*Some cons might by considered pros and vice versa.
And if you are intrigued by the story but are too discouraged due to the other factors of the game, there is a remake in the works that is bound to be a vast improvement in almost every way.

A town in the middle of nowhere, blessed with unique and almost magical architecture, ravaged by plague. The player has 12 days to stop it.  You can play as one of three main protagonists- all of whom are different from one another, yet still interact with each other throughout the game. That is, while you pick one of them, the other two will still exist within the universe and go on about their stories, sometimes even sabotaging your plans. Each of these characters have their bound- a set of important characters that support you throughout the game and are required for your victory. If you fail to complete any quest until midnight, one of them gets sick and dies. Thus, time has to be planned (and definately not wasted). Also, keep in mind that each character is harder to play (Bachelor being easiest and Changeling being the hardest).
The game has a rather large world (town) map and a large set of characters, all of whom are unique and have their own agendas. Recources are a large part of the game- exhaustion, hunger and infection. All of these will drop as time goes by and between your seemingly impossible battle against the plague, you'll have to keep a close eye on them. Reputation is also important, for if you're hated in the town, it might cause some problems.
The game is very symbolic. The best example I can give is the three protagonists- the three people that ultimately decide the town's fate. Each of them represent a different view on the world and inevitable clash against one another. Pathologic has amazing soundtrack- one of the most atmospheric soundtracks I've seen in a video game.
Another very unique thing about this game is that it always tries to hurt the player. You may find yourself in a tough spot, so I suggest keeping multiple saves so that you can restart the day if you messed something up.
Pathologic has one of the best plot twists to ever be in a video game. I will not sppoil it, but it is shocking and something you'd never expect.
All of this being said, I can come to a conclusion- this game is a masterpeace. A rather unknown masterpiece, much to my surprise. It has a huge H.P. Lovecraft vibe to it and I recommend this to anyone who likes story driven games.
Beware tho, because Pathologic can be slow and hard- at times, you can wonder around the town without any clue where to go.
Lastly, if you like action driven games and prefer mechanics over story, atmosphere and music, I would say Pathologic isn't for you.
PS: I have spent around 40 hours in the game and have completed only 1 storyline. I still have 2 characters I need to play as, so this review i based on Bachelor's story only.

The sounds of people- no wait- children, laughing in the distance. The large, glass obelisk blocking out the sky near the river at the edge of town. The dread filled streets are almost too much to bear, they make you forget that you haven’t eaten since you left the capital. The sun is going down. You only have one stale cracker and two mismatched bullets at the bottom of your empty pocket. End of day one.
The clock is ticking, Bachelor.
Tomorrow, the first man dies of the pestilence.

Ive been a fan of Shadowrun since the SNES title, even before I knew it was a tabletop RPG. After nearly 2 decades of waiting for a worthy successor to Jake Armitage's original mission, Harebrained Schemes pulls the rabbit out of the hat, only to find that its made of gemstone-encrusted gold.
Dragonfall is a fantastic tactical turn-based RPG with a great score and a storyline which will have you guessing until the end- and even then nothing is guaranteed without your own personal influence. I and my roommate both played the game through, and even though the main plot remained the same, the paths we chose and the outcome of the story based on those decisions wound up to be two completely different scenarios. With the amount of decisions that become available to you throughout the 30-ish missions depending on your stats, class, etiquette, race, ETC...this is a game with a LOT of replay value.
If you loved 'Shadowrun Returns', do yourself a favor and pick up Dragonfall- it makes 'Returns' look like a beta in regards to how much is offered as far as gameplay is concerned. If youve never played Shadowrun before, I can only describe it as "Blade Runner" meets "Lord of the Rings". How cool of a concept is that alone??
There are few things to gripe about in this game, but here are the things which I would like to see fixed:
-When you find an item you are allowed to send it to your stash (which is only accessible pre-round) or swap it with something in your inventory. However, when you hover over your inventory, no popup appears, telling you what that item is- and until youre familiar with the item icons it can be tough to judge what to keep and what to swap.
-Similarly, when you find an item, you cannot give it to a fellow teammate, even if they have inventory room...kinda sucks to find a really good grenade and then have to decide whether to swap it for one of the 5 items you can carry to battle, or just ignore it til next round because you cant offer it to someone else.
-Sometimes, AOE (area of effect) attacks will not display the targetting ring at the feet of target until you cancel the move and re-select it.
-While shifting between the Matrix and "meatspace", the music will sometimes bug out and play the wrong track, or simply stop altogether.
Small complaints, but its hard to find faults in such a great game. Dragonfall delivers a package more solid than John Holmes...I cant wait to see what theyre doing with "Hong Kong". Check this one out!!

This game is tough until you get the hang of it, but also absolutely great.  I'm only on the 2nd mission at the moment (and having difficulty getting thru the Simulations, which I'm currently attempting) -- and it took me MANY tries to get thru the first mission... but like any good platformer, keeping at it pays off and the game keeps you thinking "just one more try".
Really, Gunhound is like an awesome 16-bit era mech game... with modern design sensibilities.  You can attempt the missions individually, with the game saving in between.  There are Steam achievements (based on score) and trading cards.   And the control scheme is fully customizable for keyboard or gamepad -- and, for me, this is a game that BEGS to be played with a nice gamepad.
The only negatives I can think of at all really translate into positives for a lot of people.  The first is the difficulty, as I mentioned.  Part of this is because certain enemies and obstacles are very difficult to deal with, due to the difficulties of piloting a mech.  Also, aiming takes a bit of time to get used to, and getting the hang of the boosters.  But the control scheme really does make it seem like you're controlling a heavy mech -- and ditching your armor makes it MUCH more nimble.  In case anyone's wondering, the controls are NOT in the least unresponsive... just heavy.  The difficulty of the levels themselves is likely a positive for many people, and there IS an "Easy Mode" that you can turn on if desired.  Other than that, some people may be turned off by the fact that there's no English full-audio.  Even with all in-game text and subtitles in English, the audio tracks are in Japanese.  Personally, I don't mind this one bit and many people would probably see it as a positive -- being able to hear the original (high production value) voice-overs rather than some (potentially crappy) dub.  Lastly, and the only aspect of the game thus far that I can say is truly a net negative, is the fact that you can't skip thru the introductions / voice-over segments.  While the story is one of the high-points of the game, sometimes the levels will take a lot of dying and trying again... so it sometimes gets tedious hearing the same thing over and over without any ability to skip it.  This is the ONE change I'd like to see made in a patch -- but that's it.
Highly recommended for fans of 16-bit games from the golden days of 2D action, fans of mechs, fans of anime, and anyone who enjoys a challenge!  And, this game is quite likely worth the full asking price... but the Holiday Sale price is absolutely nuts!!  This game is DEFINITELY worth a lot more than $2.99!

I bought the game a while back and just picking up again to see if this really is fun or not, as I'm interested in survival games. This game is a cartoon style tongue-in-cheek look at a stereotypical family that is 60 seconds away from an apocalypse.  The presmise of the game is the father has to gather up his family (those he can) and as many supplies as possible in 60 seconds. 4 modes of game are available, but 1 mode is a tutorial, and the other modes are just parts of the main game, being, 60 seconds scavenge only, survival only (using random supplies) and the combined apocolyse game being the scavenge plus survival aspects.  There are 3 modes of difficulty for each scenario.
My rating for the game is 'neutral', but I rate it as recommended (just).  The game is just about worth its ask price, but if you can get on sale it's worth waiting for a discount.  This is certainly a casual game - for deeper survival games take a look at This War Of Mine. There are around 14 items only of equipment to collect, use and trade.  The scavenge part is no more than a 60 second awkward dash, bashing around the house, picking up what you can.  The main game is story driven with, at its core, simple choices. Simply - who eats, who drinks, and if there's a special event you either have the equipment or not.  And the story will tell you when someone is hungry or thirsty, driving that choice too.  There's not much the player can actually do to change things, only read the story as it unfolds.  So repeats of the game may get stale after a while, but you might pick up the game every other month or so for half an hour of fun.  Certainly, you will uncover unique story lines, but it will become limited after a while. While it's a stereotypical game, it does represent some themes well - you can't survive without food and water, and a few other items might be useful.  But it's simple in strategy.
I rate slightly higher and positively because I love the graphics design in this game, very unique and attractive bright colours. The scenes change each day you survive to reflect what's going on - are people happy, sad, sick, thirsty, hungry, etc.  And the visuals change to show what items, food and water you have in stock, with empty bottles showing once you've used drink, for example.
What keeps the game alive after an hour or so is the fact you can go for a number of achievements.  Achievement hunters will enjoy this aspect.  Also, for traders, a nice set of trading cards are included in the game, worth about 5% or so of the buy price (when bought full price).
I'd only recommend this game if you're interested in survival or looking for a casual gaming experience and don't mind paying the price for a few hours of fun.  Better 'value per hour' will be found elsewhere for strategy, survival and importantly, casual game fans (which this game seems to be squarely targeted at). A good attempt though at something different and fun for a while. My rating is 5.5/10 (55%).

You remember Pac-Man? Well, this it, although with some new ideas and it's still fun to play once in while.
It's not only about clearing the screen anymore, but also about some tactics, because most of the time clearing the pre-set-up-screen won't suffice, that's where the new ideas come in.
Often you need to gather as many fruit as you can, sometimes because it's the main objective to gather x fruit from the left and the right side of the screen, and sometimes just for points.
But the fruit does not just lie around anymore, it spawns when you cleared the respective other half of the screen, so planning with that while being chased on high speeds can prove a challenge, because it's not only your typical four ghosts that chase you either.
There's sleeping ghosts, that wake up once you come near them and others that spawn from the middle once any ghost comes in close range to you, so you will find yourself dragging around a long tail of ghosts most of the time, while some don't just enqueue but rather try to come from another side to get you.
You still can fight back using the power pellets and some ghosts grant you another power pellet when eating them to extend your combo, but eating ghosts always increases your game speed. To slow it again, there are just two ways: die or use a bomb.  Bombs send all ghosts chasing you back to the middle and they - as well as lives are given to you at the beginning of each level and it's up to you how to spend them.
For both time trial and score attack you will want to be playing on a decent game speed though, because it increases the things you can do in a certain amount of time, obviously, although in the classic Pac-Man game going around corners could be difficult - it also does here but they included a mechanic to counter that a little: instead of perfect timing you just need to plan ahead, your input is buffered, so if trying to go right at the next corner, just press right against the wall and Pac-Man will remember to turn right as soon as he can. If the speed gets really high, the usefulness of this feature vanishes of course, so yes, it's making the game easier but only so much.
Also if you're about to get caught, time slows down so you have a final chance to react, but again on higher game speeds there's little difference.
Last thing to mention is the screens change while playing: If you cleared out one - let's say the left side - of the screen and collected the fruit on the othere - right -side, the first - left - side may change the layout of its maze and its contents.
The only thing that's a shame is, that if it wasn't for the free weekend, I wouldn't have given this game its deserved second look.

This game was a pleasant surprise. The graphics may be off-putting to some, but the game more than makes up for it when it comes to controls and gameplay. Bear in mind this is a game made entirely by one person (minus music), and for what it is it's pretty damn impressive.
Super Panda Adventures is a typical metroidvania, where new areas become accessible as you lean new abilities. Sadly there is no map, so you can't tell where you've already been and where you still need to go. It's rather frustrating, because obviously you have to backtrack a lot.
The overworld map should also have some sort of an indicator to tell you how many collectibles you've already found in any one level, so you don't replay levels which are 100% complete. If these two issues were fixed, the game would be perfect.
Gameplay is the most important part here, and that's where SPA really shines. The controls are tight and perfectly responsive. The story is a bit silly, but no one really plays platformers for their complex story. The music is cool and enjoyable.
If you look past the graphics and are willing to tolerate a bit of frustration due having no map, you'll have a lot of fun. Besides, it's just a dollar. I'm even willing to say that for the value you get out of this, the game is actually quite underpriced.

The look of this game makes people think it's simple or childish, but that couldn't be further from the truth. Whether you are a casual gamer that just wants to enjoy a fun game with a good story, to a hardcore gamer who prefers roguelites and rage-quitting, this game has you in mind!
Super Panda Adventures is a one of the best examples of the Metroidvania genre on Steam.  It has solid mechanics, fluid and smooth controls, an excellent soundtrack, fun shoot-slash-and-jump combat, and is genuinely funny.  Super Panda Adventures is different and really took me by surprise; so much so, that it has made my list of all-time favourites PC games. With a slew of RPG elements in the game, you can level up your character all the way to Level 50 with several weapon, armour, skill and spell choices to make along the way.  How you build your character ultimately affects how you play the game, and visa-versa!  Along those lines, it has a lot of stats to explore: HP, MP, Shield, Regen for MP, Crit, Melee damage, Magic damage, random-events skills like "Chance to gain 5 Hp when you attack an enemy," and shops to spend collected coins on items and potions!
+ 8 to 12 hours of gameplay
+ Full controller support
+ Well-written and amusing dialogue
+ Adorably cute, deceptively challenging (at higher difficulty levels)
+ Varied, colourful and thought-out level designs that always keep it fresh
+ Many RPG elements for levelling up your character (up to Level 50!)
+ It's not a platformer, so there is no platformer rage-quitting in this game
+ Good for all skill levels (from Casual to Srsly Hardcore)
+ Level-up, gain new and significant powers, skills, magic, weapons, armour, and more
+ Character appearance changes based on selected weapons, amour, and skills
+ Excellent and catchy soundtrack
+ Hidden / secret rooms filled with treasures to find
+ Fluid, smooth, and superb-feeling controls
+ Suitable for all ages and skill-levels
- Once a difficulty setting has been selected, it cannot be changed without starting a new game
- Sudden, unexpected difficulty spikes (see note below)
Frankly, some of the bosses are surprisingly over-powered and this can result in some unexpectedly frustrating boss battles.
Say you decide to play on Normal, but it gets too hard 8 hours in, you can either push through, in which case, watching a youtube video may help with your strategy; or, start the game over and select a lower difficulty setting.  May I suggest a better-safe-than-sorry approach to this game:
The typical gamer should play this on either the Cakewalk or Easy difficulty setting, which will provide a rage-free (not challenge-free) ride through this game. Only experienced, pain-seeking gamers should attempt Normal or Hard.
Either way, enjoy the game, this is a great one!

Look, I get it, It's a childhood trip, for all those that played the original machines (like myself) and would like to revisit them, but the physics of the game just doesn't feel right to me, and therefore I will never play this on a serious level.

*TL;DR*
An Oldie *But a Goodie* with clunky controls, strange jump physics, and a plot that involves shooting Commies in the face? Sign me the hell up!
*For those of you still reading, read on*
Project: Snowblind puts you into the shoes of Lt. Nathan Frost, a self proclaimed grunt who wound up getting enhancements due to a tiny bit of stupidity during a bombing. The Coalition, which Nathan is a part of, is fighting the thinly veiled People's Republic of China *It's just called The Republic but you can definitely see the communist overtones with them* Fighting a war to liberate China from The Republic's attempt to take it over during a time of weakness in that nation.
Gameplay is pretty solid overall, having guns that feel powerful and with the secondary fires and utility uses, have purpose outside of a few levels, so there's no moment of one weapon outshining the others, leaving them to collect dust. Ammo is plentiful yet scarce in the right way. Forcing you to the other guns when the need arises, including some guns that take the same ammo *Pistol and Carbine take the same bullets for example* though there are only two cases where this is true...Controls are a bit awkward at first but once you get the hang of them, you'll find your fingers naturally hitting those keys like Clockwork *EXAMPLE: Ctl is PUNCH *Probably one of the most SATISFYING punches of all time by the way*, Alt is Augs, Shift is Grenade, etc. etc. etc.* Though do not ask me about Multiplayer as I do not know if that still lives. There is also a Stealth Mechanic that isn't OVERLY Necessary but it is an option. It can feel pretty good when you take out an entire room without them realizing you were there until only one remains and you reveal yourself, taking your sweet time in ending him.
Music is rather generic at points but it can at least strike a few chords that make you go 'F'n A.' though otherwise they are forgettable.
The Story is rather slapdash at parts but consistant all throughout the game, so there's some Kudos, not much I CAN say about it partly due to spoilers but also because its not always there, though that CAN Be a good thing if you just want to play and not give a damn. *You can skip cutscenes too, which is good if you forgot to save* And Checkpoints are more or less just save rooms which allow you to come back at any time to that section either if you die *and lack Nanoboosts* OR If you left and returned at a later time.
Either way, I recommend this game if you're up for some gunplay and well applied Stealth, the Augmentations are fun and boring *The factor being your playstyle, though some are more fun than others universally.* and the game is a decent length, around 3-4 at least if you're just blazing through it, a couple more if you are being stealthy or playing Hard Mode. *Or better yet, both*

Blade & Bones is an action/adventure souls-like yet colourful rpg/metroidvania combat driven game (wow what a mouthful but it delivers enough to validate all these tags) and it caught me by surprise, as it will catch everyone who comes across it.
This game is, according to me, the quintessential indie game. It is casually self aware while being incredibly fun at the same time.
For me it was the best surprise from the indie side this year, although it is a little on the short side (around 4-7 hrs depending on playstyle it does also have a NG+ mode which significantly alters the experience)
Gameplay-
The gameplay consists of exploration and combat basically, both can be fun and not very tedious. Combat can turn from easy to unforgiving in just a short while as you run out of health or stamina. It is basically swordplay and some relics found through the world.
You have 'lives' called purity (total of 6 purities) and if you lose all, there is permadeath and the save game is erased...
But you can find the lost purities, BUT they are scattered at random places after you lose them.
Exploration is mostly fun and the world design is expansive, vibrant yet compact, I know it sounds contradictory but just play it and you'll know what I mean.
You can access some areas only at some specific nights and you can control when to summon those nights through a contraption of stone.
Character design is nice and hits a lovely spot between scary and aesthetically pleasing.
Graphics and performance have been good for me and I run a gtx 970 with 8gb ram and i5 4690k. No crashes, no memory leak, no bugs..
Lore/Story-
The lore is deliberately vague, obscure and fragmented and is explained through hieroglyphs and some character dialogues here and there. It is interested and fun all the same, replete with references and hints of cosmic horror. You have to collect seven swords to break an ancient curse, in those terms, the objective in game story is pretty clear but the world lore and origin is somewhat lovecraftian, as in not unknown but unknowable.

The original Defense Grid is one of the best Tower Defense games in existence.  Heck, it probably is THE best.  Incredibly fun and addictive (in a good way), with a lot of content, varied gameplay and clearly coming from a group of developers who care for their audience and know how to make fun games (as evidenced by the minigames they created for the Portal 2 ARG).
At first sight, this sequel looks to be the same.  A fantastic entry in the genre with the same basic gameplay and enough upgrades to justify it being a sequel rather than just DLC.  There are new tower types and upgrades, new enemies, new special weapons (the original had only one), a new story and lots of new characters.  There are also new modes to play (with advantages or handicaps) and extra abilities that can be setup before starting each stage.  In short, there's A LOT of content here.
But, it's an impossible to ignore fact that, when compared to the first game, this one is still inferior.  And this is mostly because of a couple of factors: freedom and balance.  The original game pretty much allowed you to play however you wanted.  It gave you a lot of freedom on how to approach each stage.  This one, though, requires certain stages to be played an exact way if you intend to finish it with a decent score.  This issue causes the second one, as there's a couple of ridiculous difficulty spikes, as in a few stages the game forces you to change your playstyle to something specific if you want to have any chance.  Now you're basically following orders rather than playing for fun.
To be fair, if you don't care at all about getting medals or keeping all the cores at the end then the difficulty is not a problem.  This is a very easy game in that respect.  Much easier than the first one, actually (there aren't even flying aliens here).  But if you do care for a question of completionism, challenge or achievement hunting, you're going to have a lot of frustration and you'll probably be forced to look for walkthroughs (something that rarely if ever happened on the first game).
In short, it's still a good game.  Great even if your expectations for gameplay end with "being able to advance to the next stage".  But it's still an undeniably inferior product to the original in aspects that are quite important for this genre.

(This review is mostly for Supreme Commander as a whole, not only the FA expansion)
One of my absolute favourites in the RTS genre, this game creates the sense of an actual war with its immense scale and (for its time) very good visuals (still looks pretty good).
4 nations, countless units divided into tiers, a fairly standard for the genre resource collection, and a fresh element (intel gathering) ensures a game with nigh limitless options for strategies, especially on the bigger maps (the largest ones are 80x80km in size, that can give you a rough idea just how big this game is).
The expansion (Forged Alliance) brings in even more units, rebalances for existing ones and some new effects as well as a brand new faction (the Seraphim) that make it well worth the price, not to speak of the fact it's a standalone so you can play it without the original SupCom. The game also has mod support, and there are a few really good ones that were made since the game was released (some are still being updated).
Simply put, a must-have for any RTS fan, few games will be able to bring you a similarly amazing experience such as this one.

A friend, DontBlink+_-UrDead, recommended Watch_Dogs.
I played about one hundered hours and really enjoyed the game. Set it to the side for a few months, jumped back into it and WOW! It still made me laugh and grin!
Of course by now we all know what Watch_Dogs is all about and it is like GTA (which I never cared for) with an added twist. Hacking and THATS what sold me on this game and has kept me hooked.
Whats extremely cool about WD is the people, the environment, the city. When I first began WD I knowtist the people in the streets were skittish. Somtimes over reacting to my simple movements. I figured the devs really goofed up on making that aspect.
Then it dawned on me. Since we are trying to avoid or find the opposing player, use the city to flush them out! So I put on the headset, turned up the volume and the idea WORKED!
What ever you are doing while playing WD, pay attention to the ambience of the city. Any out of place noise like a trash can falling over. A car skidding. Rattling of a chainlink fence. People yelling, "Watch it!" or "What is your problem!?!" Odds are it very well could be an opposing player.
Although....
So I figured my idea of listening and keeping an eye on things to flush out the other player was a sure shot idea. Well, sort of....
I'm guessing the Devs anticipated us players figuring the whole, "listen to the city" idea and made Chicago almost seem realisticlly alive.
The AI of the environment sometimes fools me to believe that it is a real player when it's not.
Just one example: I was travling down the street in a car, pulled over to check on things and a car pulled up next to me and stopped. FOR NO REASON!
I figured it was a player trying to hack me! I shot the car and the driver and it turned out to be an NPC, causing the entire police force to chase me down.
This will require a player to "learn the city". Pay attention to whats going on and see if you can pick out the opposing player.
You will encounter "Hey! Thats not fair!" moments when others set them selfs in an alley way. Or perched on an inaccessible sniper position to easily one shot you and then there's my favorite, drive by in an Icecream truck and hack you. I really believe this is intentional. If it wasn't, there would not be so many places to hide and there are a lot of them! So turn the tables on those people and make THEM say, "Hey! Thats not fair!" Because, this is a game about hacking ;)
This game is the best to have fun attempting to out wit the other person. Keep your calm, know the city, stop and look both ways before crossing. It may save your life. Seriously.

By far the most fun I've had playing a turn based strategy game in a long time.  Re-playability still being tested.
--The Good
- The gameplay was intuitive and (with a handful of exceptions because Trolls are tall) fluid.
- Soundtrack was always on point with the 'feel' of the gameplay.
- Despite being 2D the game's graphics grabbed me; sprites and backgrounds were bright without falling prey to being cartoony, or dark without being drab.  Most of the time it didn't even register with me that the game wasn't 3D.
- Both micro (battlefield) and macro (character-building and story based decision making) decisiosns felt like they influinced the other in a variety of ways.
- Storytelling was top-notch from the over-arching tale down to several NPC's stories.
--The bad
- Unable to re-size fonts, and high reolution with a ton of reading made me need to walk away a few times.
- Game-play challenges do not come from AI, but from volume of opponents - this frustration is not unique to this game, and it does not suffer from it as badly as many others, but it is still present.
- While Karma was balanced (Never felt like 'super-man'), money was never in short supply.  I frequently used combat drugs, always updated my gear, and yet I always felt like I was in the black... even though one of the main points in the game involves scrambling for money.
--The Ugly
- The only major frustration I had was mis-clicks that resulted from trying to move my team to squares immediatly above other actors.  For about 1/3rd of a second it shows movement to that square, then it highlights the (again, drecking Trolls) sprite in the square beneath my real selection.

The Shadowrun series is a bit of a mixed bag for me. Neither the first nor this one has really produced a gripping story. Combat options are limited. I HATE HATE HATE the hacking sequences. There are a lot of flaws in this series.
Yet I play these and have a great time with them. The exploration is good. The world of Shadowrun is so compelling that you just have to see what's around the next corner. The art style is simply one of my favorites in any game, ever.  The gameplay is cool - you will not have the skills to solve every issue and you have to learn how to deal with it. That might be maddening to some, but it makes it all the sweeter when you do have the right skills to take advantage of the situation.
Plus, the dev is awesome. Not only do they release a good game at release, but they've gone in and added real content as a "thank you" to their customers. Who else really does this? Which is why I backed their latest kickstarter.
This won't be your GOTY, but you will get 20 hours or so of great enjoyment from it if you like the subject matter. Plus you're supporting one of the "good guys" in gaming development.
Now that is all said, let's talk about Drgonfall. Shadowrun Dragonfall is the highlight of the series. With very similar gameplay mechanics between the three different games n this series it boils down to which game has the best and most comprehensive story. Dragonfall's story is - IMO - the most memorable of the bunch. It's interesting, it's complex and it's there are some very good NPC characters in this game world. It's not the most brilliantly written RPG but Dragonfall is above average (while the other two are fairly average). Combat options have been improved from the first game and the Director's Cut additions do a much-needed job of fleshing out the game world.
Thus I recommend this to RPG fans. If you're going to play all 3 Shadowrun games then I suggest you do so in order they were released. If you're going to buy just one, this is the one to buy.

Ignore those who say the game is dead and that this remastered version is bad because the doors are not functioning as in the original, although it's true this remaster is missing 2 very cool features (functioning doors & elevators) of the original, it shouldn't stop you from enjoying a truly unique gameplay of this gem.

Is it missing something from the original? Oh yes - as mentioned before, being able to open/close the doors is a very nice feature of the original game which is missing in the remaster. Also, interactive elevators are just so cool and add so much fun to the original that it's a pity they're missing in the remaster. However, it doesn't kill the game and it doesn't make it a bad remaster, it's just a trade off as of now, which hopefully will be fixed by developers. Still, the only way to play The Ship in Hunt mode with bots or with real humans is by installing the remaster version, so it does it's job!

BuriedTown: Imagine This War of Mine and Zafehouse Diaries birthed a mobile-port love-child. And it's decent...
I would recommend this to anyone who enjoyed either of these titles...
Your shelter/resource contains the genetics of TWOM, including: crafting. cooking, defense, sleep/exaughtion, weather/temp, and health/mental upkeep. The military-time day/night counter runs continuosly, with every task requiring said amount of time to complete. It's a pretty basic formula for those familiar with TWOM, mostly proritizing what to build to initially survive versus the race to prepare for, and survive, the oncoming winter...
The DNA of ZH:D is found in the travel/exploration/combat aspect of the game. Diffrent area nodes will become available as you progress in the game. It consists of timed travel, requiring a few hours to traverse the debris to each destination. Each node has a set number of rooms to explore for potential resources required to survive, occasionally finding secret areas, or you could get attacked... Battle is pure RNG with fast flavor text, there is no "action" here.
Before initializing combat, a threat level is given indicating the severity of the encounter. Low threat means fewer and weaker zombies, with higher threat levels sometimes raising not only enemy numbers but their severity. And yes, you can avoid battles by either not walking into the next room containing zombies or by running away if attacked while traveling. Enemies will usually start four meters away. As the distance closes, you will fire your ranged weapon, if you have one, and then engage in melee combat until victory or defeat. Ammo is universal for each gun, but save those bullets for tougher battles later in game...
This is a tough little cookie, but doable after you figure out how to proritize your base growth. Also, there are crucial NPC's that will eventually appear asking for resources. Each can be visited at a stationary node after they make initial contact, trading necessary materials and accepting favored items as gifts to raise your companionship level. Higher levels means not only better trades, but also more varied items. Dont ignore your neighbors...
All in all this is an enjoyable game if you don't mind rage-quitting a window mode only mobile port with little to no feed back from the developer. I'd sorely love to see a full screen mode with a pause option, other than the quit/continue screen, in shelter strictly for viewing resources/stats, but the non-stop timer otherwise adds to the direness of the situation. Also, while outside of your sheleter, there is no way of identifying the materials you gather. Some icons are self explanitory, such as food and wood, but otherwise it's memorization of what's what till you get it home to inspect...
All negative reviews and aspects aside, I personally rate BuriedTown 3.5 out of 5...

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
BuriedTown is a fun casual game that doesn't really fit that well into any of the most common genre definitions. The Steam game page for BuriedTown suggests that some popular user-defined tags for it are as follows: Action, RPG, Strategy, Indie, Adventure. But this really doesn't define it well at all.
In BuriedTown, you are a survivor of a zombie outbreak. There's no information provided in game regarding where you came from, how you managed to avoid the zombie virus (?) outbreak, or even who you are, but none of these things is really important for playing the game anyway.
BuriedTown has received some pretty negative reviews on Steam, but in my opinion they're not really justified. The game is addictive in its own way, but it is also frustrating. A short run of bad luck can have terrible consequences, ruining in just a minute or two a game that you have been playing for over an hour. But it's pretty original and has reasonably high production values.
Coming into this review after reading some of the others I was expecting the worst, but I was pleasantly surprised.
Graphics - The graphics in BuriedTown are a bit of a mixed bag. No, there are no graphics options, and no, you can't play it in full-screen graphics mode. BuriedTown opens up in a resizable window and doesn't know anything about bloom or HDR or ambient occlusion. There aren't even any fancy animations to speak of! Instead, the game's graphics take the form of a number of stylised icons that all fit within a single theme, placed over two-dimensional still backgrounds. And in my opinion, they're mostly quite nicely done, and fit the game well.
The game screen is divided into two sections, with various statistics, your character's five attributes or needs, and a status window on the right; and the relevant world screen on the left: either your home, the world map, the current location you're visiting, or one of the utility screens used for combat, inventory management, improving your shelter, etc.
It took me my first game to familiarise myself with the meaning behind each icon and the features represented by the graphics, but once I had encountered each one once, that was enough.
Sound - I believe there's only one music track used throughout BuriedTown, but it fits the mood of the game very well: a sort-of gently mournful instrumental piece that's blended nicely with a thunderstorm. I haven't yet found myself bored with it, and it blends into the background while playing. The game's sound effects are not quite so good, with zombie combat sounds especially being extremely repetitive and lacking. Other sounds in the game tend to alert you to your character's status changing (usually for the worse), and are passable, but nothing special.
Gameplay - The goal of BuriedTown is to survive for as long as you can. You start in an abandoned house that you call home, and each day you need to maintain your character's five needs (mood, energy, hunger, infection, and injury) while exploring the mostly abandoned town outside your door.
Unfortunately it's not quite as simple as it seems, with your mood, energy, and hunger constantly decreasing and requiring you to find and use various resources recovered from the town in order to replenish them. This usually results in your other needs -- infection and injury -- taking a hit from the zombies you'll randomly encounter while exploring, which then prompts you to find still more resources to replenish these needs as well. And so on.
To explore the town you leave your shelter and select a destination. The game gives you a confirmation screen showing how long it will take your character to reach the destination, and away you go. Once you arrive at your destination, you can there explore up to a certain number of times for each location, either encountering zombies that you must fight or discovering a hidden cache of loot. The town's locations are the same each play through, which I found a little disappointing, but I was pleased to discover that the encounters for each location seemed to be at least partly randomised.
And that's basically it. The central idea is very simple, but well executed, if perhaps a tad too difficult for my liking. My first game I lasted two and a half days, my second almost double that, and then in my third I survived for over 12 days before falling afoul of a continuous run of zombies in the local movie theatre. But each game was a precarious dance of balancing needs, collecting loot, automated zombie battles, and crossed fingers -- hardly a relaxing pasttime.
The game is quick enough to play just for a few minutes and then put down again, but addictive enough to keep you busy for hours if you let it. The implemented Steam achievements and in-game trophies increase the addictiveness, as would the world-wide ranking list, if I could get it to work.
The whole game is played with the mouse pointer and left mouse button and could easily have been made for a mobile device, which I believe it originally was. But it works well on Windows, too, and once you've learned what all of the icons do you'll find the interface simple and straightforward.
Pros:
+ Addictive gameplay with both in-game trophies and Steam achievements, as well as a ranking system
+ Great music
+ Simple interface that's very easy to learn
+ Stable: no crashes or bugs encountered yet
+ Translation to multiple languages, if you want to play in something other than English
Cons:
- Ranking system doesn't seem to work; ranking lists are always empty
- Very hard; there are Steam achievements awarded for surviving whole seasons! I thought I was doing well making it through 12 days ...
- Locations are the same every game, making it more repetitive than it otherwise could be, although encounters and loot do change
I'm going to go against the general feeling of the other English reviews on Steam and say that BuriedTown is a really good little game. I've only played it for a couple of hours so far, but I can easily see myself playing it for quite a few more, struggling to survive just that little bit longer, upgrading my shelter and befriending other survivors as I go.
Is it an action adventure RPG, as suggested by the current popular user-defined tags on the Steam page? Most definitely not, in my opinion. But it is fun, and that's exactly what I wanted from it!

I figured I'd write in my thoughts after 42 hours of playing this game, right before I uninstall it.
This game is a match 3 or more style game.  You have up to 4 characters in your party, one match causes the top most character to attack, any other match usually just gives a type of energy to the topmost character of its color.  And they may eventually use a spell (specific to the character) that has varying effects, moving enemies around, destroying gems on the board, changing the color of gems, doing damage, various drain, heal, immunity, and some status effects.
With that said, this game has a very very bad swing to it.  It is too easy for 'skyfall' to happen and randomly help you or  hurt you.  Some characters also have extreemly powerful abilities that you may not have access to, mostly from sheer luck.  I have seen a game suddenly go from positive for me, to me losing from one random skyfall that I was incapable of controlling the outcome of.  And that quickness of turning is it's strongest and weakest point, the outcome very often decided by pure random chance, or owning a powerful character who wins the game once you activate their ability.
There is a mechanic for leveling up characters, but it involves using a resource you gather very slowly in game, and you have a cap on level, that is only raised by randomly getting more of that character, and sacrificing multiple copies of the character to allow it to have higher stats, and make its ability more powerful.
I gave this game a good attemp, multiple hours, but time and time again just found myself frustrated when my entire strategy was 'kill this one character before they use an ability they have an easy time activating.'   And I found myself pretty much pushed into using certain team builds to even have a chance to survive, when what I wanted to use was nowhere near a viable strategy.  Or I had leveled up the wrong character.
But in the end, it is the games swingyness that throws me over the edge of not wanting to play, and why I give this a negative review.

anticipating this game since it's release on PSP. A professional mech side scroller shooter. Short game but has a "nice" low res 2d graphics that is so appealing to retro fans. replay value is high due to unlocking new weapons for your mech. The only problem is that there is no adjustable difficulty level in this game that kind of a let down for a shooter game. there is also a simple but solid story element that accompanied by a sweet Japanese voice acting. Pick this gem up. Because every 10 year only one game like this reach the English language audience. And i repeat: This is no indie ****. This is a pro game by pro developers of the genre.
When this game's music is composed by the same person behind Thunder Force V, it must be good. It is.

It's a nice throwback to older mech games, much like Gigantic Army. Has a lot of positives, though they are tempered by the negatives. I'll explain below.
-For those of you who want to use a controller, you'll need to set it up in options first, but otherwise it works just fine with most controllers. I personally use a dualshock3 with a USB attachment.
-Gameplay is responsive, difficulty is decent but not overbearing (I recommend the simulator since you'll need the training beforehand). Please keep in mind that if you're a real go-getter and you don't take things slowly, you'll find yourself beating this game in a matter of hours.
-The story is not that good, it's not bad, but let me save you some time and recommend skipping them wherever possible. I forget if there even is a button to skip them.
-graphically it's very nice. Spritework is almost top notch, and you won't get that taste of "8 bit retro hipster" in your mouth. However it's a little confusing sometimes since the sprites can often leave you dazed and they'll group together, but in most of the missions you can tell what you're firing at and what's firing at you.
-the OST is okay, nothing to speak home about
Okay, so I have to be blatantly honest here. There is one huge negative.
-the mech customization is actually pretty bad. Without spoiling the game, the unlock system requires blatant ingame grinding, and since the game is so short, you'll just be grinding one mission over and over again to rack up the points. To put it in perspective, the very most points you can get in a mission is 500k, and you need at least 3 million to unlock your first weapon. To get everything, you need 100 million. It's a very awkward design flaw. You do unlock some stuff while playing through the game, but it's very limited and you won't notice much difference.
Overall, as a robot enthusiast, I would recommend this game, but under the pretense that you get it on sale. If you want my honest opinion, the game could still use some improvements, but you get what you pay for at least. Don't go in expecting a timeless masterpiece.

I couldn't not. Supreme Commander: Forged Alliance is one of the
examples of large-scale real-time strategy out there. This game is how I want most RTS games to be, and to be honest, I think most RTS games
to be SC:FA.
Let's start with the campaign. I won't put any spoilers, but I will list off a few things. Like most RTS games, the focus is not on the campaign but on the gameplay, so don't expect much from the story. One thing I do like is how the main characters of the game interact and talk to you depending on which faction you're playing as. It's a nice touch, however you put it. I can say that the campaign can be fairly challenging your first time around. Enemies can often send powerful units and even experimentals (We'll get to those later) charging at your base without giving you much time to react. This is fun, but can often slow the pace of the game down to a snail's speed if you want to prepare accordingly before the event takes place. I said before that the focus is on gameplay, and even the game agrees with me. When you fail a mission, you have the option of skipping to the next one to see what onslaught awaits you there. Very nice, considering RTS games are not known for their story. The characters are each fairly memorable, but none of them ever seem to have much personality. (Although, I'm not entirely convinced that Fletcher isn't Ben Stiller) It's a futuristic army vs. bigger army simulator, and that's all it wants to be. Frankly, that's all I need it to be.
On to gameplay. I thought it couldn't be done, but somehow SC:FA made it's gameplay even simpler than Dawn of War. Starting with the fact that there are no counters. Most tier II units can destroy tier I units, most tier III units can destroy tier II units, and experimentals decimate everything in their path. Speaking of experimental units, I don't believe I've told you about them yet. Experimentals are a faction's endgame units. They are the biggest and meanest superweapons out there, each more powerful than the next. Heck, there's even one that drops a mega-nuke. Did you know mega-nukes were a thing? Neither did I. In SC:FA, there is no lack of awe-inspiring combat. Seeing massive armies clash on the field of battle sounds epic, doesn't it? Well, how dare you even question the fact that it is so totally unbelievably epic. Shame on you. The resource management is quite unique, and something that I have never seen in a game like this before. Put simply, you have resource intake and resource storage for two primary resources: Mass and Power. The former being your source of unit and structure production, and the latter being to power things like a unit's special ability, or base defenses. While you can construct power generators willy-nilly all over the place, take caution as the bigger generators may provide more power, but they are also incredibly volatile and can wipe out weaker structures in the blink of an eye if they are ever destroyed. Mass on the other hand can only be acquired from certain points which you can build Mass Extractors on. Most of these are scattered about the battlefield, so protecting them may be a pain. Let's say you now have a good intake of Mass and Power and are ready to build some units. Well, each unit or structure will drain you of a certain amount of Mass and Power, the more powerful units often devouring hundreds of each resource. However, if your Mass and Power intake is more than the unit needs, you should be in safe ground and the unit will be produced as normal. If you run out of Mass or Power storage when the unit's drainage is bigger than your Mass or Power intake, your production will slow to something akin to the Heavy spinning up the Brass Beast while being hit by Natascha. Take note that Power has no impact on this, but will disable things like shields if it runs out. I hope at least some of that made sense to you.
Talking graphics, the game doesn't boast anything too great, but looking at the attention to detail on some of the units leaves me feeling impressed.
The soundtrack is meh. That's all I can say. None of the songs are too memorable, at least as far as I can recall. You won't find any Baba Yetu in here, that's for sure.
The multiplayer is dead. But not really. Although there are multiple services that have restored Forged Alliance's multiplayer on their own servers, Rock Paper Shotgun stated that this game is best played with your friends against AI. I don't blame them, because what better parter to help obliterate armies of uncountable size than your best friend?
TL;DR: Supreme Commander: Forged Alliance is excellent at what it does, and doesn't try to be something it's not. I give huge props to this game and it's devs for making it, and may future RTS titles learn from this game for years to come. The RTS genre is dying, and something like SC:FA is just what we need to revive it.

I have come to this game very late, but then I have a real pinball machine and saw little point in trying a virtual equivalent. However, I am very glad that I did.
The best way to test out the game is to play Roadshow, the pinball I have owned for 16 years. The game simply plays brilliantly, though I have noticed that there are one or two subtle differences from the real thing. The essence of the table is fully captured and it is a joy to play. I cannot recommend it highly enough. The differences from the real thing are as follows:
Loops and ramps feel easier to hit in the virtual table, perhaps because they are not subject to the vagueries of real world physics, wear on the tables rubbers, inexact table angles and leg heights, etc. Likewise, it is possible to hit the skillshot on ball launch by missing the shot and overshooting a little, allowing the ball to roll back into the blast zone hole. I definitely can't pull that off on my table.
More problematic is the simulated shaker motor. Even on its strongest real world settings, whilst the table rattles the walls of my whole house, the ball itself is not subject to the dramatic changes of flight which occur in the virtual game. I have lost the ball in the virtual game where I never would have done so for real. This is really the only material issue with this virtual table affecting gameplay.
More general problems with the game are the failure to implement a better menu system and to not have simulated the buttons on the machines fully. I want to be able to cancel a game by holding the start button without resorting to menus which break the sense of playing a real table. Unless I hit the escape key I do not want my sense of playing the real game to be interrupted. Another issue is the changing viewpoint when playing. The default height setting to view the table is too low, and whilst it shows off the acuracy of the virtual tables to best effect, it is unnaturally low and makes following the game more awkward than in real life.
In terms of the price, the game is free and includes the truly excellent Arabian Nights table, enough to keep you interested and playing for a very long time. The table packs are very expensive though, £30 a pop is like a whole new game's worth of money to expand an existing one. I realise micropayments and downloadable DLC are great for games companies, but they do not offer good value to the player. As the game stands I would need to part with £180 to have my own pinball arcade, and my wife, whilst tolerant, is never going to allow that! Pick your packs or individual tables carefully though, and you can have a smaller pinball arcade containing only classic tables. Hell, you already have Arabian Nights, were you to buy Roadshow, The Twilight Zone and the Addams Family, maybe Circus Voltaire too, you could probably play for a lifetime without tiring of them. In any case you can try all of the tables for a few minutes free play so you can always find something to suit your tastes.
So, not a perfect simulation, not a perfect menu system, but if you cannot afford thousands on the real thing, it is as close as you are ever going to get. Download and get playing.

I have decided to change my review. I've gotten a lot of fun out of this game. But I wish there was a middle of the road option. Even if you enjoy the game, doesn't necessarily mean the game is as good as it could be, with even small changes. I found out the game is locked to 60fps, which means if you have a nice high frequency monitor, then it's useless. And it's a real shame too, because there are other pinball software options out there that allow you to use high refresh rates and it's really awesome and helps the game feel immensely better. This is especially frustrating on tables like Black Knight which are so fast that it can be hard to even keep track of the ball on a 60hz monitor (and it happens to be one of my favorite tables). This is fine in real life, because we have 3d depth perception and 'endless' fps effectively, but on a monitor at 60hz, it's really difficult to play. The other problem with this game is that it is clearly made for consoles. The menus just don't work well no matter how you use them. And certain tables under certain configurations seem to constantly crash the program. And, when used in portrait mode, it isn't compatible with 16:10 monitors, it ends up cutting off a rather imporant section on most tables: the flippers. So I like pinball software. It's a fun quick way to spend some time. And between recommending this and not recommending it, it's hard for me to choose. I think PinballFX2 gives you a much better bang for your buck, on sale or otherwise. In part because the tables are designed to be played on computer. But also because of all the options, smoothness of UI, and pricing structure it offers over this. But I still enjoy Pinball Arcade and recommend it to all the more hardcore fans of pinball.

First some background:  I played the Linux version.  I like RPGs, but have never played a Shadowrun game before.  I played the game maybe 20-30 hours (Steam thinks I played more than that because I left it going overnight a couple times).
Shadowrun Dragonfall may have been my most pleasant gaming surprise this year.  I was expecting to try out a low-budget, rough experience (because indie game) with technical issues (because Linux).  Instead I found that this game was ton of fun, polished both technically and in gameplay/story.
The Shadowrun universe combines Gibson-style cyberpunk (e.g. deckers, cybernetic augmentation) with traditional Tolkien fantasy tropes (e.g. magic, elves, dragons).  Some people might find the world too weird, but for me (and I suspect a lot of game players, who have experienced a lot of sci-fi and fantasy already), it was a refreshing twist.  The story takes place in a gritty city, which seems to be on the brink of chaos.  Different factions and corporations plot against each other for control.  Think Planescape: Torment meets Deus Ex.
Besides a thought-prokoving setting, the game also has a well-written plot.  I don't want to spoil anything, but suffice it to say that the beginning of the game springs a plot-twist on you, and the intrigue builds from there.  There are often moral dilemmas without clear-cut right or wrong answers.  The plot builds to an exciting climax, and at the end I felt like my choices had real consequences.
I also liked the gameplay, but I admit that some gamers will think this is the weakest aspect.  It's a straightforward turn-based campaign.  And in the past I've found turn-based games like Fire Emblem: Awakening or XCOM:Enemy Unknown to be boring and repetitive.  What saved the gameplay of Dragonfall for me were two aspects.  First, excellent pacing.  The game doesn't just give you wave after wave of enemy to mow down.  Most encounteries have some twist to them, or advance the plot or characterization---the game doesn't force unnecessary repetition on you just to pad the game's length.  Second, I enjoyed the character customization, which gives you plenty of flexibility.  For instance, my character was a physical adept, who used magic and cybernetic implants to run up and attack machinegun-toting enemies with a sword.  There's a lot of reply value---I'm curious how it would have played if I had focused on sniping, or casting magic spells, or controlling drones.
About the technical issues, the game never crashed on me.  Other than one mission (involving a powerful computer system) which seemed a buggy, causing me to have to reply sections, I did not encounter any issues.  The game's art style is consistent and detailed and builds atmosphere well, but is all in 2D.  The interface was very streamlined and never got in my way, which is more than I can say about a lot of AAA games.  The soundtrack became a bit repetitive, but set the mood pretty well.  There was no voice-acting or animation.
In summary, Shadowrun: Dragonfall has a well-written plot that takes place in an interesting setting.  Its turn-based gameplay appealed to me because of the good pacing and interesting RPG aspects.    You may not enjoy it if you're looking for innovative tactical gameplay.  And you definitely won't like it if you're looking for state-of-the-art graphics and sound.  However, you'll probably love it if you enjoy games that have good writing, setting, characters, and RPG aspects.

where to begin, Harebrained studios has deffinatelly upped their game.
I'm told that Dragonfall was origionally going to be an expansion for Returns, I'm glad they made it stand-alone, because it does stand alone. it has been some of the best Shadowrun experiances I have had outside the pen and papper games I love.
so what's in the tin? 41 hours of single player campaign, that's how long I played it. according to steam anyway, a couple of restarts in that, but the single player campaign is epic. it did have some moments where it started to feel like it was grinding down to a crawl, but it was always a worthwhile moment at the end of the run, very few happy ones, but such is the world of Shadowrun.
The biggest let down for me playing the game was that my character didn't work, in pen and paper I play a Face, I talk, I bribe, I swindle and I intimidate. I solve problems with my brain and my mouth, and when it goes sideways I bring along an old friend of an LMG to bark a little louder. that doesn't quite work in this game, skills like "intimidate" are nowhere to been seen, there are ocasional etiquete and charisma checks in runs, but not every run, and I never had a run that didn't go squirrelly and end up with blood spilt. but that didn't take away from the fun too much, and I can see why they did it, that was always one of the problems, when new guys came in it took almost a full session to go through the books with them and build a character, too many skills to dabble in.
the brightest thing in the game for me, was character devolopment; I loved my runningmates by the end, especially Glory. each of the major characters had a history, and a personallity, and you could get them to open up to you, and devolop that personality. I found myself rushing through paid jobs so I could go talk to people again and learn more, and try to help them. It made me drunk with the possibilities of the world again, like it did when I first cracked open the books and started reading, there was a world behind the characters in the game, and I got to be a part of it for a while.
the only thing I would want to see in a next game at this point, is to see some of the origional skills put back in, and maybe the ability to get a closer to some of the characters, I wanted to kiss Glory by the end, but never was that an option.
one last parting remark, this game convinced me to break rule number one, ashamed as I am to admit it; I made a deal with a dragon...
