The devs did a great job in crossbreeding match-3 mechanics with a rather eclectic in style but funny looking CCG, & the components have blended well. You collect cards which drop randomly as prises, then choose 4 characters from your collection & take them to battle, every unit is capable of doing some sort of magic or special move as soon as it fills its mana gauge, everyone uses 1, 2 or 3 mana colors to get their specials ready, the more you match on board the more mana they get. Then you throw all your might at the enemy's 4, trying to eliminate them. The cards have 4 stats - Health, Armor, Attack (direct hits through matching skulls on board) & Magic (special power). The player who was able to form a synergetic tactical team where cards help each other (i.e. generates additional color drops for the others) has better chance to succeed even despite being unlucky. Still luck always plays a big part.
The cards have great individuality - the types of creatures you may encounter are hard to imagine! For example you might choose a kung-fu dragon to fight alongside an undead fairy princess against a giant poisonous mushroom & a pirate shark armed with an anchor - much fun just to study the qualities of those monstrosities. Every unit could be upgraded with 3 unique traits with the help of special colored stones which drop randomly & get its stats boosted up with souls of fallen enemies.
You may continue to play this forever, the process is potentially infinite - levels rise, cards get upgraded higher & higher, you continue battling against more experienced players. The game is colorful, it sounds juicy, everything's large & clear, the art looks cool, everything works fine (devs fix bugs soon & response quickly), I believe that if you look for a free time killer, especially on mobile platform, you may look no further!

If you like 90's mecha anime and difficult Japanese arcade sidescrolling action games, this might be the game for you. If you don't like BOTH of those things, you'll probably find pretty much nothing to enjoy in this game.
This game's weaknesses are easier to describe than its strengths. Its graphics are dated, having been made for the PSP years ago. It's a very transparently low-budget game (with remarkable ugly menus). It's an extremely barebones port with almost no PC-specific features or enhancements. It's singleplayer-only with limited replay value (achieve high scores to unlock extra weapons). It's also short, at about 3 hours from start to finish.
Lastly, the controls can be a pain, literally. The game's more difficult fights can require you to juggle between pressing, holding, and possibly double-tapping upwards of 6 different buttons on a controller as you dodge enemy projectiles, fire multiple weapons, jump, dash, and block. Sometimes you even have to do this in zero-gravity where you hold a button to toggle your directional controls between lateral motion (movement) and angular rotation (aiming). I typically couldn't play for more than about an hour at a time before stopping because my hands were aching so much from the finger acrobatics.
In spite of all of that, I found the game had old-fashioned charm and was quite satisfying to overcome as a challenge. Like any good Japanese action game, you can feel your mastery of the game steadily increase as you play it. Persistence, pattern recognition, and plenty of patience are required to succeed. I approached this obscure little game with no, or maybe even negative, expectations, so I am surprised and satisfied at having ultimately enjoyed it modestly.

60 Seconds!
SOME STYLE, NO SUBSTANCE
Developer: Robot Gentleman
Year: 2015
Genre: Casual Strategy
Franchise: N/A
Engine: Unity
TL;DR
This is little more than a weekend project. It features clumsy writing, repetitive gameplay and an irritatingly long list of bugs. For the same price you could be playing FTL, so don't waste the money here.
REVIEW
Story:
One paragraph in and we've already hit a snag: This is a primarily text based game with mediocre writing at best. The humour falls flat more often than not and key phrases are repeated so often it may as well be a children's book. For an FTL style game about text based choices, tight writing and variety are essential aspects. This game has neither. 2/10
Graphics:
The hand-drawn style is cute, but lacks variety. The game attempts a miserable, oppressive atmosphere by having you stare into blank faces and stone walls, with the characters moving only occasionally. While they technically succeeded, it feels less like a design choice and more like laziness. 4/10
Gameplay:
What little gameplay there is can be experienced in under 10 hours, and even in that time repetitiveness is guaranteed. The events are remote controlled, and aside from a few RNG based choices you have little to no agency in gameplay. Even some sort of wasteland exploration minigame would give the game some meat, but as of now it's so content lacking that there's nothing there. It reminds me of Fallout Shelter but with (Dare I say it!) Less to do. Honestly this feels like a tablet port, and a slapdash one at that. Interminably long load times, lag and a lack of variety make this game about as fun as being in a real bunker without a checkerboard. 3/10
Overall:
60 Seconds is a dull, content-lacking experience that is is no way worth the price of admission. If only you could refund steam gifts, huh?  2/10

Supreme Commander: Forged Alliance is an RTS classic. Featuring four diverse & unique factions and a massive scope, it is the ultimate evolution of a decade of RTS game development and design. It is frequently on sale for less than ten dollars, which is most certainly worth it.
I have only two complaints. First, don't forget that Supreme Commander was released in 2007. The graphics and gameplay are still immersive, but unfortunately it is not programmed with modern hardware in mind. So while it runs perfectly fine, it is not configured to run on multicore processors and does not benefit from advanced hardware, which can lead to performance issues with thousands of units at once.
The second complaint (a facetious one) is that the commercial and critical success of this game provoked a horrible, dumbed down sequel (Supreme Commander 2).
Also, be sure to check out Forged Alliance Forever, an online community dedicated to the game!

This is hands-down one of the best games I've ever played and it's about time for another play through!
Pros
- Very Addictive
- The kind of game you play when you're in a crap mood to brighten your day immensely!
- Amazing Music. It's very appropriate and sets the atmosphere incredibly well for each level
- Incredible Level Design (gameplay and atmosphere). One of the things that makes the game design so incredible with this game is that the game acts as its own tutorial as the player plays through. The player gets some help but most stuff is pretty forward to figure out because the levels are designed to make the player think about how to use the skills they've got. Also, there are challenges in all areas that make it obvious that a player requires a skill they don't have yet, but it gives the player a really good idea of what kind of skill they're expecting to find. This really helps keep player engagement high because there's always something really cool to look forward to!
- The artwork is very crisp, clean and bright
- Very Solid controls
- Awesome skills and lots of fun to use
- Epic combat
- Very well thought out sounds that keep player engagement high and really allow the player to feel the game
- Excellent game progression and plenty of challenges that unlock as the game progresses.
- Plenty of game to get through
- Solid levelling system
- Kind of like Adventure Islander meets Kung Fu Panda with Doom Imp fireball sounds :)
Con's
- Bosses are too unpredictable and have too many unavoidable attacks for a platformer. It's more a case of luck than skill to defeat a boss. Basically, you have to grind the same boss over and over again until you get lucky enough to have lucked avoiding enough attack changes in a row to win without taking too much damage. Each attack has an unknown timelength before the next attack and you don't know which attack is coming next, so quite often you'll jump straight into the bosses next attack and die too fast most of the time and combined with the unavoidable attacks, this becomes frustrating.
- Diversity of enemies could be increased. This can be forgiven to a degree because of the excellent level design
- Would have been good to have the option to bind Dragon Punch to its own button because the skill serves 2 functions
- A map function would have been useful
- Occasionally crashes... mostly after a save when I'm trying to exit the game, so this is a small issue

The game is horrible. Horrible not in it's controls, story or graphics. No. The game is horrible because it will constantly taunt you for your every error and misgiving. It's a true survival horror - you're in the middle of a plague trying to survive and your only way of survival is making tough decisions - stealing, looting, trading for outrageous prices. It's all comes down to understanding how desperation can bring a human to the brink of being an animal
But also you're the key to curing the plague. And the game taunts you for every day you will not do it. Every day starts with a death count that you couldn't prevent. Is it fair since the key lies way outside of your graps? Hell no, but the game isn't fair. It will throw punch after punch to the point you're lying there in the puddle of your own tears asking it to stop.
The game is a simulator, simulator of how pitiful life can be if faced under extremity. And thus it's probably one of the most important games ever made - it's unique, amazing and terrifying. It's a horrible fever dream on a steppe that wish you never experience IRL.

This is based on one playthrough of one character.
Likes: Very atmospheric, excellent soundtrack, forces you to make choices and pay attention to details, doesn't hold your hand, allows room for some strategy, time is always against you (12 days total, 1 game minute is 5 real seconds), voiceovers usually have purpose, game clock is stopped during conversations and while checking status or reading notes/maps so you have as much time as you need for decisions (but it's not stopped for inventory stuff), you can do a one-key quicksave (two quicksave slots) and as many permasaves as you like, plays well on older hardware.
Dislikes: The narrative seems forced, the game works hard to be mysterious to the point of diminishing the relevance of choice or strategy, there is intense use of the mouse where keyboard activity would be way more efficient, you are the only thing in the game that can't run, you can only walk and a lot of your time seems purposefully wasted by forcing you to walk on long errands, unable to switch weapons while moving and can only use the mouse to do that or anything regarding inventory, hit boxes are sometimes flakey and getting through doorways or around objects is a bit of a pain.
In spite of the negatives I'd still recommend it, but the negatives affect my desire to replay.

Сама игра это большое театраное представление и на сцене — три фигуры. Жертвы обстоятельств, как часто бывает. Судьба приготовила им нелегкое испытание: ближайшие 12 дней будут настоящим кошмаром, своеобразной борьбой за жизнь, в заражонном городе. Спастись самим, а так же вытащить из капкана добрую половину населения, заодно навсегда поставив крест на заразе, охватившей город.
Захватывающая история — ценнейший компонент «Мора». Ложь, предательство, интриги, неожиданные доброжелатели… Витки событий следуют один за другим. Так, крупные правящие семейства — Каины, Ольгимские и Сабуровы, растащившие во владение отдельные участки города, — все время пытаются подмять нас под себя. «Не верьте соседям» — напутствует отпрыск погибшего властителя. Странно, но «соседи» столь же убедительно твердят о его нечистоплотности. А с приездом Инквизитора накопленные сведения вообще отправляются на свалку. Здесь никому нельзя верить!
Диалоги потрясают насыщенностью. В меру литературный текст иногда достигает огромных размеров, превращая приключение в некий аналог интерактивной книги. «Интерактивной» — потому что для большинства реплик предусмотрено несколько ответов, причем разные варианты зачастую по-разному влияют на дальнейший ход дискуссии, а то и всей игры. Ну, а «книги» — в силу отсутствия озвучки.
И да чуть не забыл! Давящая, депрессивная обстановка сразу   приходит от прогулки по зараженному кварталу, мимо покрытых плесенью «плачущих» домов, ядовитых испарений и зомби, закутанных в грязные простыни, становится не по себе.
Несмотря на то, что развернуться здесь почти негде, побегать предстоит от души. Без карты и навыков владения ею соваться в жуткий лабиринт из петляющих улочек, ветхих построек и непреодолимых препятствий (заборы, ограды и всякий мусор) опасно. А чтобы игрок не заплутал в хитросплетениях сюжета, авторы выдали ему специальный блокнотик, где отмечаются основные и дополнительные задачи (подобных квестов редко бывает более трех штук, их скрупулезное выполнение не входит в раздел обязательств, но попотеть, тем не менее, придется). Имейте в виду: не успеете до полуночи проставить галочки рядом со всеми пунктами — ровно в двенадцать страницы дневника опустеют, незаконченные дела так ими и останутся.
Всем приятной игры, выбирайте правельные решения.

So. I don't often write reviews and the last one I wrote got several die hard fans of the series rather upset with me. But, all the same, here goes.
Damned, at its core, is a wonderful game. Of all the "Monster versus survivors" games, this one has been the most enjoyable for me. I found myself thrilled with the different monster choices, as well as their mechanics. I played this with four of my friends and, honestly, it was some of the most fun I had.
So...why am I NOT recommending it?
Content. I'm sorry, truly, but this game has been all kinds of dead for a long time. Little issues with server connection and the main menu have plagued the game since launch and have never been fixed. I forgave that for the sake of them adding a new monster and APPEARING to be working on the game. But then it just went...quiet. I sympathize with how hard making a game is, I really do. But check the update news. The last thing they did was last year and it was updates on a map editor. Still menu issues and a few game play bugs here and there and absolutely no new monsters or anything. I fear they may have given up on the game. I don't mean that as an accusation, just a genuine fear. I WANT this game to get finished and worked on. I loved it. But I've had it uninstalled forever, for frustrations involved with trying to get the game running for everyone.
So, in the end...if you can endure a lot of menu issues or, perhaps, are one of the lucky ones that bypass all those issues, it's not expensive. Get four friends together and play, it IS genuinely fun to play. But the issues and lack of updates outweigh the fun. Please, PLEASE keep working on this.

The pros: This game is fast, it's slick, it's exciting, it's really everything that a classic arcade game should be. The cons: DO NOT PLAY THIS GAME IF YOU ARE PRONE TO SEIZURES.  This game very well may cause you to go into full on brown acid flashbacks if you play it for too long.  Also, sometimes there is so much happening onscreen that I literally lose track of my guy and end up losing a life.
Bottom line: It's fun.  And for this weekend, at least, it's free.  Play it.

I played my first game of pinball about 15 years ago. There was a pub right next to my school where we used to skip classes, hang out and play pool. And there was this strange machine. I didn't know how to play. I kept mashing buttons, hoping the fippers would hit the ball. And when they did, sometimes the machine shook violently, simulating a quake. Almost two decades later I found out that the table was called Earthshaker!. They also had the one with the funny talking clown head — FunHouse. It was partly broken, some of the lights didn't work, but I didn't care. I had fun.
The pub is still there, though the tables are long gone, sold to save electricity. Pinball is rare where I live in Eastern Europe. FunHouse and Earthshaker! are the only tables I've ever played in real life and they're both included in Pinball Arcade. What luck! Although pinball might not be as popular as it used to be, people like me, who haven't found many real tables, can now experience it virtually. That, I think, is how pinball will survive forever, even after the production of physical tables ends. For me Pinball Arcade is not just a game, it's a great effort to preserve a unique art form.

I've been asked by many friends what the difference is between the Shadowrun Returns DLC for Dragonfall and the Director's Cut.  I'm going to write from that perspective; there's already plenty of reviews telling about the game itself and I will be using spoilers.  Let the reader beware.
First off, the overall plot reminded me a  lot of Baldur's Gate II.  Divine being-type entity split from its divinity and that problem becomes the player's problem, the player is required to raise a ridiculous amount of money to chase their adversary, along the way the player gets to know their companions better if they care to, and the player is offered side missions for each of their companions that gives each of them a slight boost.  Despite all the similarities, I very much enjoyed the Shadowrun take on the story idea; enough to play it through several times and grab every achievement - as there are many "hidden" achievements tied to how the game ends, that's saying something.
Where the Director's Cut differs from the DLC is mostly the inclusion of the companion missions, the Black Lodge audition, and missions on behalf of some of the Kreusbazar vendors [the majority of these are in both games, but I know the mission for Ezkibel was missing from the DLC for sure].  There are some other noticeable, but minor differences like less dialog options when dealing with Doctor Ezkibel after taking care of the sewers, but they do not really impact the game at all.
Edit:  playing the DLC after the Director's Cut allowed me to notice that for some reason there are some dialog triggers and conversations that somehow failed to fire in the Director's Cut.  For example, meeting Audran for the first time in the Director's Cut he just starts shooting when you meet him.  Playing the DLC, he actually explained why the player's intrusion could not be forgiven and finally some companion lines made more sense as they reference that later.
I found that the missions and dialog included in the Director's Cut greatly enhanced the story and gave it a lot of depth that the player wouldn't know was missing until they experienced it as the DLC is not incomplete without it - it's just more complete with it.
The display and inteface is also slightly different between Dragonfall Director's Cut and the base Shadowrun Returns.  While both games made use of keyboard shortcuts for things like inventory items, spells, and personal skills only in Dragonfall are they labeled on the display - playing the base game I never even knew those shortcuts existed and they enable the player to enjoy a quicker and smoother combat experience.
I also like how the weapon display was laid out in Dragonfall over the base game with all the information made available at a glance and number hot keys to switch to specific weapons.  The only thing I would consider missing from Dragonfall that was present in the base game was the "F" key to cycle through weapons when my attention was too focused on the scene to look up what number would correspond to whatever weapon, especially for a character whose loadout changes or an unfamiliar character.
Another item that is an improvement in Dragonfall in my opinion is the ability to lend not just consumable items to your team, but also weapons.  In my first playthrough, for example, I made use of rifles and shotguns so whenever I could afford to upgrade my own gear I was able to lend my previous weapons to Eiger as they were better than her in built gear for a while.  It also gave me the ability to outfit her with an assault rifle while the Shadowrun Returns Dragonfall DLC does not allow that to happen.
I'll be honest, I backed Shadowrun Returns on Kickstarter so the Director's Cut didn't cost me anything additional, but having played both I would gladly pay for the extra content and story that the Director's Cut offers and consider it money well spent.

This is a fun little FPS game. It was released back in 2005, and this is the first time I've played it and thought it was pretty fun. Don't expect a masterpiece or hours upon hours of gameplay, but if you like a short single-player focused sci-fi shooter with a cool setting, then give it a try.
The setting is a near future and really reminded me of Deus Ex (from what I've heard, it was initially planned to be a sequel to Deus Ex, but later turned into a standalone title). You play as military commander who gets injured in battle and implanted with combat augmentations, which become available for use over time.
This is what I really enjoyed about the gameplay. It's not just your bog standard corridor shooter relying on twitch reflexes. It has a bit of a strategic edge, as you acquire a number of interesting augmentations throughout the game, such as the ability to slow time, ballistic shielding (temporary protection from bullets), cloak, enhanced vision, and so on. In addition to augmentations, you also find some cool gadgets to use in battle too, such as spider bots to act as your little pets and aid you in combat, deployable force field to act as cover, a large variety of grenades (most of the ones from Deus Ex), and even a nanoboost, which is like your emergency revive that you can choose to use if you die in battle.
The game seems to have only one difficulty mode (I didn't see how to change it), but overall it's paced really well. I didn't come across any difficulty spikes and the game never throws anything unfair towards you. In some levels it's just you infiltrating some facility, in others the combat takes on a large scale assault and you have many of your squadmates with you and witness battles between large groups of soldiers. It's all really well done, even if graphically the game aged a fair bit.
I only have one big gripe. The game crashes from time to time for no reason. It only happened about 5-6 times for me during my playthrough, but because you aren't able to save anytime you like, at times you could lose chunks of progress. Saving can only be done in special save rooms and also at the end of each level.
Overall it was a fun game. Aside from the crashes, I thought it was well done and would certainly recommend it if you like FPS games with a story and a bit of a tactical edge.

Project: Snowblind was initially a Deus Ex game, before later being turned into a new IP after the poor performance of Invisible War, and it doesn't do a very good job of hiding the fact. You play as a soldier who was forced to become nano-augmented after suffering heavy trauma in a battle, and fight for a peace-keeping group called UNAT- no, wait, I mean the "Liberty Coalition". There's a character who acts as your commander who is mechanically augmented, and frequently laments that he's become outdated. The items all look like they were taken straight from Deus Ex, like the energy cells and health kits, and you fight a lot of familiar enemies like bipedal mechs and mechanical spiders. Even the hacking tool is named after the ICEbreaker hacking interface from Deus Ex.
However, it's probably for the best that it never ended up being released as a Deus Ex game. In many ways, this game is sort of like the Bioshock Infinite of Deus Ex, right down to replacing the actual hacking of the real games with a gun that you shoot at panels to instantly hack them. Rather than being an RPG with shooter elements, Project Snowblind is a full FPS. There are no wide open maps or choices to make, just enemies to shoot and objectives to move towards. The game does a loose job of allowing both shooting and stealth playthroughs, but the stealth half is pretty horribly done and not all that viable. The radio contact in the game is also somewhat schizophrenic about this; in one particular mission where you have to get up a few levels of a parking garage, he initially contacts you to tell you that it might be a good idea to sneak through it due to high guard activity, then almost immediately tells you that you might be able to cause some real chaos with one of the vehicles in the next room, only to go back to telling you that stealth might allow you to listen in on guards' conversations on the next floor. You get a handful of augmentations throughout the game, but instead of being able to choose which ones you get or being able to upgrade them, the game just hands them out as you progress, using the same story justification as the reason they later used in Human Revolution. The game doesn't feature very many characters, and while the few it does feature aren't bad, they're barely used, and after you first meet them they tend to disappear until they're needed for a dramatic moment. The story in general is pretty poorly paced, and you fight the final boss of the game about 3/4 into the game. The game is also pretty short, only lasting around 6 hours. The game also has a tendency to crash, particularly when you minimize it, which is a problem since due to being a console game, you can only save in designated save rooms rather than having a quicksave or even checkpoint system.
On the other hand, as long as you can see it as its own game instead of a Deus Ex main game, it's a pretty fun shooter. It's interesting to see it as a spinoff where you play as just a semi-regular member of not-UNATCO instead of "that guy who single-handedly unravels an Illuminati conspiracy", and while the stealth is generally awful, the shooting is done pretty well, and the weapons and their secondary functions are all pretty fun to use. While it does have a lot of faults if you compare it to Deus Ex itself, as a standalone game it's pretty fun, and it's only $6 at its base price and presumably much less on sale. It's interesting to try out, if only to see the lost Deus Ex game that almost existed. If you do decide to buy it, be sure to check out the widescreen patch on pcgamingwiki if you have a widescreen monitor.

Some games growing old with dignity and still performing just as good as they did 15-20 years back. No, that’s not about Project Snowblind. I remember playing it 10 years back, just after release, and even then it was not so pleasant experience, with all that console-style shooting mechanics. Replaying it now, I see that the best part of this game is its plot line, which was called “generic” even by backers of this “Project”. So, in short, that’s not a title you really need in your collection, unless you have some personal history with it.
The story in this game telling you about a soldier who got under missile fire, and recovered in hospital, with half of his body replaced with implants. After some petty missions he found himself behind enemy lines, with a few support, against some evil plan to bend over the world. If you think it sounds like Deus Ex, be sure it does: that game was supposed to continue named franchise, adding multiplayer experience, but all of sudden, was released as a standalone title. If you consider that Project Snowblind was just as bad as Deus Ex Invisible War, you'll agree that that was a smart move from Eidos.
For a count of pluses of this game I can say, it gives you opportunities not to simple shoot in people, but also cloaking from them with one of augmentations, see through walls with another, hacking computers and turrets… And lurking in the air ducts, of course! Everybody love air ducts.
Also it is quite short – you can finish it in less than 10 hours. Yeah, it is a plus for a game like this.
For contras I need to say, that the major part of the game, its essence, a gameplay process – is quite dumb and boring. For real, in the year 2005 we had Far Cry 1 and F.E.A.R., which gives you much better FPS experience. Even if we remember that Project Snowblind is a multi-platform, nesting on XBx, PS2 and only then on PC… There are still a great Psi Ops: the Mindgate Conspiracy game, which was also from PS2.
Multiplayer in that game wasn't really entertaining from the day 1, and it is obvious nobody will be playing it for MP now.
Finally, the reason why I decided to put the dust off from this generic shooter was a hashtag “cyberpunk”. Sadly, but the dose of cyberpunk theme in the Project Snowblind is much lesser than in real world around us. So it’s not cyberpunk. Even with all those augmented superpowers that game gives you. A first Robocop movie have tons of cyberpunk of better quality than Project Snowblind.
Summarize:
Obsolete title deserving only a small R.I.P. commemorative plaque, with mark like 5.5-6/10, and not your actual time. All the better stuff you could possibly find in this game was moved into Deus Ex: Human Revolution. See it for much better experience.

At the first glance this game is a mediocre console shooter that has nothing in common with Deus Ex.
However, the moment you stop rushing through levels and start poking around, you will notice that despite the linear structure almost every level has some useful equipment stuffed a few rooms away from the main path and sometimes you can find a shortcut or an alternative way to approach a certain situation, and while it doesn't feel as exciting as in the original Deus Ex, it keeps the game from becoming yet another dull console shooter. Unfortunately, augmentations feel unnecessary due to the rather low difficulty, but they can save your butt if you've ended up getting caught with your pants down.
Tech-wise, this game tends to crash a lot unless you set the affinity to a single core and the graphics appear washed-out no matter how much you try to tweak the settings.
Overall, this is not a great game and it's miles behind the original Deus Ex, but it can provide a few hours of fun if you're craving for a cyberpunk-ish shooter and pick it up on sale.

Apart from being simply very well designed, the maps also have goodies in them that you can grab once you got more skills from the story - so you have something to do on revisits. An old recipe, but it works well for this game.
I also never had much problem navigating them despite the absence of a minimap. Every area in a level looks more or less unique and quite easily identifiable.
I feel that there is one problem with this game, and that is that the bosses usually seemed pretty tough to me. They were often quite a bit harder than is actually enjoyable. They have so much health, and in my case, most of the skills that I had picked were are useless or really quite weak against them. I needed to grind level ups more than once to not have to play quite so perfect to win.
I still liked practically everything else - this was a fun game to play through!

This is one of the best RTS games as of 2015. When it launched it was an incredible resource hog as it suggested 2 monitors and required a great deal more processing power than most people had. It is a beautiful game overall and the balance is quite good. The ability to make massive super weapons is a real joy because they are quite powerful but they take a long time to build and can be a gamble if the enemy blows them up before they are finished.
This game is oldschool in the sense that it doesn't have cheating AI that always knows exactly what you're doing. It will build the tech 3 radar that has a massive detection range... but that's a structure you can build as well. (you can always blow it up or take out his power to turn it off).
This game has a slight degree of technicality with your base setup (the wiki can explain it very quickly with a picture). Long story short you can put power plants next to factories and each will reduce the cost of things you build in the factories. The other game resource, mass, will also reduce building costs if you build a factory on top of a mass extractor (often called a mex). The danger with this is that a tight network of touching/linked buildings is more effecient but it is much easier to destroy because power plants are volitile,
The bad news is that the AI can't really compete very well on water maps. The AI is also somewhat weak to turtle strategies involving large defensive structure batteries. However one of the interesting aspects of this game is that you kinda need to learn which thing to build to counter what your opponent is building. Did I mention that anything you send at the enemy's base that gets destroyed can have the mass reclaimed by the enemy?
One more bit of bad news is that I don't think a lot of people play so you'll probably be playing against the AI. That being said the AI is a good opponent. There is a built in "cheater" option if you want to play against a crazy tough AI opponent who will always be 1-2 steps ahead of you.
This is a really good game and the first time you see a nuclear missile hit the enemy base you will really be in for a treat. If you hear the words strategic launch detected and don't have countermeasures built you'll be in trouble.
This is one of those games you can play for hundreds of hours and never feel like you're still playing to get your money's worth.

I’ve never had such a split feeling on a game before. As a set of pinball tables, Pinball Arcade is phenomenal but as a piece of software, it’s a complete mess.
Pinball Arcade’s main competition on steam is Pinball FX2 (AKA Zen Pinball). Both games strive for something different- FX2 is impossible fantasy pinball whereas Pinball Arcade emulates real critically acclaimed tables. Both are equally valid but I definitely prefer the ‘realistic’ take; part of pinball’s appeal to me is the physicality of the mechanics involved. Arcade’s tables were all hand-crafted and manufactured, meaning they’re generally more carefully designed than FX2’s pure-fantasy offerings. Your own preference may differ but its why Arcade and FX2 are the dominant pinball games on steam without competing directly with one another.
The tables in Pinball Arcade are very diverse and you’ll likely find yourself cherry-picking a few favourites you keep coming back to. Acknowledging that I am still a novice player, my favourite tables so far include The Creature From the Black Lagoon, Black Knight 2000, Junkyard, Star Trek: The Next Generation, Funhouse and Taxi. I was very lucky that my favourite tables happened to fall into Seasons 1 and 3 (I have since also purchased Seasons 2 and 4). The tables are pricey although this is forgivable given the overwhelming amount of licencing agreements required (The Addams Family was particularly gruesome in this regard). I would not recommend buying the tables individually. The number of tables in a season is roughly the same as you’d find in an older disc-based pinball compilation for consoles. Even if a season contains a few duds you don’t enjoy, they typically should each offer a decent variety to make the price worthwhile. There does however seem to be a lack of balance between seasons even though they all cost the same. I also don’t recommend the pro versions unless you’re a pinball-superfan. (On a really bizarre note- at the time of writing seasons 1-4 are on sale with the pro versions costing *less* than their regular counterparts).
The most crippling aspect of The Pinball Arcade is the software holding these brilliant pinball tables together. The interface is horrendous. Previous versions of Pinball Arcade I’ve seen on YouTube presented all of the tables in a large list you’d just scroll through, one table at a time. This is fine for maybe the first season or two but when you have 30+ pinball tables the devs quite rightly decided this interface needed to change. Unfortunately, while the new interface is an improvement in principle- it barely functions at all. Its heavily reliant on the mouse and seems to randomly decide if it wants to recognise your controller d-pad inputs or not. I’ve had to create a steam controller profile just so I can comfortably navigate the menus without having to reach for my mouse. Even this solution doesn’t let me adjust the light sliders for some unknown reason. As well as the unpredictable interface I also frequently lose high scores (the entire driving force of playing pinball), goals I’ve completed and even the list of my favourite tables. The only thing that stopped me from just uninstalling the game after losing my original set of scores is that my top score on each table was still saved on my
profile (also the scores weren’t exactly exceptional in the grand scheme of all players). I believe this is related to steam cloud saves so beware when playing this game on a new machine. Pinball FX2 has none of these issues and if I didn’t prefer the tables of Arcade, it would definitively be the superior pinball game on steam.
Its also not a good idea to have music with lyrics for your video game menu. I used to like Pinball Wizard but I now loathe it based on the sheer number of times I've had to listen to its opening lyrics in Pinball Arcade.
The one saving grace is that I’ve never had Pinball Arcade outright crash on me, otherwise this would have gotten the dreaded thumbs down. Perhaps I should give this a thumbs down to encourage the devs to get their act together but the ultimate truth is that Pinball Arcade is still extremely addictive and in a class of its own so I can only hope the devs fix the numerous issues and make this a more comfortable recommendation.

Alien Rage is sci-fi first person shooter that will probably only appeal to masochists.
The game simply isn't much fun to play unfortunately.
The first problem is the poor optimisation, regardless of settings there are frame rate drops all over the place.
It turns out if you install a third party program and turn Texture Streaming off in the .ini file it runs a lot smoother (for the most part) but why should people have to do that?
Secondly the game isn't balanced at all.
A game can be difficult without being unfair, this game isn't though.
Enemies are bullet sponges (especially the bosses) and you can take very little damage before you die.
It doesn't help that checkpoints can often be quite far apart and cover is very hit and miss sometimes.
And you will need to use cover, again because of how little damage you can take but also because your health takes forever to recharge.
One section in particular stood out where two snipers (who can kill you in about two hits) were on a walkway in the distance firing their at least 1 shot a second rifles at me with nigh perfect accuracy.
The encounter boiled down to strafing out of cover, firing a couple of quick shots and hoping they hit (most weapons are about as accurate as a horoscope) and ducking back in before you're torn to shreds.
It wasn't fun or interesting or engaging, just tedious.
Some people might enjoy the difficulty, I just found it frustrating.
The third problem is it's really buggy.
In one area I fought a ton of enemies and reached a checkpoint then died in the next room. When I restarted the checkpoint the enemies from before had respawned, despite the fact them dying is what gave me the checkpoint in the first place. My only option then was to run back to a previous area and hope I didn't die in the process.
Another area had me shoot a switch to make a bridge appear but the middle was missing. I assumed I needed to do a running jump or find another switch or something but no, the bridge just didn't work for no reason.
It was only after dying in that area five times that the bridge decided to work as intended.
If this were some kind of physics based game I could maybe understand but it's not.
There are a ton of these kind of things, most recently a boss fight where the exploding tanks you use to injure the boss weren't shootable. They were visible on screen but mine and the enemies bullets just passed right through them.
There's no rhyme or reason to these things either, it's pure luck when you reload a checkpoint whether something will work as it's supposed to or not.
Mechanically some of the guns are fun to use and when you fix the texture streaming issue the game looks nice and runs quite well.
The story is little more than an excuse plot (at least at the point I'm at, about half way through the game) and the characters are all entirely unlikeable.
For the right price some people will probably really like this but I can't recommend it I'm afraid.

My review of this game is easy.
If you like cleaner FPS games like Red Faction, Star Wars Commandos, or even original F.E.A.R., then you should love Snowblind.  It has all the things I love about those games.  Here are just some of them:
1) All environments are "real".  By that I mean that they are all rendered in the 3D world.  Anything you see, you can probably jump or stand on.  No invisible walls except in the sense that the levels have to be defined by something. They aren't infinite after all.  But it is usually something believable like a wall or fence.
2) Along with the above, and the addition of many game elements like alarms, being able to hack terminals and so on, you have many options for how you want to defeat your enemies.  This ranges from a full on berserk attack to stealthily creeping around or hiding.  Lots of air ducts to crawl through.
3) Plenty (and I do mean plenty) of weapons, additional equipment you can use and augmentations to you personally.  Some of these are
-Increased vision abilities
-Spiderbots that follow you around, like the insects in Half Life, and help you out.
-EMP, poison gas, and frag grenades
-Cool shotgun, Carbine, Sniper rifle, and pistol
-Reflex augmentation that functions like the reflex boost in F.E.A.R.
-...the list goes on.  This is only a very small part.
4) Lots of environmental elements like steam, lighting, being able to break windows, opening cabinets and breaking some crates for items.  There also is a weapon similar to the gravity gun in Half Life that lets you move some things around and you can pick up certain objects.
5) Fitting AI and com chatter voices, for this kind of game.  So, that means coming across humorous conversations as you sneak around and a CO that is pushing you ahead.  I really appreciate all the background talking that is going on in this game.
There are lots of other elements that I like too.  But, if any of this interests you, than I would just go get this game.  I bought it for not much from BundleStars since it had been on my Amazon wishlist for some time.  But, now that I know how good it is, I would pay the full $6 price for sure.
One final caveat:  There are some graphical issues with this game.  Mostly that it looks kind of washed out and low contrast on modern systems.  BUT, I easily took care of it with a little trial and error in the Nvidia control panel.  But, even without that, it seems like the biggest thing that helped was turning off "Fullscreen effects" in the games own options.  You have to run its separate option utility to access it.  Its not hard to get to.  It just pops up when you go to play the game.
While trying to troubleshoot this issue, I ran across a lot of hate for this game.  It is completely undeserved.  Its an awesome game, if you like these kinds of games.  Its NOT a COD clone or FarCry or Splinter Cell.  But it is interesting and a lot of fun.  Give it a try!
Its not a pay to win which is a good thing. This game is very rewarding and competitive. A great time killer.

Watchdogs is a mixed bag, but is ultimitely is a good game to me. I enjoy it despite its setbacks, and there are some big ones. But first, let's go over what is good. (Note: I beat this game on PS3, so my playtime is about 5-6 hours more)
The biggest thing I love about this game is the hacking. It's original and unique compared to games like GTA. It's done well, and is executed in a clever way, though I wished there were more actual hacking actions you could do. The open world of Chicago is large and done well with great detail and a little bit of variety. The cover system is smooth, and the guns are easy to shoot and control, and sound nice, which is always good when you're murdering people. There's also great animations. Aiden, the protagonist, has difference animation sets when he's out of combat and in combat. There's fun street games like the ball and cup game, which I get addicted to playing after I start playing. The story missions are pretty good, and are the best part of this game, my notable favorite being the prison mission.
Unfortunately, that's about where it stops. Now it's time for the negatives. The worst thing a PC game can have is unopimization, and this game suffers from that. I am past the recommended specs, yet I only get around 40 FPS with dips into the mid 30s when I'm maxed out. I have to lower everything down to High and Medium, sometimes Low, to get a stable 55-60 FPS, which is  frustrating. There was even some graphical downgrades, and it's still this laggy? Luckily, I run a mod that re-enables graphical effects that were disabled due to downgrading and even adds some graphical enchancements. It's called
if you're interested. Anyways, back on topic. The main protagonist, Aiden, is rather dull and shallow. You never really learn about his past except for what the game's story is based off of. I barely cared about him the whole game. He's just some dude in a trench coat that can hack things. That's about it. The side missions feel more like padding and are very repetitive. The gang hideout missions are great, but the others aren't, and are the main side missions that repeat in formula very often. The driving in this game is stiff and slippery. You'll find yourself slamming walls early on. Even when you get the hang of it, you'll still slam into walls every now and then. GTA V is extremely superior when it comes to driving. The story is average, and the ending is abrupt.
Although there are more negatives than positives, I still think this game is worth it
It's fun, and I enjoyed it the whole way through. I got the complete edition of this game, which includes the season pass and deluxe edition content during the Summer Sale 2016 for $14, which is actually a steal. That's a VERY good price.
Should you buy it?

This game definitely requires a second and a third playthough with the other characters - and the Bachelor scenario alone took me over 35 hours.
It's quite tricky to describe Pathologic - Is it a detective thriller? A survival game with elements from various genres? An interactive Arthouse movie? A Role Playing Game with a complex structure of decision making? Walking simulator? A subliminal Horror story?
The overly long errand running (or rather walking) may not be for everyone, but once you dive into this bizarre world with all its dangers, miracles and oddities, it's hard to put this game aside.
The Good:
+ Absolutely unique ideas and gameplay
+ Terrific / Terrifying atmosphere
+ Eerie soundtrack
+ The plague
+ Three characters with lots of different outcomes
+ Interesting barter and inventory system
+ Immersive open world and NPCs
+ Basically complete freedom how you approach problems
+ Different endings and outcomes
+ Hours and hours worth of gameplay
The Bad:
- Sometimes clunky combat
- A bit of a harsh introduction into the strange environment
- The game's pace may not be everyone's taste
The Ugly:
-- Nothing really...
Whatever you make of it, it's definitely a unique yet a satisfying experience. You have to see for yourself what the hype is all about.
PS: After this trip you'll end up being best friends with trash cans and alcoholics...

The Short: A solid metroidvania with RPG elements and a decent number of collectibles. Good graphics & sound. Simple but meaningful upgrade system with several styles of play. Gameplay is generally unchallenging yet fun, but the few bosses in the game are substantially more difficult. Suggested buy at $5 or less.
The Long:
1) Gameplay: it's a 2d platformer with rpg elements, so you should have certain expectations going in. Levels are accessed from an overworld, and, in the mode of many games in this genre, you will find yourself returning to old levels with newly gained powers in order to access new areas and gain new items. There are a decent number of collectibles in the game, and it will probably take you 10-15 hours to find them all without use of a guide.
The general gameplay is fairly unchallenging on normal, though I have yet to try harder difficulties. There are many abilities which increase survivablity to the point where you won't even worry much about getting killed from mid-game on. There are not very many enemies in the game, either, and you will have their attack patterns memorized fairly quickly.
The very significant exceptions to the above statements are the boss battles. The bosses are few in number, but I had significant difficulty with all of them; they clearly represent a substantial increase in difficulty relative to the rest of the game. They were my main motivator for finding all of the extra powerups.
2) Graphics and sound: I'm not much of a buff on either of these things, but I was happy with both. The music is very pleasing, and the graphics look clean and well-done. I am glad that this game, unlike so many other classic-style games, did not use classic-style graphics that looked like they were ripped from RPGMaker.
3) RPG elements: I would classify this game as having "soft" RPG elements. While you do level up and it is important for progression, there is no pressure to pick the right skills to advance each time. You will get 2 points to spend after each level up on 1 or 2 skills of your choice. These skills can be roughly divided into melee, ranged, magic, and general, but I personally ended up using a little of each. As I said, you will not find the game becoming unbearably hard if you pick some skills before others. The bosses are going to be difficult regardless of the skills you choose, and while some some of them can make these fights easier, your reflexes and your ability to not get hit will matter a while lot more.
Those are the major points I wanted to make. Overall, this is a fun little game that's defnitely worth at least a few bucks. My suggested buy price is $5 or less.

This is an updated (+) version of a tweaked (DX) version of a revamped (Championship Edition) version of a classic we all know. It plays fast and bright, with colours exploding all over the screen (during ghost gobbling) and offers a great way to battle it out for higher scores each play.
There are many mini goals to play against, liked timed scoring or timed ghost catching, though I didn't spot a continuous play as long as you can mode (maybe I've not played it enough to open one up... or I've just missed it!?).
Anyway, it doesn't take too long for it to dawn on you that each goal is oh so very similar to the last and all it is doing is finding ways to add tiny variety to the same bunch of moves. In short it gets repetitive.
Don't get me wrong... for the first hour or so you will be amazed at how exciting Pac-Man has become, but once you've pretty much cleared all goals on the first course and begun the second, the rot will set in. I knew that stretching far ahead of me were the same set of timed events and fruit grabbing cut-down versions of a full score run, merely with different map layouts... and the novelty instantly wore off.  I have played this in demo form before and played recenty as the free download was available for a few days. It's cheap and it's almost a no-brainer.... BUT, I just don't think I'll spend much time on it, striving for ever-higher scores. The nuances of the best scores is something that still far escapes me, so I'd not so much be working on strategies as just running around blindly hoping I'd score massive runs of ghosts for each pill.
In summary: good fun, but gets samey after an hour or so.

Ever wanted to play Deus Ex and actually utilize all these awesome combat augs and loud guns instead of sneaking around? (well, technically you can, but...who does, really?) This is the game for you.
While technically not a Deus Ex game, in fact pretty much everything screams otherwise. The design of some stuff - like the energy cells and the spiderbot grenades - is literally straight out of Invisible War (hell, they probably lifted the models). The gear, like the guns (it's not as apparent here, since nothing's straight up reused, but they're definitely the work of the same person who designed the guns in Invisible War - or at least someone imitating the style) Obviously the nanoaugmentations are too, but that's enough of a broad, common idea to not really support the idea. But that's not really the point.
The point is... it's fun. It's fun to go balls out for once when playing a Deus Ex game. It's fun to pop the slow-mo aug and jump out of a window exchanging gunfire with Chinese soldiers like a lost scene from a Ghost In The Shell episode. It's fun to watch someone's bullets bounce off your shielding aug as you run in to sock 'em in the face with your fist (with blue circuitry running along your forearm to make it feel that much more ~cyberpunk~). It's fun to tag a bipedal combat robot for a joyride by tagging it with the Icepick - the game's one-stop shot hacking solution - and then letting loose with its laser minigun and rocket launcher on the unsuspecting soldiers.
Project: Snowblind is just a fun game.
Now, it's got a heap of problems, too, to be frank. The interface just screams "mid '00s console port" - it's giant and really unsuited to a pc screen. To add insult to injury, there's no widescreen resolutions to be seen anywhere in the options, so you gotta play in 4:3, which further limits your field of vision. The gamma's absolutely screwed, with no way to change it I know of. Same with the bloom - oh my god, does this game love its bloom.
And despite these, it's still really enjoyable, which I think speaks even higher of its quality. Definitely a game I'd consider more of a Deus Ex than Invisible War. If you can stomach the interface, and want to feel like the Major while wiping out faceless mooks in style, look no further. For the price of a beer, or a coffee if you don't drink, it's an absolute steal - and then more.
Oh yeah and the spiderbot grenades are my favorite thing. They're like tiny adorable chirping Tachikomas.

A fun but flawed first person shooter.  AI has shown the capability to flank however the appearance of rushing the player is apparent.  Aliens do have the ability to melee as well as stasis the player so I won't hold AI rushing against the game.  Aliens can and do flank though they are not the brightest bulbs and will get themselves killed rather easily when isolated.   Boss fights are numerous but straight forward not showing much imagination.
The game has three difficulty modes each increasing in challenge.  I started with the middle difficulty but initially my life lasted as long as a Gastrotrich, so normal it was as my mood was for limiting restarts as much as possible given the game's propensity to kill you.
Story elements in the form of recordings are spread around the levels but I only found one third of the content. Whether I missed their obvious placement by chance or because they were hidden is unknown though the story can be ignored from the small portion I heard.  Bonus mini pyramids are also strewn about, three per level but again I never completed a set.  The pyramids add to your score as Alien Rage awards points during game-play and includes leader-boards as well.
Secondary ammo is also strewn about.  They look like suitcases so they aren't hard to miss although initially I wasn't sure what they were which brings us to the weapons.  An important part of any shooter.   The weapons are imaginative.  You get to carry only two plus a revolver.  There is a high reliance on secondary fire in order to implement much needed crowd control.  Primary ammo is picked up through gun pick ups as a dropped gun retains it's ammo or by walking over the same gun as you possess.   Weapons in the game consist of both alien and human.  Human weapons consist of differing semi automatic rifles, a sniper rifle, mentioned revolver, shotgun and rocket launcher.  Sounds and reads standard however each weapon has an important secondary fire mode as mentioned.
The rocket launcher, for example, when equipped will affect your sprinting ability and to use or un-equip the launcher the full animation must be run through making the weapon a bit strategic and difficult to use, a welcome feature considering the weapon's ability to quickly change the battlefield.  Which reminds me of enemy hit-boxes which I found to be well implemented.  I can remember shooting a rocket through enemy legs and cursing myself for lack of careful aiming.
The alien arsenal consists of energy weapons and is somewhat more limited.  No rocket launcher for example but the weapons are fun to use.  The alien rifle for instance has no reloads, however the weapon will overheat, again ensuring the player makes strategic use of the weapon.  The alien shotgun is very cool and very powerful, the cool anti gravity  secondary fire helps immensely.  To summarize the S in FPS, the shooting is exceptional, it's explosive and fun.
Some reviewers have panned the levels as being too generic.  So what.  The game looks and sounds great.  You feel Alien Rage, your feel of the game, both visual and auditory is significant.  Many of the levels have nice set pieces and it's great to see a publisher like City Interactive enable their development team to build a game with strong immersive environmental elements.  Great explosions not only permeate the combat but play a central role.  Graphically the game is exceptional though performance will vary but not enough to detract from the game.
Lastly I will address the utter disaster that is
.   Wait, it is not a system.  Systems by definition imply some sort of systematic routine.  No, the check-pointing, no, make that the checkpoint restart logic in Alien Rage is not just buggy.   I've come to the conclusion that it is unfinished.  There is no other reason for checkpoint restarts missing assets, many of which will prevent you from continuing the game.  Explosives for blowing apart levels to continue, needed secondary ammunition for combat , platforms not reset so you're left looking like a shopper waiting for a mall elevator.
I've found that after each death, instead of using the checkpoint continue, I had to exit to the main menu and continue from there.  It is beyond my wildest imagination how the developers obviously knowing that there checkpoint restart system was broken could not of just rewired their checkpoint code to use the continuation logic from the main menu.  From the continue on the main menu the game loaded correctly every time.  As the game loads very fast,  circumventing the intended method for checkpoint restarts is not a significant issue.
If you enjoy a good FPS then Alien Rage presents itself as a very challenging fun FPS that will satisfy most any FPS urge.

Hey, it's actually pretty good first person shooter! Graphics are amazing thanks to Unreal Engine and what I have to especially compliment, FOV adjustment that actually works, something you hardly ever see in any modern games these days. Player movement and aiming feels the same as all UE3 engine based games so that's an awesome start, because some games just feel awkward to move around. Not this one. Weapons feel pretty solid and destructive, ranging from projectile "human" weapons to energy based alien weapons. There are tons of bosses to fight and they aren't just gun them down, you sometimes have to think a bit to make them die.
Only downside are sometimes really crappy placed checkpoints where you might die a lot. And by a lot i mean A LOT. However, despite all the rage (funny how they placed that in teh game title) you'll have, the game will just keep on pushing you forward. You know those moments when game throws this seemingly unbeatable challenge at you and even though you're so close at throwing the game in the bin, you just keep on trying and trying. It's like that. It makes you hate the game so you love it. Weird, I know. The main reason for this are also player perks that give you special boosts. I'm not gonna tell you what they are, play the game and seeing how much you need to unlock them will make you want to play further. I'll just tell you they are so worth it, especially in the last 1/3 of the game. You can also change these perks on the fly so you can adapt to the given combat situation and they can help a lot especially for boss fights.
It might not have the most complicated story and it took me only a bit over 7 hours to complete, but I have that satisfying feeling in the end. I think the game is greatly underrated and should get a bit more attention. And I think this is by far the best game from City Interactive and actually very decent in general. They used to release very mediocre games, but this one certainly stands out quite a bit. And they even prepared it for a sequel. For a change, I'm actually looking forward to it. is a dark comedy adventure/survival where you'll need collect supplies and rescue your family before the nuke hits you. The characters are 4: you, Ted (as the patriarch), Dolores (the wife), Mary Jane (the daughter), and Timmy (the son). The goal of the game is that you and your family stay alive in your bunker. As each day passes, you'll need to make difficult decisions, ration food and water, and hunt mutant cockroaches. And the goal is always survive as long as possible.
You'll need to decide about some events too, such as a weird smell coming from a wall, someone banging on the door to your shelter, or family members getting sick, to deciding who, if anyone, should undertake an expedition to the surface to found supplies.
It's a one trick pony that gets stale in minutes. As I said before, your objective is to collect supplies and family in 60 seconds and then survive. That's it. There are some survival choice but it gets repetitive extremely fast. The game looks interesting in the first minutes but quickly becomes very boring and repetitive.
Events are generate randomly and most outcomes are random. You can't really make an informed and intelligent decision in most cases. Gameplay is just about clicking on choices. No recorded dialog, no animations, no level design. The whole thing becomes quite repetitive, as does the soundtrack.
After that, there is very little to talk about. Got bored in 20 minutes and never gonna look back at it. Thankfully, this game came in a bundle that I bought. Would be €9.99 most wasted in my life.

The Ship is an overlooked gem! The remastered version introduces some nice polish to the original an with a few more tweaks it will be an even more enjoyable. I have been a gamer for about 25 years an this game really hits the sweet spot for me.
It has:
Strategy:
*Micro-managing your characters needs. Think of yourself as a murderous sim. It adds a layer of depth to the gameplay an forces the player to interact with the env.  if you want to keep your character functioning. It provides hunters oppurtunities to take out their prey in a moment of weakness (like sleeping, socializng, showering, eating).
*Collecting items- Whether it be food, books, or weapons. Your always in search of that big ticket item to either defend yourself or get a kill with a nice reward for choosing a weapon high in value.
*Trying to find out who your prey is an not getting taking out by your hunter, or your prey once they realize your hunting them, and also avoid getting caught by security in the process.
Atmosphere- Amazing Ship designs! I enjoyed them so much I looked forward to memorizing there layouts in my head each time I played. The music an design really gives off a nice 50's vibe or whatever that era is in a colorful engaging way.
Imagination - The Ship oozes with imagination from every crevice of the hull. I just noticed playing earlier there was a skeleton tucked away in a corner on top of an elevator shaft. The environment is very engaging an highly detailed. Everything has a purpose.
Creativity- Many different ways to go about how you approach the game. Will you be a brute an go in guns blazing, or be more cunning an use trickery an deceit to take you to the top?
Suspense- One of my favorite concepts this game executes so well is the mystery of whom your prey is an who your hunter is. Everyone is on guard an highly suspicious of other characters. Addicitive Gameplay- For me, the replayability of this game is off the charts! This is one of those games you can leave (original ship)  for a few years, come back and recognize some names of players you played with in the past cause it is not an easy game to stop playing once your hooked.
Balance- I think the Remastered version could do with a few more tweaks an balancing out the level of character needs. Other than that, for what this game has to offer it has great balance that gives everything meaning an purpose.
I really want more ppl. to find this game, that is why I tried to write a detailed an extensive review.

This is a really good game.
You have to complete your bug-free game by release day which requires fixing some buggy code packages. Every "package" (i.e. stage) contains several "files" (i.e. levels) that have bugs which must be found and fixed. You need to avoid obstacles like enemies and spikes along the way, as well as surviving against the package's glitches. Each package has a set of glitches across all the files which change characteristics of the world (such as enemy size doubling or low gravity). As well as finding the bug in each level, there are also secondary objectives to be found that let you play a fun mini-game for a chance to permanently remove a glitch from the package to make those levels a bit easier. There's also glitches that you can find along the way to collect and use for yourself as a special move to help beat the level (such as jetpacks or inverting gravity). If you have a tough time or don't like the glitches for a particular package, you can refactor it which re-assigns a new random set of glitches to the package at the cost of losing deadline time.
I've been having a lot of fun with it. The gradual build-up of difficulty on each package feels great and gets fairly challenging toward the last one. The inventive gameplay feels very well balanced in many ways and makes you want to immediately keep trying again after death. The game has a very unique feel to it with well-designed graphics and sound. I didn't experience any technical issues and the user interface is solid too. If I had to choose, it kind of reminds me of a hybrid of Pony Island, Rogue Legacy, Broforce, and Super Meat Boy. The only thing that I could see some people not liking is the character's jumping/movement which is very quick/fluid and tends to overshoot easily such as in Super Meat Boy.
Definitely worth the price!

I'd played a lot of Bejeweled games before but I'd never played the Puzzle Quest games when I decided to try this out from a friend posting a screenshot on Steam about 2 weeks ago. It has a neat mix of CCG style game with match 3 in that you collect creature cards and unlock attacks and abilities by matching 3 or more gems together. Each card has a physical attack, magic, armor, and life stat that increases as you level cards with souls that you can get from battles or rewards, and that you can increase by fusing multiples of the same card together to create a higher rarity card. Each card also has passive traits that can be unlocked with trait stones that are won during battles or from opening chests. Your character also participates in these battles and has their own stats that increase with level with your ability being whatever weapon you have equiped at the time, which you unlock by increasing your element affinity during character leveling.
The AI is fairly competent and does a nice job of offering matching suggestions during the players turns though these suggestions (and what the AI plays) follows a priority list that may not be the best move to make, especially if you are trying to keep your opponent from filling their ability bar by matching their cards' elemental affinities. I really like that even if you lose the match whatever rewards you've gained during the match are kept (gold from cards/4 or 5 gem matches, keys to unlock chests, souls from defeating cards, treasure maps for the treasure mini game) as that was one of the things that annoyed me the most in a lot of other CCGs in making matches lost a complete waste of time. You can also quit out of a PVE match with no penalty and try again for no cost if you have bad luck at the start. This is also the type of game that is easy to play in the background while working on other things. I haven't explored the PVP much but I like that before the match starts you can pay a small amount of gold in PVE or PVP (50, which you can often win back that much or more from matching large chains) to see the creatures you'll be battling to help you plan a little strategy beforehand.
Now that said ultimately I think it's a really fun and pretty well designed game that is hobbled in the PVE by pretty much requiring the player to grind PVP or pay $ to advance at a certain point. There is a huge variety of cards but every card you receive starts at level 1 and requires souls to level up to being more useful so if you want to try a new strategy because you just got a bunch of new cards you're going to have to use souls, which you can win quite a bit in battles and Challenges, but is quick to burn through. PVE is primarily through Kingdom Quests that you unlock with gold as you level up and Challenges, which you unlock by progressing in the Kingdoms' Quests. I'm not sure if AI character card levels are determined by progression through the total number of quests completed, player level, or from unlocking new Kingdoms but I feel I'm increasingly only beating quests by primarily luck and spamming the heck out of status effects and dropping  enemy physical attack to 0 with my level 6 cards (I keep switching out to try new cards or in upgrading cards) against now level 16 AI cards with my level 29 player (which has a much lower effect since the player's stats raise slower than creature stats). Early on in the game the problem I had was getting useful cards; now some of the quests are just incredibly difficult if not nearly impossible to do with my lowish leveled cards.
I wonder if perhaps the best thing for me to do if I want to continue playing is to find a way to completely start over and use player guides to help me plan out my advancement in the game prior to. As a FtP game the pay to win mechanics seem moderate but have a larger effect on PVE (I've played several games with terrible pay to win mechanics but that mostly just affect PVP). It's possible this is going to be one of the shortest FtP multiplayer games I play online; not because I don't like the game- it's an awesome game and I wouldn't have played it for so many hours in my two weeks of playing it; but because I'm eventually going to be unable to advance the PVE without grinding PVP or paying $ and I haven't yet decided whether dropping $10 or more would give me much long term enjoyment in Gems of War.

EDIT: Just reached level 100 without buying into the game, and got all achievements!

This game was one I got into.  It was simple, it appealed to my want to collect things like cards and engage in competitive play to see what interesting combos I could come with.  I went on hiatus for a while and came back to find a host of new regions and features, including some significant synergy boosting abilities with the Trait system as well as major events, new chests to unlock and many more cards and heroes, as well as a really great Class system that I took  advantage of, since I had maxed out my party already.
Sadly, this game has a major fault.  Having re-joined after this overhaul the game didn't do a great job in emphasizing some major benefits of the online play, namely the guild system.  First of all, I'll tell any new player, join a guild at the first convenience, the benefits are utterly broken!  If you don't, you're just missing out on a HUGE advantage, that's just the bottom line.  Sadly, there is no effective way to search for guilds.  If you have a friend that's in one, you have to hope you can somehow get an invite as only a selection of guilds with openings are available to you via the "search" option.  You don't actually get to "search" for anything, the game just finds a handful of available guilds and displays them.  Furthermore, there's an immensely benefit to joining a guild over a high (in this case the lower the number the better, which is counter to how the PvP ranking works) Rank.  Unfortunately, there's no way to view any of the guilds stats besides how many openings they have, meaning that your only method of really deciding would be to randomly join one, view their benefits and rank and then decide whether you want to leave then.
Here's my biggest bugbear with this game...I've spent 274 hours on it in total so far, unlocked every region, maxed them all out, refined my team and leveled up my class so that I had one that worked efficently...I thought I was playing well, but I was wrong.  In less than 70 hours, I friend of my mine has immensely more to show for it and not just a matter of RNG either.  Having joined a guild fairly early on, he gained immensely more than I had in nearly half the time, leaving me feeling rankly like I had done nothing but waste my time when I could have had a lot more to show for it.  So yes, join a guild right away, you have nothing but to gain from it and quickly.

If you didn't play Pathologic in 2005 (or haven't heard about it at all before 2015), now is the right time to do it. Probably you already know about Ice-Pick Lodge's plan to release a remake in 2016, but, listen, it's going to differ from the original (and you don't know how much, which is not a bad thing at all, but that's not the point), while this one is the good old Pathologic with minor to zero changes in graphics (such as additional blur) and more friendliness to English public (if a surreal survival horror can be called friendly).
In my first playthrough I used to describe this game as "Dostoyevsky on psychodelics". Later on I submerged deeper into the plethora of contexts of this product, but such a dsecription can probably give a hint of what Pathologic is. This is a very Russian product. It means neither that it is of bad quality, like some of Russians themselves think about their countriy's videogame industry, nor that it has scenes of bears playing Prokofiev on balalaikas. Rather than that, it means that the images which this game contains are very close to Russian art in general (mostly this is about literature). The visuals strangely help intensify the feeling. A yellowish gamma, properly selected textures (can't really explain it in details, but they add a lot to the style of the game), overall design (sometimes crude which actually does the game good) - everything works in such a way that you experience the plagued town deeper.
Please keep in mind, though, that Pathologic can go hardcore on you - not because of difficulty (it's quite easy once you get the survival basics - especially after the first playthrough, and you need at least three to get the whole picture) or some mistakes in game design (Russian fans usually say that these "features" are a part of the dark atomosphere). The challenges are psychological. Sometimes it almost seems the game doesn't want to be played. But that was the goal of the authors (it's a totally different topic which can be discussed in the community or Ice-Pick Lodge forum). The Plague, the main antagonist in the game, is repulsive. The town is filthy. The dark secrets are dark. The strange things are driving you mad because you don't understand what's happening (especially, once again, in your first playthrough). Everything is against you. But you need to pass this resolve test to get your prize, which is experiencing one of the most unusual and deep videogames.
So take some immunity pills and jump in.
