Pathologic was always a remarkable game. Tense, atmospheric, unforgiving, completely exhilarating. It captured the essence of player choice better than just about anything else - of reward versus cost, the now versus the potential future - in providing a constantly evolving world where everything you did always had to be measured against what you could have done instead.
None of that has changed in this newly translated version.
What has changed is that Pathologic is now also a truly impressive piece of comprehensible fiction. Carrying forth the great Russian literary tradition into a new medium with an intricate web of a story that tackles subjects such as state, religion, addiction, mortality, family, mysticism, ethics, murder, clinical research and individual ideology and ambition. All told through monomaniacal character dialogue and the stark scenery of the world.
It's a story and world building that works on many simultaneous levels, and the things it has to say about both the human condition and the video game medium itself - and by extension, art in general - is deeper and more poignant than anything I've witnessed before in video games.
It all adds up to an extraordinary experience, and also one of the very best games I have ever played.

Not for the faint hearted. Pathologic is a game about making hard decisions both in the short and long term whilst coping with a constantly ticking timer of 13 days.
Released in 2005, winning Russian Game Of The Year and getting a poor english localization the game was fated to never succeed. It had lots of bugs and an awful translation that often left players completely unaware as to what to do. This new HD release doesn't fix all the problems the original had but it does smooth out the bugs as well as completely retranslating the game into something far more sensible.
At it's core, Pathologic is very much like any other first person western role playing game but leans towards a survival horror take on the usual genre.
The game is extremely difficult, dying is common, sometimes you can die in your sleep and the game won't help you, it'll just give you a big fat GAME OVER. The game requires quite a few hours of experimentation which can be easy if you quick save and quick load often; just be ready to sacrifice your sanity as you attempt to balance drug taking with disease, starvation and exhaustion all while selling your gun to get a can of peas so you can live another day. If you are unable to spend the time to learn the game and it's strange and nerve wrecking mechanics you might want to skip it altogether, but you're not a coward are you?
By far the most unique and avant garde video game you'll ever play. Get ready to laugh, cry and breath in the miasma that is Pathologic.

If you were to read the steam reviews for this game you would assume you were playing an absolute masterpiece.
In reality, it's a clumsy walking simulator with a plot that got lost in translation.  Characters spout cryptic gibberish and direct you around a largely empty town, urging you to speak to various NPCs who can shed light on your predicament.  You play as one of three (only two are available from the beginning) characters whos fates have been somehow entwined in a dusty town on the edge of nowhere.
If you choose to play as the 'Haruspex" , you have unwittingly opted in to a harsh survival sim, where everyone is out to get you and careful management of health , fatigue, hunger, and reputation is crucial.  If any one of these meters reaches a critical point,  you are unceremoniously greeted with a failure cinematic and dumped back to the main menu.  There is no warning, no second chance, just failure.  And loading a saved game.  Some times it even happens when the HUD says you're ok.  Why not.
Proponents of 'old school' games, and masochistic players who enjoy being subjected to obtuse mechanics will probably laud this unforgiving attitude toward progression.  Kill a man so you can loot his organs, and sell them to a weird little guy who lives in a swamp on the far end of the map.  He will give you herbs in exchange.  What can you do with these herbs? Something.  Probably.
On the plus side, the atmosphere is pretty awesome here,  evoking memories of S.T.A.L.K.E.R, with its hunched characters and ramshackle environments.  The audio is also strong with a disturbing score, that seems to be comprised of a mixture of tribal chanting and hiccups.  Gameplay wise however, there's not much to like.  The world may evoke a powerful atmosphere but it is largely static, with almost zero interactive objects.  Get used to looting the same two garbage bins over and over again ....
If you are willing to put up with all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t this game throws your way,  and slog through the inane, poorly translated dialogue, I'm sure you would find some kind transcendent experience here.  The city is some kind of metaphorical purgatory where doomed souls go to live out their nightmares.
I played two days but found little to no players online so unless you get a group of friends together to play its not worth the money.

Damned is a flawed game with a tremendous amount of potential.
The basic premise is an asymetrical multiplayer FPS horror game.  Four players play people and one person plays some sort of monster.  The monster is invincible and can kill any of the players instantly.  The players need to navigate their way through frequently labyrinthine levels full of locked doors and... well locked doors.  If the monster kills all the players, the monster wins.  If the players find the exit, the players win.  The monsters can only hunt the players at certain times in certain circumstances.  The rest of the time they are trying to keep tabs on the players if they can, and generally keep the players as scared as possible.
The things about this game that I love:
- As a player, because you have no real defenses of your own, the monsters are terrifying.  Seeing one always elicits an immediate and frantic attempt to escape.
- The 3D attenuated sound means that the monsters can really add to the experience by acting in scary (or funny) ways.
- The complicated level layouts leave lots of time for the players to get lost, get separated, be hunted, etc.  Games almost always last long enough for quite a few good scares and intense moments.
The problems with this game:
- Horribly buggy.  We have never had a gaming session that hasn't been marred by game crashes, freezes, etc.  It can be tricky to recover from some of these crashes, and sometimes they'll require a hard reboot.  Also, the game requires a login, and if you crash sometimes that login gets locked in a session meaning you can't rejoin for a while.
- The monsters have very little to do in the periods when they aren't being a direct threat.  Sure you can "place traps", but that entails nothing more then clicking on objects.  Not particularly exciting.
- The players have only one puzzle to solve.  Find the key that fits the door.  And there are no clues as to which key is for what, so not only is it a very boring puzzle, it's extremely tedious as you try every key you find on every door that's locked.  Sure, there are also boarded doors and safes, but they are still the same mechanic, it's just that the key is named "hammer", or "crowbar" or "safe code".
- The maps and monsters are terribly balanced.  Some monsters will wipe out the players very quickly.  Others will make for excellent experiences.  Some maps fit certain monsters very well, but fit other monsters very poorly.
All in all I want to recommend this game, and have marked it as such.  However, it has some serious issues, and I would caution against buying it without being aware of the issues it has.

Damned is a great first person survival horror, played best with close friends. Four survivors are forced to try and escape, as a monster with unique abilities is trying to hunt and kill them.

Super Panda Adventures was a surprisingly enjoyable throwback platformer that I couldn't put down once I'd started.  Anyone with a love of the genre, and particularly those who enjoyed early PC platformers, will find a lot to like here. Your objectives are laid out in a multi-quest fashion, and levels are not beaten but rather explored in parts to achieve these missions. The levels are not particularly numerous but they are vast, to the point that you will still find yourself on unknown paths on your 3rd or 4th visits. These replays are also enhanced by a Metroid-like collection of upgrades combined with a classic colored-key system that provides for a persisent sense of exploration alongside a growing feeling of power and mobility.
There are no inconsequential collectibles, everything that doesn't fill a meter either directly makes Fu stronger or is money which can be used to  buy additional experience. After a semi-casual 8 hour playthrough I did not hit the level cap, and expect it would take a long time to do so. I think a normal player will likely only acquire about half of the skill points it would take to fill everything out, so your choices in this regard do matter (to the game's credit). They may matter more than you expect though, as there are a few boss fights which unexpectedly and dramatically shift into a much higher difficulty than the levels themselves. 3 different bosses each required several attempts from me and forced me to adapt to a more "pro" block-oriented combat style, and while I felt a satisfying sense of achievement after each, a more casual player might find these to be too much of a challenge to proceed.
The plot and dialogue are kid-friendly but also dryly amusing for an adult, poking light fun at various game tropes and dashed with a touch of real warmth. The interface is almost perfect with tight controls (bolstered by a nice built-in joystick/gamepad mapping feature), an excellent all-in-one character inventory/menu, and a comfortably traditional HUD. My only interface complaint is that there is no way to tell from the overworld which keys or collectibles you already have in each level, leaving a bit too much to memory. The music is excellent throughout (though after repeat level visits may wear thin for some). The game's art is done in a simple but charming low-res hand-drawn style with a nice variety of theme and color. The levels are distinct and pretty, though the overworld maps are a bit crude and flat (perhaps also in homage to the oldies?).
All told, Super Panda Adventures is a great little indie platformer at a great little price. It's obvious that a lot of love and thought went into this title. It takes some of the best elements from some of the best games in the genre and smartly combines them into something familiar but fresh and, most importantly, fun.

They Breathe lets you loose amongst strange, dangerous creatures, and the threat of suffocation is ever-present. To survive you need to observe the creatures and experiment with how they interact with each other and with the environment. There's no real tutorial, no point system or power-ups. The only way to survive and progress is to further your understanding through play. The story is also developed through play, and by understanding how the creatures work you'll start to understand the story, without a single line of dialogue or text. The short length of around 30 minutes is perfect - every wave of enemies presents you with something new to overcome and understand, and not a minute is wasted.
The only real thing I feel is lacking is an options menu. There's no way to adjust the audio or resolution from within the game since there's no options menu. I also ran into a problem getting the game to work in fullscreen (the default mode). Starting the game would make my monitor go black for a second and then the game would minimize and every attempt to bring the game back up would result in the same thing happening. I ended up having to go into the Config.cfg file in the game's directory to set it to windowed mode, which fixed it.
Aside from some fairly minor technical stuff, the game is impressively and elegantly designed to reward play without any immersion-breaking gamey stuff. It's short and sweet and immensely satisfying to play.

This review is related to the Shadowrun: Dragonfall director’s cut (my review of the older version is together with the Shadowrun Returns, as the older version accounted hours in that game). This version of the game brought some modifications to the older version that significantly changed the gameplay, in some ways for better and in other ways for worse.
The new missions included were very nice, besides giving you the opportunity to gain more karma and increase your stats to a higher level by the end of the game. I really liked the missions entering into the story line of the team characters, something that I missed in the first version. Also, the additional ending that allows you to complete the project is really really nice. It definitively made my replaying of the game worthy. Finally, now you can improve certain characteristics of your team mates to make them less useless in combat (most of them still pretty useless in the hardest difficulty, but it was an improvement).
However, the new rule for critical hits really sucks… You cannot give a critical hit when your target has any cover. So, you have to break their cover somehow in order to deliver significant damage - by unbalancing them, hitting them on melee, whatever… In the hardest difficulty level, this new rule made the combats last an eternity (and not more difficult), especially on the final part, which has a lot of enemies and the first thing they do is take cover. I hated this modification as it made the final part of the game boring. Even though, the game still great to play and the history lines should please any Shadowrunner fan. Definitively worth playing.

Watch_Dogs is probably the best game among those which received mostly negative reviews. The fact that it is not following in the footsteps of the GTA franchise (that series focuses on r.e.t.a.r.d.e.d characters having to kill all the time) greatly enhanced W_D's appeal. W_D is a sandbox style game which combines GTA's "driving to mission trigger icon" mechanics and Ubisoft's own "climb tower to see details on map" obsession.
The main story is about a hacker, who has to deal with his own past while solving several mysteries in Chicago. Sounds nothing extraordinary, but in my opinion the details of the storyline are very refined and that's why it never becomes boring. After 3 full playthroughs of the base game and 2 full playthroughs of the Bad Blood DLC I can say with confidence that this game is much better than anything other games in this genre can offer. The original Mafia was too hard (it not even the difficulty that bothered me, but the lack of save points which made it extremely annoying to replay large sections after something had gone wrong) and the world didn't offer too much. Mafia II was short and also lacked content. GTA (from Vice City to IV) on PC was a pain to control (flying especially), and I could never enjoy playing dumb characters. Then I'd played Ubisoft's open world attempts from Far Cry 2 to AC Unity (that is at least 10 games) which were sometimes entertaining, but mostly making me shake my head in disbelief.
W_D combines the best aspect of all of them. Driving is fun. Some might say controls are disastrous, but I think on PC with the keyboard it is in fact (except for the superfast supercars) quite predictable and comfortable. All vehicle classes handle differently and the damage model is amazing. The action is very realistic (not much blood or anything too obvious, but the physics and animations are very lifelike), and the missions are challenging and fun. The side quests are somewhat repetitive, but the living, breathing environment makes up for it big time (weird, though, just as all the other games with similar settings, there are no kids anywhere and no one rides motorbikes). The hacking mini-game is brilliant and there are tons of things to do in the city in the main game as well as in the DLC (one playthrough with “completionist” attitude easily lasts 30 hours). But at the heart of this action packed game there is one of the best stealth mechanics in existence. Based purely on scores I am in the top 30 on all Splinter Cell Black list missions. My point with this is that I love and know how to utilize the tools of Ubisoft's latest generation stealth games and what I'd learned playing SC Blacklist was a big help in getting used to W_D's stealth game play. And luckily almost all main story missions (and the Gang Hideout missions too) can be played sneaking in the dark, using purely non-lethal takedowns. And when I say dark, I mean not just nightfall, but creating my own darkness by overloading or permanently disabling power transformers to cause blackouts. The game offers Aidan, the protagonist of W_D a wide array of upgradable skills from driving and weapons to hacking, sabotaging or distracting enemies. All in a fluently usable interface.
Some of these skills help creating lures, improvised explosives, and jamcomms. These items also require parts that can be found or purchased and then crafted. Crafting is easy, unlike in the AC games, and can be done during missions without any special tools or crafting table. But the most useful skills (besides the hand to hand close combat skills used by a stealth player) are the hacking skills. From ATM machines to traffic lights almost anything can be manipulated by Aidan's smartphone.
There are dozens of driving side missions, about a dozen Gang Hideout side missions (basically the player has to sneak in or fight their way in to a hideout to take down the leader without killing him), several investigations including one of the creepiest serial killers who leaves foil wrapped, dead bodies and scary video tapes at the crime scenes. The well known Ubi tower climb (which is even copied by Crystal Dynamics in their new Tomb Raider) is now replaced by tower hacking. That is a combination of climbing (finding the way to a small computer by solving puzzles) and installing a backdoor. Hacking the towers reveals collectibles, side missions, hideouts and fast travel locations.
When it comes to the action, the enemy AI in general is quite good. They are fast to react and can flank the player in seconds. Unless their phones are hacked too, they call for backup. The car chases are very difficult sometimes, the bad guys are hard to chase down or evade. The traffic density makes it difficult to just speed mindlessly. Hacking underground steam pipes, activating blockers, spike traps, draw bridges makes it fun to take on several enemy cars at the same time. There is just one flaw, an "error in the matrix". Hilariously, it seems Ubi uses behavioral codes similar to the Assassin's Creed series, because the enemy AI responds to a certain situations in the same manner. When I'm in a chase, being the mouse, I can't really lose the "cats" inside the city. Unless... unless I hijack a boat (even the slowest water taxi does the trick) use the river to escape. The enemy AI simply cannot follow the player. Cops and gang bangers have no interest of hopping on a boat or just afraid to get their tiny toes wet. Just as in AC, whenever I jumped in water the chasers almost instantly lost interest! Is this a coincidence?
I couldn't find anything really bad about this game even though I've tried. A small thing was bugging me in the plot. Way before Aiden is revealed to be the Vigilante, the radio announces his name and background, even though he is not shown on any tape and he wears a baseball hat and his face is shrouded by a bandana. Or the fact that the story is predetermined, nothing can be changed or altered with decisions or more heroics, it is always the same. I would have loved to see something like Mass Effect and also being able to carry the saves over to any upcoming sequel. But, unfortunately it's never gonna happen, since Ubi abandoned Chicago and my beloved characters, Aidan, T-Bone, Frewer and Clara and started another one, which by the looks of it doesn't have half the appeal this one has.
And where the hell is Brad Keselowski?
Anyone who is curious about why things happened in the first place... the Bad Blood DLC might shed some light on previous events, and one particular villain's past. Also, the DLC comes with an excellent new story and many new side quests that allow for another good 20 hours of game play. Not to mention the online challenges which rank (and give XP) players (based on time and efficiency dealing with enemies and objectives) after every 3 and a half hours.
The multiplayer aspect is rather weak, for me it was best turning it off from the menu. If the option left enabled, other players will enter your game trying to hack your phone, unless you find them first and dispose of them in a flattening (driving a cement mixer for example) of explosive (well, what the word suggests) way. And of course, you can do the same, enter other players W_D universe to hack their phones unless they kill you first. It sounds fun (in a masochistic way), but it can happen in the worst moments (whenever you are not playing a main story mission), making it a nuisance.
The graphics engine called Disrupt is breathtaking. On PC it runs at whatever resolution (unlike consoles where frame rates and resolution is locked) very smoothly. Unless you run the DLC, where suddenly choppiness becomes an issue due to bad optimizing I guess. Anyway messing with settings solves it fast.
Music by Brian Reitzell is excellent, the voice acting is top notch as always from Ubisoft. Years after it's release it is an affordable game that would entertain the fans of this genre for weeks.

Fair warning: This game is not for everyone.
Pathologic is hard to describe. It is part survival, part exploration, part role-playing, and part first person shooter. The story is confusing, intentionally so, and the game does not hold you by the hand. You are expected to pay attention, learn the lore and story behind the events taking place, and generally invest into the experience. If you do that, you will find no other experience like it. Your choices will matter. If you just want a casual learning curve, skip right on to something else because Pathologic is not for you.
The gameplay is clunky, old school, and the graphics are very basic for a game re-released in 2015. But as you play Pathologic, you will figure out the inner workings of the game just as you explore the innards of the town, quickly find what best to do and not to do, and generally get over the mechanical hurdles. If you want a quick start tip: buy food on day 1, stock up as much as you can, because prices skyrocket on day 2. Check the trash bins and learn to trade. Trading with the townsfolk is probably the best way to acquire wealth in items, especially bullets.
You will be walking from place to place a lot, and it is important to learn the layout of the town and how to best hit your objectives. This is something you will do over the course of the game, so it's entirely okay to look at your map to find proper placement. Do note that time does not pass while you are looking at the map, letters, or quests. But time does pass otherwise, and any quests not finished by midnight are dropped.
If you are still curious just what is going on in that town by the river, give it a shot. Play the Bachelor first, as it's a good introduction to the game. The first few days are slow, but once you are past that things quickly pick up. If you want hard mode, where you are dropped from orbit, battered, and then left unconscious in hostile territory, play Haruspex. Do note that Haruspex basically assumes you are familiar with most of the mechanics, people, and methods of survival. I highly recommend doing a Bachelor run first, and that should be anywhere from 20 to 30+ hours.
Note: There is a re-release of Pathologic on the way; if you enjoyed the HD release, throw them some cash for those stretch goals. Or just wait for that game to hit instead of playing the HD release.

Pathologic is a survival game about a town that's been affected by a seemingly incurable plague. You play as one of three characters: a charming bachelor doctor, a ritualistic healer, and a mysterious young girl with an unusual set of powers. Your enemy is invisible, but incredibly dangerous - and every day is a fight for survival.
It's a dark, haunting experience. And I absolutely adore it. Your choices have immediate and often far-reaching consequences. All of the quests are optional. Sometimes you won't even have time to complete quests if you need to find food or rest, but people are likely to die as a result of your decisions - even when you think you're doing the right thing.
This isn't the prettiest game by any stretch, but the world is fascinating. If you're concerned about the graphics not being up to par, there's not a whole lot to be concerned about. It's a game from 2005, sure, but the art, music, and overall design of this world are still captivating. And luckily all of the murals and posters have had their textures updated in this release. Plus, the added visual effects (depth of field and motion blur) do actually add to the mood considerably.
And that mood is phenomenal. Pathologic is a terrifying glimpse into a place that was crafted by a team determined to work towards creating a unified, hollistic vision. I've heard that the concept for this game came from a dream, and in playing this game, I certainly feel like I'm exploring one. It's a sometimes terrifying place, with weird citizens and strange cultures where you're never sure what's real - or who you can trust, for that matter.
I love this game. I love the people who made this game. It's fascinating. I can hardly stop thinking about it. It's like being a stranger in a strange land. I feel like I'm exploring Morrowind for the first time all over again, except it's brutal and tragic and I'm not the hero.
I can't recommend this game enough. It's rough around the edges, but it's fantastic. The new translation is also beyond my expectations. The original, for those who don't know, was often incomprehensible - but with the new one, you don't even need a map. I'm deighted Ice Pick Lodge decided to revisit a ten-year-old game and fix it up. This is the remastering this game deserved.
However, all that being said, I still hope that the "Pathologic: Remake" (expected late 2016 or possibly later) makes the experience even better. If you don't feel like diving into this rich, incredibly realized fictional universe now, wait for that release. Ice Pick Lodge seem to be incredibly passionate about their games and I have no doubt in my mind that their latest re-imagining of this title is going to blow away all of my expectations. But if this universe piques your attention, then I can't see any harm in diving in right now. This is the best version of Pathologic to date, and probably one of the most important games I've ever played.

Speaking of design, the user interface recently got a "modern" and "sleek" update, which is both hideous and completely out of place with the medieval fantasy theme.
Another problem: bugs. Many of the card's abilities don't function as described, especially those that attack multiple targets and then inflict them with a status effect (Emperor Khorvash, I'm looking at you).
I'll be honest: I still play the game. Possibly out of the desire to remain in my guild, possibly because I can't abandon the troops I've painstakingly collected so far. But if you are considering the game having never played it before, you'd be better off investing your time somewhere else.

Cannon Brawl is a RTS game with giant cannons. Who doesn't like giant cannons?
Basically the goal is to destroy your enemy's castle using a strategically chosen set of cannon types. Turtle Sandbox has given you a variety of methods and combinations of cannons that allows you to decide between decimating your enemy entirely, or (if you're like me) slowly wittling away the ground underneath your friend's castle, giving them a small gleam of hope. Of course, for them, there is none - something you illustrate by using your drill or laser cannon to knock out the remaining support below their castle, making your friend watch their base (and hopes) fall to its demise. It's sophisticatedly savage.

Project: Snowblind isn't going to go down as one of the great legendary FPS games, but it is a very good game for the $1.50 I paid for it. The structure of the game is that of your usual single-player fps campaign (beating a linear series of levels), but it does some interesting things that make it worth playing.
The combat in this game is excellent. Each weapon is interesting and fun to use, but more importantly each weapon is useful for different types situations, meaning you'll be switching which one you use frequently. Furthermore, they all retain their usefullness throughout the campaign, meaning you won't be lugging around a bunch of useless weapons by the time the endgame rolls around. Each weapon also has an alt-fire, which expands their possibilities even more.
This game started off as a spin-off of Deus Ex, and even though the final product no longer shares that title or universe (and doesn't have any rpg elements, being a pure FPS), it does let you use the same of type nano-augmentations to give you the upper hand in combat. This ranges from making your self invisible, to shooting electric bolts, to becoming completely invulnerable. These augmentations let you try a variety of different strategies for approaching each battle and did a great job of spicing up the game (although I did find myself using the invulerability one pretty much exclusively it was made available). Also like Deus Ex, there is also a hacking element. You have a device called the "icepick" that lets you fire a dart onto anything that's hackable and then take control of that thing remotely. This allows you to take control of turrets and mechs, and using them to turn the tables on the enemies is hilarious and awesome.
The last thing in terms of gameplay I want to bring up is that the level design is excellent. Even though the levels are mostly linear, each area gives you a handful of options and alternate routes, meaning you could go in guns blazing, or you could try to find a sneakier path and do things stealthily. Overall, the gameplay is Project: Snowblind's strongest point, as the weapon design, level design, and augmentations blend together brilliantly.
Despite the excellent gameplay, there are a handful of areas Project: Snowblind falls short in, some of which were detrimental to my enjoyment of the game, some not so much. The biggest issue I had with this game is that the saves are handled using manual checkpoints you must find and activate within the level, as opposed to being able to save where you want or using automatic checkpoints. Normally, I don't mind checkpoints too much, but Project: Snowblind only has one or two of these points per level, meaning that if you die, you usually have to replay much more of what you just did than is desirable (usually about 7 or 8 minutes worth). What's even worse is these checkpoints are sometimes hidden in obscure, out of the way places and in some levels I couldn't even find them despite the game having a feature telling you what direction you should be heading to find them. These checkpoints really drag down the game, and whenever I found myself quitting the game, it was usually because I was tired of having to replay massive swaths just to retry one point.
On the technical side, Snowblind has a few glaring issues as well. I had the game crash on me several times during my playthrough. This was especially annoying because they usually happened once I finally overcame whatever section of the game I was stuck on (meaning I would have to replay that part yet again once I restarted the game). Annother annoying bug is that there is something wrong with the game's contrast, making everything look extremely washed out making stuff that's supposed to be black more of a gray. This seems to effect everyone's copy and I haven't found any kind of workaround or fix. Take a loot at the user posted screenshots on this game's Steam community hub, then compare them to the screenshots on the Store page, and you will see that something is very wrong. This is extremely annoying and even makes the game hard to look at in places, which is unfortunate, because you can tell the game has decent art direction and isn't supposed to look like this (videos I watched of the PS2 and Xbox versions seemed to be fine however). With that said, I was able to look past this and enjoy the gameplay (which again, is excellent), but this is something you should know about going in.
The storyline is a weak point as well, but it does have some merit. The overall plot is completely forgettable, basically serving as an excuse for you to shoot your way through each level (as an aside, nearly every cutscene contains a helicopter either destroying something or getting destroyed. This is not a problem). The most interesting thing about the storyline is that the big evil plot that you try to prevent is almost identical to one of the ending options from Deus Ex 1, but that's about it. With that said, the character themselves were actually pretty likeable and distinct, and there is some pretty good voice acting as well (the game also has a surprisingly decent sense of humor that pops up now and them). You won't care why you're fighting this war, but you will enjoy the company.
Overall, Project: Snowblind is pretty solid for a budget game, thanks to fantastic gameplay (even if it doesn't have much else going for it). I don't think I'll be playing through it a second time, but for $1.50, the ride was a fun one worth taking.

Obligatory header to the review: I focus on four primary areas whenever I review a game: gameplay, story, graphics, and sound/audio/general things that go into your earholes. Gameplay and Story get a rating scale from 1 to 10, and the AV stuff gets a rating from 1 to 5. My philosophy on this is that there are some instances in which a game may not necessarily have that much in the way of gameplay (take Amnesia for example), but the story/atmosphere/whatever it may be is reason enough to pick it up. Also, take the cumulative score with a grain of salt; it's just a numerical feeling about the game as a whole. That's part of why I do these subscores. Also, keep in mind that I'm not going off of school grade based rankings. A 5/10 denotes what I feel to be an average game. Likewise, 7/10 is a game that I think is pretty cool, and something that gets a 2/10 is near-abomination level. Pinning scores to an even further obfuscated rating scale is kinda senseless, but for the sake of my backloggery, I'll repeat again that 1.0-2.7 is a one-star game, 3.0-4.7 is a two-star game, 5.0-6.7, 7.0-8.7, and 9.0-10 are three, four, and five stars, respectively.
Gameplay: Project Snowblind, as you may or may not know, was originally intended to be a more multi-player focused game in the Deus Ex series to be called Deus Ex: Clan Wars. Then Invisible War came along and utterly tarnished the Deus Ex name.  Despite the abandonment of the namesake, the game still retains a lot of the level design sensibilities that Deus Ex had, albeit a lot more straightforward here than in Deus Ex. By that, I mean that the player has plenty of choices on how to take areas. You can run in, guns ablaze; pick enemies off from a distance with the sniper rifle; sneak through the area entirely; hack any nearby electronics to kill enemies remotely, etc. etc. Since I often opt for the most meat-headed approach to gameplay, I was a guns blazing kind of player, although there were a few chapters where I found that it wasn't the best approach.
As I said earlier, this game is pretty much Deus Ex Lite. It has pretty much everything Deus Ex had, although much simpler to suit the very action oriented gameplay. All the RPG elements are gone, which can be disappointing for some. Hacking is done with an Icepick; a weird sort of EMP hacking kajigger. This does mean that you are limited to how many things you can hack throughout the level, although I found that ammo for the Icepick was easy to come by, presuming you looked around for it. Augmentations are here as well, with a few abilities being cloaking, slow motion, and bullet shields. They don't last forever and do use up Bioenergy, which you can find both replenishing items and increases to your maximum Bioenergy (the same for health, of course).
Unfortunately, this game is very much a port. Autoaim is on by default, and I found no way of disabling it. Some people talked about the game crashing all the time; it crashed a couple of times for me, and both times it was just after a cutscene started. After looking at what happened in the Event Viewer, I wasn't able to make certain what it was specifically in Snowblind.SP that crashed or why it did so. This could have also been because of a thing I did to make the game run at 1080p (I'll talk about that later). I did rebind a couple of keys; namely rebinding augmentation usage to Tab and getting rid of the weapon menu altogether. It's just more fun frantically scrolling through weapons in the heat of battle (to me, at least).
The levels themselves are short, usually lasting about ten to fifteen minutes, and have at least one savepoint in the area. This game doesn't have checkpoints, so be sure to make use of the savepoints. These levels are pretty well paced and often feel reasonable and fair without being completely boring. Enemy variety isn't the greatest, and I would have liked to have seen a few more mech enemies, but it's not too big of a deal. Overall, if you're looking for a dumb mid-2000's shooter to play for a night, you really can't go wrong with this one. For the price of $6 (I picked it up on sale, so it was even cheaper), I can say that this is a very worthwhile purchase, even if you do have to do a few things to get it in reasonable working order. 8/10.
Story: Again, it's pretty much Deus Ex Lite. The game did open with some actually quite good exposition of the main character, Nathan Frost. Unfortunately, it does kinda turn to the same old military hoo-rah schtick after a while. There really isn't much in the way of character development for Frost, much less for anyone else. At least it's not Russia being the bad guys, so I guess there's that. However, at least it's pretty well directed, even if the source material isn't the greatest. The cinematics are pretty well done, even if they do have some questionable choices in filters from time to time. They do start to feel like more of an action movie than a Deus Ex intrigue, however, so take that as you will. However, for what was there, it was pretty enjoyable, if rather cliche at times. 7/10.
Graphics: You're gonna need to do a bit of work in order to get this game running decently on a modern computer. For starters, this game only runs in 4:3 using the default resolutions in-game. I looked a bit on the Steam forums for this game, and I came across a fix that had me download an over-riding DX9 .dll file and its associated .cfg. In that .cfg, it's rather easy to set the resolution to that of your monitors. Some people have said that the fix doesn't work for them, but it worked well for me. Perhaps they didn't put the .dll and .cfg file in the root directory of the game; I dunno. Nevertheless, if you do a little searching on the P:S forums for a topic on widescreen resolution, you'll find what I'm talking about. I will be keeping that file around; it seems to be a pretty neat little multi-purpose DX9 "modernizer". Just don't be dumb and drop it in System32.
As for how the game looks in the perspective of art style, this is what I talk about when I bring up realistic graphics not standing the test of time. It doesn't look god-awful, but it isn't the easiest thing to look at. Probably the best looking area in the game is the last level, which goes for a very Tron-esque look. Again, the game as a whole doesn't look terrible today, but this is yet another reason why art style should always trump realism when it comes to visual direction. 2/5.
Sound: The soundtrack is pretty much a generic action movie soundtrack. It's not bad and it does pump you up, but it's still not that musically interesting. Voice acting is alright; it's certainly not going to be winning any awards, but it's probably not going to put you off, either. I'm running out of space, so I'll just say it's alright. 3/5.
Overall scores are: 8/7/2/3; cumulative score of 6.7/10.

Difficulty isn't as bad as it may seem... perseverence and old school pattern recognition pays off.    If you rush in guns blazing like Master Chief, you WILL DIE.  Even at the beginning.  You must have tactics and use cover, playing defensively.  The game is rarely, if ever, "cheap" with its difficulty.  You usually die because you screwed up.  Weapons are satisfying and fun to use.  Enemies are diverse and aggressive.  Soundtrack is decent, and I began to warm up to the quippy companions you radio chat with and the audio logs tell a decent story, even if I was underwhelmed that there's basically no closure to it by the end.  This game is basically the love child of Doom, Halo and Gears of War.  "I was told there were no gears in this!?!"  Self-depricating humor for the win.  I was sad it was over, which is rare for me with shooter campaigns that last more than 8 hours.

Alien Rage seemed to me like a very generic FPS. I found it very hard to follow the story due to the only source of it coming from a fifteen second intro on each level, but my guessing is that the devs weren't intending for the story to be the main attraction to this game.
As you battle through the 14 increasingly hard levels, you encounter lots of different types of enemies and scenarios which will probably kill you over and over again until you finally work out the optimal way around. I started out playing on a controller but it quickly became apparent that a keyboard and mouse were needed because this game is brutal. I only played on easy difficulty and this is one of the hardest games I've ever played.
The graphics are brilliant. It runs on the Unreal engine which sparks good reason for it to run very well, awesome physics engine and destructible environments. This is definitely an old school shooter which has plenty of repeatability for high scores and different achievements.

Well this game has rly mixed reviews on the Internet, and I wanted to find out why. At 1st it looks like an oldschool shooter with an awesome sci-fi setting but as soon as you start playing you realize that it's more like Duke Nukem Forever. Mixing Old and New stuff but not doing a rly good job with it.
So the game looks quite nice. However the textures are low res. Sometimes I felt like playing Darsiders II because the game has rly cool aesthetics but the tech is inferior. It runs fairly good on my PC tho there are some places when I felt some FPS drop. The other problem is the variety. You are in a spacestation, a mining facily, an alien mothership, labs....and all of them look the same! Thats a rly big problem with the game. These should have been different from each other in aesthetic wise.
The game uses many public domain sounds but in a good way. Every sound effect sounds right and nothing feels out of it's place. The weapon sounds are punchy too. The voice acting is nice especially the announcer who sounds almost exactly like Don LaFontaine. The dialogs are funny and cheesy but in a good way. I had some smiles listening them. The music is okay.
So I mentioned DNF at the begining now I tell you why. You have a weapon limit system of 3. The 1st one is the always the same backup pistol and 2 other weapons you can pick up. This means you have basically 2 weapons and a pistol. There are alien and human wariations of the same weapon which is cool but they are basically the same. You can also pick up a minigun but it's basically a carry weapon which means you have to drop it if you wanna use any of your other weapons. Another problem is the regenerating health. I've found myself in cover almost every time I had a fight. And sitting behind chest high walls waiting for my health to regenerate is not fun. And the game is difficult. I died many times on the middle difficulty  (Normal, Hard, Brutal). You can get scores from kills, bonuses and other destructive stuff just like in Bulletstorm. If you have enough points you can unlock perks. These perks can add more firepower, defense, or other bonuses for you. This is a nice little feature but nothing special. However the last perk is cool.
There are collectibles like Bonus points and Audio logs, but these are not rly well hidden because of the extremely linear level design. Seriously you are always walking in 1 lane. Sometimes 2 but thats extreme stuff.
You can earn achievements for multiple playthroughs but I think the game is not that great. If it had more variety in aesthetics and level design I would recommend it but in this case it's just a one time run. And it lasts 7,8 hours if you are exploring the levels for hidden stuff.

For ten dollars, I figured this game would be a good bargin.

While it is a step up from City Interactive's previous work on 'Sniper: Ghost Warrior'... it's not really a step in the right direciton.

But, the game grinds to a frustrating hault due to a pathetically balanced regen health system that doesn't mesh with the fast paced nature of the enemy actions.
The alien enemies can rush you in a split second, flood the screen with numbers and explosive rounds that damage you through walls and various cover.
Leaving you clinging to cover while your health regens painfully slow.
The game itself comes across as tedious, boring and a lifeless grind that is simply not worth it.
Uninspired level asthetics and bland level design fades into a "meh" feeling. Every area of the game looks the same... the same cliche' metallic sci-fi location we've all seen countless times.
With dull aliens that do nothing interesting or creative to make them memorable or fun to fight.
There are better games. For cheaper prices.

Where do I start with this...?
Yeah, this game is absolutely brilliant. The music is delicious, the art is clean and consistent, and the gameplay is quite diverse.
You go into the game getting a bit of backstory and some nice visuals which clearly portray the world you've been dropped into. You have your base abilities presented to you immediately, aaaand then you see some blocks you can't yet interact with—a glowing orb floating only a foot beyond. The exciting thought creeps into your mind, "Yep, this is a metroidvania."
Every new item you discover makes exploring and backtracking all the easier, whether the new item you've discovered required the former item in order to be obtained or not. You've got a level system, with experience pickups as well as experience gained based on your combo counter, not killing, which is definitely a quirky, fresh concept you don't really see nowadays. Leveling up is quite crucial, however collecting a certain collectible is all the more powerful. Basically what I'm boiling down to is that you are not required to collect
item to beat the game—but the nature in which the items and their collection are presented will entice you to 100% it.
There are multiple difficulties, the hardest of which,
, doesn't really show its effects until you're fighting a boss, where it shines in hellish delight. There are some ever slight, ever rare bugs here and there, but overall it's an extremely stable game.
In order to complete the game, getting all collectibles, on Ridonculous difficulty, it took me 11 hours in game time, 19 hours real time. For $4.49 CAD, I feel Super Panda Adventures exhibits a tremendous amount of value. I'd recommend this to any platformer-brawler-exploration-delicious gamers who like the idea of a little panda with a small sword and big dreams.

This is one of the best games I've ever played.

Even though you can 100% complete the game in about ten hours, those ten hours feature pure entertainment. From the open world & world map (featuring two different worlds), experience gathering, levelling up and spending skill points on abilities, doing side quests for NPCs which often contain good humour, to cute graphics and light-hearted characters who actually point out some of the real-world problems and give the game great depth.

The only negative thing I have to say about the whole thing is the fact that some of the game's bosses feature large difficulty spikes, especially the last boss. I think you'll always feel like the boss is one scale higher than the difficulty you're currently playing on (there are about five difficulties, if I'm not mistaken). But if you like to play on easy, then you should be able to beat it without any major issues.
So if you are still thinking about whether you should get it or not, go get it right away! The 4€ price is super small considering how good the game is, and this is coming from a guy with some serious budget issues. I got the game on a discount for 3€ and I feel like I ripped off the developer.
I seriously hope for Super Panda Adventures 2 or something like that.

A snake's tale is a unique Puzzle made on iOS, Android and Computer OS which is inspired in some ways by the original concept of the snake game in 1976. The snake behavior and the eggs concept have been kept. You help a Brown Water Snake to reach the hole of each level to his long journey. (Well if you are a snake specialist you can tell me if that's a Brown Water Snake but it seems to be one.) Several gameplay mechanisms are added to the game : snakes with different behavior, eggs and buttons.

Graphics are nice despite they are minimalistic : they look like 3D models. And the 5 worlds as well as the 7 snakes will not let you bored. Only the levels overview is the less attractive part of the game.


Nice music with fine sounds.

You begin with the map with overview of the unlocked levels : only one at the beginning. As long as you clear a puzzle you unlock the adjacent ones. This is a really nice concept as you can skip or play any unlocked level you want. Also the title of each level can provide a precious hint on how to solve it.
To clear a puzzle you need to move the brown water snake to its destination : the black hole. There are no time or "step" limits and you can use the Undo and Restart features whenever you want.
You can move any snake you want in any order, just be sure to not get a snake stuck unless you need to do it. Anyway you can always use the Undo or Restart feature at any time. Also you will encounter mostly 3 unique snakes which make the game tougher.
Adding to that you will encounter some eggs in several levels : the regular one and the black one. As you may think the regular will increase the size of any snake by one tile. I say any because it's not mandatory that your snake eat it as some puzzles requires you to have another snake that eat the egg. And the black eggs are rotten eggs so it will decrease the length of a snake by one tile but if the snake is already small he will die and disappears from the level.
Finally you will encounter some buttons - switches that all need to be pressed in order to open the hole.
The first levels are obvious to clear : they are small, easy and includes a few gameplay mechanisms : including snakes, eggs or buttons.
The later levels can become a bit tedious as they are medium-sized and sometimes includes several gameplay features.
Finally after you beat all the regular levels you unlock the final level which includes most of the snakes and gameplay features you have previously seen.

There is only one achievement you get after you beat the game.
An excellent game. Simple controls, nice looking snakes, casual play, new puzzle mechanics are introduced as you progress. Reminds me a little of Stephen's Sausage roll, though not as hard.

Looks like a very cinematic, detailed, complex game. The story and characters seem appealing and the concept seems like it could be a lot of fun - but for me, it was too complex or too cumbersome or just too... much. I only played the first mission, up to where you get to your safehouse. I hacked a bunch of things, I built a lure, I drove around and eluded the police. But I could feel myself getting weary already. Tedious maybe. The "me" in the game just stood by a door while cameras were hacked to enable unlocking a door. I snuck around police, unsure if they'd see me or not (once they did; once they did not). By the time I got to the saferoom I was ready for a break from the hacking and the dodging. I liked the story. I liked the mysterious phone call. I liked reading silly one-line bios on random NPCs. But it just felt... boring. And then I realized that the star gets his family killed in the opening sequence because, essentially, he's a hacker and a thief who steals other people's money and what does he do next? He continues hacking and stealing other people's money. Maybe that's meant to feel ok because of the one-line bios, such as the guy who searches the internet for &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; a lot, or because one person is a known art thief. It just feels odd that my family was killed because of MY actions (hacking) and yet here I am, still hacking. I'd like to think *most* people would realize that their illegal, immoral actions had consequences and would try to rectify things - you know, like grabbing a bunch of guns and killing those responsible. Maybe that comes later in the game but, for me, I'm done.
Now, if you like stealthy games where you'll be spending quite a bit of time surveying the environment and hacking things and luring people away so you can sneak past, and doing it from a safe distance - then this game might be ideal for you. I've played Dishonored and the Thief series and numerous other games that feature stealth as a key component. Those games were better, I'd say. The action felt more real. The stealth and the takedowns felt more compelling. In this game it feels dry and empty.

MOAI 4: Terra Incognita is already the fourth installment of the story of "our hero" and just like the previous games it is captivating in its simplicity. For people who are into casual games this one is a real gem.  The levels are bound together by the story of an island community which is tormented by a big wave, after which a new group of islands appears. For those who have played the other MOAI games there are some characters you will recognize and a few references to the other games, but it is an all new story. The short cutscenes and conversations allows the player to immerge in the story and to be taken from a ravaged beach, over an island full of birds, to an underwater city and further.
Aside from the storyline, the gameplay is much like the previous games. This  means that you will have to think about the order in which you do things, but most of the time you will get there anyway. Although the levels do become harder when you progress. They changed the way you get your equipment; while playing you are gathering crafting supplies which you use to craft items to give you speed or production bonusses. This means that you can  focus on the bonusses you like best.
The game also has a good Steam integration, which includes achievements, trading cards and a background and emoticon. Especially the achievements will keep you busy for a while if you are a perfectionist ;)
In short, I would highly recommend this game. The levels are well balanced (although they could be a bit harder sometimes) and strung together by a nice storyline. When I play this game time flies.

Deus Ex: Invisible War is a terrible sequel in regards to the original, but I defend the game on its own merits.
This is the case with Project: Snowblind, comparing it to its heritage will result in the game being slammed. But is it a bad game? No.
Project: Snowblind is a interesting game, granted the game is easy as hell and the main protagonist isn't particularly likeable, but the game has some interesting ideas, and some kickass weapons. My favourite of these is the Flecette.

A very fun but very poorly balanced game. I want to cover four quick points.
In Gems of War the primary gameplay is broken down into games you either play against AI created teams in a variety of scenarios, or in games you play against real teams created by other players that the AI controls. The balance for the AI created teams is a bit messed up. It starts out trivially easy but scales up incredibly rapidly and caps at around level 50. The problem is that you'll soon find yourself unable to effectively compete against the AI teams. At this point it seems lots of people decide it's either go pay-to-win or call it quits.
There's a much better solution. Go play PvP. PvP will pair you against more fairly matched teams. You'll get better rewards and be able to continue leveling up your cards and team. Since the AI team scaling stops at level 50, by the time you come back to it - it'll be a cake walk. It's counter intuitive but yeah. Start by playing against AI teams and then after that do PvP until you're ready to face the AI...
The cards in the game are in no way balanced or is there any major attempt to balance them. Rarer cards tend to do everything less rare cards do... and more... and better. The problem is that this strictly caps the room for creative team design. You are left to take your best/rarest cards, add a mana generator (turning gems of a certain color into the one your 'win card(s)' need), and that's pretty much going to crush any other team you could make. This is really fun at first when you're regularly finding more rarer cards and your decks are constantly shifting and changing in new and interesting ways. But as you start to collect most of the top cards - the fun starts to stop. Suddenly there's not much to look forward to, and since less rare cards tend to just be worse in every possible way there's not really any sort of room for creative team design.
The major 'grab' in this game is chasing the carrot of rarer cards. With real money you can buy these cards - or at least keys to chests that give you a very high chance of getting them. However, everything relevant that you can buy you can earn through regular play as well. I actually find this a bit frustrating. I'd love to toss the developers a few dollars since I've gotten a lot of enjoyment out of this game, but just about everything you can buy is going to just decrease the hours of enjoyment you can have with the game. A recurring problem with free to play games that don't just focus on aesthetics purchases.
Overall yeah, give it a go. It's by a wide margin the most fun I've had in this sort of game and there's hundreds of hours of entertainment in this game for those that enjoy the fundamental gameplay.

Supreme Commander is a realtime strategy game featuring gameplay similar to Total Annihilation and Planetary Annihilation. Forged Alliance is the standalone "expansion" to the original Supreme Commander, where all the factions are featured including Seraphim which apparently is the alien race that Aeon got it's technology from.
Supreme Commander is a game about macro-strategy and production above micro-strategy. There are no "unit abilities" in the same vein as in games such as Starcraft II. The game features a "Streaming Economy", where you can build anything regardless if you have the resource stored or not, but the building speed is dictated by how much resource you can stream into said building. So if you only have 5 metal to stream into a building but the building speed maximum would require 10 - you would theoretically only build at 50% speed. You can store more resources through building storage buildings, which acts as a resource buffer for you, but storage of resources are not infinite - the production that exceeds demands is simply lost.
The game features a lot of UI improvements like being able to set up ferry lines and limited automation, repitition and the like. It lacks a few of the improvements from Planetary annihilation but so does planetary lack from improvements from this title.
In the end it's just a great game overall, while it doesn't have the best of themes like the drama involved in even regular games of Company of Heroes - it's still a great game in its own right. It is deeply underappreciated game and one of my absolute favorite games of all time.

Honestly, if your going to get Supreme Commander, this should be at the top of your priority list. This adds another faction as well as tweaks in the gameplay and mechanics that allow for more play time and more interesting strategy styles. The game itself may seem standard for RTS games but that is more a strength than a weakness. Some more modern RTS games (talking to you Supreme Commander 2) can create a more simplified experience and cause the game to easily become stale and dull, whereas this game follows in line with classics like Age of Empires and even Command and Conquer with a larger unit management and a fun/ever changing atmosphere sure to entertain any RTS fans.
If your looking for online play, this game has lost a large fraction in its community in the years and it may prove difficult to find other players online. There is a community online called Supreme Commander Forged Alliance Forever where people looking to play online and continue the life blood of the game gather, so check them out for the best way to find other players online.
All in all, this game is fun and fresh for new-time players, and entertaining at least to veterans. Hope you enjoy it as much as I do!

They are without question the worst final boss fights I have ever had the misfortune of playing. All the other boss fights are bad too and overall the game is just really hard for the wrong reasons.
This game uses the same control feel and engine as the game Bulletstorm. Even the main assault rifle is the same and the main voice actor is the same guy from that game as well. The main difference between the two games is that this game is very sub-par and Bulletstorm is a good game and a cult favorite.
Unless you have some good twitch style gaming skills you will be doing parts over and over again. I am a pretty solid oldschool twitch gamer and I was re-doing parts a lot. This is without question the hardest FPS I have ever played and I wouldn't say that it is hard in a fair way which is unfortunate for this game and is its only real major downfall. It is hard for no other reason whatsoever other than it floods you with enemies and your guy can quite literally only take a slight few bullets then lights out. Two or three bullet hits puts you in red-screen heartbeat mode then one or two more hits and you are dead. Possibly the worst are snipers that can kill you in two shots and their sniper rifles can fire about 4 times a second. You can barely pop out of cover to shoot them so good luck with that. No single cover spot in the game is safe: you will get killed by a grenade shot or aliens will run up to you with super speed and use a melee stun move and you will get shot to death in two seconds or less while you are stunned. So far the first two boss fights are among some of the worst I have ever seen. They are not fun in any way, just getting a boss' life down low then dying over and over and over again is not fun. This first boss is only beatable by staying behind a pillar and fire/hide the whole time i.e. not fun. The second boss you can only dmg him when you explode a tank next to him and other than that you are exposed and will be constantly hit by him and die repeatedly. Enemy weapons fire a near constant laser stream of bullets at you and can even destroy your cover leaving you exposed. Another major downfall of the game: p-ss poor checkpointing which is a staple of many bad games. It makes you replay large sections, killing dozens of aliens over again. You can be doing really well, clearing an area of a swarm of aliens that takes what feels like an eternity, then one alien can just inexplicably finish you off or take you out entirely on his own, forcing you to redo a♥♥♥♥♥♥load of work. So like I said, if you have some good oldschool twitch FPS skills then you will not have a huge amount of trouble with it, but you will for sure have at least some trouble no matter who you are. And all of this I have said is on the second difficulty out of three possible. It goes from 'challenging', to 'hard', then 'brutal'. As incredibly hard as it is now, I have no desire to ever try it on 'brutal'. If skill was involved then sure but not when the only reason it is hard are the reasons I pointed out.
Being extremely difficult for the wrong reasons aside, this game gave me some fun times, however much so that now that it is over it is uninstalled and will never be played again. The graphics look very good and it sounds good too. The story is... I haven't been paying close attention to the story. It's a game called ALIEN RAGE who gives a♥♥♥♥♥♥about the story lol. It controls well, mostly runs smooth (minor slowdown/lag), and can even be sorta fun for a brief while. It would be even better had it not been difficult for the wrong reasons. When I got to the level that had me riding a mine cart and you die in a fraction of a second around every turn and I retried the sections probably twenty times each, that was the last straw and I lowered the difficulty, in which it did not make the game too much less frustrating and definitely did not make it any more fun. This game would have been a lot better had it been much more balanced. You will never feel like "oh man I legitimately died". You only ever will feel like it is hard for the worst possible wrong reasons that the developers could have made it be.
4/10 Not worth the headache even if it is on sale for a dollar.

"Alien Rage - Unlimited" is a great FPS game with lots of alien enemies to shoot and blow to bloody pieces.
Yes, there is a storyline to it all: In the future, humans and a race called the Vorus are both mining the same asteroid for Promethium, an extremely valuable source of energy in a world depleted of fossil fuels.  In the beginning there is peace and cooperation, but then something goes wrong and carnage follows.  You will figure it out as you move through the 14 levels, picking up audio logs along the way that tell of the events that led to you being sent in to mow down any and all alien opposition.
Apart from the lesser enemy types, the game features a whole range of enemy bosses, each requiring its own set of tactics to defeat.  There are some really tricky parts - for example, the final boss can be quite difficult at first - however, once you understand how to best use your weapons and environment for each situation (and remember to keep moving), it gets easier.  There are three difficulty levels, the lowest (or normal) level being called "Challenging" - an indication that your first tour isn't necessarily going to be a pushover (depending on your unique experience with FPS games, of course).
Weapons can be divided into two types: projectile and energy, all with secondary fire modes.  You can only carry three weapons at once.  Of these, only two can be changed for other weapons, because the unlimited ammo pistol (your default weapon) is a fixed necessity - don't underestimate its use, though, for it's a formidable weapon and one can finish the game using it alone (especially with perks tailored to maximize its use).
Players gain a selection of "perks" (advantages) by stacking up points made from kills, modifying the abilities of weapons, armour or the player's health.  For instance, the Mega Pistol perk supercharges the default pistol to give it way more punch.
At times you are able to also pick up a mighty minigun, although it will hamper your speed.  The game's shotgun may not be very useful (personally), but there are enough weapons to experiment with as well as a melée attack.  In one level you also get to drive a mech, squashing the enemy under metal feet and spewing bullets from your rotating machinegun barrels (it overheats quickly, but this can be helped by chosing the Heavy Weapon Recovery perk).
There aren't all that many controls, which is great - and it can be customized. The jump function very rarely comes into play since the game is structured in such a way that jumping over cumbersome obstacles is eliminated (assisting fast-moving gameplay).
The game has autosave checkpoints, no manual saving.  Some players might have an issue with that, for it sometimes means that one has to repeat easier bits before getting back to the action that got you killed.  Not really a problem, though.  The game has real replay value, especially since global leaderboards are kept: you can try to improve your overall score by replaying individual levels, maybe also to go back for pickups you've missed before, all the while keeping tabs on how other players are getting on.
The game has amazing graphics and scenery/environment.
If you're a fan of the FPS genre, then "Alien Rage - Unlimited" is worth it.
Enjoy.

A fast paced hardcore first-person shooter with arcade elements implemented. The level design is somewhat all very similar, like they were dipped in metallic paint. However, given the context of the game - you are fighting an alien robot race - it fits pretty snug.
Like I said above, this game is very fast paced, giving you little to no time to stop and think. Your finger must stay on the trigger at all times if you expect to survive.
There are ten weapons found throughout the campaign. You can carry two side weapons and one main weapon (Pistol) that has infinite ammunition. Each weapon has an alternate firing mode giving you multiple advantages in battle. Killing enemies skillfully increases the points given, and you can unlock perks for your character. There is an entire perk tree to choose from, but you can equip up to three at a time.
Fourteen levels to play through and eight huge, tough♥♥♥♥♥bosses to mow down.
True to it's hardcore reputation, the easiest difficulty is called "Challenging", with the next two being the "Hard" and "Brutal" difficulties.
Very highly recommended to fans of first-person shooters that like a heavy challenge.

This is a re-review of Alien Rage. If you want to compare it to my old review, follow this link:
I was very disappointed with Alien Rage, back when I first played it in October 2013. My biggest issue with the game was how incredibly unfair it felt, how little health your character had and how often I had to seek cover and let my health regenerate, completely killing the flow of gameplay. But since then I always had a thought at the back of my head that maybe I just didn't "get" it. Perhaps I was doing something wrong. I decided to give the game another spin and I actually ended up enjoying it a little. How come I am still not recommending a purchase? Let me explain.
At first glance, Alien Rage appears to be a score-attack shooter similar to Bulletstorm, putting an emphasis on acquiring high scores by successfully executing headshots, killstreaks and explosion kills. But the games' scoring system is quite limited compared to Bulletstorm. There is no incentive to try out different combos as shooting the highly destructible enviroment around you is the fastest and most reliable way to get rid of the evil Vorus scum and will net you tons of points regardless. See something glowing red? Yeah, shoot at it and watch half the level blow up in a spectacular fashion, which is fun to watch but gets extremely monotonous few levels in. The Vorus are quite bulletspongey if you don't focus on headshots. Not a bad gameplay element at all and I do view on it favourably but pulling off headshots with hipfire is a real pain. Weapons become very inaccurate during prolonged fire from the hip and paired with the visual feedback from recoil makes it unnecessarily difficult to hit them. Yes, you can toggle ADS on weapons but it feels out of place in a fast paced shooter like this. It'd have made more sense to get rid of ADS entirely (except sniper rifles) and to give the weapons accurate hipfire instead. ADS not only obscures vision from the battlefield but it also makes you move slower which is in odds with the general pace of combat.
Alien Rage's gameplay can be best described as a flawed mixture of old- and newschool shooters. Movement feels fast and fluid even without sprinting, gunfights are at their core hectic and fun and weapon feedback is for the most part really good. But for every good thing it does something else wrong. Why does my character have so little health? Why do I find myself constantly seeking cover, sucking my thumb because those mean Aliens jerks keep turning my screen into greyscale? Why am I constantly getting killed by Snipers, Heavies and Grenadiers that I couldn't react to in time? You are simply too weak to sustain enough damage which works against Alien Rage's idea of being an oldschool score attack shooter. Building up truly impressive combo scores is often not possible because you need to regenrate your health. Keeping the pace of gameplay up is difficult since there are no health kits lying around which could speed up the healing process. Alien Rage doesn't seem to know what it wants to be and ends up being an unfocused mess that could have been pretty decent for it's 20€ price tag.
You might be asking, if there are any rewards for getting high scores and well, yes there are. After getting certain amounts of points, the game will reward you with perks, which you can utilize in your playthroughs. Up to three perks can be chosen and swapped out for other ones at any time and some of them are more or less game changing, like the overcharged pistol or health upgrades. Truth be told, I didn't even notice that I've unlocked those in my first playthrough and it's one of the key reasons I'm doing this re-review. So I started a new game on "Challenging" difficulty, decked myself out with Armor, Health and Explosive Resistance and surprisingly, I had a good time with Alien Rage. I can't think of a single occasion where the game came to a standstill. The pace of gameplay was fast and constant. Alien Rage was... good! The big issue however is that you'll have to complete the game atleast once to get access to those goodies. This makes for a terrible first impression and may explain why opinions on this game are so controversial. Admittedly playing Alien Rage with those conditions made it a bit too forgiving so once I was done with the campaign, I went straight to the second playthrough on Hard and unfortunately the gameplay turns into the same boring slow cover-shooter affair despite using perks.
Presentation-wise, Alien Rage is serviceable. Enemy and weapon designs are great. The game has a very distinct artstyle with its copious shades of blue and contrasting orange for explosive level setpieces and it does offer some visually interesting levels, especially once you get to the planets' surface and beyond. Particle effects and lightning are very nice-looking but some of the effects like heat and blastwaves from guns and explosives respectively can be annoying. Enemy AI is quite aggressive and will try to rush you down but path finding issues exist and it is possible that enemies don't react to your presence at all but that happens very rarely. Exaggerated head bobbing while running and visual distortion when getting hit with certain attacks are an issue and afaik can't be turned off. The FoV can be set up to 120° in the options menu but the gargantuan weapon FoV can only be altered with third party tools. Alien Rage's soundtrack is okay. Tracks vary in quality but are never outright annoying. Sound effects are good. PC Performance however isn't amazing. During firefights, FPS will dip from 144+ down to sub-60, even on a GTX980/i7-4770k setup. Very disappointing. Alien Rage offers very little in terms of video options and none of them seem to affect performance in a way.
Change weapon FoV - Flawless Widescreen
Edit encrypted config files - Bulletstorm INI Editor
(I assume Alien Rage was built with Bulletstorm dev tools and assets considering animation work for enemies and the encrypted INI files are similar)
Talking about difficulty is always going to be a controversial subject because it's highly subjective what a person finds fair and balanced. Alien Rage's gameplay elements of old- and new school shooters contradict each other so much. It wants you to go fast and take on hordes head-on and when you're able to it's quite entertaining. But it's also throwing roadblocks at you all the time by making you as resistent as wet tissue paper, forcing you to take cover and waste your time doing nothing interesting. Playing Alien Rage as an old school shooter will leave you frustrated. I've given it another chance and in the end, I can only recommend it if you're either 1.) fine with cover based shooters or 2.) going to play this on Challenging only.
Otherwise stay clear.

As fans of the original "The Ship" game, me and some friends decided to try out this new "remasted" version.  At first it seemed good!  The gameplay was a little smoother, the graphics were improved, and I liked the addition of an HP bar.  Then the problems began to arise...
To put it simply, this game is not finished.  It was likely rushed out of early access with the World Leader mode in an attempt to cash in on the recent election.  Various members of our group ended up having crashing issues.  Only 3 of us were able to log onto the World Leader mode server, despite it only containing bots.  Oh, and some bots/players would frequently show up as invisible too.
On top of the bugs, the game just seems like a downgrade compared to the first one:
- For one, doors can no longer be closed.
- Despite the patch notes saying that bot AI has been improved, this was not the case on our games.  The bots would barely react and just kept walking when we'd attack them.
- Speaking of bots, they seem to have 10x more HP than players.  Multiple people in our group reported smacking a bot over the head more than 10 times with a 5* weapon, and still couldn't kill them.
- No more secret rooms. #sadface
- No more functioning elevators.
- Most 'needs' now seem to be completely pointless and forgotten about, except for sleep.  Running for several seconds will often result in you falling asleep.  I lost count of the amount of times my character passed out whilst trying to evade my hunter, only to then hear the familiar "THUNK THUNK THUNK" sounds of my character being whacked repeatedly whilst I'm standing there asleep and helpless.
The potential in this game is there, but it still needs a lot more work in order to surpass the original.  As of right now, I cannot recommend this game over the original.
