Celestial Command is a true Indie-title being lovingly made by three Developers. I dont know if these guys really have a solid longterm-roadmap on what this game will really be when its done but does that bother me? Not at all.
Right now what 'CC' is is fun to toy around with. Obviously there are still some elemental things missing und weird stuff can happen like you would expect from Early Access, but steady progress and the friendly & responsive Devs make it fun to watch this game take shape. Whether this will turn out to be an arcadey deathmatch in orbits or an everlasting exploration game with proper mining and manufacturing of parts - ill take it all.
In a way this game is like KSP in 2D - so expect meneuvering being tricky at times. Use proper orbital-mechanics like you would in KSP to get around and conserve fuel. If youre having trouble start by googling the terms "Apoapsis", "Periapsis" and "Hohman Transfer".

Having only played the game about an hour, it seems to be headed in the right direction, but it definiely isn't there yet.
As the warning in the "Early Access" window clearly says, this isn't a playable game yet.  The obvious comparison is with EVE Online, but there is a lot this game wants to be that Eve is not; mainly, a physics-realistic, 2D, space sandbox that isn't MMO and riddled with microtransactions.  On the downside (IMO), this is much, *much* smaller scale than EVE is.  On the upside, it's far more intimate than EVE - I could easily gather one or two friends and start playing around with no issue,  I could see some people having fun with this in single player, but it's multiplayer where this game really stands out, which is good since it's multiplayer that seems to have the most potential.
The game itself looks good, albeit simple.  This isn't a limitaion of the game, it's a design choice made by the devs, leading this to be a game that's easily accessible to all, and even opening the possibility of a mobile port waaaaay down the line.  I really appreciate this choice, if only because I've lived the majority of my life gaming on low end machines.
The sandbox aspect of the game is embraced whole-heartedly, giving absolutely no tutorial or instruction aside from a popup windows in the beginning that's shorter than this review.   The game does help with the more difficult stuff, like rendezvous with meteors and other ships by showing relative velocity vectors, but it took me a while to find them.  It definitely reminds me of Minecraft, but Minecraft could get away with it on account of it's relative simplicity.   Learning orbital mechanics without any help isn't my personal idea of fun.
All-in-all, I like the direction the game is going, and I can't wait until there is more of it to play!

I picked this up because I liked the idea of a space/orbit mining simulator.

The physics are broken - the orbital mechanics aren't close to real-life.
They are close enough that you start playing thinking this is awesome and then weird things start happening.
e.g. I deconstructed a large thruster and suddenly my ship achieved escape velocty from the planet.
Despite the description on Steam that they are aiming for a good physics simulation the devs have posted that is not their intent and do not consider these things bugs.
Unfortunately that makes this sim garbage.
Also, bugs that are claimed fixed are still present. I believe that they fixed something but this suggest they are struggling with code-quality which does not bode well for the long-term playability of the game.

So far? It's pretty great. It's more of a simulation than an action game.
Getting your orbit trajectory right, managing fuel and thrust, and power; it's all pretty interesting and adds some depth to simply flying around space collecting resources.
See that asteroid with the ice you need? Well you've only got about 1 minute of thrust left, total, and it's going faster than you around the sun.
You'll need to slow down and widen your orbit so it can catch up to you, and you can reserve fuel.
That sort of thing!
At the moment you collect resources to build modules for your ship, sell excess for funds to buy food for your crew, and defend yourself against the occasional space scum. More will come.
If you're looking for a faster paced space game, this won't be for you. If you're looking for something more akin to Interstellar, or creating your own space stations with really well done top down graphics? This is a good buy.

Oh Watch_Doges, you hurt me.
This is honestly a game I wanted to enjoy. I wasn't hyped, my expectations were of my own accord, and I was aware of the issues with it when I purchased this during the Summer Sale of 2016. 15$ for all the content. I figured, ♥♥♥♥ it, I can sacrifice a pizza. This'll last longer...
Well, the core aspects of this game are basically the same as any other open world third person game. Shooting, and driving. The better those aspects, the more fun it is to play the game. If those aspects are simply BROKEN, then you're not going to want to play for long. Take a look at GTA V. The driving and chases are addictive, and the gunplay is fairly solid!
Unfortunately, in Watch Dogs, the driving is arguably the worst I've ever dealt with in a video game. Before you ask, no, a controller does not make it any better at all. I died on the first mission because of the sheer clunkiness of it all. Now I'll admit, I didn't take the time to follow the guides that reduce stuttering (also a problem), so I imagine that would help to a small degree, but even at good frames, it's just really shallow and dull to tiresome to work...
I said okay, fine, driving is bad but maybe the game has great gunplay! No, no it doesn't. The cover system is nice. The controller shooting feels fine. It's not remarkable, but it works and that's okay. I prefer using a mouse for shooting aspects however, and that, is where issues arise. The mouse, as a whole, suffers from some form of delay. Even when the game is running at it's full 60fps, the mouse has an odd response delay. It annoyed the hell out of me and even after disabling mouse acceleration, (on by default, had to navigate config files, no option in game menu), I saw little relief.
The game suffered from some odd pop in and stuttering on high/ultra which is odd considering my system is more than capable, and you'll see this is a common trend in other reviews as well.
As far as the world goes, it's pretty, it's got some unique stuff going for it, but it feels very shallow. The profiler was the redeeming factor to a world full of lifeless, generic NPCs. Once more I'll refer to Rockstar and GTA V for how to do an immersive open world because this is just sad.
Story is as generic as it gets, but I didn't give much a ♥♥♥♥ regarding that, to be frank.
Overall this is a game that I tried to embrace, I ignored the hate wagons, and I caught it on a $15 sale. Even then, I cannot recommend this. I don't know if the console version is any better but as far as PC goes, I really wouldn't wanna pay more than $5 for this. Call me cheap, but there are many better games in the Steam sale this year, and more genuine studios, that deserve that $15 and then some.
I'll keep an eye out on Watchdogs 2. I feel they have a shot at pulling it off. I just cannot endure this♥♥♥♥♥♥ RIP. Papa Bless.

An addictive Puzzle Quest-like game made by the same devs that I have sunk several hundred, almost a thousand hours into now. Early game is a bit rocky but once you get going, there is meaningful experience through the early-mid, mid, and early-late game in both PvP and other modes.
Don't like PvP? Don't worry, Gems uses an AI to control player-made teams that you can set to defend for you and go against whenever you please. Gems is fairly well balanced, with a couple VERY powerful troop combinations, but it is possible to make anything viable for as far in as I have played.
Would I recommend this game? Hell yes. And I have, and I've gotten several friends playing now as well and they love it, too. So jump on in and give it a try. It's free, so the only thing you stand to lose if you don't love it is a bit of your time.
Oh, and as a final note, the developers are incredibly awesome and come on from time to time to talk with the players. They take feedback into consideration and have a fairly transparent design process and are open to discuss anything from in-game topics to daily life with anyone. Wonderful dev team to match this wonderful game.
Many negative reviews there... but this is simply the best match-3 game ever. If you like match-3 genre, I definitly recommend this game.

Lara is introduced as an unexperienced adventurer, although the way she picks up after being shipwrecked and thrown on an unforgiven island is feral. Survival is right. Despite open wounds she wades through waist-high baths of blood and guts. One would expect her to have raging fevers as one moment she dashes through volcanic caves and the next she’s climbing a radio tower that sways dangerously in a snow storm. This is no survival, it’s mythical. While her diligent band of cardboard friends struggles to find important things to do, she risks her life every single minute. That is, of course, how Lara ‘Grave Robber’ Croft came to be – as the first true female video game hero – but why, then, would the writers cast her in this at times toe-curling, teeth grinding fantastical pseudo-realistic-American-soap-like plot? Was it the contemporary fad of rehashing the heroes of old (e.g. Batman) in an emotional and profoundly human way? If we, one can hear the developers assert, salten Lara’s adventure with themes of loss, maternity, insanity, mass murder and resurrection, we surely will learn more about her, understand her,
for her?
The beauty of the first games was the fact that the introduction to the player was neutral and short, providing just enough incentive to become Lara.
- which wouldn't be that bad if the writing was engaging. But
, and I did not care about any cutscene, journal or conversation (except maybe for the sake of being a completionist, which is no accomplishment on the developers’ part).
Nevertheless, I actually enjoyed the gameplay very much. As with in all probability the entirety of the former Tomb Raider games, and similar third person (acrobatic) adventure games like the Assassin’s Creed series, it is troubled with moments of utter frustration, whenever there is a discrepancy between how you want to control the character, and how this gets interpreted by the game engine. Fortunately, this is not as common as in some parts of the aforementioned series.
(though their animations sometimes leave something to be desired), the input-to-control ratio is up to par, the weapon handling and ammo switching are good. And, above all, stealth is a welcome and well-implemented, albeit at times glitchy, addition.
Autosaves are frequent (at times too frequent even), and any kind of statistical progress is, as common in this genre, saved immediately.
. It really is okay; it spices up the gameplay a little, but only a handful of skills actually give you an idea of improvement; these are mostly included in the brawling and weapon upgrade trees, adding new moves or types of ammo.
. The atmosphere is arguably the best in the series, and the level design is rather good as well, as long as you don’t care too much about examining every nook and cranny. It obviously has been designed for a linear playthrough, turning the completionists’ endeavour into a galling burden.

Tomb Raider ( 2013)
-Over all what can i say about this awesome great game ? Best storyline game
i ever played so far . Excellent Storyline , Almost like  a movie . The Way The
game present Each Characters , What happen them through out the game and
the duration of my playthrough the game  ,It made me curious . Amazed of the
graphics as it came out 2013 . The Documents ,  Diarys and the Easter eggs the
game carries spent most of my time as it is hard to find some , ending up not
finding all the easter eggs . Over all this game is intensive as many killings and
anytime there will be something hidden in the shadow to catch  you...
The journey Begins !
- Open World is a plus. Yikes ,I really liked how the developers made the environment open for exploration in each level, which really encouraged you to look around for secret areas, items, etc. that would spawn around the map.
-Fighting is well programmed. Fights in Tomb Raider always felt smooth, and through the style of the game, it put YOU in the driver's seat on how to engage enemies. The variety of weapons in the game match these various styles too, and they sometimes even have uses outside of fighting, which I found interesting.
- The Goal in the game is clear. Tomb Raider is a perfect example of great script writing in this sense. I never felt like I was aimlessly doing something in the plot. I felt like every action I made had some meaning that pushed me closer to the end of the story.
- The game is challenging, but not overly so. Playing my first run-through of the game, I had no idea what I was getting into. At the same time, the game can be very conducive to new players, teaching them the mechanics of each tool early off in the game without deliberatly giving you a tutorial that has no meaning to the game. That being said, I died many times, but quickly learned how to avoid the situations that had killed me in the past.
- Game Environment is gorgeous, VERY immersive. Each scene has a picturesque feel to it. You can be running through an environment and be awestruck from just looking out into the distance. You feel like you're there beside Lara Croft.
- No substantitive DLC! The DLC for Tomb Raider consists mostly of player skins, but I would've loved to see another few missions added as something a little extra. I understand the studio that made this game was planning to make Rise of the Tomb Raider and didn't want to creatively drain themselves, but I would've loved to see some post-story missions or thematic material.
This has to be one of the best games I've ever played. If you're still looking to buy Tomb Raider, it's always on sale during Steam sales, but it is always worth it to buy this game. I literally have nothing bad to say about it functionally or about the story. You WILL be amazed. 10/10 Highly Recommended

As I'm writing this review, I've only played 10 minutes of The Ship: Remasted, and I can tell you now, with strong intentions, that this game is a masterpiece.
Stunning graphics, great atmosphere, 3 seconds into a game I'm already bursting with nostalgia as I hear that main menu theme song.
I load up a game of Deathmatch on my all-time favourite map - Krassin.
I spawn in and open up a cupboard straight away, to find a find a classic weapon - an old friend, if you will; the repeater rifle.
I enter a corridor where I find people ruthlessly hacking and slicing at each other, but I take a moment to survey the area. This game is beautiful.
I take 2 minutes out of my time to say hello to all the NPC's around the map and visit Boris - the security guard.
I purposely show him my weapons to get into jail (bet you've never heard anyone say that before) and I'm astonished by what I've seen.
The jail feels depressing, and makes you want to get out of there immediately, as a jail would, and this is a great way to teach you to hide your weapons when sneaking around guards or cameras.
As of now, that's all I have to say, but I urge you, I urge you deeply, to buy this wonderfully exciting and weird (in a good way) game.
"WHAAAAAAAAP WHAAAAAAAAAP!" - The Ship: Remasted, 2016.

I greatly enjoy tactical RPGs when they're done right. I'm a big fan of the Tactics Ogre and Final Fantasy Tactics series, and that plus an affinity for cyberpunk novels are mainly what drew me to Shadowrun despite never playing the original SNES or the tabletop RPG.
I played Shadowrun Returns and enjoyed my time with it save for a few key complaints, mostly around the pacing, shallow combat, and characterization. I'm pleased to say that all of those issues are cleared up with this game, and that it's an utterly fantastic title. I went so far as to recommend that people skip Returns completely in my review of that game and proceed onto this one instead. It's that much of an improvement.
The pacing problems I had with Returns often caused me to lose interest in the game and stop playing it for weeks at a time. Those issues are completely alleviated here. The game seems to have taken some inspiration from the Mass Effect series, as missions are structured in a similar manner in Dragonfall. Something happens in the first mission of the game that creates an overarching plot, and you're gradually working towards the solution of that by taking odd jobs to build up your bankroll. You're also conversing with your regular allies--something else that Returns lacked that I disliked--and completing missions specifically regarding their background. It worked excellently in Mass Effect, and it really works well here.
The combat has taken even more inspiration from XCOM: Enemy Unknown, and it now feels far more fleshed out than it did in Returns. Each class has far more depth than it did in Returns, and there are more opportunities to utilize the environment in interesting ways. Some of my favorite missions in the game involved the opportunity to have your computer hacker operate in the Matrix, simultaneously fighting a tactical battle in a cyber world with the aims of unlocking doors and disabling or even turning the security systems to your teams side while they proceed with a battle in the real world. There are some incredibly compelling race-against-time type missions in this game that require that sort of thing. It creates a ton of suspense and allows you to take combat in exponentially more directions than the first game did.
The characters and the story in this game is the largest improvement over Returns, though. Your squadmates have obviously been crafted with a caring touch, and they feel like well-rounded human beings (or metahuman beings), which is a far departure from the hire-a-mannekin system that Returns did. They've got their own motivations and their own reasons for being there, and they're not always going to agree with the path you're taking. I even feel like I got a deeper roleplaying experience out of my player character than in Returns. I felt like I had more opportunity to inject my own desired personality into him, which I hadn't realized I was missing in Returns until playing this game. Even the minor characters are compelling, from the civilian engineer dwarf roped into a job she has no interest in doing to the loving Grandfather who works as an accountant but also moonlights as an assassin for a loanshark named Meat Grinder, who he hilariously refers to as "Mr. Grinder". Writing is the strength of this game, and it would have compelled me to continue onward and finish even if I didn't really like the combat.
I should also mention the music, which was of quality in Returns but seems improved here. I read somewhere that the composer for the music in the original SNES game did this one as well, which was interesting to me. It's very good, and it properly encompasses the mood of a world that's caringly built as an homage to William Gibson's in the Sprawl Trilogy.
Gibson, for those who have never heard of him, is to cyberpunk what Tolkien is to fantasy. His novel Neuromancer, released in 1981, inspired a great many of the ideas included in this game, particularly the Matrix, which is nearly unchanged from those novels. I'd highly recommend the fans of this game pick up a copy of Neuromancer and immerse themselves in the grassroots of the cyberpunk subgenre.
The only real gripe I can think of is the way the game depicts corporations. It's utterly cliche, uninteresting, and tiresome. Look, I'm no fan of stodgy, bureaucratic, inhuman multinational corporations. But not every company is Comcast. Literally every corporation in this game is depicted as maliciously evil and self-serving to the point where the player is dealing with atrocity after atrocity. The one "good" CEO in the game is promptly fired for not putting the bottom line first. That's just boring storytelling. There's great value in turning the cliche on its head, and it would have been nice to see a depiction differing from norm since the writers did such a good job of that otherwise.
In conclusion, this is an excellent tactical RPG set in a well-crafted world. It's beautifully presented, beautifully written, and just a hell of a lot of fun. Hairbrained Schemes has met all of the potential set forth by Shadowrun Returns, as this is probably the best RPG I played in all of 2014.

Dragonfall is a great--excellent even--game. This is your true to heart and classic CRPG. Good, solid turn based mechanics, varied character building, engaging and excellent narrative and storytelling, characters you grow attached to, and an immersive and expansive world.
Dragonfall fixes pretty much all the problems with Shadowrun Returns.
Dragonfall retains what made Shadowrun Returns so good: an immersive world, incredible storytelling driven by excellent and plentiful writing, and tangible characters. It takes what Shadowrun Returns did right, fixes its weak points and made everything better.
If you liked Shadowrun Returns do yourself a favour and play Dragonfall. If you thought Shadowrun Returns was too linear or lacked a truely compelling plot gives Dragonfall a shot. If you haven't played Shadowrun Returns but like turn based RPGs and/or cyberpunk play Dragonfall over Shadowrun Returns (but I suggest you play Shadowrun Returns anyway). They're standalone titles. If you like anything to do with cyberpunk, Dragonfall Director's cut does it right.  I mean, they really hit a grand slam on every aspect of the game. And... if that's not your thing... don't talk to your team mates.  If you do listen to them, you'll feel for them.  I have to say, not once, in any game ever, have I felt an attachment to any character, until now. I get chills playing through most of the missions, reading the deep well written back story for each and every mission.  The AI seems semi-intelligent as well... they always go for my shaman, as he's my weakest link, survival-wise.  And choices... so many choices.  Many skippable runs, some minor, some major. So many different ways to overcome obstacles... locked door?  Send a drone throught a vent, or have your "muscle" break it down, or have your decker hack the security terminal, or have your shaman astral plane and see the keys that have been pressed, etc.
If you don't like to read, well, you may not like this game.  However, it really is a good mix of reading a compelling story and interactive elements.

I've probably played every Pinball game in existence on various systems but to me "The Pinball Arcade" is easily the best of them all. No need for Gimmics or Special FX it's as close as you can get without playing the actual Pinball table. Although come to think of it sometimes it's better because there's no dodgy flipper or bad reflections as many Arcades place the tables (in the UK at least) too close to a window.
The DX11 version is the Mutts Nutts (or DB if you prefer !) and with season 5 upon us there are now over 40 tables available. Sure there are a few crap one's but with 3 of my all time arcade favourites in Fish Tales, The Getaway High Speed 2 & Funhouse faithfully reproduced I can't really complain.
The interface is getting a bit clunky now with the number of tables available as you have to scroll through a long list to find the table of your choice. Perhaps a future update will address this with search options or being able to arrange the tables by say season, year or manufacturer as well as a favourites option. When the disc versions of Pinball Arcade
Hall of Fame came out on PS2 & Wii all the tables were represented in an Arcade with so many tables in each room which worked well so something along those lines would be good as well. My only real gripe is the Pro version of the tables which is just a rip off. Why not make them available for free if you achieve all the wizard goals on a table ?.
Above all it's so much fun to play and although I'm a seasoned player I still get frustrated when a ball drains unexpectedly or I tilt the table just short of my all time high score !. But that's what it's all about realistic gameplay that draws you in to having another go. I'm sure you won't regret buying it but I would wait for a sale before buying the earlier seasons. Who know you may get as good as me with lots of practice but I doubt it ! :).

Defense Grid 2 is a good tower defense game, but not the best. The best is still the first game, Defense Grid: The Awakening. If you've played the first game, they have basically improved the graphics and added/tweaked some things (not necessarily for the better). If you haven't played the first game, buy that instead. It's a much, much better game, with much higher replayability and a lot more levels.
The main differences in DG2:
- Instead of command towers you now have boost towers. They end up being a bit of a resource burden since not using a boost tower is always worse than using one and you can't go back and add one later. They are useful to cheaply control the path of aliens though.
- Flying enemies have been removed, although missile towers remain and now fill the same role as meteor towers.
- You can sometimes alter the terrain and create new build areas, although this feature wasn't explained and I didn't learn about it until almost finishing the game. It is not actually needed to succeed, so kind of pointless.
- Towers now have passive upgrade items of different rarities, and at the start of a mission you can choose which one to have for each tower. You randomly unlock them after finishing a mission. They slightly alter the way towers behave, for example making lasers slow down foes, making guns pierce shields or making cannons damage multiple enemies. They come in different levels, so eventually you can have quite overpowered towers and these are needed for playing on higher difficulties.
- There is now a level editor and people can sell their levels via Steam Workshop.
- There are now some multiplayer modes, which I haven't tried yet so can't comment on, however the co-operative mode in which you share resources seems pointless. Considering you normally know where you want to put your towers, I'm not sure how having another player placing them would ever be helpful. Seems like it would only make things harder. The other multiplayer modes might be more worthwhile.
- There are now alternatives to the orbital laser that you unlock as you go along. These are quite useful and suit different playstyles (e.g. slowing aliens, giving you some free resources).
- Tower balance: from what I remember of the first game it has been tweaked somewhat. It's not so reliant on guns and cannons, while other towers like lasers and concussion are more valuable.
- Scoring: they have changed how scoring works and the game also feels easier (I got gold on every mission very easily). The scoring seems more focused on killing aliens as fast as possible, whereas the first game involved more careful resource management to get big scores and you had to be more careful about when you built towers if you wanted to earn the most interest. The scoring seems much more variable now and less precise. However, a recent patch added the ability to play with the old scoring style. It also shows you your score on a graph while playing, with someone on your friend's list to compare with, which is a really nice feature.
I found the campaign to be a bit short, the voice acting is very annoying and distracting and continues for too long after you finish a level, and the story is bad (although I guess in this kind of game that doesn't matter). But the game is also not challenging or compelling. Replaying levels in different modes is boring.
Ultimately this is a fun game, but they have lost the perfect formula that made the first game so addictive and replayable. DG2's biggest fault is that it is not DG1.

Defense Grid 2 is a solid Tower Defense game. It's fun for at least 10 hours, which it took me to pass through it once plus a bit on top of that. It may sound silly, but to be honest, when asked "what new does Defense Grid 2" bring to the table, the game chokes. I don't see why you would play this instead of something like Onslaught 2, which is a free flash game. This game plays the safe game, which in this genre is kind of silly considering the amount of copycat TD games that exist.
One thing that the game has going for it is relatively high production values compared to other TD games, but that's not what you're really looking for in this genre, now is it?
All in all, if you've ever played a TD -game, then you've already played Defense Grid 2. It brings nothing new to the table and is therefore a creatively low-effort game. If you get it for 1$ in a sale, then it can't really harm to get it, but there's no justification for a full price purchase.

Metal Drift may be small, but it's incredibly tight. It's like someone took Battlezone's agile hover tanks and stuck them in Hyperblade's extreme sports setting, giving you a variety of weapon and equipment options while they were at it. I'm always pleased when I can pick up a competive game and immediatelly excel above other entry-level players, though Metal Drift's tiny community means that you're always going to run into one of the few veterans, who will inevitably demonstrate why more people don't stick with weird little games like this. I encourage you to overcome the inherent butthurt in playing aginst such individuals and engage in a unique and thrilling multiplayer experience.

The fast-paced, arena action of Metal Drift will easily satisfy your craving for a quick action game, and the multiplayer is phenomenal.  The graphics are nice and the framerate is steady.  The controls take some getting used to, but are actually quite good. As long as you know what you are buying when you purchase, you will not have any regrets with this title. It's not a new $60 AAA game, it's not a mobile game, and it's not a single player campaign story mode with a multiplayer mode. This game came out before the current crowd funding alpha-release indie scene blew up. You might want some more features after awhile, or expect a larger community, but what this game offers is polish. It's not a broken release with a promose of "Bugs will be fixed later," it's polished and *released* as a full game title.
Some people will not enjoy this game, it doesn't appeal to all audiences and isn't trying to. However, the people who don't enjoy the game generally don't enjoy the gameplay - the game itself runs and handles fine. If this game looks like the type of thing you might find fun to try, don't think the negative reviews are due to this being a broken mess with wonky physics and terrible graphics - this isn't Fireworks Simulator or something. If the idea of getting in some tanks and shooting friends in a soccer match sounds fun then this is a great way to do it. People who complain about the weapon unlocking don't realize that the first weapon and upgrade are some of the best in the game.
Metal Drift is what you make it, and I can tell you personally that it has a ton of potential for people who give it a shot.
Oh and if you're on the fence about it, there's a free demo.

I originally reviewed Celestial Command (CC) on 21 October 2015. Since the game is being actively developed and updated, it's only fair that my review reflects that. As such I updated my review last year, and now again.
CC is a pretty unique game and a great example of how Early Access could work. Developed by three friends that care immensely about their game and are very much in touch with their player base, I would recommend the game on the basis that these people deserve support to keep going alone. However, as it happens, the game itself is quite fun too!
At present, CC's largely a sandbox in which you can build space ships from the ground up and then control them. Design matters - proper balancing, fuel/power distribution and engine placement to name a few can make the difference between thriving and failing miserably. Failing miserably generally means you die.
With your ships there are several things you can do: Mining, Trading, Fighting, Salvaging and the occasional mission. Most of these are pretty worked out although still subject to continuous change. If you just want to design cool ships, there is a sandbox option where you can build anything you can come up with.
You can save and load ship designs and share them with other players. For now this is done by sending save files, later this will be done using the Steam Workshop.
The best part of CC for me however is just how involved you can get with bringing out the big potential that is obviously present here. The developers are responsive and responsible, read every message on the Steam forums as well as the game's Discord channel. They listen to suggestions and feedback and have let the community contribute to the game, for example by submitting ships to serve as NPC pirates, or by letting players translate the game into other languages.
I hope of course that my review will help to bring other players in. However, there are also a few things that you should keep in mind before getting the game.
Again, I highly recommend the game, but make sure you know what you buy before you buy it. If you have any questions you're always welcome on CC's Discord channel, or just leave a comment here or on the Steam Forums.

A lot of people seem to be having difficulty with the game, so here are a few tips to get started:
Mobility - you need fuel to move and mine astroids to survive, making ice a priority. You will not get a container for ice so build a large ore container for it.
To mine - install a beam structer infront with a mining laser right beside for precision mining and install a grabber on the beam structure to grab astroids.
FIND THE ICE FIRST - start mining ice which will go into the large container and install a fuel generator. Install 2 huge fuel tanks for the hydrogen. Transfer the hydrogen to the huge fuel container and connect the oxygen node with the fuel container that once contained hydrogen. this should take care of the fuel as long as you have enough ice.
then get solar panels, use them to charge the power storage to be used by the fuel generator and the mining laser.
Install 2 - 4 booster rockets (first rocket in the build menu for propulsion) for evasive manuver to either quickly get out another astroid or station's way and to break the gravitational pull caused by planets or just for a speed boost. You can also add more RCS rockets for a increase in speed without spending oxygen for the bigger rockets.
Thats pretty much what you need to start with.. weapons and other stuff comes later. Also you need lots of aluminum since that is a very commonly used material to build with.

Definetly an amazing concept. As a Kerbal Space Program addict I must say this is one that you should pickup if you are too and would like to support its development (it is EARLY ACCESS after all).
It is in essence a 2D space sim where you build a ship part-by-part in space and go about mining (so far) and surviving. Your crew will need food and your ship will need power and fuel. Build a bigger ship with more storage and more power, lasers and crew, and you will find yourself having a blast.
It's space physics/orbital mechanics is quite well simulated but do note, this is an early access so expect there to be lots of work to be done until release. You will find there is little content but the devs are working hard at it. For now your challenge will be trying to get more and more food and fuel to survive without flinging yourself into an asteriod.
It has a fairly steep learning curve for new-comers and even more so new-comers to the space sim genre but I'd highly suggest to take a peak at the guides and experiment how modules connect and transfer resources.
More parts will be coming as well as AI ships filling the universe with life and dangers throughout its systems.
A work in progress but looks very promising thus far. Going to keep an eye on this one as it develops.

If you've played the excellent SimpleRockets, you are already familiar with terms like gravitational sphere of influence, apogee, perigee, Hoffman transfers, retrograde and prograde burns. If not, you may want to try playing SimpleRockets to give you the basics or read up on the terms online. You will need to know what these mean.
To begin, this is an awesome game. You can travel within a solar system using several modes of propulsion. You can orbit planets and go to space stations. You can mine asteroids and shoot at things with a ship of your own design. You can do all of this in sandbox mode (it will give you things you need from a sandbox menu) or not (in which case you better know what you are doing). I really suggest using the sandbox mode until you are comfortable navigating and modifying your spaceship.
I haven't tried muliplayer yet but I did start my own instance of a server so I can experiment in. Set a password you will remember so you are the only one to get into your instance. In this mode you are given a ship and are in orbit around a planet randomly spawned. Read the F1 help text carefully as it will get you familiar. Anything you need to build or remove from your ship is done in engineering.  You can build and destroy engines, power sources, solar panels, , reactors, corridors, cargo holds, command decks, struts, fuel tanks, a radar system, various weapons, a grapple hook, and a mining laser.
Before you can use the object, it must be either connected to a power source or a tank. That's done easily by dragging and dropping nodes from the source to the object. You can connect multiple objects to a single tank or power source but remember you will empty that source faster if you do. Adding more sources of fuel or power will help, but it will increase the mass of your ship which will make it slower to turn.
Moving around a solar system is not a simple manner of pointing your nose at a planet, star or asteriod and then firing your rockets because everything including you is in Newtonian motion. It's like trying to drive a car on ice. You have to kill one direction of motion before attempting to move in a new direction (retrograde burns come to play here) or slow down or speed up at the apogee or perigee points of your orbit. Failure to do this will result in your ship skidding and slidding off course.
For a game that is in alpha, it is very stable. The game cost is insanely reasonable and there is a lot of play value provided you get past the learning curve. There's very little tutorial info here about the game to explain all the basics but two guides written and available on Steam will help you get started. If you keep in sandbox mode, experiment with ship design and orbital mechanics, and ask questions in the community area, you should get the hang of it.
One  thing I would like to see added as  a feature is the clicking of planets to show info on your approach vector (both tangent and radial). You can do this with asteroids but not planets.
A ship editor for creating and modifying a library of ship designs before entering the game would be great as well.
Time dialation for up to 8x speed is not enough to see a discernable change in orbits and intrasolar system travel...perhaps 24 would be more appropriate?
Buy the game! For 3 cups of coffee you get something that will keep you entertained yet challenged for days.

I've always loved the cyberpunk setting in videogames. Transistor is one of the highlights of 2014. This game here is no different. I won't lie, I've never played any of the Shadowrun games before this (I read that they weren't as good as this here) but this game made me want to delve deeper into the Shadowrun world. Set in futuristic Berlin, the story plays out at a nice pace though you would probably get confused with all the terminology and lore going around (Google is your best friend here) if like me, you are new to this universe. The branches in the storyline offer some replay value, and your decisions do affect the storyline. Strong supporting characters also help give the story some life rather than a Y/N kind of game.
The artwork is to me, pretty good. Reminds me a lot of the aforementioned Transistor, in a good way. You don't really get super detailed character models but it doesn't matter since the game isn't meant to be played with you zooming in that much (Plus, it's all about the STORY). One of my only complaints about the artwork (graphics or whatever) is that the Matrix (it's the digital world where deckers can "jack in") looks like it came out from one of those crappy Android games. But then again, it IS the digital realm we're talking about here with all the 1's and 0's.
The turn-based combat is solid and plays out as you'd expect. In terms of upgrades and the like, there isn't really a lot of things to do. There is no one God-tier 'class' or gear to get. It's all up to your imagination and how you want your character to play. Support with spell buffs (yep, there's ♥♥♥♥ing MAGIC), long range combat with sniper rifles, close range melee and many more ways you can decide to play.
This game makes me want to get the previous one (this game was a DLC for it, but has since become standalone), Shadowrun Returns. Also with the next game confirmed to be set in Hong Kong, I can't wait to see how Harebrained Schemes steps up the game from this masterpiece.

Harmonia is a kinetic visual novel by Visual Arts Key who are known for their tear jerking visual novels. If you have an hour or three for a quick burn of a feel sad feel good kind of thing, then Harmonia is the game to read.

*SPOILER FREE REVIEW*
Key is pretty much one of my fave companies of all time, as their content is whimsical, romantic, thought-provoking and fully of emotion.  Harmonia is another good example of what they can do.
Harmonia is a kinetic novel, meaning that there are no choices to make - it's more like reading a book or watching a DVD.  It took me about three hours to complete.  Technically speaking, there is only one slight issue that I can report - when I booted up the game for the first time, an error message occurred telling me that the game's default font was not available on my computer and I had to choose another one.  To be honest, this wasn't an issue as I could choose a new font with ease and it had no effect on the gameplay - I could start the game straight after choosing with no issue.  Just beware that you might have to choose a different font from the in-game menu.  No big deal though.
Story wise, Harmonia touches upon themes that Key have covered before, and a lot of people have criticised it for being too close to Key's other kinetic novel Planetarian.  After playing Harmonia, I can both agree and disagree with elements of that comparison.  When you put it down on paper, the similarities are astonishing; both stories feature a post-apocalyptic world caused by human error, where the protagonist wanders a desolate Earth, dealing with phenomena like acid rain from atmosphere pollution and attack from roving bandits.  Both stories also feature a type of humanoid android/robot/computer that has survived events so far and is attempting to fulfil its original purpose.  Both stories also feature a theme of fixing or rebuilding physical objects.  Both stories ALSO feature the struggle for survival and the emotional connotations of trying to help people even if it seems pointless given certain circumstances.  After reading all that, you'll probably agree that it doesn't look good for Harmonia being an original, fresh experience.
However, all of that being said, what makes Harmonia great in its own right is its story and characters.  Despite all of these similarities, as the story progressed and I was introduced to the different characters, their struggles and their experiences, I happily fell victim to what Key do best - making great, 3 dimensional, genuine and entrancing characters that you really grow to care about.  Despite noting myself at the beginning that the themes were similar to Planetarian, I quickly found myself forgetting about Planetarian completely and instead becoming attached to this group of characters that felt authentic and unique to Harmonia.  By the story ended, I felt like I'd really gone on a journey with these people and that it hadn't been like anything else, especially with the twist in the tale I did not suspect.  So in contrast to my earlier comparison, I genuinely recommend Harmonia because its story is its own, and it was very enjoyable.  Its CGs and soundtrack are also up to Key's usual memorable and effective par, and all in all, I'd say that Key are definitely on form with this kinetic novel.

I was disappointed with DG2 unfortunately.   The main reasons for this:
1.  The graphical upgrades from DG1 actually made it harder for me to work out what was going on.  Lots of bells and whistles, but they don't add to the core gameplay, which felt a lot cleaner and more precise in DG1.
2.  The voiceovers.  Goodness me, these are... terrible.  DG1 was characterised by a really quirky voiceover whose occasional glitches and obsession with raspberries was amusing and sometimes a bit sad.  For some reason in DG2 this has been "upgraded" to a banter between at least 3 different characters, that really pushes hard for laughs and fails miserably.  Not funny, just cringeworthy.
3.  Gameplay generally; again the feel isn't there from DG1.  Having the option to build towers on top of other blocks and upgrade them both should in theory have added depth and complexity, but the beauty of DG1 was in figuring out the patterns and where you could divert the enemies to.  The levels of DG2 I was able to grit my teeth through just seemed really dull by comparison - more thinking about which combination of upgrades, and less thinking about pathing.
Like most things, it's just my opinion based on playing for a little while and really failing to enjoy it at all.

Where is my wife!! For the love of all that is holy, why is my daughter so fat! Timmy!!! Dammit Timmy where are you!?! These questions and many more will race through your head the entire time you are rushing about collecting soup, water, tools and other supplies mere moments before nuclear energy obliterates your home.
Once inside the dank, often bug-infested shelter below the wreckage of your domicile, the race against the clock begins. A playful jab at Cold War Americana, a choose your own adventure serial that could use more effort overall, and a game, in that order.
The art style effectively parodies the Reagan era suburban family.  Most of the graphics are two dimentional sketches in which beauty will be in the eye of the beholder, but I largely found unimpressive and lacking in variety.  The three dimentional gameplay segment is function, but equally forgettable art wise.  Music also fails to linger after the game is switched off.
The game is effectively two games in one.  The first being a time management puzzle evocative of the game's title.  The second being a decision driven visual novel.  The two elements don't inherently feel connected, save that your performance in the former slightly enhances your experience of the latter.  The game itself seems to realize this as either segment can be played independent of the other through some of the default options.  For two games, two reviews are in order.
The time management puzzle is a glorified random number generator.  Tasked with procuring the best and most necessary supplies for your fallout shelter in 60 seconds, the fact that all supplies are randomly scattered throughout the house on each playthrough, while the house's layout is fixed, means that you'll naturally develop an optimal path for maximum stuff accumulation, hoping that the correct stuff is in the correct place.  In short, the segment plays itself for the most part, aside from the infusion of varience in the form of player mistakes.  Controls are slippery and require spamming clicks to force the avatar to execute the desired action, no doubt to raise tension but frustrating nevertheless.
The visual novel is full of delightful anachronisms that may induce a hee hawing from time to time, but they do repeat themselves frequently.  You'll soon find yourself skipping through the family status updates and consequences of previous decisions to get to the meat and potatoes of your upcoming encounter.  Most of the decisions in the game are focused on rewarding you for having the correct tool when prompted (or inversely punishing you for not having or using said tool).  Some choices rely on your memory of previous encounters or informtion, which deliver a more satisfying sense of accomplishment when overcome and a sense of fair play on the game's part when you fall prey to them.  For the most part though, luck is a large factor, making the exercise less about achieving victory and more about enjoying the story of your family victimized by the ravages of a pulp fiction nuclear holocaust.
Your $10.00s will buy you a few hours of entertainment from this title before it starts collecting virtual dust on your virtual shelf, awaiting the next major content update that may never come.  You can do worse for the money, but you also could do better, and with the release of games like Stardew Valley, I find myself expecting more from my indie titles nowadays.  If the idea of a pulpy, witty game about nuclear war and American values interests you, the Fallout series has been scratching that itch since the 1990s (Those games from the 1990s are likely obtainable at a comparable price tag to this title and absolutely dominate in comparison regarding content).  Consequence driven visual novel lovers can get a more rewarding experience from the Telltale games or a dedicated visual novel game.

Gems of War: The more you play it, the more you hate it!
On the surface, this game seems like an interesting spinoff of the Dr. Mario ripoff puzzle genre, combined with TCG mechanics, for that extra collectability/addiction.
As you play match-3, your matches give mana to your "troops" which then attempt to defeat the enemy.
One thing that must be clarified is that there is no "PVP" in this game, despite how desperately the game tries to convince you otherwise. There is only PVE against decks the devs put together, and PVE against decks other players put together. When you play against another player in PVP, you only play against the deck he/she last used, while the computer essentially plays the deck.
The first thing you will notice, and hate, about GoW is the CPU player's rampant abuse of the extra turn mechanic.
Whenever you match 4 or more gems, instead of just 3 in one turn, you get an extra turn.
This is a huge advantage, as this means your troops will charge their attacks first, and get that much closer to winning.
One thing you will notice, is there is often no available "bonus matches" on your turn. That is, you cannot make a match of 4 or more on your turn. But then, when the opponent's turn comes, the match you made caused "bonus matches" to appear for the opponent. It is not uncommon at all for the CPU to hand itself extra turns. To add insult to injury, these bonuses matches can, and so often do, lead to more bonus matches for the opponent, leading to the CPU enjoying 3-9 bonus turns before you can move more than once. One could suggest this is merely RNG, but as you play, and you realize that these lucky bonus streaks don't seem to happen to you, but almost constantly happen to your opponents, the excuse that this is merely "randomness" begins to hold less and less water.
Another thing that you will hate is how the game scales the opponents. These are based off of your player level, not the power of your cards. Because your player level will increase waaaaaay faster than your deck level, you eventually end up losing more rounds than you win, until you're simply stuck.
While you technically do not need to spend money to unlock and power up cards, the sheer amount of time required to power up cards is staggering, paticularly the time required to gain "souls" the currency required to level up individual cards. Without spending cash, Gems of War becomes a tedious and unrewarding grind.
In short, Gems of War is technically "pay to progress faster," but in a game where you need to constantly keep ahead of your opponents' power level to stand a decent chance of winning, it ends up feeling pretty darn pay to win anyway.
In short, Gems of War will infuriate any true "gamer", or anyone that believes that games should be won/lost based on skill and wit, and not sheer luck or cash spent.

First things first, this is the first Tomb Raider game that I've played. I don't know that I was actively trying to avoid them before, but the previous ones never really looked all that great. And I'll be honest, this one didn't seem like it was exactly my cup of tea either. Holy hell was I wrong about that.
I greatly enjoyed this game. Honestly, I struggle to find anything wrong with it.
The plot is interesting. The action is awesome. Combat is balanced and fun. The exploration / platformer aspects likewise. Nothing ever seems unfair or unreasonable, but stuff is still challenging. I'm normally not too much of a fan of the puzzles involved in games of this sort, but these I rather enjoyed. Hell, I even didn't mind the few quick time events which popped up during the game.
I seriously underestimated just how brutal the game would be. Suffice it to say that Lara spends a heck of a lot of time coated in blood, only some of it hers. But when she does end up dying, due to combat or terrain or what have you, the game does not pull any punches at all.
I think I need to single out the sound effects / sound track. They did such a wonderful job of setting the mood of the game. It really allowed you to get into things. The voice acting was especially well done; Camilla Luddington obviously did a great job with Lara, but the rest of the cast were well done also. One thing that this game did that so many other games failed at was the voice acting on the various bad guys. At no point in time did we see enough repetition to make them seem like a bunch of clones. Both the lines of dialog and the different voice actors used were sufficiently varied to keep everything from going stale.
Level design did the same, mixing up different aspects of the game play in fun ways throughout the game.
As per usual, this review covers the single player only; I have no idea how the multiplayer goes, and I don't really care. If that's a big deal for you, then you might wanna look into that elsewhere.
So yeah. I highly recommend playing this game. Especially if you see this review in time, before the Winter sale ends. At 85% off ($3.74 CAD), this is one hell of a deal. And of course, as a franchise reboot, you don't need to have played any of the previous games in order to enjoy the hell out of this one.

I had quite a bit of fun with this game and I expect to probably get about 10 hours out of play in its current state. That is however because I enjoy semi-realistic simulations, love orbital mechanics, have a taste for cience fiction, and am generally going through an indecisive phase in terms of entertainment.
This game is far from finished but I am cautiously optimistic. I've been burned by titles like Starbound and Towns (early access before steam greenlight) in the past. Naturally I didn't expect much. This game however, is seeing regular updates. It's also changed a lot. Most of the guides are outdated and there seems to be quite a shift in how manufacturing mechanics work.
Lets start with what you should expect from this game at the time of writing. There are lovely orbital physics, even thought they feel a bit clunky compared to KSP (which is this game's nearest comparison). The idea of having to collect lots of resources (12 at this time) is actually kind of cool, but again clunky.
By clunky I mean the following. So orbital physics works, but as a vetran of KSP I know how imporant it is to know your prograde/retrograde vector (i.e the line that runs at a tangent to your orbit). This isn't difficult to code but is not in the game at all, all intercepts have to be done manually (you get no intercept vector) with lots of tedious course correction which would be fine if fuel wasn't such a massive concern. This leads to resources, to get fuel you need to mine ice, which can then be broken into oxygen and hydrogen by using a fuel maker. This gives you your propulsion, and you will need to carry huge quantities of this fuel to get anywhere significant. On top of these 3 resources you will need at least 1 cargo container for each of the 8 other elements which are commonly used to manufacture components. You'll find yourself frantically managing these containers because once a resource output has filled up the container it dumps it dumps it in another empty  one. This wouldn't be so bad if the same output wasn't also the input for when you want to use that resource to build things. What this leads to is a module being half built and you having to figure out what resource isn't properly connected to allow the build. This can legitimately take 2 to 5 minutes as it's like trying to untangle a pair of earphones. Resource connections being represented as lines that you have to trace to a point.
So why do I like this game and why at 3 or so hours will I play it again? Simply, it's a great idea. A bit more casual that KSP in terms of gameplay and realism. It's also fun in different ways. The nearest comparison I can make is that if Celestial Command is to KSP what Terraria is to Minecraft. They're similar but enjoyably different. If you liked KSP but had a hankering to blow a few things up or just chill out and do some silly things like destroy a station with a mining laser, then give Celestial Command a go at some point in the future. If however you're bored of KSP and want a variation on the theme, you'll get about 3-5 hours out of this game.
A final note is the game's language. I know the devs aren't native English speakers but it's just lazy. Get someone in to write tooltips for all the modules so they explain themselves properly. Otherwise it's really difficult to get into the game. Hell I'd write the tooltips for a copywriters fee. I want to see this game become a fully fledged product. I want to play it again after the major updates. So devs, if someone you know who speaks English is reading, make a few core tweaks to your resource management, orbital mechanics and your tooltips. It will make the game much more playable and much easier to recommend in it's current state. Also ditch the whole one element for each cargo container, it's just boring.

TL: DR- 10/10, literally one of the three best strategy games i've ever played, and probably the best RTS.
This game can have a steep learning curve, and campaign missions may well take you two hours to complete if you go carefully, or twice that if you go full defensive on the hardest difficulty setting, but this just means that there's actually meaning to good base design, and it is incredibly satisfying to build up an impenetrable fortress then create an army that will flatten your opponent... hopefully. Then there's also the option of building so many nuclear launch facilities that you can overwhelm your enemy's missile defense systems and drown them in nuclear fire (for reference, nukes in this game are just about the hardest to obtain in any game i've found, but they're also the most visually spectacular and you actually have cause to fear them)
There is a good variety of options for the skirmish mode, you can put yourself in a cagefight with a trio of AI opponents that cheat just for added difficulty, you can customise some major gamemode settings such as completely disallowing certain units or tech-levels, or you can increase the rate at which everyone gathers resources to speed the game up a bit.
The graphics are very nice, especially considering the number if units you will have running around the map at any given time. the textures don't look that great if you were to zoom all the way in, but if you do that you'll zoom out again to find that OH GOD THE CYBRAN HAD A BUNCH OF STEALTHED MONKEYLORDS OUTSIDE MY BASE AND THEY'RE TRAMPLING MY REACTORS!
However, the place this game really outshines anything else i've played is its interface. you can customise so easily what the map shows you in terms of the range of your anti-air, anti ground, indirect fire, etc, your sonar, radar, omnisensor ranges... it offers you so much information but if you're finding it overwhelming you can just switch it all of with about two clicks.
Unit control is so good in this game, in terms of automation. you can very reasonably set up a factory to produce infinite of a set of units, have air transports pick them up from your base, and airdrop into a different part of the map with no input from the player. this makes managing hundreds (or, with mods, thousands) of units so much eaiser, leaving you to direct your army, navy and airforce, and watch the explosions.

The culmination of nearly twenty years of evolution in the RTS genre, the last great base building RTS, and the finest example of grand scale real-time strategy to grace any platform.
Every RTS title since has failed to even approach the zenith established by Forged Alliance. With the industry switch to MOBAS and DOW clones, and the seeming death of the base building RTS, it is unlilkely that this game will ever be surpassed.

I will echo many other reviews in that I 100% agree Dragonfall is much more advanced than the recent Shadowrun Returns. I have completed the SNES version when it came out (Yes, I am a grandpa gamer), and in many ways it's better than that and other ways it isn't. The SNES version's environment was very open, so much so that it was easy to get lost. But at least you could beef up Jake Armitage which was fun to hulk him up. Dragonfall isn't as open environment as the SNES version, but it is no where the linear game that was in Shadowrun Returns. Dragonfall is very much a 'Goldie Locks' between the two. In fact at different points in the game, you need to make choices that directly impacts the outcome of runs. So although the story progresses itself in a linear fashion, based upon what you decide and act completely effects the game.
I do believe the game designers' intent of allowed the gamer to make these important decisions was with purpose. Allowing for decisions also invests the gamer in the story's plot. The main storyline is interesting as well as some of the optional side quests. As any good story or movie goes, there always is a twist that you don't foresee. I was close in my assumption. You can also become involved in your teammate NPC characters as well as powering them up.
I would definitely recommend this game. It should not disappoint. I bought this for myself during the Christmas 2014 sale, and the cost was completely worth it. I don't believe you'll be disappointed with this version of the Shadowrun franchise.

Shadowrun Returns was a bit lof a letdown. It wasn't a bad game, it was an 'ok' game, where we expected something very good. For that reason, I avoided Dragonfall for a long time, even after the positive reviews.
The wait was absolutely worth it. Dragonfall - Director's Cut is a fantastic rpg game. It's less linear than it's predecessor, the combat is more balanced. The story is exceptionally good, which is always very important in an rpg game. What makes it even better, is the fact that your decisions really matter, so the replay value is more than just rolling a different character.
Also, huge kudos for the NPCs (well most of them anyway). You know that feeling from old rpg games, where you actually REALLY cared about your teammates? What their motivations are, what's their story, their plans? Dragonfall - Director's Cut absolutely delivers in that regard as well. (Oh Glory, wish it was a Bioware game... *wink*)

This is a spoilerfree review of an entire playthrough of the game including pretty much every sidefart you could let.
First of all if you are just looking for a clue if this contains shadowrun returns: it doesn't.
Damn this was great. It's really been a while since I got as immersed in a story and this game manages to tell its story without any shiny cutscenes. The main characters are all memorable, at least if you had the option to talk to them a bit more. I only kind of discovered you could actually unlock sidemissions by talking to your team shortly before the end. So I just spam-talked myself to all the missions and they make some of the characters a lot more interesting.
If you know XCOM then you pretty much know the combat system but to those who don't: you have a certain percentage of hit chance and critical chance and different forms of cover.  The entire thing is turn-based and everyone has a certain amount of actions they can perform in a single round. That also means that walking distance is restriced. One thing I dont like about this is that the game has the habbit of missing an unbelievable amount of 95% hit-chance hits. And no there is not a decent amount of hits despite low percentage to balance that.
The sidemissions are pretty much all interesting and you dont have to be a die-hard completionist to happily have done about 90% of what the game has to offer.
Another thing I like is that you dont get XP for kills. You get XP when you finish a mission and somtimes when you for example do something important on some machine or something then you also get XP in a mission. The lack of kill-XP however means you actually look for ways to avoid a fight. Usually a game says "there is a lot of them there, better go around that" and the reaction would be "and give up extra XP? aw hell no!" but here you actually do it to not waste another medkit.
I played the game on normal difficulty and I cant say I ever really got stuck in a fight. barely ever even used a medkit. I played a troll street samurai focused on melle combat. and by focused I mean that I shot less than 20 times throughout all combats together. Dragonfall - Director's Cut continues the great line of the roleplaying game Shadowrun Returns: Deadman's Switch, and in some aspects adds to it - all of which are improvements in my opnion.
First of all, what is Shadowrun: Dragonfall - Director's Cut? Well, a roleplaying game in a dystopia future with magic, tech, drugs, politics, double-crossing and otther filth. It is not affraid to pick adult themes. Furthermore, if you look in all the nooks and crannies you can even find comments in the game that make you think about your actions; If you whipe-out that rascist organization, what about the kids that were there just to get of the street to be warm and have meal? Another example is your fellow shadowrunner who is a victim of prejudices and domestic violence. Rarely did I see this in RPGs and I played a good many. Now, not every NPC is like that and some are a bit one-dimensional, but such archtypes can be fun to have around.
Like its predecessor, this RPG has turn-based combat (like e.g. X-COM or Space Marines) but with its own unique twists. In comparison to Deadman's Switch, cover has grown in importance. So, what else is new? Dragonfall places more emphasis on different stats and social etiquettes. Spells are explained more clearly and in the Matrix you can actually find statements about meatspace that you were involved in. Also some quests have taken a lighter tone with more humor, but that may or may not be to your taste.
All in all, this game is interresting for any strategist, that has the balls to adress more adult themes, and that all in the unique and intriguing world of Shadowrun. I recommend this game (and its previously mentioned predecessor) for any RPG fan and for anyone that loves to read Dark Fantasy, Dystopian Futures, or Noir fiction.

Harmonia is one of those really short visual novels I genuinely enjoyed from the beginning to the end. Key always does a wonderful job at keeping pace and engaging the reader with great dialogue and story. Harmonia is not an exception. I highly recommend this for a short but emotional ride!

Rating: 7/10 ("Good")
Recommended for: People who enjoy VNs, people who enjoy post-apocalyptic futures, people who enjoy crying with their novels. I would recommend this to a first time VN reader.
Harmonia is short visual novel with around 6 hours of read time. There are no choices to be made; it's simply a VN to read and experience. One thing I noticed immediately upon starting the game is that the UI seems rather old what with the overlay of text over the entire image. That's not something you see in a lot of VNs released recently. Thankfully, you can remove the text to see the CG or background simply by hitting the spacebar.
The art in Harmonia is very pretty apart from one quibble I have; that would be Madd’s sprites. His nose is nonexistent and makes him look extremely unnatural. Everything else is fine and even beautiful, albeit it requires you to suspend your disbelief. For instance, how can Tipi have such long hair and wear such lovely clothes in this dystopian society? I know for sure that I wouldn’t want hair that long in a setting like that…it seems like too much work to take care of when I could be doing something else…but perhaps that is a sign of her true strength.
Jokes aside, Harmonia itself is a somewhat sombre game. Whilst there are certainly slice of life elements, it's a tragedy novel at its heart, meant to make you cry. You'll probably be pleased to hear that the ending is actually happy, in a way that fits. It's not overly optimistic but it does fit the themes and it's at least somewhat "realistic", as far as realism can go.
The plot itself is decent but feels a little too similar to Planetarian. There were plot aspects and scenes I could guess simply from reading that VN previously. And, after reading Harmonia, I can say that in my opinion Planetarian is the better of the two, but your mileage may vary. Some aspects that seemed very strange while first reading Harmonia make sense later on after finishing the story and understanding everything.
The characters in Harmonia are competently written, though they don't have an astounding amount of depth and some are rather unabashedly cliche.
The soundtrack is hit or miss. Some tracks were very beautiful and fitting to the scene, while I simply didn't care for others.
Overall, Harmonia is a decent visual novel that is a nice read, though I personally think Planetarian would be a better pick even with its shorter length.

i liked this game when i first started playing it a few days ago. but the more i played it, the more of a boring grind it became. i don't mind a grind where the payout is worth the time put in, but this one just doesn't do that. crappy rewards from the campaign missions combined with the fact that the enemies in the campaign are based off your hero's level and not your monsters' levels make this game pretty much unenjoyable after about 10-20 hours. right around level 20-25, i noticed i was losing more missions than i was actually winning. part of that i attributed to the fact that the game suggests moves to you that usually end up benefitting your enemy more than if you had picked a different move. i've tested it in many missions doing the computer suggested moves and doing moves other than what the computer suggested. i found that the enemy would benefit from my move choice roughly twice as often if i went with the computer suggested move than it was benefited by the move i made that wasn't suggested. i posted in the steam discussions and was told this doesn't happen. i did not believe that and when i came to the store page to write my review today i decided to read some of the reviews before i did. i'm apparently not the only one who thinks the computer is suggesting moves to help your enemies.
i really liked the gem swapping and matching-the games great on that and has a nice variety of enemies with their own special ability that they can use when they have enough mana (obtained by matching the gems of the same color as your monster's ability) and that provided some entertainment for a while, but like pretty much every free to play game i've played, there comes a point not long after you start playing where you hit a wall in your game you can't beat without dozens, maybe hundreds, of hours of grinding to get past or you're expected to fork over some cash for a little boost to get you over that wall until you come to the next one.
the pvp is also a lie. someone else mentioned that in their review, but i wanted to mention it as well because i also was disappointed. not just that the pvp is a lie, but also that the pvp is the main way to level up and get gold and glory(the game's currencies are gold, souls, gems, and glory. gold is used for buying new kingdoms to unlock new missions or for upgrading those kingdoms as well as for unlocking certain lower level chests. gems are used for the highest level chests (in terms of rarity of the items/creatures inside)  and reshuffling the 3 choices you have for pvp (which will always be weak, medium, and too tough for you to beat.) glory is used for the middle tier chests. souls are used to level up your creatures. the problem i have with many of these currencies is that you only get about 100 gold (plus whatever 4 or 5 gem matches you make will give you some paltry gold as well) per mission and only about 170-250 gold per pvp match. you also only get 4 or 5 souls per mission or pvp match. to get your monsters to level 10-15 you need 1000-3000 souls. you do the math. how much do you like grinding? if you like grinding or have money to throw away to avoid grinding, get this game-otherwise don't. it's not that great.

Damned is a fun, multiplayer survival horror game where 4 people (Or less) play as survivors while the 5th player chooses one of 4 monsters and has to try and kill the survivors, each monster being unique in it's own way.

Pros
*Cool Music/Sound Effects
*Allows Co-Op which most horror games do not have
*Nice Push/Pull system with doors and drawers. (Like an Amnesia: The Dark Descent)
*Unique Character models and graphics
*Tons of maps
*Unique and easy to pick up mechanics
*Simple hosting/connecting to friends
*Good Sp00ks with insanity effects
*Literally like goosebumps the game. (The goosebumps theme fits so well it's not even funny)
===
Cons
*Some maps and monster combinations make the game extremely difficult or too easy
*Some monsters are more overpowered than others
*Some maps are very hard to find keys on. Ex: Black Lake
*Performance problems on the highest settings (And I have a decent gaming computer)
===
All around very fun and unique game experience.

Damned can be a tough sell, and for good reason. Back when I bought it, sitting in a lobby for over a minute without the host starting the game basically guaranteed hard crashes for all involved. This has been (mostly) fixed, the game will still randomly kick people for no reason, and isn't very well optimized, but if playing with people you know you'll be hard pressed to find a better multiplayer horror experience when everything DOES work.
Gameplay:
The game is multiplayer slender with amnesia click-and-hold door controls and a battery/flashlight system that would make Jim Sterling cry. You find keys (rather than notes) and use them to open doors to find more keys until you escape, all while being hunted by one of the various monsters (played by a real person). Each monster has their own little twist on gameplay, and by far the most tense moments of the game are when you're limited in where you can travel (no keys) and don't know which monster's playstyle to counter.
That's what the gameplay is, but is it fun?:
Yes. Play. Damned. With. Friends. Hop in a VC, que it up, and make the monster mute himself except for the occasional brag directly after scoring a kill. You'll be amazed how quickly you can betray someone, locking them out of a room and leaving them to die in order to ensure you stay alive. You'll feel genuine relief when you cycle keys as a team to finally open that last exit door. Resource management with batteries usually feels like a tacked-on timekill mechanic, but in Damned you have to share those resources amongst 4 people, which adds to the urgency quite effectively.
Playing as the monster is a blast too. Sometimes you'll get a series of bad ports as Mary, or noone will hit your traps on Lurker, but setting up a legit jumpscare makes it all worth it. My friends and I have tons of stories along the lines of "remember that time I made [friend] scream like a little ♥♥♥♥♥?" Very few games give you that opportunity.
Graphics:
Meh. Mary and Fallen work well because they are meant to look stiff and plodding, but lurker looks like the monster from "Boogeyman," and only will make you jump if he pops up right on your♥♥♥♥♥(which he often does). Character models are functional, as are animations. Environments are sufficiantly mood-supporting, but a LOT of the levels are "re-arranged assets from our asylum level." The most important thing is that the graphics rarely detract from the horror experience.
Audio: Absolutely essential to have a good headset in order to get the full experience with this game. Most monsters set "traps" by interacting with objects in the environment that give off a sound que when the players pass by them. There is no worse feeling than stumbling through a hallway and triggering 3 or 4 traps in close succession, basically ensuring the monster knows exactly where you are. Ambient sound when the monster is close or is attacking further crank up the intensity, and the plinking minimalism of the rest of the audio just accents these bombastic moments even further.
Overall: 6/10, 8/10 with lobby of friends. If you can, buy it on sale or in a 4-pack with friends pitching in, but $20 is a relatively fair price on its own.
