Conquest of Elysium 4 is a unique game that mixes 4X (eXplore, eXpand, eXploit and eXterminate) with roguelike elements, such as permadeath and procedural generation. The game has 21 classes (nations), six dimensions (being Elysium, the initial dimension, similar to the planet Earth), hundreds of units, seven kinds of universe (societies) to be generated, five different map sizes, support for up to 16 players and / or CPUs, up to six teams, 10 levels of difficulty, support for mods and full customization of UI size, graphics and sound effects.
The game's battle system is quite different, as it's not possible to command the units. Although this seems somewhat pointless in theory, in practice it works very well. Battles are resolved according to the pros and cons of each unit, their current status (blessed, cursed, poisoned, for instance) and battlefield conditions, which may contain hiding places, walls and gates, among others. This system also causes epic battles involving hundreds of units to be completed in a much shorter time than if we needed to control each unit. It is also possible to accelerate the battle or to pause it, but it will never be possible to interfere with it after its beginning, and the best phase of preparing for the fight is recruiting varied units according to the weaknesses of a certain class of enemy and adding them before the match starts. The organization of the troops is done automatically and follows a pattern, and it's not possible to take advantage or disadvantage in this aspect, so take your time while you think what kind of units must be recruted.
The graphics are all made in tilesets and are somewhat reminiscent of Tales of Maj'Eyal. The sound effects part is quite simple, being only functional, but on the other hand, the soundtrack is exceptional. Not surprisingly, the developers at Illwinter Game Design have been granted permission to use Adrian von Ziegler's songs in the game, providing an epic and Celtic atmosphere for the Elysium universe. The interface is the elephant in the room. With unconventional controls (such as movement using Q, W, E, A, D, Z, X, C instead of W, A, S, D), several essential shortcut keys, no information on options, and also the lack of tutorial, the game is certainly intimidating and practically impossible to be played efficiently without at least reading a little of its 72 page manual. The good thing is that the manual has a nice and pleasant reading, and it is not necessary to read it in its entirety. Just follow the part about the controls and the interface while playing and you're good to go. Even though it was the fourth title of the franchise, if only the game came with a small tutorial, this would help give it more visibility, making it more accessible to more people.
Speaking of gameplay, Conquest of Elysium 4 classes are so different from each other that if we learn to play with one, we will need a good time to adapt with another, because besides the universal mechanics for all of them, there are some mechanincs that are unique of certain classes. Not to mention the dimensions (called "planes" in the game). For instance: there's one in the game which is the true hell, with diabolical creatures and other creepy things. It is possible to travel between them, and this causes the generated maps to multiply their size by six, since they are six dimensions, and sometimes some monsters and creatures escape these dimensions and spawn at the quiet Elysium, bringing chaos and destruction to a relatively peaceful world. With all this in mind, you can have an idea of ​​how rich this game is.
The universe of Conquest of Elysium 4 is so extensive and deep that it is impossible to discover everything in it in just a few games. It takes dozens, if not hundreds, of hours of gaming to see everything. Even more impossible is to speak of all this in this humble review. So here's my recommendation for you to get to know the game. If you like strategy, planning and tactical thinking, take time to learn how to play this game. It's worth it.
* Rich and deep universe with a ton of content
* Many customization options, with variants for both beginners and experienced in strategy
* Great and immersive soundtrack
* Support for mods
* Constant content updates
* Unintuitive UI
* Lack of tutorial

This is how all the new games should be. It is not a pay-to-win like a lot of people have claimed. It is simply a pay-to-progress faster. There are no cards, equipments, or skills that only people who pay can get. And there are multiple ways to gems to be able to get armors and high level trait stones that seems like you have to pay for them. Yes your progress will be a lot slower than someone who paid, but you'll know that you earned it.
Also I've seen a lot of people complaining about the new pvp system they introduced. But really, I think it's great. I felt like the old pvp system was way too easy and was getting a little bored with it. I haven't spend a single cent on this game and I'm still 170 wins and 4 losses with pvp. The amount of money and items you can gain per week has been greatly incresed.  It might seem intimidating playing against someone who has more than double your attack, life, and armor, but that doesn't matter if they rarely ever get the chance to attack. Days Under Custody, developed by Abraham Carreola, is a side-scroller horror game with a lot of heart, but not enough presentation.
You play as Duc Parkings (Yes, you read that right. Your name is Duc. I could hardly believe it either), who’s been taunted by horrible nightmares. One late night, after another fit of bad dreaming, Duc falls under a sinister impression; his inner demons are manifesting themselves into reality, and their trying to break into his apartment. It’s the player’s job to escape whatever madness peruses them, and to uncover the truth behind Duc’s murky history.
We’ll start things off with the graphics. The quality isn’t terrible, but it’s pixel art at its simplest. There’s nothing in the design department that’ll keep you hooked, and character models and animations are very stiff and barebones. There were some moments when the game looked aesthetically pleasing, like the dancing of dust specs beneath the grimy light of a sewer lamp, but those moments were few and far between.
As for gameplay, it’s what you’d expect. Puzzles with some survival mechanics thrown into the mix, with a side of item collecting. Duc’s movement speed is terribly slow, and walking down one long hallway to the next, only to realize that you missed something down the previous hallway is not a fun experience. Occasionally, an axe-wielding killer will appear at scripted moments, and you’ll have to hide yourself inside dressers to evade him. But these scenarios can be very cheap. The killer’s appearances are so random and misplaced that (unless you’ve played the game before) a first-time player will have to learn from his/her mistake on the next go. This is why I highly recommend you save game as frequently as possible, lest you have to trek all the way back from your last save point.
Lastly, the story…
Eh… It’s a stunted mess of scatterbrained mystery pieces and untapped potential. I won’t spoil anything for you, but the twist ending is so cliché that I couldn’t help but roll my eyes. The story can be uncovered by finding notes, which are hidden all over the game. But the dev must’ve used Google as his main source of translation. I’ve seen bad grammar before, but sheesh. A word of advice to all indie devs: If English isn’t your first language, it is VITAL that you hire a professional translator, if possible.
What makes me sad is… Days Under Custody has the heart and soul of something great, but it lives in the body of a mediocre product. Some real effort was put in, but there are so many better games you could buy for 5 bucks or less. But I’m confident that this developer will make something great.

After some much needed updates, Days Under Custody is a pretty good short horror adventure title. Initially, a lot of the mechanics were confusing and worked in wonky ways, but much of that has been addressed and fixed in updates.
Graphics: The game is meant to look like a classic pixelated title, so the visuals are simple, yet effective if you are a fan of such a style. If you are picky about realistic graphics however, you will not be impressed. But that should go without saying.
Sound: The music, like the art style, is simple yet effective. The score isn't brilliant by any means, but it sets the tone acceptably and never gets irritating to listen to, even if playing for more than 20 or so minutes at a time.
Puzzles: The puzzles aren't going to be anything you haven't seen before if you are an experienced adventure game player, so don't expect much innovation in terms of puzzles. The puzzles that are there are mostly inventory or code based, with the final one being a little more tricky and of a different variety (I won't spoil it). The puzzles are not central to the plot, and mostly serve as filler gameplay between the main plot "events" that happen with the spooks in the house.
Story/Plot: Frankly, I'm not entirely sure what exactly happened or why any of the details presented mattered, but for a game that lasts around about an hour, I wasn't expecting anything either deep or profound.
Value: The game is only a few bucks which is not free, but there are much worse games available for 15 or more dollars here on Steam. From that perspective, the hour+ of gameplay you'll get from Days Under Custody is well worth the money, especially considering the entire game was produced by one guy (apart from the music apparently).
Overall Score: 6.7/10, I really look forward to future titles from this developer!
P.s. I am a new Let's Player who uses Pop-up commentary, if you'd like to check out my playthrough of this video game, look me up on youtube!

It's bad.  This game is more than just poor quality, it also is pretty much broken.
So here is a rundown of my experience.
- In the startup launcher, every resolution option was duplicated 10 times at least.  Like, 1920x1080x32 is listed 10 times, same with 1680x1050x32, and so on.  Strange.
- No controller support...  I know it does not imply to have any controller support on the store page, but it is a huge setback for the experience requiring the user to use the keyboard.
- No mentioning or list anywhere within the game of what the controls even are.  You have to play with it for a few minutes to figure out how to move your racer.  Spoiler: you go forward with "w" and you steer with the left and right arrow keys.
- No options menu AT ALL.  There is a space in the menu for where it COULD go one day, but yeah, there's no options menu in this game.
- Only options are quick races and career mode.  First I tried career mode...  It seems to function, you go through the races and if you get first place you can continue to the next race.  If you fail, you have to restart that race.  There's no indication of what progress you have in your career, just that at first you will be one dirt track and on the next race it's a different track.  You get to choose a rider model, but when you race, it will not be the model you chose!  Brilliant!
- When you create your "career", you enter your name.  But when you finish the race, it instead displays "aaaaaa" as your name.
- The game has weird quirks to it, like if you are headed down a straight away and you go 1 inch outside the course (still headed in the right direction, maybe just cutting the corner ever-so-slightly. a big "WRONG WAY" is displayed on the screen.
- Sometimes the computer's AI will need to respawn back onto the track, and they might just spawn right on top of your head, and you can keep racing with them on top of you.
- When you "restart a race" because you didn't make first place, you might break the game.  As in, there are no textures, and you are racing in a black world which is impossible to see what you are doing.  I did race 1, got 1st place, race 2, failed, restarted, and then got to no-texture-world on that next attempt.
- Even on a high end system, the rain seemed to break the game.  I went from a super high framerate to almost unplayable when the rain started.
- When "restarting a race", the game did not load, basically crashed.  I waited 10 minutes, nothing happened, had to alt+F4 to get out.
- Frustrated with career mode, I then chose the quick race mode.  I did one race.  I stayed exactly on the track.  I was far, far ahead of everyone else.  After 5-6 minutes, I noticed that I was in last place.  And I was still on my first lap.  Just for fun, I kept playing and playing, enjoying myself at the fact that it was not triggering +1 laps every time I crossed the finish line.  I went on to do 3 more laps, and still was on lap 1.
- If you get stuck, you cannot "reset your ATV" back onto the track.  There is no button on the keyboard to do this, nor if you hit 'escape' can you expect a 'reset your ATV' option.  You have to exit the race, or restart it from the beginning.
Should I keep playing or is this enough reasons to not recommend the game?  Oh yeah, I forgot one more thing:
In quick race mode, there is a big button (when choosing your ATV) that says MODIFY.  As in, modify your ATV... but it does nothing.  I assume it's a placeholder button.
Okay I'm done.  Don't buy this game!  :)
I'll add in a compliment: there seemed to be quite a bit of variety in the quick race mode level selector.  The tracks themselves are done fairly well and is around a dozen of them.

A round-based board game at heart, Greed Corp makes you fight your way through a 24-map single player campaign, destroying your enemies with your workers, cannons or by just removing the ground they are standing on. It's definitely following the 'easy to learn, hard to master' approach, with just a few possible moves working together to create a surprisingly sophisticated strategical challenge.
The original idea is that your main source of income comes from harvesting the ground below you -- which then quickly breaks down, so you need to keep moving. Gaining money is closely tied into gameplay, as in that being greedy really limits your other options a lot.
Clean graphics, day/night cycles, cleverly written mission briefings and debriefings, it all adds up to a astonishing level of polish for an indie game. The swingy and jazzy music isn't the obvious choice, but it's great and ends up being surprisingly fitting by giving it all a lighthearted feel.

I'm quite a huge fan of Key as a studio.  Rewrite and Little Busters! are some of my favorite games of all time (despite them just being Visual Novels). I have played most, if not all, of the Key Visual novels (aside from the extremely heavy adult ones because playing the 18+ version of Kanon almost ruined one of my favorite characters.).
When I heard about Harmonia, I was pretty excited to see that It would be getting an official English release on steam, not that it matters to me since I can competently read Japanese.  With English being my native tough, however, there are certainly times when reading a Japanese text can leave me a little lost (mostly due to slang and wordplay).  Unlike many of the Key library, Harmonia is a Kinetic Novel; you don't have any choices, you just read, look and listen.  Also, like Planetarian before it, it is quite short clocking in at about 3-6 hours depending on how fast you read.
The music is quite amazing, as expected of Key; there are some extremely strong tracks here that are very memorable and really good at setting the mood.  The story follows the usual Key formulae of being a "crying game".  The first few acts are slow and mainly for character development. The final few acts are where the emotional &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan", as they say.  The voice acting is superb as expected and the art is very impactful with some panels being extremely vivid and memorable. Character design follows the typical "moe" style that Key is known for though don't be fooled; the characters are designed this way so that you will grow attached much easier.  Then when the story decides to rip your heart out of your chest and stamp on it multiple times you will be even more devastated.
If you like Key and like visual novels then this is definitely worth it at 7 dollars. Bring a box of kleenex when you read Harmonia (not the happy kind) and enjoy the ride.

Where the original Shadowrun Return campaign was easily outdone by community made campaigns, Shadowrun: Dragonfall shines on its own.  What was great about the original - beautiful 2D isometric artwork, modability, variety in character builds, good combat with some tactical depth, and an OK story - has been double downed on in Dragonfall.
The story's easily the most talked about strength of this game.  Where other games will rush to establish most of the characters you meet the moment you meet them (looking at you, Borderlands), Dragonfall takes its time to let characters develop over time.  There's plnety of opportunity to establish your own protagonist too throughout dialogue, which doesn't reward the nice guy choice every single time.  In a way, the game is sort of like what would happen if Telltale decided to ditch their amazing voice talent to do an isometric tactical RPG.
Combat is notably stepped up.  While the original Shadowrun Returns had massive balance issues that made the game way too easy, in Dragonfall there's considerably more care put into crafting tense firefights.  Very Hard difficult is actually fairly difficult, with massive shootouts being hard enough to justify sometimes avoiding them by using your skills.
Character building in particular is a lot more rewarding.  There's a lot of skill checks in the game that expand on the story or give you something extra or allow you to tackle a mission in a completely different way.  You could of course look up a guide to figure out the exact point totals you need to succeed every check, but the result is a spread out character that might have some trouble getting through the game.
And, of course, there's plenty of beautiful artwork to go around.  Character portraits and backgrounds are as great as they were before, evoking the tropes of the cyberpunk setting.  The only complaint to be had is the low-poly character models.  The less you zoom in on them, the better.
Once you finish the main game, there's plenty of high quality user-made campaigns waiting for you.  There's plenty of junk, sure, but stuff like From the Shadows, Run are worthwhile in their own right.
For $6, it's a steal.  There's a version on Android for the same price right now, but from what I recall it lacks modidng support.  The game isn't exactly graphically intensive, so if you don't care much for user generated content or if Harebrained Schemes brings in modding support for it later, the mobile version should be just as good and way more portable.

I bought this and Dragon Age: Inquisition on the same day. This was on sale for $5, and Dragon Age had just been released and it was full price.
I put 30 hours into completing this masterpiece before spending more than an hour or two into Dragon Age.
Let me preface this review by saying that, while I enjoy cyberpunk themes, I had never played anything in the Shadowrun universe. I discovered after I played and beaten this game that this is a stand-alone DLC to Shadowrun Returns, so this review is also focused on having zero experience with Shadowrun Returns before playing and completing this game.
The biggest positive for me was the story. The story was well told, gripping, and satisfying. There are some elements about the ending I didn't understand, due to lack of knowledge of the Shadowrun universe (for most of the game I assumed when they referred to "dragons" that they referred to some sort of augmented superperson.. not actual dragons themselves). The core characters are supremely polished and satisfying.
The world is realized very well with fun and immersive environments. There were a lot of options on how to finish each mission and I really felt my choices had an impact on the story, even at the mission level.
I'm generally not a fan of tactical combat. The combat is in this game, while not amazing, is pretty good. I realized pretty quickly that there is no "RPG" benefit to combat, and if you could it was generally best to avoid it. The game gives you lots of (sometime subtle) options on avoiding combat.
I ran as a Decker: a character who jacks into systems to control them. One flaw in the game was that I'm sure I went 10-15 hours into it before the first time I could jack into something, so my character was kinda underpowered otherwise as most of his skill was in decking.
This game is a great value. A great story with fascinating characters (you often delve into their backstories quite a bit) and an immersive world that you feel like you actually have an impact in.
Highly recommend.
It's sort of like Mass Effect 2 meets Planescape Torment. Unreservedly recommended.

I like the game, but I am not excited about it.
The graphics are pretty basic for a game of 2016 and the fourth instalment in a series. The two-dimensional top-down views both on the map and in battle are functional and consistent, but as unimpressive as the 20 years old Civilization 2 after playing Civ6. No cutscenes, no character portraits, no animations at all. Sound effects are sparse as well. The background music is nice though.
The gameplay is accessible and easy to understand: Conquer resources, levy troops and hire commanders, defeat enemies - repeat. The depth of strategy is based on the procedurally generated maps and the bandwidth of different factions you can play, and that latter one is indeed a big plus. A baron with his knights and crossbowmen actually plays differently from a druid who uses the powers of nature. I don't mind little flaws - e.g. I did not understand how a single wild deer could prevent a whole village from yielding taxes until you conquer it a second time. I do mind that the AI does very stupid things occasionally, but I have yet to see a strategy game where this is not the case, so this is forgivable.
A big minus, however, is the fact that you do not get to command your troops in battle. This feature, or rather lack of features, was the biggest disappointment for me. It all plays out automatically, with a step-by-step battle report on the side (which impairs my immersion, because it is stat-related and technical). You cannot even give basic commands like "retreat" or "defensive stance". Neither can you influence the battle formation, and in large armies, that can lead to archers being useless because your own ranks in front of them prevent enemies from getting into shooting range. Maybe, the developer wanted to spare the player too much micromanagement, but this could have easily been solved by making such interventions optional. Also, I do not understand why castles and watchtowers are all represented exactly the same. At least, you don't have to watch every skirmish play out, but can increase speed or skip to the final result, which I ended up doing regularly after an hour.
This quite decent retro indie game does not actually offer a lot of production value, but it manages to stimulate your imagination to make up narratives while you experience a minimalistic strategy game with an exceptional variety of different units. 6.5/10.

Conquest of Elysium 4 is a 4X strategy game that looks simple on the surface but has loads of depth. Every peice on the board matters, and every soldier is represented. The sheer number of units and strategies available puts other 4X's to shame. Yes, it is not as pretty as the latest Civilization, it's battles are not as detailed as Sins of a Solar Empire, but if eye candy is not generally a selling point for you, Conquest of Elysium 4 will reward with hours upon hours of intense strategic gameplay. Most people seem to like when I do a Pro/Con list, so here you go.
PROS:
-20 different factions with a variety of play styles for each one, ranging from a medival baron leading knighs and foot soldiers, to cults of tentacle beasts, to dryads leading continuously spawning hordes of upgradable beastmen. There's something for everyone. Yes, everyone.
-6 maps every game, most of which you will never visit, but are there in case you have to, or want to. Elysium not enough? Take over the other realms as well.
-A wide variety of terrain features and five time periods (as well as hidden alternate timelines) makes every game different and unique.
-Different resources required for each faction. A baron will require mines for metal to make armor, an enchanter will require them for gemstones for constructs, and druids won't care, because they will use herbs from forests for thier summons. In fact, resource denying other factions by destroying resources yours don't use is an oft effective strategy.
-A wide variety of magic, with availablity differing among the numerous factions, creating another layer of strategy as each faction tries to get thier wizards to godlike power, or prevent others from doing so.
-So many individual units you'll only have seen all of them after having played many games.
CONS:
- RNG plays a significant role in terms of events and resource/terrain placement. Some will like it, other's wont. I tend to, but it can get annoying when your playing a 6 player game and you get relegated to the center of the map, inbetween the other 5, and right next to the most powerful neutral towns.
- Neutral unit spam. Another matter of contention between players. Some like it, others don't, and it can be controlled through the use of the time periods, and close attention to realm logisitics. Still, it doesn't make having to recapture that same settlement for the 4th time because a group of stealth theives jumped your village idiots, again, any less annoying.

Postal III is a third-person shooter in which you… ehh… uhm…
Alright I’m going to level with you – don’t buy Postal III. Seriously, you’d regret it. Hell, you’d regret playing it for free. It’s a borderline-broken, boring, frustrating, unfinished mess, and there was nothing we could do stop it.
What happened is that we agreed to let a big Russian publisher develop and publish a third Postal game, which we would handle the design for. It was actually going well for the initial development time, but then the economy crashed especially hard in Russia and the project was handed to a smaller, less experienced team that didn’t have the skill or resources to make the game we designed, and they were forced to rush development to meet unreasonable deadlines. Corners were cut severely, dramatic changes to our design were made, and the game was put out in an unfinished barely-Alpha state. The game is simply unfinished and broken. And when it does work, the game is just boring and frustrating to play. The sad part is that the publisher made little-to-no effot to fix it themselves, nor did they ever give us access so that we could try patching it up for them. We are stuck with Postal III as it is.
You’re a responsible adult (we hope), so I’m sure you’re capable of making your own purchasing decisions. I just want you to consider all of the above, before you make the leap of regret into paying real hard-earned money for this title. We don’t own the game, we can’t support it and we don’t get anything from its sales, so if you decide to risk the purchase – you’re on your own.

Call this the Counter review.   Countering a lot of the negative reviews here for 2.0.  I didn't play the previous build, so I don't have an axe to grind.  I'm not really invested in the game, so I don't care if it's different than it was before.  There are lots of reviews here from players who feel wronged by the game's changes.  Since those changes didn't impact me, I'm just going to talk about the game as it is and the experience of playing 2.0.
I played Puzzle Quest 1 and 2 a lot.  And several of the other Puzzle-type games from this and other publishers.  And while I really enjoyed the earlier titles, after awhile they just got boring.  They were slow and it was more fun to go play Diablo or something else with a little excitement to it.
So I'm very happy to report that this game is fast.  The animations are fast, the tile moves are fast, the tutorial is fast, the interface is fast.   But at the same time, you're totally in control of the speed.  If you like to spend time stratgezing before making a match, you can.  If you just like to play oh-what-thehell and make matches as fast as possible, you can.
There was a certain amount of grinding in the other games and a storyline to follow.  There is here, too, but much more rewarding and no where near as tedious.   Every match gives you something.
When the game opens, after a 3-step tutorial, you'll end up with a few important things.  Your first town, your first troop cards, your first rewards, which consist of some chest keys, some soul stones and some gold.  You can spend the gold leveling your town, which will give you more daily gold or you can spend the gold in other ways to improve your game.  The keys you use to open chests that give you more souls, cards and trait stones.   I got an epic troop card from my second chest.
I took that epic card and upgraded it with my soul stones.  I then put it on my team (not sure why they call your troops a team, but whatever).   I equipped my hero with a new weapon, added a few common troop cards I received in my other chests and started on my first town's quest.
Pretty soon I had enough gold to buy another town, which contained another quest string.  I now have four towns, each with their own separate quest string.   I received an epic troop card for completion of the first town's quest line, upgraded that and started playing PvP.
I really wish they had not named it PvP, even though it is, it isn't.  One reason I wish they had not is because a lot of players have negative views of PvP, since it often engenders a toxic community, loss is often ridiculed and the pressure to compete leads players to make ill-informed or just plain poor decisions regarding their real life money.   Another reason I wish they had not named it PvP is that you actually don't play another person.  You play against the AI, which is using the other person's team (of cards, like yours).
So, I gave it a whirl and it turned out to be no different than playing the quest line or the PvE challenges.  The game is exactly the same.  You simply get some different rewards and rank up, which gives you more rewards, gold and soul stones, to improve your game.   There's nothing horrible about it.  No one makes funny noises or calls you names.  Because there isn't anyone there.  The AI loses gracefully or wins gracefully and you move on.
Pros:
Fun graphics
Plenty of PvE
Fast gameplay
Sense of advancement
Enjoyable PvP
Classes as you level up
Troop card animations
Troop card improvements (leveling, new traits, ascend in rank)
Cons:
No cursor tooltips
No explanation of the icons of which there are a great many on cards, on character sheet, on the UI, etc., etc.
The Cash Shop:
Will give you an advantage on how fast you level, acquire gold and other in-game currency.  Whether you can parlay this into a top spot on the leaderboards depends on whether you have a good, basic strategy to begin with.
Rating:  8/10
Quite enjoyable and fast-paced.  Great way to spend a few hours.
Pay for continue wall  before end of second city questing. Save your time.

168 hours edit:

Wand Wars is an frantic arena-brawling game for both single and multiplayer, where you have to catch and toss a killer orb at your opponents while trying not to get turned into a chicken.
The orb mechanism is easy to grasp and you'll be an expert in no time. Press a button when the orb is close and you capture it for a short time, giving you just enough time to aim and fire it at the nearest opponent. Once fired, the orb just keeps going, bouncing off walls. As the match proceeds, the orb gets larger and faster.
It's about timing, basically - hitting the button just before you get smashed in the face, then turning the tables on whoever threw it. With the full 4 players, it's pure twitch gaming.
Wand Wars gameplay review video:
On its own, that would be a decent but limited game. But your second ability is to fire black arrows. If you hit an opponent, they briefly turn into a chicken, whose only ability is to run away. The arrow can also be used to neutralise the orb, making it slow and harmless until next caught.
Together, these two things add an element of strategy to your attacks, although nothing complex or clever. The only way to really add strategy to the game is to play in teams, 2 vs 2. So perhaps one player would be on chicken duty, the other orb. Or you could pass the orb between you (you can only harm enemies when firing the orb), and only strike when the time is right.
Powerups are sometimes added to the arena (and you can optionally start with some in Versus). They're massively powered deadly attacks of different kind, and can turn the game into chaos as everyone tries to fire them off at once. When you fire them, the game pauses for a couple of second for an animation, which can get tiring!
The singleplayer Story Mode is split into the stories of six unlockable characters, each consisting of several matches. Each match has something unique about it - number of players, teams, weird levels with moving walls, different game types etc - so it never gets dull.
Versus Mode consists of single, customisable 1-4 player matches (including however many bots), with a choice of 5 game types. This includes the basic battle type, a type where your team has to get the orb into the opponent's goal, and more.
Pleasingly, Wand Wars works well in singleplayer. The bots are well programmed in the basics (with multiple difficulty levels), so it doesn't feel like you're not really playing the game properly. They're not so clever at guarding the goal in that game type, but that's a team-focused game and should really be saved for humans.
Wand Wars feels slick, it's easy to learn and not difficult to master. Pulling off a good move is very satisfying - stuff like turning an opponent into a chicken just as you're about to grab the orb, then bouncing it off the wall into their stupid clucking face.
The limited strategic potential means this game will have an exciting but fairly brief life in your library, but if you have a good local multiplayer scene going, it'll fit happily into the rotation. And if you play it singleplayer, the Story Mode keeps changing things up enough for you to want to keep going.

SPOILER FREE REVIEW~~
Harmonia is a beautiful game. Everything about the production is top-notch. From the visuals to the music to the voice acting, Key is in top-form here. The concept and characterization are both exceptional.
It's a shame that in the end, the story fails to deliver.
Which is unfortunate, because everything preceding the story's conclusion is amazingly well-executed. Our main character, who is desperately in search of a way to fix his absent emotions, is a compelling, earnest lead whose desire to help those around him fit his background. The upbeat, yet level-headed Shinoa is a perfect compliment to this goal. The reclusive librarian, Tipi, and the grumpy owner of a general store, Madd, both provide interesting contrats and conclusions one can make from Rei's straightforward, earnest attempt at friendship. Better yet, the story takes several surpsing, yet well-foreshadowed twists that will catch even the most savvy of readers off-guard.
However... The ending is emotionally tone-deaf. It has no respect for the events in the earlier portion of the story, presenting readers with an over-the-top resolution that is intended to be immensely satisfying, yet flies in the face of the grounded narrative the story tries to steep itself into.
Regardless, it's definitely worth a read. Harmonia is an experience I won't soon forget. However, in spite of it's good intentions, the ending casts an unfortunate hue on everything building up to it...

At the time I'm editing this review I've put close to nine hours into playing with Pinball Arcade.   I'm having an absolute blast so far.
Honestly, all I cared about with Pinball Arcade was getting the Attack on Mars table.  I adored that game as a kid, and it still rocks as a young adult.  Playing it again is such a delicious rush of nostalgia for me.  Several of the other ones I've tried, Arabian Nights, Star Trek, and Medieval Madness are pretty awesome too.  The attention to detail in recreating these tables is staggering.
However, there are some potential drawbacks I've encountered too.   These weren't deal breakers for me, but they might be for others.
First, the choices for camera control are minimal.  This wasn't a problem for me because the default angle of the camera is pretty much what you'd get playing at the arcade.  But compare this to Dream Pinball, for example.  Dream Pinball had six or seven different options.  If I wanted to follow with the ball I could.  If I wanted to the camera facing more directly downwards, I could do that.   If you don't like the default angle with this simulator you're out of luck.
Second, if you want individual pinball machines there are some inconveniences in your way.  I actually did not know that I could buy individual tables at first.  I thought they came in either smaller packs or seasons.  As of right now, I can purchase a single table if I want.  The price is $4.99 for a single table or $7.99 for the pro version which includes additional options.  However, I have to buy this in game with Steam wallet funds.  My guess is that this is because it would be ridiculous creating individual steam pages for the dozens of pinball tables.  A lot of people may not even be aware that they have this option, so keep that in mind.
Also, $4.99 or $7.99 may sound a bit steep for a single table.   I will say that the "pro" option in my opinion is customization that should be available in the base game, not stuff that should be hidden behind a paywall.  If it was just $4.99 for one table, and you could customize it then I think people would be a bit less annoyed about it.   However, I ask you to consider the alternative.  I haven't seen an Attack from Mars machine in YEARS.  I could travel hours to find an arcade that has one, and then pay dollar after dollar.  Or I could shell out $7,000 dollars and have to store and maintain it myself.  Or I could pay a measly $7.99 and have all the customization options and have access to it forever.  All in all, I will unquestionably get my money's worth and then some.  However, it all depends on how badly you're hurting to play any of these tables.  If you buy the season at a discount, which I did, then your average price per table goes down drastically.  I'll probably upgrade the few tables I enjoy the most to pro and pretty much ignore the rest.
The last potential negative point that I will mention is the ball physics.  I personally did not notice anything wrong, but I know that there have been some negative comments about that from people who were experienced with pinball machines.   As an ordinary consumer who just enjoys pinball now and then, I can't really address concerns that hardcore fans might have, so you should probably read a few negative reviews just to get a balanced perspective.
If you're squeamish about trying pinball arcade, then let me set your fears to rest.  You can try Pinball Arcade for free.  When you download the free platform it includes trial version of ALL the tables.   So, all you have to invest up front is enough time to install the game.  Try it out, and find out which tables or seasons might be worth your money.
I'll conclude this interview with a brief and very sincere thank you to the developers.  You have brought a piece of my childhood to life that I'd never expected to get to experience any time soon, if at all.  I really appreciate the work you're doing, and hope to see more familiar machines on your platform.  Now let's kill some Martians!

I never thought I would enjoy a game that treads to close to the "note collector genre" so heavily, but here I am. Damned is  an asymmetric 5-player multiplayer game where one player controls one of three different monsters, each with different abilities and methods of detecting the humans, and the other players play as humans trying to escape by finding keys and tools in the environment to make it through to the exit. The game has 12 maps, giving it a good amount of replayability. The voice chat system was one of my favorite parts of the game, featuring a 3D audio option that makes each player's voice come through their character's position instead of being global, encouraging them to stick together in standard horror movie fashion while also allowing the monster to taunt them.
The thing that I like about this game is that unlike other asymmetrical games like Evolve, Damned isn't afraid to kill off players. It treats the humans the same way that any horror movie would, and if they don't stick together and find a way out quickly they aren't going to survive. The keys can be pretty well-hidden, and Damned is the only game where I've ever seen a group of players slowly succumb one by one to the realization that they might not ever find the key they missed somewhere, if the key even existed at all. The tension of new players figuring out what to do and what not to do to avoid alerting the monster while finding their way out is a lot of fun, and while I haven't played past that point to know what it'll be like once I know all the tricks, I think there's enough content to it that I would still enjoy it.
The big problem with the game is that it's pretty buggy in its current state, despite no longer being in early access. When I first started playing the game it had capped itself to 15 FPS, and the only way to fix it was to restart my computer. Even after that, the game is generally poorly optimized from what I've seen from other players (I was able to run it at a pretty consistent 80-90 FPS, which isn't really ideal since I have a 144 hz monitor and a computer that should be running it at far past that framerate, but oh well). The other issue is that the game isn't exactly populated. A quick look at the server list showed 7 lobbies, 3 of which were public, and 1 of those had a ping of over 1000. This is the sort of game where you should buy a bundle and play with a group of friends instead of relying on random players, but it's more fun with friends anyways so I didn't mind.
In its current state I wouldn't recommend this game at all for $20, but it seems to go on sale in various indie bundles fairly often (I bought a four-pack of the game for like $1 or so at some point or another), and if another four-pack deal comes up and you can get it for cheap it's a great way to spend a few nights with a few friends.

It's Defense Grid again. It's solid tower defense. They've shaken the towers up so that cannons aren't the be-all and end-all of defense, an in fact rather than needing half your maze be ballistic to knock down shields, shields are reworked to the point of almost being irrelevant if you place the disruption tower upgrades appropriately. (As a final insult, level 3 cannon towers are now ugly wheezing bellows. This is not how recoil works, animators. The aliens tend to largely all look the same, too.) Airborne enemies are gone completely, although drop pods make for a tactically interesting replacement, running the maze in reverse.
BUT. Big but. Hairline of negative review but.
But it's deeply, deeply marred by the godawful AI banter. Everything that was mildly charming and background in the last one is now rubbing in your face like a chinchilla-urine-soaked cheese-grater as a badly-written soap opera unfolds between a half-dozen scenery-chewing unlikable characters. Yes, even he from the first game has become insufferable, and they predictably take his one little quirk and roll a whole stupid plot point around it. Do yourself a favour and put the dialogue volume slider down to zero. Then turn off the subtitles too. The story in this will just kill braincells you need to play the actual game.
Oh, and there are persistent unlocks, because boy we've sure gotta be next-gen. I've yet to see if they ruin multiplayer, because that was so ill-designed in the beta it discouraged the other player from buying it.
It also feels short when you put it up against the ridiculous amount of content the first one got. As always, wait for a deep sale. This review would certainly be negative at full price.

Not as good as the first, but I'm enjoying it. The addition of different commanders that give you different super weapons is cool. Th new graphics are problematic. Certain towers in DG2 look a lot like other towers in DG. For example, at a quick glance, the DG2 gun tower looks a lot like the DG flame tower. I would have liked it better if they'd modelled the new towers more on the old ones. That would have significantly reduced my learning curve.
I dunno. I kinda feel like this is a DLC that's priced like a full game. So far the only real difference I've noticed is the addition of more super weapons (DG just had the super laser, whil DG2 has a different super weapon for each different character). I'm sure once I play it more I'll see new enemies and new towers, but my first impression is that this is mostly a graphics update and new missions.
I don't like the new touch-oriented interface. It's just okay on my actual touchscreen (DG1 works better with my touchscreen), and if I'm playing on my desktop (no touchscreen), it just makes things awkward. Long story short: the controls don't work well. Touch or not, I frequently have to click things more than once and the graphic that you're supposed to click on rarely lines up with the actual place you need to click to register a command. So I find myself using the mouse to select towers and locations, then using the keyboard to navigate the resulting menu. Even then, I find myself having to hit "enter" more than once very often, and the controls are just overall bad.
So... Yeah. Bottom line: I can't recommend this game. I feel like it takes a lot for me to say "don't play this," but broken controls is pretty much a deal breaker. DG2 would be as good as DG if only the controls worked. But there's not enough new/better (there's really nothing better that I've seen) about it to balance out the fact that the new interface completely breaks the controls.

If I could describe Danganonpa in One Sentence it would be: Ace Attorney meets Persona 4 meets Saw, while also being infused with pure anime.
Danganronpa is a weird Visual Novel/Murder Mystery/Courtroom Drama, that also mixes in some dating sim elements. In it, you play as Generic Anime Protagonist #1137 aka Makoto Naegi, an Ordinary High School Student who was chosen to go to the prestigous Hope's Peak Academy via lottery. After arriving at the school, Makoto suddenly falls unconcious and wakes up inside a classroom. He soon discovers that he and 14 other students who were supposed to be attending Hope's Peak have been trapped insdie the school with no way to escape. They then meet Monokuma, a robot bear and so called "Headmaster" of Hope's Peak. He tells the students that the only way to escape the school is too kill a fellow student and not be found out during the following class trial. Of course the students say they won't kill anyone, but as the game progresses, the bodies pile up. It's up to you to find out who was the killer and find a way out of the school.
The game itself is split into two sections, Daily Life and Deadly Life. During Daily Life, you are given Free Time to explore the school and spend time with your fellow classmates. Spending time with your classmates will slowly fill out their Social Link-I mean Report Cards (they're basically the same thing), which will net you Skills and extra Skill Points for class trials. During Deadly Life however, you must investigate a recent murder by inspecting the crime scene, talking to possible witnesses, and finding evidence to help you out. After your investigation is over, you must then take part in a lengthy Class Trial, which is seperated into three sections. First up, the Nonstop Debate, where the students talk about a certain aspect of the murder, while you have to find any potential holes in their statements and shoot them with your Truth Bullets. Next up is the Hangman's Gambit, where you have to shoot down floating letters to fill in a keyword related to the trial. Finally is the Bullet Time Battle, where you have to shoot down an oppoents statement to get an arguement to them by matching the beat of a song. After that, the killer is chosen, and is executed (normally in some brutally ironic way).
Pros:
A Compelling Plot that can keep you on the edge of your seat at times
Great and (mostly) Likable Characters
Amazing Style and Presentation
Great OST
The Class Trials can actually force you to think about whats actually going on
The Executions are amazingly brutal
Cons:
Hangman's Gambit is probably the worst part about the trials because of how weird some of the words you have to guess are
The Trials can get very long in the late game (thankfully you can save during them)
Late Game Pacing can also be a bit of a problem due to some dialouge heavy sections
Your Best Girl (or Guy) will probably end up dying
Overall, Danganronpa is an amazing game that managed to keep me interested for the entire game, with some suprisingly  good gameplay outside of the regualr Visual Novel stuff. I highly reccomend this game

You can play this as a repetitive PvE game or a pay-to-win PvP game that still feels like PvE. Either way, it has a compelling set of core rules but lacks enough confidence to let them shine; it's buried in a 5-pronged progression system that discourages experimentation. It's an acceptable way to kill time on your phone but isn't worth any more than that.

This PvP update (2.0) is a typical example on how to switch from a "free-to-play" game to a "pay-to-stay" game.
First of all, before update you needed 10 gold pieces to change opponent if you found it was a mismatched fight. 10 gold is nothing even for new players.
Now, you need 5 diamonds!
Secondly, the rewards are ranked for the whole server and only the few top ones will get the best rewards (diamonds and arcane traitstones used to unlock special abilities on high end creatures).

Harmonia is a short, linear novel roughly
in length. It has everything that Key is renowned for; introspective characters, atmospheric soundtrack, and writing.
Harmonia definitely seems like a spiritual successor to Planetarian, Key's other kinetic novel that was roughly the same length. Perhaps too similar. The setting is the same: a post-apocalyptic future where robot servants are struggling to cope with the reality that the remnants of humanity are on an inevitable course for extinction. Even certain plot points are repeated exactly as they occurred in Planetarian.
What sets Harmonia apart from Planetarian are the characters. Whereas Planetarian centered on an odd couple, a soldier with no hope for a future and a girl whose mind was stuck in the past when humanity's future still seemed bright, Harmonia brings together a small cast of characters who must come to terms with their limited set of emotions as they interact with one another.
The missteps that Harmonia makes are a combination of short length and poor plot decisions. It might have been best to remove one of the characters entirely if only to give more time to the other two. The emotional impact of the finale is still there, just as it has been in other Key novels, but the events immediately leading up to it aren't satisfying and the resolutions to the characters are delivered in rapid succession.
Overall, Harmonia is still decent enough to check out if you're a fan of the genre or Key's previous works. Those who played Planetarian may find it a retread and will want to base their decision on how much they enjoyed that story.
Unless you're a major fan of Key who can't wait to read this story, it's best to

Key's newest VN, Harmonia, has been a long time coming. When it was announced to be coming to Steam in English alongside CLANNAD's English release before being released in Japan, I was excited beyond belief. It was a very unexpected move on VisualArt's part, but a welcome one nonetheless. I knew I would be buying the game Day 1. But the game was constantly delayed due to various conflicts, until finally the game reached the quality VA expected from it.
So was Harmonia worth the wait? Well, let's look at the story first. A young Phiroid with no memories of the past awakes from cryogenic sleep, and seeks out civilization in order to find humans to serve. He stumbles across the residence of one Shiona, a priestess who takes him in and names him Rei. Quickly growing attached to Shiona's infectuous smile, he decides to help her as she sings to the townspeople and makes them happy. But there are some in the town who are not as happy, and Rei takes it upon himself to solve their lingering regrets.
I won't spoil the rest of the story, but while it does take some pages from previous Key games to make it more accessible to their audience, it does become something all its own. I can at least say that it's a shorter and easier read than Planetarian, although don't let that dissuade you from checking the story out. It's a hard sci-fi story that knows what it wants to do and accomplishes it fairly well, although personally, I've seen this same kind of story before on a few occasions.
Each of the four principal characters leaves an impression upon the reader, setting up an allegory to drive the novel's message of cherishing the human trait of emotion. Shiona represents happiness and warmth, Madd represents anger and stubbornness, and Tipi represents sadness and loneliness. Rei is the vessel that receives these feelings and emotions, learning through his own common sense what is good and what is bad for these individuals. Out of all the characters, Tipi is definitely my favorite, and it's not just because she's a loli~ :P
The artwork is unique among Harmonia's elder siblings, as it has more of a stencil drawing feel to it. I praised Sepia Tears for this same unique take on spritework, but Harmonia shows you how the professionals do it. The pencil gradient adorning each character sprite moves subtly, giving them an earthen, sketchy feel. Considering that the outside world is very dirty and polluted in Harmonia, this makes sense storywise. Itaru Hinoue's art in general has always been beautiful regardless of how old the game might be, and while she left VisualArt's a few days ago at the time of this review, this could be counted as a fantastic swan song to her days with Key. I wish her luck in her further endeavors, and hopefully this won't be the last time we see her work in a Key game.
The music is also worthy of note. With Key's in-house composer Shinji Orito and freelance prodigy Ryou Mizutsuki at the helm, the soundtrack is almost exactly what I expect from them. The music paints a picture of a desolate world that yearns to a single ray of hope, and it also captures every emotion Rei experiences while in the town or the outside world. I feel Mizutuski's pieces are much better composed than Orito's, and that's usually been the case even in Rewrite, but here it's especially noticeable. Not that Orito's music in this game is bad, but it pales compared to Mizutsuki-san's softer, simpler tracks.
Harmonia is not a perfect visual novel by any means, but it's a pretty darn good one. It has every right to stand with its elder brethren in the hearts of many a Key fan, and I'm glad it was brought over to English-speaking countries, even if it took a while to get here. If you are a Key fan, you likely already have this game. But for those who have no clue who Key is or have any passing interest in Key, do I recommend this visual novel to you? Almost certainly yes. Be prepared to cry, though. This is one journey you will not come back from emotionally unscathed. :)

I'm totally in love with the concept behind this game, and while it can be clunky and rough at times, it succeeds in being an actually scary multiplayer experience that offers a unique kind of fun you won't find elsewhere.
While this is a recommendation, there are several things I should note before you make your purchase:
- $20 is quite high for the amount of content currently in the game, and updates seem to be coming rather slowly. The developers have not yet abandoned the project, but they are a small, inexperienced team. This may be better as a sale purchase if you're uncertain.
- There are a high amount of technical issues in the current build. Many players report unplayable, slideshow framerates no matter how powerful their rig, though this sometimes randomly resolves itself through reinstallation or other fiddling. There are also occasional crashes that can ruin a match. I've only had one so far after several hours of play, but it's still frustrating. Thankfully, host migration is fairly seamless.
- The playerbase is fairly small at the moment. While it's possible to fill up a lobby with random players, and there are generally a small handful of public servers running at any given time, you're much better off having a consistent group of friends to play this with.
With all that said, I'm having a ton of fun with this game and it just comes down to the great idea and clever design behind it. The levels are all creepy, dark abandoned buildings like hospitals, asylums (lots of asylums), hotels, a factory, etc. The monsters themselves all have unique mechanics that require patience and vigilance from both the human and monster players. They're all deadly and can take out a survivor in a single blow, but have some sort of limitation on when they can attack, or how they move, or even how they see. It means that even as players become more experienced, the battle of wits and "does he know that I know that he knows..." mindgames make for exciting matches. Despite the competitive nature of the game, there isn't a big emphasis on the competition and it's more about having fun. The monster player has to be very very patient, naturally keeping twitchy, aggressive players out of the game.
The simple requirement for the survivors to explore and find keys keeps things active and prevents extended campfests, though it can be rather difficult to coordinate an escape in a public game with all the different players grabbing different keys and not communicating about what they're unlocking. But it almost doesn't matter, because even with random strangers the tension and buildup and panic make things exciting and fun, and creates one of the most friendly communities I've encountered in a PvP game so far, mostly devoid of the usual rudeness you might expect. A shame there only tend to be a few servers at a time, because managing to keep a full lobby going from beginning to end of a match makes for a great time even with strangers who don't speak your language.
I really hope the devs continue to add to this product, as the groundwork here is already a lot of fun and there are a lot of great ideas on display. I also wish this game would have caught on a little more, because the idea of a competitive game with emphasis on wits and evasion and awareness rather than just fighting each other is a sadly untapped niche for the most part that could do with more love. Pure, strategic Tower Defense with a lot of depth thanks to a wealth of play modes, difficulty choices and most importantly tower customization options.  A good sequel to the famed original, 'Defense Grid: The Awakening' which is hailed by many including myself as the best TD ever made.
The sequel plays more different than it looks, resource income and scoring is tweaked a bit which has put some off, but is in my opinion an improvement. Boost towers is a great idea which offer extra upgrade options and can be used to adjust towers' line of sight and range.
All is not perfect however, and here's a few things that should have been better:
- The aliens are poorly designed and it can hard to tell the different types apart at a glance.
- Bad sound track.  One track for menues and one during playing is extremely repetitive to listen to.
- Ugly low quality FXAA that one has to fiddle with Steam launch command lines to disable.
- Leaderboard cheaters is still a thing,  taking some of the drive to replay levels to improve your scores away.
- UI is clearly designed for gamepad or tablet navigation.  It is so awkward to navigate with mouse+keys I've actually given up and now play this with a PS3 pad instead.  Big disappointment.
- Monetized Steam Workshop for custom maps that is poorly maintained.  Charging money in a retail product for user generated content is a massive slap in the face, this needs to STOP.
Outside of that, DG2 is very enjoyable and can offer dozens of hours of well designed tower defense gaming for those that must gold medal various game modes.

I first stumbled upon Supreme Commander when it come in a glorious steam bundle filled with big name titles. I owned the game for nearly 3 months before actually playing playing it. (You know how it is.) Never heard of Supreme Commander or the series and passed it off as a generic knock off from Command and Conquer. WOW I WAS WRONG. SC and SC: FA are 2 of the most underrated RTS games I have ever had the privledge of playing. The progressive scaling of units and map size where hundreds of units engage in epic land, air, and sea warfare is something very few RTS games get right. NIce blend between theoretical technology and pre existing war machines with armaments that can be found in armed forces around the world.  But what impresses me the most is how smooth the games run, even when 2000 units are "in play." The interface is very polished and easy to navigate. Simply scorlling the mouse wheel immediately zooms into full view of the map where units are displayed by icons instead of smaller models, allowing for fluid macro play even when your 3 bases are scattered across the map. Has all the elements that one would want in an RTS which include but are not limited to:
4 playable factions. All with their own unique flavor and yet are still balanced.
4 Tier(s) of technology and units that are EPIC when engaged in combat.
A challenging campaign with 8 missions that can last between 1 and 5 hours. (5 if you're like me and enjoy building more automated base defenses.
Incredibly fluid gameplay that is challenging and rewarding.
And finally it is quality mental exercise when you've got 10 macro'd unit groups and several dozen unit production buildings gaurding your commander against endless waves of enemy units that often have an unfair advantage.
If you're a true pc game elitist and you enjoy games of strategy that are aesethically pleasing then definitely grab SC and SC: FA next time you get a chance.
PS - could care less about any grammar or spelling oversights. (Its a steam review that no one will read anyways.)
PSS - Do not buy Supreme commander 2 unless you are a HUGE fan of the serious. Square Enix produced the 2nd installment and completely re modeled all of the units and maps and turned it into shallow, brightly colored, and insignificant shells of their former counter parts.

Conquest of Elysium is a game of... conquest, as you might expect. Sieze resource and magic sites, build up your army, and conquer. Yet at the same time it is also a game about discovery, about unlocking new magic and forces, about discovering new locations, and trying to make it gel together to become more powerful - and often without knowing for certain exactly what you can unlock as you progress. It's an entertaining premise on a simple turn based format that flows effortlessly forwards.
As with the Dominions series, part of the real joy of the Illwinter games is the imagination and ideas that are included, and this game is no exception. The game's graphics are basic but in the main work well - though as monitors get bigger it is coming to a time where the beautiful sprites are simply too small. Illwinter's UIs also still need much work, but the apparent simplicity of the game belies something more complex under the hood - yet with the enormous advantage that you don't have to delve into the numbers and abilities unless you want to.
Each starting race/character plays very differently, and Illwinter truly understand that the art of 4x is to ensure that discovery remains past the early part of the game - and on this Elysium delivers in trumps. It's not an easy game though - don't run into the gamer's habit of picking any of the higher difficulties; you will be frustrated!
What's it worth? £17 / $20

After watching a Lets Play of "60 Seconds" I got curious and grabbed it.
The gameplay is obvious: the first 60 seconds are spent gathering supplies and family while the rest of the game is largely RNG events. Eventually the family dies or gets saved depending largely on how the dice roll more than anything else.
The game is low-effort as far as development goes. No animations are involved after the first 60 seconds - you just stare at an unmoving image for about 20 minutes at a time. There are little changes here and there that visibly show changes in the characters' statuses as well as what items you have and what shape they're in.
For the majority of the game you're at the mercy of randomness. Even if you played an event
game it very well could be a different result if you picked a yes or no
time. The only ones that have predictable results are the events that require you to pick and use an item in the shelter - often at the cost of the item.
Would the game be better if there were more active events that went beyond reading RNG event text? I don't know. It stands out as it's own game even if it lacks for excitement or effort. It doesn't strike me personally as
, but it
have a charm to it.

Well, I don't really know what to say about this game, I don't want to spoil anything, I don't want to tell you - the reader - anything other than Danganronpa is a murder mystery game similar to the Ace Attorney series which you may or may not have heard of, and I think it's likely if you're into the idea of a visual novel relatively light on gameplay but heavy on the story, this is a great one to try. So, yes, I recommend Danganronpa whole-heartedly. Go on, grab it.
So, I guess I'll just talk about some other stuff since I've got a nice big empty space. There's an excellent story here that does a great job of dropping hints and clues but never too much at once, nothing you can't keep in your head all at the same time, and nothing blatantly untrue - the game sometimes drops red herrings and will do it's utmost to give you a huge amount of possibilities as to where the story is heading, then perhaps direct you down one path while secretly laying the foundations for it to suddenly veer off onto another with little warning.
There's a lot of fun to be had guessing where everything's going to lead throughout the story, and it's satisfying when you're right, and usually not disappointing when you're wrong. I managed to vaguely guess some of the big plot points myself, some of the more obvious stuff, but you'll only really get this if you do what I did and just analyze every single piece of text you receive, all of the visual clues, and match them against tropes and story elements likely included in a murder mystery game like this.
The gameplay's a little off at times, some translation issues I think. The basic gameplay is, you walk around and look at stuff and grab clues. Then later during a trial, you work to find the hidden contradictions in the statements of the other characters as you work to figure out the truth behind each murder. To find a contradiction, you look for yellow-coloured 'weak points' and 'shoot' them by clicking on them with the correct refutation. This gets a little messy down the road if you're playing on higher difficulties when you have more possible refutations for statements, so if you're not on top of things yourself, if you can't figure out what the game wants you to click on with what, you can spend a bit of time retrying the same section until you get it right. Not really a big deal since it's only in a few areas, but it's frustrating to be so stumped.
I should mention the characters. While I think most of the cast once you spend enough time with them is likeable enough, these are still 'people' you have to stick around with for hours and hours, talking with and such, so if you don't like them you're not gonna be very incentivized to keep playing - if you don't care about them, then the effect of seeing certain characters die won't do anything for you. So for my part, I like most everyone, but there's a few which are so painfully grating you'll hope they die in awful ways.
There's not much else to talk about. Being a PSP port, I think the game looks pretty good myself, it doesn't look amazing or anything but it's held up by the style. It's not really too hard even on the hardest setting, you can muddle through the game without much caring about skill points (though there's definitely a few certain skills which make life much easier than certain other ones). Great game, I love the cynical humor of the characters (don't skip the chat!) and the way you don't always know if you are helping the good guy or the bad guy until the story plays out.  It is hard to work a decent story into a match-3 game, but they managed it pretty well.
There is PvP in the game, but at this point, it is totally optional.  You can and will get attacked by other players, but they are limited to taking a certain percentage of the gold you accrued while offline, not emptying your bank account.
The PvP ranking system is a little sketchy, but can work in your favor as often as against it.  You can be level 100 and get ranked against a level 295 but then 'try another match' and get a level 45.  I have no idea what stat it matches you up by, but be patient and you can do well.
There are guilds in the game.  There is no guild chat as you may know it in other games, but instead there is a message board.  The advantage to that is the messages STAY, so you can talk or give messages to players who aren't on at the same time you are.
Guild quests are simple.  Give a little extra gold when you can.  You pay to fill the quest bar.  You don't need to be uber skilled to help your guild.
The skills and abilities of your troops was greatly expanded about the time I quit playing, so I can not add a lot to that, but it creates a lot of depth and customization for fighting style and powers, that you really would not expect in a game that seems so simple on the surface.
Pay to Win.  Nope.  Simple as that.  Pay to speed things up?  Yeah, of course.  Dev's don't live and work for free.  But there is no gameplay advantages to buying other than to get stuff done faster.  You can patiently grind away to get those runestones and still get those talents on your troops you want without paying.  It will just take a bit longer.  I really like that.  It kept the game from feeling like it was descending into a stale cash grab.
The game is still vibrant and alive with active devs and a lot of players.  I hope it continues to thrive.

I downloaded this game off a whim, expecting it to be a fairly generic match-3 game, that would probably devolve into pay-to-win rather quickly. I was pleasantly surprised to find it otherwise. The RPG elements actually intergrate surprisingly well with the puzzle match-3 elements. Now, there are rather a lot of options for microtransactions, and, when I first started playing, it seemed like levelling troops would be extremely painful. However, this was before I discovered the minigames.  Both the arena and the Zhul'Kari Treasure hunt give potentially high yields of gold and souls, with the Zhul'Kari treasure hunt providing free to play players a means of slowly acquiring gems, and thus high rarity units. Once you start playing those two minigames, the power progression proceeds at a quite reasonable rate.
The most obvious complaint I have about the game is that the quests are written, well, kinda terribly. The characters you quest with are rather centred around a very basic archetype with no development beyond that, and the player character has no personality whatsoever. While I haven't seen anywhere near all the quests, the four I've started on (three of which I've completed) have all been a fairly formulaic near-solitary lawful good hero campaigning against large chaotic evil force. Maybe I'm just refusing to see some elements somehow, but it's almost impossible to get invested in the stories. I do understand the plot isn't the point, and the brief dialogs are not really enough to convey any depth, and the attempt at plot is appreciated. Nonetheless, how flat this falls is my one true complaint about the game.
tl;dr Gameplay's great; story, though the attempt is appreciated, kinda sucks.
