After years of our voyage to Saturn's moon Titan hyberpods have awaken us as we started to decent into the lower layers of the atomsphere. Something went wrong and only 4 members of the crew have survived the flight - lead biologist, chief engineer and two technitians. We had nowhere near enough resources to build all essential domes, so we had to priortiise - most resources were spent on building the largest available power storage unit, sollar pannel, water extractor and lightning rod. Remaining resources went into building a landing pad, small oxygen generator, canteen and medium garden.
Most constructions were finished past midnight. Since we cannot afford a storage dome, my crew watched spares, medkits and remaining provisions to rot on the landing pad under the methane rains. As we waited for a trading ship, we were growing medical plants that would be sold in exchange for metal, spares and interstellar currency.
We have requested additional biologists to manage the garden that is not only providing nutritions to the colonists, but it is also our sole source of exported gppds and therefore fundamental for our medium-term survival.
Only trading ships we have encountered were carrying medical goods, which were of no use to us due not having any operating mines. While we had more than enough food, we were running low on spares. Only two parts lefts and we still cannot produce our own bio-plastic.
With 1 spare left, finally a cargo ship has landed with 10 metal and 5 spares. This would allow us to survive for another week. As we commenced construction of a small refinery, storage and a lab, I was running 1 metal low. It became apparent that the only bot we have will need to be broken down into raw materials to complete the essential constructions. As the lab was nearly completed, 2 medics have arrived and started to working on the pharmaceuticals, which was expected to increase our export value. It was a relief to see the degrading spares being transferre to the storage dome, where its quality would not affected by time.
Colony now has 20 people, which means that we can no longer accept new members until we build a new oxygen generator. Yet we have not even built a dorm, where the existing colonists can sleep - everyone sleeps where they can, normally at their work stations. It was essential for us to start harvesting our won ore, but at this point our electric consumption has now put a risk at any futher expansion. We soon ran out of storage space, which meant that any new imports would be left at the landing pad and degrade over time.
We have finally built a dorm dome, alongside with a large turbine. However, there was little space to expand due to vast methane lakes. We needed a new lightning rod or risk losing key domes and personnel due to a lightning struck. Equally, even if we had enough metal, building a mine would risk puting health of workers at risk, which would mean that we could lose ability to produce bio-plastic.
We ran out of spares, but there is still time before the equipment will stop functioning. Engineer refuses to comment on how long we have.
Shipment of metal has finally arrived for us to construct a mine and sick bay. We still do not have enough resources for a lightning rod, It is a risk that we will mitigate as soon as we harvest enough metal.
We can now finally produce our own spares and started building a new large storage unit as we remain low on space. I made the executive decision to priortise this project over a new lightning rod.
New power storage has been built alongside with more turbines, water extractors and pannels.
Lightning has struck the gym dome, killing 5 people. As tragic the situation was, we started to run low on food, so this incident will allow us to restock our food supplies before any futher expansion.
I woke up today in darkness. Electricity was off due to a quiet windless night. Nex project was to increase the number of power storage units.
With a new power storage, lightning rod and even a large garden, it looked that we can now start accepting tourists. Base is protected by 3 trained guards, but we are yet to start production of weapons.
Days of resource storage and sleeping in the canteen seemed in the past. Base keeps expanding, resources are flowing, power is well managed and even cashflow is rapidly increasing. Our defense squad is now 10 people strong.
This morning 8 armed people have entered the base. It was the first time we used a red alert as 9 of our guards were killed in close comabat and 1 died later in the hospital. Number of civilians were killed or wounded. I have stopped all current projects and requested to put all effords on weapon crafting.
Starport-3 has now been built and our 12 person defense squad is now properly armed to protect us from any future attacks.
Several problems have been reported across the base - We are low on food, water and power outage are now becoming a new norm. Most of our trades focus on buying food at all costs possible to build several largest bio-domes and meat-labs.
Lightning struck the new bio-dome, killing 8 biologists and the yield.
Power outages are becoming less frequent. Traditional ways of harvesting electicity that worked perfectly well in previous colonies do not seem to be as effective on Titan. This needs to be urgently addressed as motivation of the colonists is rapidly become below the norm.
Perimeter of the colony is vastly covered by large lightning rods, which surprisingly generates enough electricity to compensate for innefective wind and solar power sources. Motivation issues have been addressed through a construction of a number of bars.
First Titan colony size has now reached 200 people and mines are now fully operated by drill-bots. It is also now becoming a rare sight to see people carrying items over delivery-bots.
Minor epidemy of space flu that was brought by one of the tourists has been timely detected and successfully treated.
We have now reached a population of 250 people and met all other milestones. I declare this colony a success and now pack my things for a trip back home to my family. There are still a few colonies I will lead in the next decade, but I dream of the interstellar journey to the mysterious planet Rim that orbits the newly discovered star, only a light year away. Our technologies are nearly ready to build the first drive that will humanity to that exoplanet. It feels like a holiday - building a colony on a planet with rich oxygen atmosphere, where it rains with water rather than methane.

Now, I know what everyone means, and I get exactly why this game is so negatively graded, and perhaps I'm blinded by the vanity that i've been with the POSTAL series for years, but I honestly quite enjoyed this game. There are a lot of bugs, no doubt, such as mapping problems where you'll spawn in from a cutscene and the map doesn't exist anymore, or AI bugging out and getting stuck between props or other AI, and not to mention the often crashing; these are all problems, but you can easily look past them, in my opinion. Take into consideration all the problems this game has is the same problems that are often found in Valve games, speaking of which they both use the Source Engine, which isn't perfect by any means. It's kind of a shame that the levels are very simplistic and unclear to the storyline oftentimes, but it's worth the value of doing it most of the time, as it does lead up to something in the least. The factor of having two different game-styles based on your choice of Good or Bad is a nice touch, and alternate endings based on what you do throughout the game is a fun factor to work towards. Additionally, I will mention that the game is not really lengthy, unlike POSTAL or POSTAL 2, where you can make the game pretty much as long as you'd like. But on a positive side, after you've beaten the story once, you do unlock a free-roam mode, which is much like POSTAL 2, but in Catharsis, not Paradise. Bottomline, there are a lot of features in the game that are good, and it's a solid Third-Person Shooter in the least, but yes, there are gamebreaking and annoying bugs. In the sense that the game itself is disowned by Running With Scissors themselves, as it was mostly developed by Akella and Trashmasters, I understand why, But, despite it all, if you are a
of the POSTAL series, like myself, do give it a try, but I do feel like the only ones that are able to stick with the game are the super-fans, and I totally understand why anyone would overlook this game and play POSTAL 2 instead, because it is a lot more fun, and cheaper. Conclusively, I recommend this game to primarily huge fans of the POSTAL series, but for those that aren't and are looking for a better game, I would recommend getting POSTAL 2 and overlooking Postal 3 here for now.

The (actual) bad side of the Postal franchise. Postal III is too glitchy, too prone to crashes, and too unfinished to recommend.
I do like the ultra violence, the humor, and the voice acting, though. The Postal Dude is voiced by Corey Cruise rather than Rick Hunter, and while some people aren't happy about that, I personally love Corey Cruise's work. He makes the Dude seem more relaxed and chill, and it's an interesting take on the character.
But that won't save the game. The game's got performance issues, often severely dropping in framerate, even if you have a powerful PC. This makes the already difficult aiming worse, where sometimes bullets seem to pass right through enemies; you have to be really accurate when you aim, but sometimes that doesn't help anyway.
If there's too much going on in the level, the game may crash. If you have a save file where there's a lot of stuff going on, it may become unusable and you'll have to revert to an older save. Even if it's not that far back, it can undo a short but difficult part (which wouldn't have been difficult if the game was done better).
Postal III uses a sticky cover system, where unless you're close enough to a cover object, you may find yourself getting shot by hordes of enemies because you can't crouch. Sometimes the cover is too sticky and you can't escape fast enough. Or you can't find a good position or angle to use it. I'm sure this system was implemented to capitalize on the whole "realistic", "tactical" cover shooter craze; thanks, Gears of War. Okay, I do like Gears of War, but that game did its cover system better.
Unless you're a die-hard Postal fan, skip Postal III. Or even if you are, you'd probably be better off skipping it anyway.

Better than the original campaign, but still most of the same criticisms of that apply: very strong dialogue, decent plot and characters, a fun setting and lots of atmosphere. Still very linear and with clunky equipping UI, but now you can save anywhere (including in combat) and overall the story arc of this campaign is more impressive. Environments remain low on interactivity and colour text, and the lack of looting means the already somewhat linear path of the game can feel very rationed-off with no real opportunities for grinding or over-leveling, but the experience of the game is highly recommendable to CRPG fans, and one of the most accessible CRPGs too, thanks to the 2 action point combat system also used by the new XCOM. Perhaps most importantly, you can actually do runs now - that is, feel as though you have control over a homebase and go out on missions at your leisure. While it only comes about because of a contrived plot-feature, and it's not a substitute for true non-linear gameplay, it makes the game feel a lot more open and overall better-paced.

An excellent isometric RPG, enjoyed playing through the entire set.  Music and good storytelling, I feel like I'm ready to run the shadows after playing this.

I recommend this game as an expansion to the earlier Shadowrun game by the same company; it uses the same engine and has some expanded content for those who like to use the Workshop.  It also has a much thicker and more meaningful plotline than the prior Shadowrun game, especially within the bounds of character development for your team.
There's less to micromanage this time around; when giving a team member an item, it's explicit it is being "loaned".   You run with a team instead of just whoever you can afford, and you spend time doing actual runs instead of constantly following a linear sequence of events.
My one complaint is one mission: APEX Rising.   Without spoiling too much, you get your typical choice with an AI at one point; set it free or kill it dead.   This mission was really phoned in, not because of it's particular story, but because I think it was developed by the dev team's unpaid intern.   No matter which you choose, what happens next is the same: kill an endless wave of robots that all have a rediculous amount of health and junkies that all carry stun guns while defending a computer terminal.   There is a timer you have to wait out; this timer is only triggered by having your decker(s) hack two terminals.   There are also two turret terminals to give you some automated help, but only on one side at a time (both terminals cant' be active).
What isn't obvious is your team of four has to defend the central computer from robots and junkies trying to kill it, but also defend the terminals (which are far from the central computer) from hackers that can pause the timer by getting a full turn near the terminal.   If this happens, you have to re-play the entire hack to get the terminal working again.
The end result is a mission where tactics mean nothing; you're entirely at the mercy of the Random Number Generator.  It all depends on whether or not all those taser shots connect, and which targets the turrets pick (they pick enemies at random).   Some of the junkies take a stim (also at random) which lets them move three times, enough to run past the turrets in one round and lock down the timer.
I'm not one to normally complain about difficulty.   I was already a gamer when the NES was new.   The problem here is that you cannot save during this mission once any enemies have spawned as a result of the hacking.  The save file corrupts when you try, and you have to force-quit Shadowrun and re-open it.  Forum searches tell me this is a common bug, in this mission only.   This game is the kind of game where it's reasonable to expect dinnertime or a phone call or something to interrupt a long battle; you can't do that here unless you leave the game running.  Other bugs (which force you to quit and reload from your last functional save) include parts of the Matrix disappearing and trapping characters in it, a sudden inability to issue commands, and stuttering when trying to hack a terminal.
Two hours of trying to get through that one section of that one mission and no luck.   I probably won't come back to this until it's been so long I start over.

This is a review based on playing through the first chapter of the campaign missions in Defense Grid 2.
The tower designs seem more modern than futuristic this time which is good for me. The gun turrets look more like AA guns now and the cannon turrets look and move vaguely like the mechs in Battlefield 2142.
The Medals are back but are purely points based now instead of points and cores like before. I had one core get taken by the aliens in the 2nd map and still got a gold "medal" for it.
Other tweaks like the graph showing your score over time with the bronze, silver and gold medals appearing at fixed point values for each map make it easier to tell how you are doing on the map.

The AI from DG: tA is back of course but you also have 2 other AI helping you as well and the banter between them and the other AI you encounter is an interesting change.
Being able to upgrade your turrets with mods before starting a mission and the new Booster unit with the Overdrive ability are also cool. For a total cost of 250 energy (50 to deploy and 200 to activate Overdrive) I can see them being used in a few strategies.
I will post an update as I play through the rest of the campaign.
If you liked DG1, you'll like this one. Highly Recommended.

Let's get something out of the way. The game looks ugly to the outsider. But let me reassure you – when you're ravaging the countryside with your necromancer's army of the undead or laying siege to coastal towns so that your demented priest can summon Cthulu-inspired monsters, the graphics won't matter one bit.
This is one of the rare games that challenges the imagination as much as it does your skill. Though the game is addictive and complex, it really shines when you allow yourself to get sucked into its universe – when you assign histories and personalities to the bizarre commanders and heroes you recruit to lead your armies. When you visualize the fear of your enemies as you approach them with your army of flame-breathing demons.
Too many games hold your hand and get in the way of letting your imagination run wild. Great graphics and 1,000-page RPG scripts are an example of this. It's hard to imagine your own heroes when you can see the individual specks of beard stubble rendered on your character in 1080p. This game trades those luxuries for some rich lore, deep gameplay, and graphics that are just good enough so as to not be distracting (as Dwarf Fortress is for me).

If you grew up during the late '90s and the start of the new millennium, then the name SNK has little to no bearing on you as much as other fighting-games, and that’s a shame. History has often forgotten games not because they lacked quality but they were behind the times, and The Last Blade was most certainly an aging, though as strong now as it was back in the past, relic of arcade fighters.
Beneath the quarter-eating exterior that we may liken to modern microtransactions without the nostalgia of their novelty, these games provided short, worthwhile experiences that could not be done on consoles or PC hardware at the time. The Last Blade was one of those unexpected gems that has the distilled greatness of SNK like Shock Troopers, King of Fighters and Metal Slug with its own unique take on fighting games as well as 2D pixel-art presentation.
Now on Steam, you can replay this forgotten gem without the constant gouging of your wallet for your failures, though you certainly are getting what you paid for as with every other SNK game PC Port developed by DotEmu.
This is an emulator job of a game from arcade cabinets instead of remastering the classic or offering new content for both casuals and hard-core fans, which is a shame the sequel is not packaged along with it to justify its asking price for fighting-game enthusiasts. The game has only two main-modes: The Arcade/Campaign mode where you fight all the fighters and a final boss designed to be brutally difficult well as a timed horde mode to defeat as many fighters as possible. Versus is strictly player-vs.-player mode, no bot-matches or a 1:1 fighting mode. Unfortunately, my experience has shown that the online capabilities are not playable enough to warrant purchasing it for nostalgia fans, so local-only games are your only other means of replayability. As a result, unless you really want to replay a forgotten SNK fighter because you are curious enough to try one or have friends around you who would be interested, this game does not warrant a full-asking price.
However, if you are a seasoned fighting game player who has never played a SNK game or if you are a fan of other SNK classics like King of Fighters, then The Last Blade can be a pleasure to behold. Unlike the archaic lane-switching mechanics of Fatal Fury and Samurai Showdown, The Last Blade incorporates many modern fighting game mechanics such as balancing offensive-and-defensive play with parries, rolls and characters on the roster balancing one-another. Something oddly unique to The Last Blade is a Speed/Power playstyle option humorously referred to as “Orgy Mode”, which is more of two specializations of playstyles. This classic also understands a major appeal of fighting-games is the importance of character and style not only as a visual spectacle but also in the unseen complexity within a fighting game tiself.
Each fighter controls slightly differently with different types of combos, special moves, speed, offensive and defensive capabilities that is countered by a rival character. It's difficult to go into details without becoming too technical but the important take-away is that you can feel the changes in-battle, and it's mastering this self-imposed challenge that is the core appeal of SNK. The simplicity of the four-button design undersells the polish and the depth of a game you can discover.
This polish is what leads to the greatest quality of TLB; it oozes style with all its substance, and that alone may be worth the admission price. Characters' animations are highly detailed, even in stagger animations or the "cutscenes" that play in-between battles that establishes the darker tone of the game. (I only wish there were subtitles or English voice-overs to let the banter add to the spectacle.) The visceral nature of the battles is emphasized when the final blow is struck, the game literally cutting the music with the final blow in a silencing red-flash. The synesthesia rush of gameplay, music and visuals all come together in this one distilled game of SNK greatness, which is only marred by its current developers.
It's no secret that DotEmu spent as little as much on polishing up this game for a Steam release with the 24 SNK bundle from HumbleBundle. Coupled with monitor frame-rate issues, graphical glitches and other technical details. TLB is no different than other SNK games available on Steam as well, along with the health issues common to '90s games (flashing lights and colors).
However, in DotEmu's defense, the game has fully configurable control schemes for two players that work with controllers (at least with X-Input devices), and other than a few strange quirks and blemishes on an otherwise flawless classic, the technical issues should not discourage you. These are blemishes when it does impede on the overall experience, although I found it hilarious that the developers wrote the cheat-codes on the Steam store-front page to unlock the hidden characters. As previously mentioned, the multiplayer lobby system is so broken that if it was even possible to establish a fighting-game scene for this game the developers ruined whatever possibility for enthusiasts to get together every now and then to reminisce on gaming from the past.
As the Shogun from Total War would say, “A shameful display!”
Sometimes games are entertaining for their gameplay, narrative and the like, but sometimes the historical and artistic value alone is all that is needed to play a game. SNK classics, such as The Last Blade, manage to hold up because they are mechanically competent as they are beautiful. One can only hope that the popularity of SNK games from the past as well as bringing back King of Fighters to new audiences will also encourage SNK to revitalize series like The Last Blade. Until then, The Last Blade is a bit of history that shows less of its wear than its greatness from another time and the possibility of a future built upon its legacy. .

I've played Planetarian way back and oh boy I lost count how many tissues I've used in that novel. This visual novel has no choices so you just get to enjoy the ride in one way. Finished reading this. I must say I immensely enjoyed it.
Story
- Post-apocalyptic setting about a boy who wakes up with no memories. Yes, we know it's kind of tropey or not that unique but the way the story builds up definitely makes up for it. The pacing may seem a bit quick as there are little to no fillers for this novel. I frankly believe it's enough for anyone to digest what's happening in the story.
Sound
- Normal ambient music that accompanies whatever is happening in the screen. And does it's job well.
- BGMs. I think this is probably the strongest part of the novel as it accompanies the scenes well. If you're familiar with previous Key games, you know what to expect as I think Key's in-house music people are the same people responsible for the music in this novel. I've always enjoyed pinball games. Unfortunately, given the fact I live in a very rural area I've always had to make do with video game pinball tables, only having played real physical units a time or three. Despite that the history and design of the real tables have always fascinated me, and I've longed for a way I could experience some of the real classics.
Well, here's the answer.
In terms of production values as a video game Pinball Arcade is a little lacking in some areas. Overall visual fidelity isn't the greatest given the simplicity of its subject matter, and in all honesty the presentation of the game's menus isn't the most user friendly, with a strangely syrupy-feeling lag between menu selection inputs and their taking effect on-screen. In-game, though, things are completely different, with tight controls and a solidly reliable camera that makes actually playing the tables themselves a joy. Perhaps its simply my inexperience, but the physics of the tables do, at times, feel a bit on the floaty side, however.
What really takes the cake in the game's presentation, at least for me, are the snippets of table background available when you launch each table. For players just looking to play some pinball these might seem like a bit of an annoyance, but for those who appreciate the history of the industry, or the history of games in general, these blurbs are fascinating and offer insight into the development of pinball games as a whole.
The visual issues and physics mentioned above are nitpicky issues, but part of what makes them stand out is the price of the overall package. At thirty dollars or more a pop for each "season," or five dollars a piece to buy tables individually, the tables in Pinball Arcade feel like they come at a stomach-churning premium, especially when compared to its competitors. Doubtless the premium is partially due to licensing costs for the various tables from their original producers, but when alternatives like Pinball FX offer cheaper tables with arguably (from a video game perspective) more complex gameplay and higher production values, it can be hard to justify to oneself the pricing here. That said, there's something to be said for featuring "real" tables as opposed to completely unrealistic fantasy models, and when the content of each season is taken into account the price discrepancy isn't as great as it at first seems, since each season consists of 10 or more unique tables, meaning tables average out to about 3 dollars a pop if the basic version of each season is purchased, less for the Season 1 tables since there are 14 of them.
If you're a pinball aficionado, Pinball Arcade is definitely the game to look at, and I would highly recommend it to anyone who appreciates more about game design than just the latest graphics engine and online shooting. The tables play nicely, and the extras make for a unique, well-valued package. If, on the other hand, you're turned off by the idea of solid-state hardware and often incredibly dated table aesthetics, then look elsewhere.

If you haven't seen the videos and the summary they provide, you are in a bunker with your family and you basically just try to survive. This is a game about a 1950's family living their lives, enjoying life as it is...
Until a fallout happens.
You have 60 seconds to grab your family, along with supplies and 4 slots worth, to put them in the shelter. If you don't get into the shelter in time, you immediatly perish. You can choose to leave all of your family or collect all of them. You have 3 family members, including you, Ted. Once 60 seconds are up, you get into the shelter.
You can choose 3 modes: Little Boy, where you get longer exploration time, a hefty stocked shelter/briefcase, rare problems, and good opportunities, Fat Man, where you get average exploration time, problems, average shelter/briefcase, and decent opportinities. Then, Tsar Bomba: the hardest difficulty where you get no exploration time, no stocked shelter/briefcase, often there are problems, and no good opportunities. This gamemode is for the adept player, and for the most hardest, realistic fallout gameplay.
Once you are in the shelter, you have until you die or until you get rescued by the government. You can choose to send people out into the barren wasteland (yet full of suprises, good or bad) to scavenge for supplies and food/water. There are also sometimes where you play a game of chance: for example, an empty suitcase appears on your doorstep. There's no one around, and there's no writing on the case. Do you open it? There are a few possibilities: there could be water and food in it (ONLY water and food), it doesn't have anything in it, it could explode and hurt someone, or it could have food/water, but it makes your family sick. See what I mean? It's all about skill, gambling, and achievement.
This game is EXTREMELY worth the $10 bucks, and has extremely high replay value. All in all, this game has:
-No story, you make your OWN story
-Gambling and risks
-A dog! (you have to earn the dog)
-Desision-making and strategy
-Fallout survival
Survive as much as you can with this amazing strategic game! 9.7/10, needs just a tiny bit more time when collecting supplies.

The timeless classic from Namco Bandai that gave a name to the video game industry has been remastered into a wonderful new game that tests problem solving skills, reflexes, and more, all while delivering an exciting experience that those who grew up in the 1980s experience. The ability to use alternate designs from other Pac-Man titles such as Pac-Mania, and even offering DLC that includes skins based on other games such as Dig Dug and Rally X makes this game as entertaining as eye candy as it does in gameplay. The additions of the game that include slow-mo effects to help avoid ghosts, bombs that can help you from getting trapped between two ghosts, and the auto-adjusting of the speed of play based on deaths and bomb-use are excellent additions that make the game a lot more interesting and lowers the chances of a reallly cheap death.
My only concern is that there is no Classic Mode option that only involves the title character the four main ghosts, and the classic gameplay of the original game. And while there are plenty of modes to choose from, this game isn't going to keep you busy for very long if you don't buy the DLC. But other than that, any fan of the arcade classic this was based on is sure to enjoy this blast from the past.

PAC-MAN Championship Edition DX+ is an arcade game based off of the original PAC-MAN arcade game. The game centers around two ideas – speed runs, trying to eat all the pills on a stage as fast as possible, and point runs, where the player tries to score as many points as possible within a 5 or 10 minute timespan. The game differs significantly from the original game in many respects, but is still recognizably related to the original game.
Story
There is no story. This is PAC-MAN!
Gameplay
The game, while recognizably very similar to the original PAC-MAN, is also very distinct from it. There are a number of different mazes (stages) for you to play in, with the completion of time trials and point attacks on earlier mazes necessary to unlock later ones. The gameplay is pretty simple – PAC-MAN moves continuously in the direction he is pointed, and can be turned into side passageways. All passageways are exactly as wide as PAC-MAN and the ghosts, so the levels are a series of paths.
Unlike the original PAC-MAN, the stages in the game are not static. Each half of the maze contains a number of pills; once all of the pills on one side of the maze has been collected, a “fruit”, which can take many different forms (some of which are not fruit) appears on the opposite side of the maze. Once that fruit is collected, the cleared side of the maze shifts to the next pattern in a series. The series of patterns is preset, not random, and there is a path through each pattern which is “optimal”, and this path is continuous between patterns. Thus, at its heart, the game is one of memorization, and most of the mazes have at least one path from the top of the screen to the bottom of the screen, and from one side of the screen to the opposite side of the screen, wrapping around and allowing for swift navigation across the stage.
In addition to the pills, there are two other important features in the mazes. The first is ghosts. These enemies come in two flavors; the first flavor is the wandering ghost. Early on, there aren’t any of these, but as the game progresses these continuously spawn, until eventually there are at least four of them, and possibly an infinite number of them – the maze seems to get increasingly crowded as time goes on. Some of these ghosts carry power pills, and some of them carry bombs, but the vast majority of them carry nothing.
In addition to the wandering ghosts, there are static, sleeping ghosts in each pattern. These ghosts are woken up by passing by them, and will start chasing PAC-MAN around the maze. Unlike the wandering ghosts, these ghosts will form a very long line chasing after PAC-MAN, though the wandering ghosts will oftentimes join the pack and join in the chase. The more of these ghosts are woken up, the longer the line will grow. One touch from either kind of ghost will spell PAC-MAN’s doom, but the game slows itself down if PAC-MAN comes close to touching one.
Power pills are much larger pills which spawn in certain patterns of the maze. These can be collected by moving over them and temporarily give PAC-MAN the ability to eat ghosts, scoring a large number of points and eliminating them. Wandering ghosts will respawn after a short period of time, while the sleeping ghosts (and the woken up ghosts) will simply disappear forever after being eaten. As some of the ghosts themselves carry power pills, eating such ghosts (or eating another static power pill on the map) will reset the time allowed to eat ghosts and score points. The patterns of the map are set up such that the player can do this potentially indefinitely, assuming perfect play, retaining effective invincibility and the ability to eat large numbers of ghosts for points. Some of the patterns require PAC-MAN to eat ghosts.
There are also bombs, which can be activated to clear the map of all woken-up ghosts, as well as of all the wandering ghosts. If this is done, all of the ghosts will be put into the center of the map and slowly escape back out into it, pursuing PAC-MAN once more. Bombs are a last-second desperation measure, but they are very effective.
Should PAC-MAN touch a ghost, a death animation is played, the ghosts are returned to the center of the map as if a bomb had been used, and PAC-MAN respawns where he died. The player has a limited number of lives, though can gain extra lives by scoring enough points.
The game itself has multiple modes, as noted. There are a series of time trials, which are intended to teach the player the patterns of the map and for the player to navigate through a few sets of patterns as fast as possible; the first six for any map are to teach the player the patterns, with a seventh intended to run the player through a full rotation of patterns, and the remaining three intended to run the player through a set of patterns with more ghosts wandering around, making it significantly more difficult. The time limits on these are generally fairly generous, but the player, once they set a top time, will change the maximum time limit on the map to the time they scored.
There is a point scoring mode, where the player must navigate a continuous, looping pattern of mazes with an ever increasing number of wandering ghosts spawning in over the course of the map; the goal in this mode is to score as many points as possible within 5 or 10 minutes. In this mode, it behooves the player to continuously maintain power pill status and eat as many ghosts as possible in order to maximize their point total, all while navigating the mazes and advancing the patterns to keep supplying themselves with fresh sets of pills and ghosts to eat.
Finally, there is a “ghost attack” mode, wherein the player’s only goal is to eat as many ghosts as possible within a single continuous use of a power pill, with ten minutes to do so.
Graphics
The game is actually very attractive; while some of the graphical modes, in particular the retro pixel mode, are a bit harder on the eyes than others, on the whole, the game does a good job of visually representing what is going on.
Final Summary
There is very little wrong with this game, but it is very simple; all it has is the very pure gameplay. The game offers little but different maze setups; as a result, it is very likely that after playing a couple hours of the game, the player will have seen almost everything it has to offer save a few more variations on pre-existing setups.
If it does have a flaw, it is that a player who is unfamiliar with PAC-MAN would be a little bit confused at first. Even still, not knowing the controls, it wouldn’t take very long to pick up.
Still, such a limited game is not worth very much of your money, and if you get the opportunity to play it for a few hours for free, you will have seen everything there is to see.

The visuals and the audio are both lazy and repetitive; the voice and sound samples used quickly become annoying. Five and a half years later the performance is still bad, you still can't alt-tab it without it hanging or crashing, and in game bugs will either make you get stuck or just halt your progress arbitrarily.
On top of all that, it's a Postal game in name only; it has no concept of "going postal". Every level simply contrives enemies to attack you and the only thing of any entertainment value whatsoever is that, ironically, in a Postal game, you're actually acting in self-defence all the time.
If you want a Postal game just replay Postal 2, it's a classic game; if you want a third person shooter just pick another one at random, it's highly unlikely you'll end up with something worse than this.

One of the best games I've played in years. It totally drew me in. The fixed cast of characters were amazing, you really grow to love all of them by the end of the game. Their back-stories are really fleshed-out with their own series of side-quests. Glory's sidequests were particularly good. I am not normally a fan of cyberpunk settings but Shadowrun's intrigues me: it seems to blend elements of traditional cyberpunk with those of high fantasy, with the inclusion of elves, dwarves, trolls, etc
The story is one of the best I have ever played through, and the choices you make really do make a huge difference in how it plays out. Your characteristics like intelligence, charisma, strength, etc. also play a big role in determining how well you're able to handle difficult conversations and situations, allowing you to convince guards you're one of them for example.
The combat is really solid: a lot of the time tactical RPGs end up boring me as the pace is simply too slow to maintain my interest. Even though this is a turn-based tactical RPG, Dragonfall's is definitely challenging (even playing on easy!) and rarely boring. The variety each team-mate brings to the team as well as the ability to specialise in various areas makes combat a lot of fun. Turns don't take forever and there's enough going on on-screen to keep things interesting and exciting even during particularly long battles.
The soundtrack is really good, fits the atmosphere and setting perfectly, and I particularly liked the song that plays during Glory's sidequest.
All in all this is one of my favourite games in recent years and I urge any fans of RPG or strategy games to try it.

While this was already a wonderful game in DX9 mode, with the recent addition of DX11 support (if you have a recent and fairly powerful graphics card, I'm using two nVidia GTX Titan in SLI with 3D surround enabled here) this game now looks utterly stunning. I couldn't quite believe it was the same game, all of the tables look so much better, especially Black Hole, Attack From Mars, and Circus Voltaire. You can even adjust the room lighting (to around 20%) so as to give the feeling of a real arcade, and adjust the lamp brightness accordingly (55% or lower seems good). When playing with the nVidia 3D surround turned on (press Ctrl T to disable/enable it), there is still a little issue with the light from some of the brighter bulbs appearing to be rendered at a slightly incorrect perspective, i.e. "floating" above the table. I'll try to bring this bug to Farsight's attention, to see if they can get it fixed, but in the meantime just lowering the bulb brightness slightly to around 45% when playing in 3D surround mode with DX11 seems to be sufficient.  Note: the room and bulb settings are under each table's options menu, they're not set from the game's launcher. At the moment, to get into fullscreen mode, you can either select it from the DX11 settings in the game's configuration launcher, or press the Alt-Enter key combination while running the game itself. At the moment, when running with DX11, the game only makes use of the center monitor in nVidia 3D surround mode (whereas when running in DX9 mode it uses all three monitors), so it feels slightly less immersive. It'd be nice to get full 5760x1080 resolution working in landscape mode like it does in DX9 mode. But overall, the DX11 support is such a huge improvement that I feel it already brings this game up to "must-have" status among all games on the PC platform. Awesome job, Farsight!

Completed the Story Mode today, after 25 hours of gameplay. For ease of reading, I'm going to start with the summary and work my way into details, avoiding spoilers. I'm assuming you've at least watched the trailer to even be here.
I'd give it about 6/10.
When reviewing Danganronpa, I think it's important to know who you are as a player, and who I am as a reviewer.
Me:
-Have played less than 5 visual novels, absolutely loved one, forgot about the rest
-Like the Anime art-style, but couldn't name my 5 favourite Anime Shows
-Really enjoyed the better Final Fantasies
-Enjoyed Persona a little less due to perceived lack of polish
I think these things matter, and contribute to the 6/10 score. I think that most people who rate it more highly will probably be a bit more enthused about points 1 and 2.
Danganronpa is a visual novel, with some basic gameplay elements thrown in. It has little inclination to hide this, and in truth of those 25 hours I played, I would suggest that at least 20 could comfortably have been put together in an unmodded Renpy engine.
The gameplay consists of the trials, where there is a combination of quick clicking, logic and rhythm to involve the player. The result is vaguely involving rather than exciting, and has a tendency to be extremely frustrating due to a lack of clarity between answers. The logic takes a back seat for the most part. The mystery of the stories will generally play out ahead of you with the gameplay only serving to act as a "next page" button. Whether or not you have been able to see the full outcome of a trial a mile-off, or have no clue as to what transpired, have very little impact in your ability to solve the cases.
Sometimes it will be difficult to understand what transpired, because Danganronpa is unabashedly wacky. It also has a very mixed tone, where it's perfectly reasonable for a teenage girl to be stabbed to death with a kitchen knife, but the blood is pink and the dialogue kooky. Whether or not that appeals is very much up to the reader, but personally I couldn't help but think that a more classic Japanese Melodrama tone might have suited the concept better (I have since read that the originally planned game was closer to this).
The characters are playing hard tropes, but are for the most part agreeable and rarely a barrier. Those with experience working in mental health may find Danganronpa's cheerfully offensive misunderstandings a little hard to bear. Arguably, it is an Anime and should be approached with a sense of humour in this regard.
The 2d art of Danganronpa does look lovely, and is stretched at times into pseudo-3d art. The 3D navigation acts as little more than a menu.
At times it bored me, and I was aching for the game to end. For far too much of the game you find yourself idly clicking through text without caring. I also found the amount of repetition to be frustrating. At times it will hammer home relentlessly a point that you got first time around.
However, I did complete it, and I don't think it ever occurred to me to not do so. Plus, Danganronpa has a charm to it that makes it a little more than the sum of its parts. It is brilliant at nothing, good at few things and terrible at many, but it does seem to possess that unquantifiable something that kept me playing.
I feel a bit harsh giving it a thumbs down, but I honestly couldn't recommend it to any of my friends who hadn't already heard of it. If you're any less involved in visual novels or anime type things than I am, then it is hard to see what you would get from it. On the other hand, if this is your bag, you probably already know.
Like I said, 6/10.

To start this review I have to say that this is my first real experience with a visual novel game. I never thought that I would ever enjoy one these type of games. I would rather watch the anime. But after sitting down and playing this game non-stop I can easily say that I am now a fan of visual novel games. I am going to break down this game into catagories to best help describe each point with this wonderful game.
So the basic understanding of this game is, You and fifteen other students are trapped in this school with no way of escape. The only way to escpae is to kill another student without being detected by other students. There is a class trial for the students to talk and vote on "whodunit". Okay so that is the basic understanding on the games story. The best part about this story is the characters. Each one of them are bursting with personality and hidden pasts. It is so much fun just watching the characters interating with one another. Spending time with charaters during your free time and discovering there past. To top it off you may invest time and energy into getting to know them better, conecting with them, for them to die. Not all characters die but you are scared when someone knew dies and it could be your favorite character. The gameplay of danganronpa is quite interesting. For starters you can walk around the school and explore. I don't know how comon it is for visual novel games to give you the ability to freely move around in a 3D space. Being able to move around feels great and when the game asks you to find something in the school it just feels rewarding to explore. Each room you go in you can click on objects and areas to investigate them and see whats going on with them or learn a bit of information. Basic stuff for a investigation type game but its well done and isnt't a boring experience. Okay so when you find a dead body a investigation takes place. You have to explore and get clues and unravel the mystery of how this person died. Sometimes it gets really easy and the characters are braindead to what has happened. But for the most part the investigations don't take up to much time and arn't a hassle at all. Not bad but not amazing. But that all leads to the juicy parts of the game, The class trials. There is a lot of gameplay features that take place during the class trials. Some things are easy like the word search thing, but using your truth bullets during a non stop debate gets hard at times and is really enjoyable. But the stupid white nosie words things are really annoying and not that well inplomented. When you fire a truth bullet on a word you object, the firing thing takes its sweet damn time shooting and I swear to god the amount of times a stupid white noise sentence pops up at what I am firing at. This gets really annoying and makes you waste time. Lastly the tempo mini game during the trial is a great breather section and lets your fingers move a little. Its a great pause and breaks up the long trial. Personally I enjoy them (Get Hina's report card maxed out to make the tempo game easier, its kinda easy but the last trial was hetic with the upgrade so I highly suggest you get her report card done during your playthrough). When you beat the original story you get an extra game mode called school mode. It acts like a dating sim and item management sim with no murders. Personally its a gimmic with its only real purpose being for getting report cards finished for achievements. The romance isnt that good, a little dissapointed in the extra mode but again it is a extra mode and it serves its purpose. Ypu may be able to get a lot out of the game mode and I still have to go and finish some things up in there. There is a lot of things to do in school mode.

Okay so this game was originally on the psp then ported to ps vita then ported to pc and ps4. But for it being on the original psp it looks great. The port on pc adds visual advancements to the game and it looks great for a visual novel game. The artstyle is great with its upbeat visuals to scary horror artwork. Overall its solid for the visual department. The music is fantastic. Honestly I love the soundtrack. From monokuma's funky and strange theme to the upbeat and groovy music of the intro. The soundtrack covers music from upbeat to creepy and horror. Its great and I know that you will take the time to just sit there and listen to the music while doing nothing in game.
So Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc is a great game. This is just a interesting visual novel game that has amazing characters and a interesting story with fun gameplay that will make you play for hours to find who killed your favorite waifu.

Postal 3... oh god Postal 3. I should have listened to the reviews!
Short Version: Don't. Just don't. Buy Paradise Lost for Postal 2. It's the sequel Postal 2 deserved, even if it is just DLC.
Long Version: I love the Postal series.  I remember first buying Postal 2, and being unable to stop playing it. The sense of humor and the open world gameplay was amazing. Then I saw the screenshots for Postal 3, and thought "Hey! This looks awesome! And it's made with the Source engine, which was the engine that was used to create amazing games like Half-Life 2, Portal, and Left 4 Dead!" and without reading the user reviews, I purchased it.
My first immediate problem with the game is the loading times. First, to start the game, you go through a loading screen. That alone is pretty normal with Source games, but this one doesn't last 10-15 seconds, it lasts several minutes! Just to load the menu screen! Then, once you've started a game, you have to go through ANOTHER loading screen that also lasts a few minutes to load the level. Every loading screen is like this, and I'm almost certain that I've waited for the game to load more than I've actually played it.
The second problem is that the game is buggy. Very buggy. This is one of the most broken games I've ever played. In the time I've played, the game has crashed so many times that I lost count at about the fifth time. If your game is unplayable, then don't release it for gods sake!
Third, the gameplay itself is flawed. Even if we look past the technical problems, the gameplay still ranges from mediocre to terrible. There's a mechanic that tracks everything you do. If you do something bad (For example, killing an innocent bystander), you become more evil. The more bad things you do, the more evil you become. This would be fine if it was excecuted well, but the way the system is set up, you can't do anything FUN. You can't do the things you did in Postal 1 and 2 because it has an impact on the story. Even if you could, there's not much to do other than kill people. Also, the world is small compared to the world in postal 2. How can you market your game as "Open World" if your world is barely oepn? Oh, and the melee weapons are garbage. They do very little damage, with the exception of the machete.
In conclusion, this is one of, if not the worst sequel to a classic game I have ever seen. You thought Duke Nukem Forever was bad? Well, at least Duke Nukem Forever was actually playable and somewhat entertaining, even if it is disappointing for something that was in development for over a decade. There is one positive, though. Because Postal 3 was made with Source, it is very moddable. So, if you're a source modder who wants to remake Postal 1 or 2 in the Source engine, this is a good foundation. If you're not a modder, and don't want to mod this game, then avoid it like the plague.

Is this Free to Play or Pay to Win? No, it's just Learn to Play! If you do, you will not need to pay anything in the store. Of course you could buy something to support the devs. I suggest a good armour that increases your winnings of gold and souls.
So Learn to Play!
Here are a few tips. This is not really a match-3, it is a match-4! A match-4 gives an extra turn. The AI is not cheating as so many lazy guys have been complaining about, it follows certain rules of its own, always! So find them out and use it against it. It always does match-4 first even if there are spells or skull moves that could make it win the game, then it does skulls, them spells. It almost never does anything clever, like a move that will create a cascade of matches. This gives you the chance to outwit it. I regularly can win an opponent 3 times stronger than me. At level 200 I could beat the level 1000 opponents. But if I am not careful or if I play a new combination of troops I may easily lose by an opponent half my level. Use the quests and the challenges to learn the best conbinations for you. Study the opponent to find which troops are the really dangerous ones. In other words Learn to Play! Then join a guild and play PvP. It no longer costs gold to play so you can play as much as you like, and you get traitstones, gold and souls to help you upgrade.

Alright, so first of all: I am a big fan of DG 1 and I like DG 2. There. This is a review to dispel some of the wrong and inaccurate information in many negative reviews, that almost made me NOT buy the game!
I am currently at Level 6 out of 20, so I have completed 1/4 of the game. This gives me enough information to write a first review. Here are some of the main complaints and what I think about them:
1. People complaining that the game is too easy and everyone can beat it on gold and that they can't show off their virtual♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and don't know how to distinguish themselves and increase their score.
A: No, the game is NOT too easy. There are 4 difficulty modes. I play on normal. Normal is pretty relaxed so far. There are 2 difficulties above that. I imagine they can be pretty hard. You also have additional challenge modes. You should not get bored unless you're maybe extremely good, but the average john will be challenged with normal alone.
Your score is calculated whenever you kill an enemy alien. The score depends on the alien, how much money you have when you kill the alien and how many cores you still possess while killing said alien, while floating cores (the ones not at your core station) count only partially. Only cores that have been taken out of the map do not count at all. Apparently, the scoring system works very similarly to DG 1, but in real time. So this point of criticism is not valid in my opinion.
2. People complaining about the resource system and that they have removed interest.
A: This is technically not correct. You now receive a fixed income rate per "tick", namely 10, that is true. At the end of a round or every second round (I have to admit I haven't exactly figured that out) you get bonus money based on how much money you have NOT yet spent, meaning the more money you have available the bigger the bonus, i.e. interest. This is explained in the 3rd mission I think. People need to read and pay attention and not provide misinformation (almost every negative review that I read had this issue). So, not only does it pay off to play conservatively in terms of score, but also in terms of money and thus longevity/sustainability. Edit: I forgot to mention that you do no longer gain credits by killing aliens, that's true and it didn't even occur to me...that's bs. That's also why the command tower is gone I think.
3. People complaining about how horrible the UI is.
A: I have no idea what they are complaining about. People just complain. The UI is perfectly fine. You can get all the required information, it is simple to use etc. You can activate paths, you can show tower impact ranges, building and upgrading towers is as easy or easier than before AND you can play the game with a game pad just as well as with mouse and keyboard, which is brilliant. I personally am a mouse player primarily but I like to use the controller for this, because I can and it’s easy to use. (Update: Just checked and you can also use it in DG 1 but it is slower. Works fine too, however.)
4. People complaining about the graphics and style.
A: I have to agree here that DG 1 simply had clearer visuals. They tried too much with DG 2. It basically still looks the same, but with a lot more clutter and effects. Aliens and towers are harder to distinguish, although I’d say towers can are still easy to distinguish. Aliens on the other hand feel a bit bland, but mostly I can still see what I’m dealing with. The UI also tells you in the wave information. Personally I wish they had not changed the engine. It didn’t make a lot of sense and probably cost a lot of money. It’s not “ugly”, however.
5. People complaining about the performance.
A: Personally I couldn’t see any real lag, even with larger alien crowds. Maybe this happens later on. I did notice, however, that the game “seems” a bit sluggish in general.
6. People complaining about the sound.
A: This is unfortunately absolutely correct. The gun towers simply drown out all other sounds. You could barely hear them in DG 1, but in DG 2 one or 2 gun towers feel like a Manowar concert. You can still hear most other towers if you are in the vicinity, but especially the concussion and the cannon tower are basically silent towers, which is very sad, at least in the cannon tower case, because that “oomph” rocked! I always did hate the concussion tower sound.
7.  People complaining about the unimaginative level design.
A: Can’t really comment on that. So far the first 5 missions were pretty basic in design. You have to keep in mind, though, that this is not an expansion, but a new game, thus early levels must be simple to have a good learning curve for new players. Will see how it will be later on.
8. People complaining about the story and the AI chatter.
A: The story is…well, it’s a TD. Who cares, really? I do partially. Fletcher is still great. The others are ok. Before each level you get glimpses into the aliens mind set…this seems “interesting”. So far the chatter has been ok. I think you can also just disable the sound for that? Not sure. Just waiting for the raspberries!
9. People complaining about the workshop integration.
A: This is actually a pretty strong negative point for the game. Apparently you can “vote” for maps in the workshop, which then become available on the official DG store. I checked and one map seems to cost TWO dollars!!! TWO. Not only is it ridiculous to sell them, but the price is so over the top it is not even funny anymore. If you value community created content, this might be the point for you to NOT purchase the game.
Now some general info:
-	Aliens: There are a few new ones. Some that regen health. Nothing too interesting. I’m not sure if they took some out. Didn’t look like it, but could be. All in all, pretty boring stuff if you played DG 1.
-	Towers: The tower encyclopedia in game does not list ANY new tower at all. In fact, the command tower is now missing…I think that’s the only 1 though.
-	Boost blocks: You can build these cheap blocks to create mazes and put your towers on to give them additional effects like increased damage or cloak detect…etc. The concept is “ok”, the execution is…meh. You basically want to build them for every tower, because they only cost 50 credits and without them a tower can simply do 20%!!!!! Less damage. That is huge. Ofc, the upgrade costs money, but still…20% more damage for 250 credits? Still a good deal. Plus you get extended range and fire arcs. I don’t particularly like it. It is a bit clunky.
-	Tower bonuses: You unlock bonus abilities for your towers, which you can choose before a mission. For example, my laser tower currently does 15% splash. This is a nice addition, but they could have added more interesting effects. Maybe there will be better ones later, but I somehow doubt it.
-	Different commander bonuses: You can now choose a special power at the start of a game. No longer just orbital laser.
All in all I would say that DG 2 is a good TD game. IF you have played DG 1 you might find that better in some aspects. It also has more maps to play on. IF you have NOT played DG 1…get DG 1 lol. No, seriously. DG 2 is not a bad game, but DG 1 is better imho. It is not as bad as people make it out to be and I will recommend it, but ONLY at a severely reduced price. Right now, it is 66% off…so only 8 euros or so, which is ok to get a few hours of new tower defense stuff.
Overall, however, the “changes” and “additions”, wherever they are, do not warrant a full price…and the community map selling is just plain evil. The creators probably get some small amount for each purchased map, but if you are a map creator and doing this for the money, you’re doing it wrong. I loved creating Star Craft Maps back in the day…it would have never occurred to me to charge anything for that…pffft.

This game is great! Think of the original Pac-Man, but more colorful, it gets really fast as you progress through the level, and 30 ghosts chasing you at a time. That's Pac-Man Championship Edition. What I don't like though, is that you have a time limit, Facebook sharing, and this did help me a lot, but it makes the game easier (And I like challenge) is the game goes in bullet-time when a ghost is about to get you.

Despite having a few weird design choices, the game is really fun.
It is worth your time, without a doubt. As for your money - the game uses a weird microtransaction downloadable content system. A few levels and skins are sold separately, as DLC. Thankfully, you can just ignore the DLC and play the main game as the extra levels and skins aren't really required to have fun and work towards better scores. I'd suggest buying just the main game or waiting for a sale for the whole DLC pack.
Gameplay-wise, yes, the game can be enjoyed by anyone. However, the game has some neon-ish colours passing through quickly (this is especially visible on the highest game speed). It's not a huge issue but if you suffer from epilepsy attacks or some form of movement-based vertigo I'd suggest checking small clips of gameplay footage first (or even static screenshots) to make sure you'll be able to play the game without any problems. There are also other, less neon-like, skins included in the game - switching to a tamer one could do the trick.
The game is using the classic PAC-MAN formula, but with a competitive twist. You roam around a labyrinth, searching for pac-dots and power pellets. You avoid ghosts (unless you have a power pellet) and try to get the best score/time possible. The difference with PAC-MAN CE DX+ is that you have various labyrinths, each with a different structure. A few of them are locked as DLC but they're not really mandatory to have. Each labyrinth has various challenges that you can play and compete in the leaderboards (time attacks, score attacks, ghost combos and even playing on a barely lit version of the labyrinth).
PAC-MAN CE DX+ is oriented more towards a competitive side of gaming. Instead of slowly roaming the labyrinths, the game quickly gains speed (and so do the ghosts), forcing the player to make split-second decisions and tests the player's reflexes at every turn. Also, instead of just a few ghosts, you will be chased by a whole chain of them, which gives the player the opportunity to build up massive combos. Running into a dead end can also be forgiven as the game uses a bomb item which will temporarily send all chasing ghosts back to their spawn, in the middle of the labyrinth.
Some skins look really good but others are just bland. You'll most likely find the skin that suits you best and you'll stick with it for the whole game.
The sound effects fit perfectly into the pace of the game. There are some moments where the sound effects become quite loud (i.e. when you eat a 20+ ghost chain) but it's nothing a little volume regulation can't handle. Music choices are quite interesting, very fun to listen to while playing. Although, there's not many tracks to choose from. A few more psytrance or euphoric tracks to choose from would be nice.
As far as I understand it, PAC-MAN CE DX+ doesn't follow any particular story or canon of PAC-MAN and honestly it doesn't need to. The fast-paced gameplay hold its ground firmly and doesn't really need a storyline on top of it.
Runs without any issues on my 5 year old PC (Dual-Core 2.66GHz, GeForce 9600GT, 2GB RAM). Steady framerate, no jittering. The game seems to be locked into a 1280x720 resolution on 16:9 monitors. The game also doesn't have a proper graphical options menu, aside from a fullscreen toggle. While not a dealbreaker, a few basic options (v-sync, resolution, etc.) would be nice.
Yes. The "PAC RAINBOW" track. A psytrance track in a game about running in a dark labyrinth with neon walls, munching down pills and seeing ghosts. There's something fitting about that.
Yes. It seems that the top places on the scoreboards have been overrun by spoofed scores. This could be a sign of very weak coding of the leaderboard. Still, it's pretty fun to watch a replay of someone who has (allegedly) 500 gajillion points and see him fail on Game Speed 5.
I give PAC-MAN Championship Edition DX+ a Wakka Wakka out of 5.

Deciding to buy this game depends on your value of gameplay vs story.  It is more like playing through a book than a game.  Content is split between dialog and combat.  Combat is mildly amusing, but does not bring anything new or complex.  However, the games strengths combine to make it immersive and enjoyable.

Shadowrun Returns was part of the vanguard of the 2013/2014 resurgence of the computer RPG and while the mechanics were well implemented, the story felt flat and linear. This is something Harebrained tackled head-on with the Dragonfall DLC, later released as a stand-alone product. While it doesn't hold a candle to some of the behemoth open world CRPGs out there, there's a great deal more optional interaction to be discovered in Dragonfall versus the original Dead Man's Switch campaign.
More than the breadth of the world, Dragonfall really adds to its depth as well. The characters and dialog are uncommonly good. If you take the time to get to know the runners on your crew, you'll find a wealth of well-thought-out backstories doled out throughout the game in well-measured helpings. I would venture that this game performs well when viewed in the light of gender equality, as well. While the Sixth World can be an exploitive place, the game empowers you to do something about that. Dragonfall features a number of meaningful major roles for women, and their roles and backgrounds perform well against with-a-pink-bow and bechdel examinations. This game isn't making a statement about gender equality (because it's in no way "about" that), but I applaud it for executing its goals well while demonstrating that a quality title doesn't need to play into shallow tropes.
I've been reading the Shadowrun core rulebook for the pen & paper game to get a group started with some friends, many of whom are newbies to P&P RPGs, let alone Shadowrun. I've recommended this game to get them familiar with the universe. I'm very much looking forward to the next installation from HBG.

Done a couple missions and I must say the game is nicely put together. Each character has a unique personality. There are different dialogue options and approaches to each battle. There are unique classes and you can customize your character the way you want it. The hacking system is also very cool and unique compared to other games. The story itself is intriguing and will draw you in.
One of the things I like about this game a lot is the karma/skill system. Everytime you complete a mission or side mission you will get karma. Karma is used to upgrade your character's skills. There is a lot of customization for this and the race you choose will even impact this. You don't get anything for killing enemies in the game. This is a fresh way to go about it since I feel like some games reward the players too much. Complete the mission first to get the reward, not during the mission. It also means when reinforcements are coming you won't be inclined to want to kill them just for extra loot/xp.
All in all, I would give this game a 8.5/10. Talking to npcs can get boring, but this game is definitely worth the sale price tag. Just make sure you enjoy turn based combat.

This is like if you took Total War, ♥♥♥♥♥ed it up a little bit, removed any form of diplomacy, and implemented a pen n paper RPG style damage system. Oh, and converted all the graphics to crappy little 2D icons.
Here's some problems with this game.
You can't recruit anywhere except your capital, and some very specific other locations, such as guard towers, and broken castles. This is only a problem because if you don't happen to have any of these near your front lines, you are going to have to run your troops up (who only have 3 moves a turn which isn't very many) all the way up. And another thing. Because you have to have a commander commanding your troops, you need to have some guy ready to ferry those troops up, and you can't just buy a commander at any time, no, of course not. So say you need to replenish your troops on your fighting commander guy. You need to go all the way back to your capital or whatever recruitment building is closest, train your troops over as many turns as you need to get back up to strength, and then you can get back to fighting. This is a problem only because you can't recruit from villages. Even big named villages. It makes no sense.
This is enough for me to not recommend this game.
There's also without a doubt some balance issues. There's also no such thing as overexpansion. There's no downside to building an empire as ungodly huge as you can build it. There doesn't feel like a lot of depth to this game beyond the combat.
Actually watching a huge combat unfold is pretty cool, it's kind of a shame that you can't direct any of your units or anything, especially since you're going to see your wizards doing♥♥♥♥♥♥like using a big damage single target spell on a frog or something, as opposed to the massive hill giant next to him. But that's okay, since there wouldn't be a way to fix this.
The actual universe is... interesting to say the least. It's always nice to see classic fantasy. You can also play as the Innsmouth cult, basically, from Lovecraft canon. So that's cool. But then you've got... weird♥♥♥♥♥♥ Like giant moose and such which can trample an entire army, or take your cities and such.
Another thing that is really really annoying is that there's no militia or anything raised to protect a town. Nothing. You can just walk onto a space, and you own it. I get that this is a kind of thing one or two of the 'races' have, but it's still stupid. I'm not even talking something serious. I just want to see SOME kind of resistance, so a single wolf or something can't run into a town and take control of the whole thing.
I don't know, I don't want to compare this so much to Total War, but that's how it goes, this is pretty damn close to the Total War formula. Except it's only about conquering.
Let's talk about some of the rumours of 'depth' and 'tactics' - now let me tell your right here and now there really isn't much of either of these. There's no micromanagement except for your commander units, like you can equip these guys with certain magical things you find... if you ever find any. My last game I found two. Just two. One on a hero I bought, was some crappy mushroom spawning thing, and the other was a lightning staff from an enchantress I murdered, which was pretty cool actually.
There's no paper scissors rock type triangle, spears aren't extra strong versus cavalry, there's no flanking bonuses, nor are there bonuses for attacking from behind, obviously, and because of this, Conquest of Elysium has little to no depth whatsoever.
Don't praise a game for things it doesn't really have.
However, this is gonna be a thumbs up now. I've played it some more, and it's grown on me. It just depends on RNG to get you to the place you need to be in to actually get♥♥♥♥♥♥done.

This game is truly a gem. Conquest of Elysium 3 was good in itself, I played a lot with it and enjoyed it. That said, I don't play thousands of hours with a single game, I'm more diversed in the way of gaming I have. But this game is absolutely worth it! Illwinter Game Design made it. They are responsible for the Dominions series as well. That is more complex. This game is simpler, but that does not mean that it is simple! In fact it is not simple at all! You have either tons of units to recruit or tons of units to achieve with your special resources through Rituals of Masteries. It is more straightforward than Dominions. but it's depth is even deeper than many of the turn-based strategies today. There are zounds of units either under your control, or seeing the game as a whole. You have a choice from the beginning. What you want to do defines the gameplay for the 20 classes not mentioned before. These 20 classes range from Necromancers to Barbarians, through Senators and Demonologists, to name a few. I said before recruitment. You either have a lot to recruit from (but usually only one per turn can be recruited, with a few exceptions) or you have not many, but you can collect resources and expand your abilities named Rituals. Mostly, there are three levels of rituals. You can repeat a Ritual of Mastery many times, but the result will always be random, granting it infinite replayability! But it's the usual explore, exploit, expand, exterminate formula many times did before. I recommend it highly to anyone, who didn't try it before and is good at English. You should definitely give this game a try and let you get charmed by the atmosphere and music it has. You can play with your friends online or at the same computer at the same time! This game deserves the "Test of Time" Award, because I always return to this one. It is easy and hard in one.

De ez a játék abszolút megéri! Az Illwinter Game Design készítette. Ők a felelősek a Dominions-sorozatért is. Az sokkal összetettebb. Ez a játék egyszerűbb, de ez nem azt jelenti, hogy egyszerű! Valójában véve nem egyszerű egyáltalán! Vagy több tonnányi egységet tudsz bérelni vagy tonnányi egységet tudsz megszerezni a speciális nyersanyagokkal a Képzettség Rituálékon keresztül. Sokkal egyértelműbb, mint a Dominions, de a mélysége még így is mélyebb, mint sok körökre-osztott stratégia manapság. Hordányi egység van vagy a te irányításod alatt, vagy egészében véve a játékot. Van választásod az elejétől kezdve. Hogy mit akarsz tenni, az meghatározza a játékmenetet a 20 kasztnak, amit ezelőtt még nem is említettem. Ez a 20 osztály a Nekromantáktól kezdve a Barbárokig, a Szenátorokon át a Démonologusokig, hogy csak néhányat említsek. Mondtam ezelőtt a bérlést. Vagy sok bérlés közül választhatsz (de általában mindössze egyet lehet körönként felbérelni, néhány kivételt beleértve) vagy nincs sok, de gyűjthetsz nyersanyagokat és kibővítheted a képességeidet, amiket rituáléknak nevezünk. Többnyire három szintje van a rituáléknak. Megismételhetsz egy rituálét többször is, de a végeredmény mindig véletlenszerű lesz, végtelen újrajátszási lehetőséget biztosítva ezzel! De ez csak a szokásos felfedezés, kihasználás, terjeszkedés, kiírtás formula, amit már olyan sokszor megtettek. Erősen ajánlom mindenkinek, aki még nem próbálta és jól tud angolul. Feltétlenül ki kell próbáljad ezt a játékot és hagyd hogy az atmoszféra és zene elcsábítson. Játszhatsz a barátaiddal Online vagy ugyanannál a gépnél ugyanabban az időben! I have been looking for a game like this since Pharoah, but nothing really seemed to fit. I think a lot can still be added to flesh it out, but this game ticks a lot of boxes as it is.
Things like experience levels to improve efficiency of specifiic colonists, or even specialising into more advanced forms of production after gaining experience.
Sliders allowing you to adjust how much resources to allocate to entertainment vs food or new builds (or monolith building) vs production would also help. At the moment new builds gets everything and production has to wait. the build limits are ok, but kind of redundant, as production is back of the queue anyway.
Make building a monolith - or similar big useless projects - a bit more exciting... like building those piramids in Pharoah, watching the slaves pull the limestone up to the top :)
Being able to select what each storage allows in would also be a great addition. This will for instance avoid flooding spare parts storages with starch or vegetables after a new farm dome starts production.
A mini game to fly and land the colony ship would also be nice - allowing you to scout for a nice open flat plain to a limited degree.
