This game isn't as bad as people say it is. Sure, it can be buggy, and the framerate dips quite a bit, but it isn't too bad.
I think most people's problem with it is it's departure from Postal 2. If you're looking for a Postal 2-like experience, don't get this, get Postal 2 Paradise Lost. It's cheaper and honestly a much better product.
This game isn't like Postal 2, it's a third person action shooter with a Postal 2 theme to it.
So, pros and cons:
Pros:
- Lots of new weapons and items - such as beehives to throw at enemys
- Lost of references to Postal 2 - Lots of items/weapons return, recap of what happened in the last game, and quite a few returning characters
- Champ... Champ is awesome
- The game looks very nice. Seriously, the graphics are amazing
- You can dash - a feature that I wish was in Postal 2
- It's amazingly fun to completely trample people by dashing at them
- Branching story with different missions for each branch
- The art is quite nice
Cons:
- The controls are ♥♥♥♥ing wonky at times. Sometimes your accuracy is really off, and everything is either above or below the crosshair. Also, you can't jump anymore. You can only vault over certain objects while you're taking cover behind them
- The framerate dips a lot
- The game crashes occasionally
- Quite a few odd glitches
- The saving system is pretty garbage. Unlike Postal 2 where it was clean and organized, this saving system has your save data all over the place
- No difficulty settings. Postal 2 had so many difficulty settings to choose from, so why can't this?
- Rick Hunter (The Postal Dude's voice actor) isn't here for this game. Instead, they have Cory Cruise substituting for him. Cory does an alright job, but it isn't as good as Rick, in my opinion
- The inventory is a cluttered mess. In Postal 2, everything was organized into catagories
Pros or Cons? - These I'll leave up to you to decide:
- The game is in third person now
- The game is much more linear. Postal 2 put you in an open world with some objectives to complete around the map, while Postal III is linear and mission based.
- The soundtrack is pretty good, but often times very oddly unfitting
- The distastful humor from Postal 2 is back, and ramped up to be worse than before
I haven't played the game too much yet, but honestly I feel like I've gotten the full experience from just my first 2 hours of gameplay.
So far I've enjoyed the game, but I'll let you weight the pros and cons and make a decisions for yourself.
Also, rather than paying for it and giving Akella more money that they don't deserve, just email Mike J of RWS asking for a key. He's often pretty generous with them.

I have put 3,000 hours into this game, made over 40 tutorial videos for new players, and it is bloody-well killing me to click the Thumbs Down button.
This game started as a simple Match 3 RPG-style game with simple quests and a very obvious method of progressing as a player.  The rules were intuitive and playing delivered a great emotional satisfaction where for the most part, player skill would triumph over whatever else was happening.  New Troops rolled out frequently which keep the game fresh.
Over time new features were added such as unlock-able Traits and new mechanics such as Freeze, Disease, etc.  Additional game modes such as the resource-grinding Explore were added plus PvP Mode which over the last year has become firmly entrenched as the core game experience. Recently a featured called Guild Wars was added and this week saw the introduction of Soulforge (crafting) and Daily Dungeons which reward new currency types.
All of this sounds good on paper: A game which is ever-evolving and continually adding new Game Modes and Troops to keep things fresh.  Sadly what has happened in reality is that this simple, humble Match 3 game has gradually outgrown itself and become a gigantic, twisted, lumbering, convoluted mess.
New bugs enter with almost every new game tweak or newly introduced troop/mechanic. Other things that are broken are game design decisions which were made solely for the purpose of wringing extra money from the player base but they went too far.  I believe every game has the right to make money, especially when they deliver the value that GoW does, I just feel like it has gotten out-of-hand.
The new Guild War mode is a fiasco which was
.  They have been designing it and tweaking it on the fly for the past 3 months or so on the backs of the players.  Imagine how it feels when the core rules of the biggest aspect of the game change every week.  And when many of the changes are held in secret by the developers.  And when the game has changed to the point where you never feel in control as a player any more.
All of this could be forgiven if the core game experience had remained approximately the same: namely a skill-based Match 3 game.  Sadly with the introduction of the Guild Guardian characters 6 months ago the game has been on a progressive slide away from being skill-based and more towards being a slot-machine, where Boosts which the player may buy ahead of time give them a better chance in the final outcome
The most recent adjustments to the pRNG and the "AI luck settings" (which in-part determine how many free gem cascades and free turns the AI gets) has made the problem absolutely lethal.  This problem multiplies further when you add in the ever-changing, hidden formula which artificially limits the number of useful consecutive actions or moves a player may take. And it doesn't stop there, don't forget to multiply this frustration by the fact that many Counters, Traits and Game Mechanics are bugged meaning many times you have absolutely no control over the outcome.
I have always been a fair and balanced player in this game, ensuring not to become emotionally excited one way or the next as this game has always been under constant construction.  It has just gotten to the point where I actually
because it is more like a slot machine now where it used to feel more along the lines of chess, and this slide away from skill-based play is something I personally detest.
Mark my words, if this game is restored to some form of skill-based play as it was before I will come back and revise this review.  But per the above complaints the game is garbage ATM and has been for at least 10 weeks, and I would not recommend anybody

I was a huge fan of the first Defense Grid. I think I have around 170 hours in it last time I checked. I was really looking forward to DG2! I pre-purchased it and played the beta a LOT!
After nearly 30 hours of game play in the final release, I feel a little let down. DG2 isn't a bad game by any means but there are a few annoying things about it that keep me from loving it the way I did the first one.
First of all, the scoring in the game makes absolutely no sense what-so-ever. Even after all my hours in the game, I have no idea which strategies earn the most points (and I've read all the posts from the developer about the points system). The point system seems very random. The tips the developer has on the DG2 Steam forum are at the very least misleading. The things they claim get your the most points, absolutely do not. The only reason I was able to put up several top 50 scores is nothing more than dumb luck. I have no idea what I did differently that got me more points than other times I played those maps.
Ultimately I find the points system extremely frustrating. If I don't know what kinds of things I get rewarded for, how can I possibly come up with strategies that will advance my skill level in the game? I don't want to win with luck. I want to win because I came up with a brilliant plan to score the most points given a known set of measurements of success or failure.
Other than that, the game is actually pretty fun. If you're looking for a tower defense game you can play for 15 to 20 hours, DG2 is a great choice (If you already have DG1). If you want a game you can replay over and over, you might want to pass on this one.

Baezult 2 is a puzzle platformer that is both incredibly challenging but also very fair and avoids being frustrating.
Most of the game is spent pushing blocks around, blowing up walls, and shooting enemies in specific sequences while avoiding obstacles and doing time-constrained platforming. However the game rarely gets infuriating because Baezult 2 doesn't lead the player running around in circles wondering what they did wrong. If you messed up a puzzle, it is immediately apparent that you made a mistake. This helps give the game this smooth flow to the puzzles, and solving them immensely satisfying.
However, I was a bit surprised by how short the game was, but I don't think that it detracts from my over-all opinion of the game. Just be aware that it's only an hour or two in length depending on how fast you can solve the puzzles and complete the platforming challenges.
PROS:
- Clever puzzles.
- Great level design.
- Solid mix of challenge-platformers and puzzle-platformers.
- Cheap
MIDDLE-GROUND:
- Very short.
CONS:
- Controls can feel a little bit too slippery.
- Music gets grating and can't be muted in the game options.
SCORE: 8/10

Stands alone in the cyberpunk turn-based RPG market.  There are other games with similar themes, but there's nothing as good as Shadowrun: Dragonfall in terms of the finished product.
-Incredible amount of character skins and specializations.  The experience is slightly different based on the race, class, and specialization of skills you choose.  My dwarf rigger uses totally different combat strategies than my human street-samaurai, and triggers different interactions with NPCs.
-Excellent ambient soundtrack music and effects add suspense.
-Better than average story blending magic, corporate espionage, and political intrigue in post-modern Berlin.
-Variety of missions including data-theft, pickup-and-deliver, assassination, negotiation, and protection.
-Optional objectives (side quests) between missions, or often within them.
-Events become available (or unavailable), based on your choices in conversations and side quests.
Usually your team is limited to 4 runners, but the combats never feel unbalanced since your team gains greater skills as you progress through the story.  Fans of other turn-based tactical RPGs like Ogre Battle, Fire Emblem, or Final Fantasy Tactics should probably own Shadowrun: Dragonfall.

Much, much better than both the story and engine of the original Shadowrun campaign. This is a solid tactical RPG with an incredibly well-written story, nested in a well-crafted future Berlin. The combat lacks the polish of games like XCOM, but when taken as a whole with the excellent story and stylized art, it packs a hell of a punch.
I really liked the first one and this one is a step up from that, cool graphics and music. For anyone looking for a tough puzzle platformer I recommend Baezult 2.
I liked the original well enough that I'm happy for the opportunity to toss the creator a fiver.  :)  Good so far, though note that this is more of a DX remake than a sequel (which is cool by me).
I love the Shadowrun world and this scenario plays better than the first offering; I look forward to more installments.

This game was brilliant.  I haven't written many reviews for games on Steam, but this one blew me away enough to take the time.
I was a little apprihensive buying this as I played Shadowrun Returns and did not like it very much.  The story was nice (if a little farfetched) but the controls were abysmal.  Shadowrun Dragonfall - Directors Cut fixed any of the issues that I had with the previous game.
Story - 10/10
It was literally incredible.  It may be text heavy for some, but if you take the time to read all the interactions it is like reading a book.  Where as most text interactions just say what the characters are saying, this game includes facial gestures, descriptions of the surroundings including sights, smells and sounds.  I would have read a book or watched a movie with the same story and absolutely loved it.  A really fantastic selling point that many games don't have these days.
Gameplay - 8/10 (28 hours to complete primary campaign)
I am not usually a huge fan of turn based combat (RTS fan), but this system was very smooth and easy to get a handle on.  There were a few points left out of the tutorials (It took me about half the game to figure out that you could activate cyberwear) and the initial exploration of your home town was a little stunted by a lack of anything to guide you (It took me three missions to figure out that there was a cyberwear shop in your home town as it was tucked away in the corner).
Graphics, Art and Atmosphere - 9/10
Everything went to setting up an excellent atmosphere for the game.  The ambient sounds were fantastic throughout the final game (A little clunky in the finale) and the effort to create weather effects and ambient lighting really helped set the picture of the world.
Final Thoughts
I waited for this game to go on sale before I bought it as I was a little apprihensive after Shadowrun Returns.  If I knew what I know now, I would have bought this game for full price on it's release date.  I also cannot wait to play through some fanmade adventures from the workshop.
TL:DR - If you are a fan of turn based RPG's and don't mind reading text.  10/10 would recommend this game.

If your looking for an awesome RTS game to curb your boredom, then look no further, Forged Alliance is my favorite RTS game to date and the fact that I have over 500 hours on record, should be good enough for me to write my own review of the game. I'm not sure I can express how much fun it is to play Supreme Commander: Forged Alliance, but I'll try anyway. I like to take my time when playing, just to make sure I have enough fire power to overwhelm my enemies, even when I'm challenging my friends, but they make me work for it so it's a fun experience overall.
If you've got the specs to run the game, I guarantee that you will love playing it for hours everyday. I know I do and even though you go through the same thing every time when going through campaign, it's still fun and makes great practice to further develop your skills. I've played this game for years and it never fails to curb my boredom. In the beginning of the campaign, you choose the level of difficulty: Easy, Medium or Hard (Do not choose hard if your just starting out, you will get owned within the first 30 minutes of starting the campaign.) When it's time, you'll choose your faction: UEF, Aeon or Cybran. Just remember that each faction has a particular strength that the other factions either can't do or do better, but also remember that you can repeat the campaign as many times as you want and you can play throught it with all 3 factions.
You can even choose to skirmish your friends or Computer AI's or both and with the AI's having different levels of skill, you'll probably have your work cut out for you. If you dare choose one of the hard difficulties, let's see if you can adapt when the AI is sending experimentals your way every few minutes among the other possible waves of units. My advice, build up a strong defense and make sure you can hold the line long enough to turn the tide.
There is also multiplayer for anyone who just wants to challenge their friends to an all out fight or you can choose to fight in teams. Let's see if any of you have what it takes to reign supreme, but no matter how it ends, you'll all have fun doing it.
Good luck to you all who are just starting out and just try to have fun.

The original video gaming mascot is back in his best game since the 1980s. Pac-Man Championship Edition DX+ takes Pac back to his roots with single screen arcade levels. The controls are simple, up, left, down and right to make Pac-Man move through different labyrinths, eating pellets and dodging ghosts. When Pac-Man eats a power pellet, the hunters become the hunted and Pac-Man will eat the ghosts to death! Think about that logic!
But that's how the classic game played, and while there isn't much difference between then and now, Pac-Man Championship Edition DX+ has different 'challenges' that you select and play. Mostly time trials that have you eating enough fruit to complete the objective after eating enough pellets to make the fruit appear. You'll also have score attacks that put you in a level for 5 or 10 minutes to get the highest score you can. There is even a ghost chain mode that will have you seeing how many ghosts you can eat before a power pellet wears off. Each challenge needs to be unlocked and for the most part they're all easy, but a lot of quick fun.
The game now has 'inactive' ghosts that stand in gaps. They don't move, they're just there, until Pac-Man sets them off, but they don't just chase him. Instead they wait for another ghost to float by and then join a ghost chain. These chains get longer and longer as a sort of centipede. Its visually impressive and adds a new dynamic of just having a long string of enemies to avoid. When you get a power pellet, it feels satisfying to eat fifty ghosts. These ghosts can also have pellets and power pellets in them, so to advance through the game, you need to eat the ghosts. It is a nice twist.
That's not the only twist, you don't clear an entire level like the original Pac-Man. The game makes lines of pellets after you eat each fruit. It might seem easy to just follow the lines, but the challenge comes from Pac-Man moving so fast and ghosts being everywhere. The maps will even get altered to block out paths or make new paths. With every complete line you eat, a piece of fruit will appear along with the next line and more 'inactive' ghosts. So it feels like there is always something changing and happening. Even the level changes colors.
Each of the game's 10 or so unlockable levels are a vibrant array of neon colors, but before you start each challenge, you can change each level's look. From old school pixelated Pac-Man to new school and even the lego block look from previous games. You can change the sprites too. Its a nice dynamic that can keep the game looking fresh. There is also plenty of DLC to buy that changes sprites and level graphics. The background music sounds great and the fast paced beat matches the arcade action.
There is even a new gameplay mechanic of ghost clearing bombs. When you use a bomb it sends all active ghosts to their penalty box in the middle of the screen. These bombs are helpful when you get pinched by two ghosts, but to to some people bombs might feel like cheating even if they decrease your scoring rate temporarily.
The game is fast paced. Eating ghosts will make the game go faster. Higher difficulties will make the game start out faster. It creates a need for fast paced reflexes, while still being forgiving, because if you are headed for a ghost, the game will slow down to give you time enough to dodge it. It is very helpful and feels forgiving.
If its too easy for you, there are three difficulties, each give you fewer and fewer bombs and lives along with amping up the game speed. If you lose a life, it simply sends the active ghosts to their penalty box, but you get to continue on after a brief delay.
This is what Pac-Man should have been all along. Just upgrading and tweaking the original classic. Well worth $10 for any arcade lover, but get it at a discount, especially since the game has so much DLC to purchase.

A few things to note, this game is not for everyone, the graphics aren't the most advanced and the fighting isn't exactly hands on, infact youre not even a general! Think of yourself as the quartermaster/recruiter/eventorganizer
You don't fight, you don't lead, you just tell people where to go and give them troops and they do the rest!
So what is Coe4 exactly?
Its a turn based strategy game where various players are competing to be crowned big boss
The gameplay itsself is quite simple, pick a class (these guys are each unique, some more so than others) You gather gold/iron/ and depending upon your class one of the following: Gems, Herbs, Mushrooms, Sacrifices, The severed hands of criminals as well as weed.
That's right weed, those cheeky hoburglar hopped up on some green stuff, no wonder their fat.
If you've sticked around for this long heres real talk.
This game fufiles a niche that is lacking in strategy games. While you can play it seriously you can also play it with a more laid back attitude, while their is some strategy and though required, for the most part the game is not balanced, their is a lot of variety and things you can do.
The gameplay itsself is quite simple to learn but complicated to master. While on the surface each class seems to be similar to several other in one way or another, their not.
Each class plays drastically difference from each other has advatanges and disadvantages, as well as various unique abilitites beyond similarites, for example: The Senator, based off of Roman esque legionaries can declare himself the Emperor which gives him a few boons, no one else can do this, unless of course you encounter someone or a bot playing as the Senator and then proceed to take control of him :p
---Now for my personal opinion
Their is a lot to be desired but I love this game for what it is: A laid back be a warlord stomp some face with your armies get conquered by deer because you forgot to leave a troop behind, reroll as a caster get mauled by a manticore on turn one, reroll again as a druid, off to a great start, what's this no special location to be able realize your full potential?
This game won't hold your hand, it is also not forgiving, but this game teaches you to learn from mistakes, to look to the future but also remember the present and most importantly scouts are not a luxury they are a necessity.
So yes I recomend it, but I also recomend if a friend has it, to play theirs, or to watch some videos on YouTube before buying simply because this game is not for everyone.

I wish there would be a thumbs in the middle option. I really enjoy this game and it is by no means a bad title but there are a few issues that just keep me from recomending it. Because for the price tag the game lacks a lot of features I would expect. There are hardly any settings. The level selection is semi-randomized and there is no way to edit anything when setting up your game. And with the rather annoying 30second landing animation it takes forever (and countless reloads) to get a starting position you like. The planets are hardly any different from each other, some are more effective when using solar powers, while others prefer wind energy, some have radiation, but thats almost all there is to it (and I am fairly sure the desert and the ice planet are just reskins of each other). The objectives are the same on every planet and they are rather boring and uninspired (get X habitants, build X of Y etc.) Especially in the late game the AI tends to go out of the window, and you could end up with scenarios where you have plenty of food, distributed over several cantinas and storage units and people still line up in front of one machine and starve. Except for building and changing a few settings in rather unintuitive menues (especially the one where you distribute percentages for new colonists AND the trading menu are HORRIBLY designed) you have hardly any real input options. No reasearch, no real tec-trees etc.
I still really enjoyed playing it. the atmosphee is awesome, the soundtrack is really immersive and it is just a grasping game, but after a while you realise that the game tries to pretend it is a broader and deeper experience than it actually is. It is basically a 2-3h game that was artifically stretched with more of the same to legitimize its rather pricey cost (for what it actually brings to the table)

This is my very first review on Steam.
The game is geared for paying players.
I only played the single player game, I'm not interested in pvp.
As a casual player you don't stand a chance. I couldn't even complete the first quest completely. My cheap units vs strong ai units (pay to win!). It was fun for a while, but then when you're nearing the end of the first quest all the enemy units seem overpowered compared to your weak units (regardless of team/color setup).
Your troops start off as white cards, then green, blue purple and pink is all I've seen. Yeah the game is really fair, my white and maybe green cards vs all the colors above in various combinations (oh that's right, I forgot it's pay to win, play for free only goes so far...). Even the ai white cards present a serious problem. You know there is something wrong when you're still trying to get enough mana for an ability, however the ai has already wiped out 3 of your 4 units.
I tried the other two (close) kingdoms, the first part of each quest I was able to beat (barely) and that was it. Exps and gold are slow to come by, so you must grind, replaying the same losing battle over and over. After a while this just gets boring.
I got the impression that the hint system is more helpful to the ai's next move. It will suggest moves (when there are multiple moves) that will help the ai's next move much more. And the ai never misses anything. And the funny thing is it will suggest matches for colors you have no use for (but if you look ahead you'll see why it's suggesting that particular move). Also noticed that when there are no more moves and it reshuffles fresh for the ai every time. Never once in my short game time did it reshuffle at the end of the ai's move. So don't tell me the gem drops are random.
Supposedly your supposed to be able to collect taxes from your kingdoms (every hour plus whatever is your daily amount). What a crock of poop. All I ever get is 32 gold next day of play. I've unlocked 2 cities, the next one will cost 1000gp to unlock, to get that I'll either need to log in every day for 32 days or win/lose 40 +/- battles or some combination of the two. Perhaps you could make your game more clear with this? What I see when I click income is gold per day (590) +35. And yet next day of game play I get 32 and that's it, plus the usual 17-25 per battle.
The only difference between winning and losing a battle is you get a traitstone, otherwise it's 3-5 exps (souls in the game) and 25 gold max. It's 10 exps to get a troop to level 2, 25 to 3, then 75 to 4 (good luck), talk about a very grindy game.
There's no random encounters, all battles are quest pre-determined. So you must constantly fight the same groups over and over......
You'll get a couple hours of fun, get bored, and then delete the game (or pay to play and enjoy it).

Once you get through that "newbie" phase you start working on completing your collection, merging multiple copies of cards to make them stronger, farming material to add abilities, etc...  The bulk of the game is your team against AI controlled versions of other player's troops to gain resources used to make your team stronger.  Even after months of play and an active guild there is still things to strive to  obtain, so it isn't game that will leave you with a "now what?" feeling.
And while you can use microtransactions to buy resources, it is by no means required nor is there any sense of "Pay to Win"

One of the most under-appreciated games of all time.
The most positively user reviewed game tagged with RTS on Steam.
Mediocre campaign generally speaking, but containing the BEST real-time strategy gameplay... ever.
When you have learned how to play it properly (50+ hours at least), you realise that SupCom FA does real-time strategy better than any other RTS in the world. An RTS should allow the player to use all the systems he has at his disposal, and use those systems -and his excellent knowledge and wisdom- to make TOOLS in which he uses to complete the objective. Let me explain.
In other RTS games, you get resources, you put those resources into aggressive units, and you attack the enemy.
In Supreme Commander, you have a basic start, and then the rest is completely up to you. There are many resources: Mass, Energy, Time, "Build Power", "Micro", but
just now on the spot. You have so many units available to you to use in new ways. These units are not limited to merely 'aggression'. The magnificent unit diversity allows for all sorts of strategic applications. And not just units, but buildings too.
You could send an engineer out right into enemy territory, get it to build a Stealth Generator, construct a Tactical Missile battery, and snipe the enemy commander. This is a logical combination of only THREE units, and none of them the typical 'go and shoot stuff' aggressive units you find in other RTS games. You could teleport a Support Command Unit into the heart of the enemy turtle base and destroy the Strategic Missile Defense in his three seconds of life so that your nuclear missile can do its job. You could send a decoy squadron of Interceptors along one flank of the enemy's base so that your transport drop of an army can get past his horde of Air Superiority Fighters and do damage to the base. You could choose to put your resources into Mass Extractor upgrades and engineers, so that your engineers can focus their build power on speeding up the upgrades one by one, and so run away with exponential increase economy. Actually, that last one is done by all good players anyway. But you can do it as much as you like. There are endless combinations.
The situation is never 'I have x resources, I can put them into y firepower' it is 'I have x spare engineers - I can put some on reclaim and use those bonus resources from reclaim to go into ecenomic upgrades', and 'I have x spare resources that are being wasted sitting in my storage instead of being aggressive units that could get me more ground and Mass Extractors or shields that could give me better hold of what territory I have already claimed', etc.. Your Mass resources can take the form of strong and heavy turrets. Your Energy resources can take the form of air scouts.
But they do not have to stay in those forms. In SupCom you can reclaim those resources by dismantling structures and units through your build power. This unlocks massive intuition, adaptation, and freedom - aspects that encourage strategy. It feels right in an RTS that you can switch up your techniques so easily. You cannot go back to the cold dark RTS games where dumping resources into the wrong form dooms you.
Reclaim is certainly not the only thing in SupCom that makes it so outstanding. It gets everything right. It is the combination of unit variety, resource conversion, scale, and control that makes up so great strategic freedom. I cannot put into words how perfectly Supreme Commander gets strategy.
Admittedly, it is quite a learning curve for the first few hours, and then you think you've got it, but then you find you got the basics, and you need to build complexity on those basics so you can unlock more learning curve. It's hard to do, but you can expect so much from such freedom. And if you can't grasp it, just play it simple: get the economy right, and turtle. Lots of players do this. They pick a map with one thin line or gap so that the two teams can hold the line or gap against the other team while everyone gets a superpowered economy and shoves firepower into the middle. Not much strategy, but enough to satisfy many.
(This paragraph: some re-iteration and self-explanation; skippable.
Supreme Commander features the most streamlined control options I have ever seen in an RTS, and a unit/race balance that is far more dependable than other RTS games. Though this may limit the diversity of faction units and maps, it is for the benefit of having a clean canvas on which the players can work fair and beautiful strategic destruction.
Personally, I find the mathematical artistry of strategy war gaming to be more greatly rendered in Supreme Commander Forged Alliance than in any game in the world (apart from chess). This aspect is what captures my interest. The breadth and depth of strategic warfare are greater in Supreme Commander than in the tens of other RTS games I have played. Behind the steep learning curve and the very small scale match start lies pure strategy that is more refined and accessible. Supreme Commander does better in enabling the player to develop their strategic brainstorming and application without restraint, achieving their own art of war through the perfect mechanics of Supreme Commander.
I know this is all wordy and may not carry much solid fact, but it is a difficult understanding to explain. For me, where other RTS games seem to sit on the same strategy of rush with the right mix of different unit types, Supreme Commander opens Real-Time Strategy to what it was always supposed to be: the set-up necessary to allow the players to continuously evolve their own strategies in matches that are as much of the mind as of the mouse.)
Short story: grand scale of war, control of your forces, freedom of strategy...
BEST RTS EVER. Get it. Or at least watch some casts by Gyle on YouTube. Be warned, many of them are epic, that means potentially hours long, and yes, skirmishes do last that long because SupCom is epic. And then get Forged Alliance Forever - the community lobby, which I could write another entire review for.

After you buy this game, (which if you haven't already, what's taking you so long) head over to
, a community lobby built by the SupCom community. It is ~10,000 members strong, with a competition ladder, up to 6v6 custom matches, a dozen+ mods, galactic war, the campaigns of SupCom and Forged Alliance redone to allow up to 4 player co-op, and more. It's free and adds far more to this game than any other RTS on the market.
Hands down the best RTS game available. This game really does things right by focusing on the obliteration of your opponents through sheer force of strength and easy economy management. Don't like the tediousness of micro-managing your economy and just want to throw hundreds of units constantly at each other? Are you annoyed that you have to wait until you have resources stockpiled before you can build units? Want to build massive units to wipe your enemies off the face of the earth? Do you enjoy being able to specialize in either land, air, or naval units, or use combinations of each? This game is what you're looking for.
Now the only question is, what are you waiting for?
Post-Robotic Revoultion Simulator.
Fordged Alliance Forever!

Gripping turn-based fun.  Would say 'strategy' but that mostly relies on metagame knowledge.
Dialogue options allow for several types of characters (bleeding heart or experienced shadowrunner).  Characters have rich backstories and optional missions to help resolve some loose ends for them.  The setting is oozing with cyberpunk charm and there are plenty of notes and emails to bring life to an already believable anarchist Berlin.  Choices have consequences, even if some are only getting some hateful email from somebody you wronged during a job.
The only gripe I have is how combat is initiated by the enemy.  This often happens when you use a dialogue option to 'Attack', open a door, round a corner, or load into a new zone.  This always happens with your main character in the lead, your group huddled around him/her for warmth, out of cover, and enemies in or moving to cover.  The enemy moves and acts first, they favor squishy targets, and they love grenading tightly packed groups of sheep.  Kicks you right out of the experience everytime you see your crack squad of shadowrunners who have seen so many raids but get caught flat-footed when breaching a room full of guards they know are there.
Lots of reading. Fantastic story. Perfect noir atmosphere. Compelling combat system. 10/10!

Brilliant game.
Pros:
Deceptively complex beneath a simple superficial appearance.
Hundreds of unit - still coming across new ones after 60 hours playtime.

Randomly generated maps guarantee replayability.
End-game spells and summoning generates even further variety and cunning interactions (like the necromancer summoned Abomination that grows more and more powerful if left on a tile with corpses from a previous battle).
Cons:
Old-school graphics, I find the sprites and tile based look appealing but mileage may vary.
Randomly generated start positions can occassionally make the early game very difficult.
Highly recommend to people who want a good game with excellent underlying mechanisms rather than just shiny graphics (looking at you Total War series).

First review (thumbed up):
If you searched Steam for Master of Magic, and somehow wound up here, buy this game.  It's as close as you're going to get, and that is very high praise.
Second Update 27 Feb 2016 (thumbed down):
Having sunk a bunch more time into this (offline mode, I probably have fifty hours offline), I'm ready to thumb it down. It's tedious. MoM was never tedious to me. There is a non-stop barrage of deer, snakes, wild life, and wandering nobodies that continually take your farms, forests, and anything else you could have possibly laid claim to. For no good reason. Two wandering deer do not chase people from their farm.
It's a non-stop game of recapture. You leave three guys to defend the farm? Four bears show up and kill them. If that's not bad enough, there are actual random factions and events that pop up for the sole purpose of spitting random extra monsters across your lands.
If you start a game with five AI, three of them will be killed by neutral "armies" (deer) in the first dozen turns or so. As far as I can tell, the only difference you get for ramping the AI difficulty up is that they start with bigger armies (and probably get cheaty amounts of resources per turn).
I assume I'm just bad at the game still, but there's no excuse for the amount of rubbish that exists just to force you to keep recapturing the same thing over and over.
Third Review  7 Jan 2017 (thumbed up):
You should probably own this game.  It's pretty damn good.  What I said before holds true, but it's possible they've tweaked the deer attacks so that there are less of them.  I think there's an option now to make more of them.  Play slower, keep all heros active and with at least a very small army so you can run around recapturing things.
If you like 4X games where there are lots of different characters / play styles, you can't go wrong with this one.

Not much there, there.
Planetbase has a great concept - build a base, in space. The mechanics are simple, and life is tough on distant worlds. Ultimately, though, the game stops being fun around the 5th hour of play when you realize there's a pattern to building a base and keeping things balanced. Once you've figured out how to maintain that balance, there's nothing left to do.
Ostensibly, a goal of the game includes building a bigger and bigger base. Which is great in theory, but not that much fun in practice. There's really no variation; build x, build y, build z to support x and y, and so on; repeat when you finish the list.
Does this game have potential? Yes. But right now it's less a game than a thought experiment. Once you figure out the build pattern, there's nothing left to do.

Gems of War is a CCG Match-3 Puzzle RPG. Every one of these elements has a pivotal stake in the gameplay, so if any of these elements are considered undesirable to you, the game could begin to feel like a slog at certain points.
Cross-Platform between PC/Mobile, while the Xbox/Playstation versions are purely independent and are unable to connect across platforms. Keep this in mind when choosing which platform to play on. (Certain features are exclusive to Xbox and Playstation, while other features might be missing.)
Gems of War has come a long way from when I first started. This is a bit of a running theme with how active patches are in the game, completely reworking some mechanics every couple or few months. Adaptability is very important to have in this case. If you don't like change, whether in your team setup, new features, or reworked mechanics, I highly recommend you against playing this game.
But even among all the differences between when I first started and now, a few things have always remained the same. The core gameplay, the weekly excitement, and the amazing developers.
As mentioned in the beginning of this review, GoW has 3 very consistent points to stand on.
- If you've ever played a CCG online game, you'll no right off the bat that trading is a no go. There's no clear plans of this changing anytime soon either. So if you're desperate to get that one troop card you really want, you'll have to leave your fate in the hands of the RNG.
- Power up your troop's spells by collecting on board colored gems. You can match skulls instead to inflict attack damage. These are both very important to your success in winning a match. Troops spells often offer board control to manipulate the playing field to your advantage, or possibly screw yourself over. 4+ matches also offer an extra turn, meaning another free match before the opponent gets to play, so thinking out your moves and observing the board carefully are important.
- Leveling, Ascension, and Traits are all key aspects in powering-up your troops to better handle opponents. Obviously some troops will outshine others, some times you'll need to use another team to handle the situation better than your primary one. There's many ways to learn how to build your teams, but the best one is the Arena, an important minigame that'll teach you team synergy and introduce you to all sorts of spells.
Weekly events are what they're known as, and are a fun way to keep you interested in playing. Whether it's a new troop or Hero weapon, not a week's gone by since I began playing that there wasn't something to look forward to.
Some months a new kingdom is introduced, and other months we've got a whole new patch to explore! The amount of content provided so frequently is mind-boggling sometimes, and keeps my interest firmly gripped for whatever may come next.
You honestly won't see them much around the Steam community or in the AppStore, but if you give their
a chance, you'll quickly realize how much attention they pay to player feedback. They keep active and enjoy chatting with the community, even when things get rather heated.
Support will also quickly look into and resolve issues as soon as possible, they've even offered apology gifts to compensate the delay on occasion.
Some people have expressed concern or a hatred for certain aspects of the game, so I'll be addressing these issues here so you can know to avoid the game if they aren't to your liking.
So is this game for you? If the idea of a Match-3 RPG with countless hours of play (700+ hours now and not even halfway done) sounds interesting to you, definitely give it a shot.

There is a lot to love and a lot to hate in Gems of War, but at its core, it is an enjoyable game to play. There is something elegent about mashing together a match 3 and deck building game. Being a match 3, there is always an element of luck to winning. There is also a lot of skill that goes into building a good deck. The two are as balanced as it gets.
Despite being an always online game with guild and chat features, it is a single player game. Even the PVP feature puts you against a player created team controlled by AI. This is the biggest thing I can fault the game for. I would love if the game were to have true PVP, or at least an offline mode.
Being a F2P game, I must also mention the payment model. The game currently follows a pay to grind less model. While everything except the newest piece of armor is obtainable for free, it will take a long time to get normally in game. Currently, the amount of available troops is expanding faster than I can generate resources to upgrade them. If you are a completionist who likes variety, this may become an expensive and time consuming game for you. However, if you can pick out your favorites and stick to them, you will never need to spend a dime to enjoy the game.

There are specialities, which focus on which gems give extra mana (which allows you to use special moves quicker)
You can also gain souls, which are used to level up your characters. With hundreds, if not thousands of different characters with different abilities and majoring in different gem colours, there are so many combinations to create to make your team all-powerful.
Guilds are also an increasing important role (ahem, mines is "WARMACHIN3"). Guild participation allows for additional keys for treasure chests (these give characters, as well as other cool stuff), gold (this helps progress to other areas), souls (help with levelling characters), diamonds (good for buying new armour)and maps (allow you to gain extra loot)
In order to go into every detail of the game I would be writing for a long time, there is plenty to do and hold your interest. It’s amazing to think that it’s been six years since Hidden Path released the acclaimed Defense Grid: The Awakening, often cited as one of the defining tower defense games. For the sequel, Hidden Path took to Kickstarter and with overwhelming support the game became a reality. And the reality is that Defense Grid 2 is just as good as the original, totally nailing the strategic and addictive elements that are so crucial for any tower defense game. Unfortunately, the reality is also that Defense Grid 2 is basically identical to its predecessor which is definitely mildly disappointing.
If you ever played a tower defense game, you’ll be right at home here. If not, the short but clear tutorial will get you up to speed. Basically, you have to defend your base and stop aliens taking your cores by building towers with various abilities. For example, Inferno towers set groups of aliens aflame at close range, Temporal towers slow them down whereas Missile towers deal massive damage at long range. All tower types serve a specific purpose and you will make good use of them all in order to defend each map. Just like the towers, the aliens as well come in different forms. Some are large and slow, some are small but fast, some have stealth, others regenerate or spawn other aliens. Naturally, enemy variety is crucial in order to ensure each tower type is useful. Sometimes the paths the aliens take will be set, other times you will have the option to block certain routes carving out the longest and most winding path you possibly can in order to ensure maximum tower usage. The map design is nothing short of fantastic walking a fine line between intentional design and player experimentation.
Defense Grid 2 looks and sounds great. Each tower is distinct and easily recognizable which becomes extremely important in later rounds. Sometimes you’ll have a bit of time to just observe the glorious carnage unfold before you. Most of the time, however, you will be scrambling to make important but quick decisions. Every wave will pose a different threat and you don’t have much time to assess what is the best move. You also have limited resources which you earn as you clear each wave. This is where Defense Grid 2 truly shines. It seems so effortless and yet so many tower defense games fail on this tactical level. It’s truly a fast-paced, action-packed strategy game.
By far the worst aspect of the game is the storytelling. The original was light on narrative, you only had a single AI advisor which had something to say from time to time about the current happenings. This time, you have six or seven badly written and acted AIs who love to yammer on about whatever is going on and even beyond that. It quickly gets really annoying and detracts from the overall experience.
Even though I am a bit disappointed by the lack of new towers and new ideas and the awful, intrusive storytelling, the truth is that Defense Grid 2 is a very good game and an easy recommendation to anyone who is remotely interested in tower defense games.
7 OUT OF 10 (GOOD)

While falling short of the challenge provided by the original, Defense Grid 2 nonetheless provides a satisfying journey through twenty stylish and interesting stock maps.
The game stumbles with a distracting and indecipherable voice-over 'story' and multiplayer problems but the coming addition of custom maps and the potential for an improved online experience make Defense Grid 2 a worthy addition to your catalog if purchased at a discounted price.

Supre Ruler: the Great War is a great expansion on the basic Supreme Ruler Ultimate. However... the problem exists that many of the bugs that have been in the series since when I played Supreme Ruler 2020 in 2009 still exist. The game works, but unless you want to sit there and micromanage your units and construction and a great many other things, it's just not fun.

These global strategy games can be complex. In pretty much all of them, there's a lot going on at once that you need to manage - internal politics and finance, military, diplomacy, research, etc. So no matter how good the game in question is, it needs a good UI and tutorial in order to succeed. Some games, like Making History as an example, have those qualities. This game does not.
I haven't played any of the other Supreme Ruler games, but after the first couple of tasks the tutorial seems to stop paying attention and assume that you've played the other versions. So at first, it gives you a task and highlights what buttons you need to press. Nice. Then it just gives you tasks. I figured out a couple on my own, then I was like, "Wait a minute. This is a tutorial. Isn't it supposed to be telling ME how to do these tasks and what they mean in the big scheme of things? I've been doing this for like 20 minutes and while I can do some individual tasks, I still have no idea what I'm doing."
You first open the game up and the UI, to me, looks awful. There are open windows covering up most of the map screen. You're positioning and moving units individually. The tutorial was playing during peacetime, which was manageable, but it struck me that when war broke out there were going to be units moving all over the place, perhaps on more than one front, and the entire screen was going to turn into one gigantic cluster****. At that point I thought I'd better quit while I could still refund.
After looking at this I'm not sure anymore if RTS and global strategy should be mixed. I see that most people are saying the other versions of the game are better, so I might eventually check one of those out. I certainly wouldn't recommend this for someone who isn't familiar with the Supreme Ruler games.

Hello Reader of this review.
so, where to start...
i keep buying the new products from this studio expecting them to actually 'improve' on the game/series but they seem to make it worse with each iteration.
an example of this would be the fact that in SR2020 - barracks seperated units by category for easy deployment, they also allowed you to select a specific barracks , and deploy units from that specific barracks.
in SRU they lost the unit dividers in barracks' , but you could still select a specific barracks , an deploy units from that barracks but since you no longer had the units divided by category , that meant searching a small window of barracks units which for a large nation could contain hundreds of units. which meant your ability to play effectively and efficently went down.
in SR the great war....they have apparently intentionally - or unintentionally removed the being able to select a specific barracks so now when you go to deploy a unit from your reserves it randomly spawns from any of the barracks you have. as a small nation with one or two barrackses this isn't a big deal. but add in a country like the US, China, Russia , or Germany who can have a  50 barracks and thousands of units, and its just a large mess trying to organize your military units in a less than tedious manner.
From SRU , this isn't really much of an improvement. it just adds 2 new scenarios - the option to start in 1914, or 1917. it does of course add in some 'ww1 units and techs' however while they weren't researchable due to the time period, these same units and techs for the most part existed in SRU, and SR1936. so they really didn't "add" anything new they just changed the starting scenario and technology level.
If you get SR the Great War and launch SRU to play the DLC version that it gives you when you buy the great war. it has a problem with flickering text. which might not matter to a lot of people but when theres text near a button constantly blinking for me this constitutes an undo distraction especially given that in some games blinking text can sometimes mean your attention is required. this however is not the case.
this as a standalone for someone who hasn't played the older games might be okay.  but as someone whose played the preceding games from this studio...i have to say its just another let down.
primarily in the fact that they seem not to actually add anything into the game  they don't expand on anything. they have reached the point of being comparable to an EA sports game. they chage the start year, give you a few new 'players' in the form of countries, who are given absolutely no TLC to make them stand out from each other in their cultural differences , or traditions.
if you wish to get an Supreme Ruler Game that is the best in the series SR 2020 , is probably your best bet , its not being updated anymore. but it was atleast more user friendly and had a decent interface for the player.
SR1936, has issues with AI garrisons engaging enemy units ,  so their garrison units often just sit there an let themselves get killed without firing a shot. resulting in them being butchered.
They also seem not to have fixed the AI in the sense that the AI still does not understand 'defense' and how to prevent itself from losing cities. its only tactic is the only tactic its ever had which is to throw all of its units at you at once, and then when that fails an they lose most of their units they'll throw one or two units at a time at you. effectively putting up no real strategic, or tactical fight in the slightest.
i really want to support this studio , because SR2020 was one of my favourite games and i keep buying their games thinking they're actually going to improve the game an challenge themselves, but that has yet to be the case.
the one thing i can say about their games is that they're atleast mostly stable in that they don't crash every 10seconds however...
the game does have a lot of other issues such as the AI never ceasing to produce units , since there is no unit limit for countries beyond what they can afford to support this results in an ai constantly adding units to its 'deployed' status which after 10-20 years in the game all of the AI's have produced thousands of units which gradually drags down the performance of the game.
which results in later slow downs. the AI also does not produce resources efficently and since the game does utilize a 'world market' for resource trading that means that eventually the world demand will exceed the world production because while the player may be keeping up with their demand efficently the AI doesn't plan or build facilities to stay ahead of its demand leading to an eventual collapse of the world market which in turn means that even if you don't involve yourself in the wars of the world , you will win simply because eventually no other nation will have the ability to produce military goods(units rely on supplies) which will result in them being unable to fight back in the slightest.
it would be a great game if the actually put effort into improving the game but they do not. and seem to only release updates as a money grab, without any actual improvements.

Okay so I finished Tomb Raider(2013) last night. Personally liked it a lot.
It was a huge "collectathon" with nice lists or items, "percentile completed" values and "find things through walls and then figure out how to get to them" focus witch really tickles my completionist hoarder nature. The whole "ludonarrative dissonance" thing I think was a bit overused since it really wan't THAT big of a deal within the game. It was poorly balanced in that regard, but it sure didn't bother me even when I was "looking for it". :P
I couldn't care much about the combat. It was good, upgrading my gear was sweet and the weapons all had a different feel to them, but wouldn't have mattered much to me if the whole thing was just a series of puzzle mazes.
What I didn't like is actually the focus on "cinematic feel". It tore away the controls from me and yanked the camera around to use a better angle for a "cutscene". I'm okay with and even like cutscenes most of the times, they are an important method of guiding the player or giving some weight to an event, but this had WAY too much of it and in places I didn't need them. -_-
The only other problem were the controls, or more like all the automation it had. A bunch of times the game just assumed what I meant and did that, but when I wasn't perfectly on spot or at the wrong angle it just thought "must be a miss-click" and it let me to drop to my death... But that's just random frustration, nothing to ruin my general experience so YAY! I had a blast maxing out this game in just 20+ hours. :)

Now to start off this review, I'll advise that I have played about another 12 hours on top of whatever it says here because I stated playing with no internet. With that out the way, know that I have completed the game at around 60% and have the single-player DLC. I'm also going to try and keep this as spoiler free as possible, but there will be some instances where it would help. That all aside let's get the review.
Tomb Raider 2013 is a reboot of the classic Tomb Raider Series and a worthy one at that, although it takes strides away from the original series, most that works for the betterment.
The gameplay is often divided up into exploration and combat with the odd puzzle here and there. While someone could still identify this as the make up of a  'Tomb Raider game', the changes are in how this is done this time around. For a start, the majority of the game is spent outdoors and not in tombs like the originals, opting for more 'Point A to Point B' exploration around an island inhabited hostile animals and other people rather than a lot of the supernatural eneimies from previous games.
While the gameplay itself is generally enjoyable, there are some hithces where it fails, such as the overutilisation of items and gadgets. One minute you'll get a new weapon or maybe an item, the next the game will continue to fall back on the use of that item to the point where it's not really fun, it's just 'I have to do this so I will'. The exploration is held back by this, making it sometimes feel like a chore rather than a game section. Some of the controls for climbing can be very clunky, leading to multiple deaths that you should've been able to avoid.
The combat is a lot better, but sometimes can feel a bit unfair or repetitive, but has smart enemy AI to make it fun.
While the main game isn't based around tombs, there are plenty around the island and lot's of collectables. Each tomb is about a puzzle or two long, but are the perfect bite sized puzzles to make you want to find every one and get all the treasure in each of them. Other collectables can be a bit more repetitve and simple, but give rewards that will make you want to keep going.
The plot is probably the bigges problem with this game. While I enjoyed it's style, basing itself around Japanese mythology and being stranded on an island, the pacing and misteps just hold it down. While Lara is a well developed character who develops further as the story goes on, the other characters are almost meaningless in comparison. SOme of them are just falt out unlikable where they're not meant to be. Which leads me to the bigger flaw, it mistakes death for emotion. Whithout trying to spoil anything, this game is almost obsessed with character deaths, falling back on them way too much. If the characters that died were memorable or interesting, I could forgive that, but Tomb Raider has characters that aren't biult up suddenly being dramatically killed for the sake of looking sad, while it's hard to care about most of them. The plot is also to some degree predictable; you see a character and the game almost points out how they're going to be involved in what is supposed to be a twist. This is worst with some characters actually having refferences and tell-tale bits that the player can easily pick up on, while Lara herself doesn't pick up until later. This can extend into the mystery of the plot, as some points have Lara realise what the player has probably realised an hour ago. All this can lead to a plot that stretches itself a bit more than it's welcome. It's all still enjoyable, but wrapped in drawbacks.
This game is a really good game, I understand the praise it's getting but I just don't see it as "Game Of The Year" or with a perfect 10/10. I'd probably give this game a 8.5/10. As $20 it's an alright deal, but getting it on sale is just a bargin. Hope this has been helpful.

To be fair, you have to have a very high IQ to understand Danganronpa. The humour is extremely subtle, and without a solid grasp of theoretical physics most of the jokes will go over a typical viewer’s head. There’s also Makoto’s nihilistic outlook, which is deftly woven into his characterisation- his personal philosophy draws heavily from Narodnaya Volya literature, for instance. The fans understand this stuff; they have the intellectual capacity to truly appreciate the depths of these jokes, to realise that they’re not just funny- they say something deep about LIFE. As a consequence people who dislike Danganronpa truly ARE idiots- of course they wouldn’t appreciate, for instance, the humour in Makoto’s existential catchphrase “Wubba Lubba Dub Dub,” which itself is a cryptic reference to Turgenev’s Russian epic Fathers and Sons. I’m smirking right now just imagining one of those addlepated simpletons scratching their heads in confusion as Dan Harmon’s genius wit unfolds itself on their television screens. To me, this game is like Johan and Kristoff took all of their really cool original ideas from dominions and mashed them together into a single world and decided to have -fun- with the whole thing. CoE has much less micro than dominions and plays a lot faster, but it isn't an easier game. It is true that CoE 4 is going through a lot of growing pains right now, but it is quite humbling how efficient Johan is at fixing things. I've reported a good handful of bugs and have seen most of them fixed. And at the same time, I can confirm that CoE 4 is a straight improvement over CoE 3 in most respects. It's more than worth every penny and I can highly recommend it. If you do decide to give it a shot, be mindful that it is made and maintained by pretty much two people. Attention to detail is kind of Illwinter's thing, and there happen to be a loooooot of details in this game, so missing a few of them is only natural. Most of the bugs or oversights aren't game breaking by any means and the game is a blast, even where it needs improving on.

In these days of bloated AAA titles, it's refreshing to be able to pick up a game that's designed to be played for just 5 or 10 minutes at a time; that said, I've lost count of the number of times that a sneaky "5 minute Time Attack" has turned into a 2 hour marathon. Tl;dr: Quite challenging resource mangament game, but events are so random that strategy doesn't seem nearly as important as luck. The static picture style and repetitive text narration results in little to no replay value and unless you are SUPER in to difficult luck-based resource management, the game consists mostly of clicking through text pages you've already seen a dozen times after playing for only an hour or so.
The game is fairly challenging. Even on the easier settings, things seems to go wrong pretty much no matter what you do. Given that every game I've played has ended in failure, I don't even know how interesting/fulfilling winning might be. If you enjoy difficult resource management games, this might be for you. However, I just got bored very very quickly. There are only so many events that can happen, and reading the same thing over and over gets uninteresting fast. As there are no animations (after the 60 second opening scavenging bit), only a single static picture and text to narrarate what is happening, once the text gets boring, there's just nothing else there to hold your interest. The resource management simply wasn't enough to keep me invested or make me want to play again, since you has so very little control over what's happening. Whether scavenging nets you the supplies you desperately need, or just kills one of your people seems to be mostly randomly generated. Sending them out with some of your precious few rare items just means if they do die, you lose those items. And since they stay out scavenging for a seemingly random number of days, the rest of your family just sits around using up supplies and doing nothing while you wait for the message that you just lost the family member you sent out and all the supplies they took. The handful of random events that occur (knock on the door, mysterious gift, etc.) are also a crap shoot as to whether they're helpful or not, so it's not like you can learn through trial and error which events to go for and which to avoid. Overall, the game has some good ideas and not terrible art, but it's simply not enough to keep you engaged for more than an hour at most.

E: This review was written a day before the July 28th update.
Hello~ as of this review, I've clocked 62 hours on Damned.
The reason why I'm giving this game a thumbs down will become apparent quite quick.
I'm not going to give overviews, so I apologize in advance if anything sounds off to someone who knows nothing about the game just yet. Simply put, despite how much fun I have with the game, a lot of my friends DON'T have fun, and I'm going to list all of the problems here.
1. The insanity system is bogus. E: This has been fixed as of July 28th, about two days after I wrote this review.
Seriously. Having so many bad effects happen throughout the game is annoying, and un-needed unless you happen to be playing against Mary (because she moves slow enough to warrant them). Late in a game, survivors see things that aren't there, but still physically affect them, turning them blind, slowing them down, or making them deaf; often all at once. This seriously needs to become an optional thing, but for now, it's extremely crippling to any survivors that manage to last long enough against monsters to begin with.
2. Mary's teleporting is bogus. - E: Still a problem, unfortunately.
Tonight I've had a game where Mary's teleported into the same general area 5 times, sometimes right next to where she was previously, successfully edging survivors closer to their spawn point with no way to progress. This speaks for herself: Mary's teleportation mechanism is NOT random, but is more biased to teleporting into the same room despite how big a map is, and needs a system countermeasure.
3. Phantom's camping is bogus. E: Still a problem, unfortunately.
This one speaks for itself. Phantom needs a penalty for staying in one place (sometimes to camp a corpse or deliberately trap survivors) for too long. Otherwise, he's fine. Applies to a lesser extent to the Lurker as well.
Those are the three big issues that my friends tend to have with this game. Personally, I've beat the odds and have continued playing despite these major flaws, and can still manage to have fun in the game to this day. And these problems don't even touch the plethora of other problems, such as...
- Frequent client crashes
- Host disconnecting from a game crashes the game
- Connection issues cause duplicates of corpses to walk continuously into walls
- Maps such as the factory spawning unwinnable for the survivors due to key placement
- Lack of care / content / fixes from the developers (E: As of 1/30/16, it appears as if they've deleted their community forum)
So with that being said, I definitely cannot recommend this game, since it's nowhere close to being worth its full $20 pricetag. Know that if you do end up buying this game, whether it's for the full price or on a sale, that you'll be paying lazy developers that are more talk and less action. If you can somehow see past that and can see a glimmer of fun trapped deep within the potential that is Damned, then I shall see you there.
Oh, and don't forget. The monsters can kill you in one hit. But I don't have a problem with that. I just want to actually SEE the monster kill me instead of getting blinded before the climax. What kind of a climax is that?
E: Having the ability for people to change their usernames was a bad addition, so I'm not going to be changing the recommendation of my review. The game's files are predominately client-sided and can be edited by hackers. Now the hackers in the game can change their names, and we'll never know who we're playing against anymore, so thanks a lot 9heads.

Alright. First things first - this game is in no f..king possible universe is a strategy. If anyone'll try to say to you that it is - you can laugh his face off. Strategy games rely on thinking more than on a pure luckfest. This is a 3-in-a-row game with fighting elements. People who gave it "strategy" tag are doomed to hell either, by the way.
So, considering that, how this thing stands? It's a "3-in-a-row" with fighting mechanic and CCG collecting - your fighters are cards. And it has positives about it. The collecting feeling is there, there is a lot of customizing for your team - every card has type (dwarf, elf, etc) level, rarity, kingdom (theme\campaign based thing), traits and color for their ability. You can take up to four cards for a team - including your hero - and based on the sum of these (except for rarity) features you'll gain team benefits. There are also banners that give +1\+2 to certain color matches to tune this up. And, of course, you've your own representation in the game - your hero. Hero gains expierence from every fight, increasing attributes (armor, health, attack and magic), color affinity (gives a chance for double energy from color matches) and can equip weapons that give him actual attacking abilities. Recently classes were presented giving even more to your protagonist - traits like those that creatures have, special class-based weapons and abilities (like mimicking one of creature types for team bonuses). So building your squad of legend is quite interesting too.
Quests here are just series of battles that have pretty uninteresting - in majority at least - dialogues and that's it. Finishing quest-lines give you more tax from kingdoms, opens challenges for gaining souls and some of them have class missions that give you certain classes for your hero. And that's it.
PvP isn't that forced and you don't actually fight players: you invade their defence party that was chosen before by the player and it'll be controlled by AI. It's just that these can be more of a challenge because of roster - some are pretty devastating if not prevented in time.
But the game can't be all pluses, you understand. First, and most obvious, it's f2p. So, a paywall is awaited. Thank Gods it's not so forcing on you, but you'll nonetheless meet people who paid and yes, they have access to ways of upping their squads to "you gotta be kidding me" levels. That's a problem of f2p in general, not just this one. This particular game problems are difficulty spikes during said quests - some fights are done easily, some are nearly rage-stomping you because of 1-2 creatures that are strong on their own. Second problem is luck: your team uses three out six colors but you can't make a single useful match while enemy spoils or takes those that you create? Welcome. Plus 4 and more gem matches give you an extra turn - so yeah "first turn and half of your team got squashed" situation is possible. Not so often but possible. And infuriatingly real. Trust me, THAT makes you rage-quit pretty easily.
So all in all, I'd recommend it. The game isn't bad, doesn't throw you into "no-pay" trash-can, has pretty good artwork, music in some areas and what it's good at doing good thing in it. Look into it yourself and decide.
