I've been following the development of Divergence: Online for some time, and believed in the concept enough that I backed it prior to its availability on Steam. So, how does it stack up now that we all have access to it? First, some definitions.
The game is in Early Access. Valve intended this program to be a kind of crowdfunding where people who liked the concept of a game enough could throw money into a development pot so that the developers could finish the game. In return, they gained access before the game was ready for a general audience. As such, reviews can't be made on the state of the game, but rather on the pace and quality of development. This is particularly true when the game has only been in Early Access for two weeks, as is the case here.
With that in mind, here's my review.
Since the game launched in Early Access, we have seen almost daily updates to the game, and each one is substantial. Major bugs are fixed or mitigated, new features are added, and feedback from the community is addressed. The pace of development is very rapid. This inevitably means that new bugs are also being introduced daily, but at this point in the game's life, a plethora of bugs is to be expected.
So how about the quality of development? Well, I can't see the code or the server performance graphs, so I have to judge this based on the rate of improvement, not just the rate of development. Visually, the game is not progressing very much. It looks better than SWG did, but it has a long way to go to be complete. A lot of the graphics are placeholders pulled from or based on SWG assets. That does nothing to solidify the game's own feel, and this is an issue the developers have promised to address. I believe they're sincere. Whether they can deliver or not remains to be seen. From a systems perspective, the game is improving by leaps and bounds on a very rapid basis. In the past few days, we gained full-loot for PvP, a lot system, new mobs, a ton of new craftable interior modules, bigger harvesters, and others. Network performance has improved, though not as much as systems have.
The community growing up around this game is fantastic. Almost everyone is willing to help each other. It being a full-loot open world PvP game, I imagine you'll start to see the usual roving gangs common to games of this type, but for now at least most people are cooperating. Interestingly, the community on the Steam forums seems much more toxic than the community actually in the game or on the Facebook group.
Not exactly. It borrows a lot of the features, yes. Crafting and harvesting are extremely reminiscent of pre-CU SWG. Combat is nothing like pre-CU, CU, or NGE combat, however. D:O combat is unique, and twitch-based. A lot of supporting systems from SWG are not yet in the game, such as missions or image design. However, this is probably the closest thing we're going to get to a SWG 2 in our lifetimes. It's certainly closer than The Repopulation was.
The one area where this game really falls down is in public relations. The developers need to improve how they deal with the public. I understand they're under a lot of stress, but the image they present is somewhat less than professional. Sometimes this is reflected in the game itself, with game text being just a little too snarky or even immersion-breaking. Thankfully, this is nothing that can't be fixed fairly easily. If they can bring on even a part-time community manager, a lot of this will be solved.
The game is very rough, with many key systems partially implemented, buggy, or outright missing. But we're two weeks into Early Access, and the game is already vastly superior to where it was at launch. The developers know what they're doing, but are in need of a community manager. The community for the game is the reason you should buy into Early Access right now rather than waiting. This game is going to be amazing six months down the road, but the community is amazing
.

TL:DR version -
Positive aspects:
+ beautiful game environment
+ robust crafting/mining system
+ robust base/home building system with the ability to use voxel tools
+ consistent updates ( in my experience since starting the game)
+real time/non turn based combat , healing
+ good in game community/active devs, GMs
+ original race concepts (synths for example)
+ Solid performance, 60 FPS on highest settings with medium draw distance.  Drops a bit when entering populated cities (my cpu is a bottle neck in this case >.<)
Negative aspects
- feature incomplete (this is not unexpected-it is an EA after all!)
- steam community/forums for the game semi-toxic
- PvE - mobs are currently bugged out, and are to be fixed
Points to take note of:
~ Recreated SWG assets. (not ripped from the game, but modeled after and used in the game)
~ Similar skill system to SWG
~ Real time, third person view combat.
~ Mining/Crafting Similar to SWG
~ Full PVP world
Long version
This review on the game is based on having played the game after 54 or so hours based upon steam's estimation.
I will start by saying that the term SWG 2.0 is a bit misleading.  Because to say this implies to me that this game and it's price tag are just a product of a few people trying to cash in on graphically prettier version of Star Wars Galaxies, and call it a day.   The more fitting term that I would go with, as coined by those who described Repopulation would be a, "Spiritual successor" to SWG.
Now granted, the initial experience of the game resembles SWG, down to the familiar UI and clicking noises for typing.  This may lead to the impression t that this game tries to be SWG. What with a UI that is very similar to what you'd have seen in SWG, the skill trees, and even how some of the classes are named.   The next point of similarity is the mining and crafting system which seems to be almost lifted out of SWG, which is not a bad thing mind you because of the complexity that this mechanic afforded.  After harvesting/mining though it is pretty much at this point where the similarities end.
The races are at this point are as follows. A little lizard race that weren't intended to be playable and yet ended up as such due to player demand (which in my opinion reminds me slightly of the Geico Gecko) . A robotic race (the synthetics) which lack the ability to use armor but rather instead are intended to focus around the ability to a) modify your body to provide you more armor upgrade stats, or b) allow you to transfer into a new body , whether it be into a larger combat mech, another synthetic chassis that was just built, or the fallen body of an enemy sythetic that was killed (or a friend who died o,O) while leaving the old body lying there.  Your typical human race which is composed of different sub types of human with different backstories and appearances (genetic lineages?).  The Lokri, another human looking race that look a bit differently and are more adept and "psychic abilities" which will have some advantages for the magic like abilities and skills available in the game.  (not yet implimented).  Another psionic based race called the D-Tanix that are going to be some sort of energy looking guys (not in game yet).  And finally you have the Veli which I would say are akin to space ninjas, and a PVP required, "alpha race" who pretty much have the ability to teleport, and slowly lose energy over time and who are required to kill on of their opposing faction (Vindicator kills Verrator, or Verrator kill Vindicator) to extend their life, which are purposely going to be made to be in low numbers.
Combat, and healing are done in third person/over the shouldver view akin to games like Firefall, Definace, Day Z TPV, H1Z1 TPV, etc etc.  And is real time combat as opposed to the turn based combat seen in SWG.  Same goes for combat healing of other players which requires the use of a medic gun for healing others, or stim packs to heal yourself.
Housing is pretty fun, and comes in the form of either house parts that you craft and plop down yourself, prefabbed housing, or housing that you build using a voxel tool, all of which are tied to a hopper.  In this game a hopper being a central terminal that you can use to tie all your items to in an area which can then be packed up and moved with little issue if you want to find a new spot.
PvE at the moment is broken with the presence of a few of the planned mobs in the game with an AI and attributes that does require  tweaking if you want to avoid a horrible death.  More mobs to be added once these issues are fixed.
As far as work being done, it must be said that this game is far from feature complete and is most definitely a game you could call an "Early Access" title, despite the fact that the game the main guys working on this project started according to some sources as far back as 2012-2013?   Despite this fact, it's not unusual to see the content constantly being updated and nearly daily patches in an attempt to work towards bringing the game towards a more complete state. With an emphasis on *more* given that an MMO is truly never complete given the addition and tweaking of content as time goes on.
The community is a mixed bag as you may have seen on the forums, or even in the reviews, or on the reddit page.  The forums seem to be more toxic in the way of community with people on both ends spewing vitriol at one another.  Whilst in game, things are a lot more sociable in my opinion especially for a PVP enabled world.  This being that as opposed to having players only interested in killing other players (you do have quite a few of those), you have those players more interested in working with each other to build things up and who just wish to craft, mine, and socialize.  Add to this, active staff who are on nearly at all times who are always happy to socialize and talk, and who jump in to make sure that nothing which has broken stays broken.
The game's graphics are quite nice looking,but  the client itself does appear to suffer from lack of optimization.  An issue most noticeable with the Nvidia cards.  (Using a 980TI here, and having some performance issues, whilst better performance is being reported with those using ATI cards). As of this review a patch was done adding the ability to turn on and off some of the visual effects, I've yet to find out if this affects the game's performance in any way at this time.
Another issue that I want to bring up is the use of assets.  This has been mentioned and will probably continue to be a bone of contention for some.  As it is now, the assets are *not* ripped from the SWG client or from SWG Emu.  They are in fact modeled after these SWG assets at a higher poly-count, and skinned from scratch.  And quite honestly, in my opinion (for whatever it is worth) I feel that it was a good choice, because the harvesters, and the assets used in the game fit in with the world/terrain.
All in all, as you can see by the time I put into this game, I am still continuing to enjoy it and if things keep progressing as they are, it is one that I will hope to enjoy for years to come.
*edit* Updated review because client is far more optimized than when I wrote the initial review.

BANZAI PECAN: The Last Hope for the Young Century, or as I would like call it, BANZAI PECAN: The Last Shred of Dignity of This Century, is a half-baked 2D brawler that tries so hard to be like Capcom's God Hand (or not at all) that it falls flat on its face thanks to its poor execution and bottom of the barrel story. I wanted to give this game the benefit of the doubt after the ridicule it got when it first showed up on Steam Greenlight back in 2012 and with all the "praise" this game gets on DESURA, but after seeing this game for what it truly is, I have nothing but contempt for this game and its developer. I could just sum this up with "It has boobs" and give it a non-recommendation, but BANZAI PECAN does so many things wrong. Oh, and don't let my playtime with this game on Steam have you thinking "You barely played it at all!", I've been playing this since I got it at Indie Gala's Greenlight Bundle, so my playtime with game has been
than generous.
Apparently it needs a lot of graphical and processing horse-power (especially with the older versions), even though the graphics look about as good as a mediocre webcomic from the mid-2000's, and the animations are terrible to the point of being a detriment to the gameplay. A recent update apparently slowed them for the regular enemies, only to make the game look even more jarring. Nothing feels "retro" at all as its Steam page claims, neither in presentation or gameplay (seriously, compare this game to something like Freedom Planet and the difference will be night and day). There's also technical issues on the Steam version that I'm pretty sure the developer never bothered to check. Oh, and it appears that the developers stole some of the animations from other games like Waku Waku 7 and some other fighting games from SNK. Lovely.
Audio-wise, BANZAI PECAN is rather unspectacular and there isn't a whole lot to say about it. The music most consists of repetitive techno beats that loops constantly, while others don't really add anything to the game. As for the voice-acting, I can probably guess the actors are amateurs but it's poor even for amateur standards. The actors don't put much inflection or any weight to what they're saying, and at times feels completely wooden. It also appears they stolen stuff other games with some of the sound effects; come to think of it, even the audience cheering whenever you do a "Taco Popper" against the Hunny Bunnies sounds like its ripped right out of God Hand.
Onto the gameplay. In theory, this should be a fun brawler, but the more and more I notice the game's problems. Now it has the usual tropes you'd expect from a beat 'em up: punching dudes in the face (mostly chicks in this game's case), eat out of the garbage for health, pepper in some special attacks for added spice (optional), fight the big cheese at the end, repeat until the you finally punch a hole in the biggest cheese of them all and roll credits. However, for every step it takes, it trips over a pebble and falls flat on its face as the gameplay stems from these major problems:
1) Repetitious gameplay that requires little skill to get through.
2) Poorly-designed mechanics.
3) Horrible difficulty balance.
You really have to take my word for it. It is shallow, monotonous, and repetitive as all hell. Most of the tools the game provides are rubbish, there's no sense of impact anywhere in this game (ironic, considering the developer's company name), nothing feels satisfactory or rewarding, and the bosses are just a test of luck rather than any actual skill. It's just one tedious button-mashing session after another, and by the fourth level I was beginning to get RSI from jackhammering the bloody Attack button! The developers may claim they're taking inspirations from old-school brawlers, but it's plainly obvious they don't know a damn thing about what made them fun in the first place.
As for the story, now why would I devote my time to criticize this game's story when beat 'em ups aren't generally known for good stories to begin with? The answer to that is simple: the writing in BANZAI PECAN is terrible, even for beat 'em up standards! From my understanding, and what the game wants you to believe, that BANZAI PECAN is supposed to be a tongue-and-cheek story. For those that never knew about this in the older versions of the game (specifically pre-v1.3 and later), within the first few minutes of the game, we're treated to a zero-effort♥♥♥♥♥♥joke.
. A lot of the dialogue between Pecan and villains don't feel like it's being tongue-and-cheek at all, but rather it's being clichéd and contrived by forcing innuendos and/or pop-culture references. And if it's not shoehorning innuendos or pop-culture references, then the tropes being used in this story are played for bland.
The exchanges with the "protagonist" and the villains feels trite, hardly even trying to be comedic, it doesn't change beyond this formula, much less even try to have fun with itself as some claim to be. The characters are flatter than a piece of paper, despite what the game's website or manual tells you, without much of a personality to make them endearing or charming in any way; they're just a bunch of big-breasted bimbos. I get that character development or any kind of meaningful story is not the reason you come to play a brawler, but in a game like God Hand it knows it's a video game and runs with it by having characters and situations that are goofy, over-the-top, or just plain silly. But then again, what do
know? According to
, I'm just another dumb 90's kid...
I like also how the one "favorable" review here claims it's God Hand meets Kung-Fu Master, it's like the reviewer never played a good beat 'em up before, much less God Hand. Here's a much accurate way to describe this game: it's Kung-Fu Master meets Eiken by way of Sailor Moon!
In the end, BANZAI PECAN: The Last Shred of Dignity of This Century is another classic example of (lousy animu) style with
little substance. I came here expecting a guilty pleasure, but in the end I feel guilty having played this. The story is a shallow, clichéd mess that doesn't even try to have fun with itself and relies too much on stale memes and innuendos to the point where comes off as just plain terrible. The gameplay fails to get any of the fundamental aspects of classic beat 'em ups that makes them fun. Combine all this with questionable programming and system requirements, little replay value, along with some stuff stolen from other (objectively better) video games and you have a game's not very fun to play. It's about as heartless as it looks, sounds, written, and programmed. If there is anything this game manage to get right, it would be re-establishing my appreciation for games where the developers put their heart into their work unlike the people at SERIOUS☆IMPACT WORKS.

I've heard this billed as 'open world' and a whole bunch of other things that don't apply.  Open world, first.  That was why I bought it.  Open world implies choice.  This thing is as linear as Rygar - an ancient 2D arcade shooter.  Yeah, sometimes you have to go left and down, but forward is always right and up.  No options.  Also, much Hand Of God in this thing.  If you vary from the One True Path that the devs have laid out for you, you fail.  Same as if you die.  So basically, it's a game of dying until you figure out what the devs wanted you to do.  Now normally, that's not such an issue.  There's usually a quick-restore to let you try again.  No such animal here.  This was done in C#, and apparently the devs are noobs, so they went with the default serializers - that save about 25 times as much information as they have to.  So load times are s...l....o...o...o...o....o....w...w...w..w.  Think loading from login in Warcraft slow.  Yeah, that slow - maybe slower.  Also, they pop up alerts every 30 seconds about alternate things to do.  Literally.  If this game is any indication, in the whole of Chicago, there are about 1,500 crimes in progress every second of every day.  I suppose they thought they were being cool.  But it's predictable as hell.  Stealth op?  No problem.  There'll be two waves of adds and car chase involved, probably police, yadda-yadda.  Figure about $150M in property damage and 50 dead by the time your 'stealth op' is done.  Lots of unskippable cut-scenes to make sure that things get a nice substantial lead on you, so that the car/foot chase will take a lot of time.  If I understand Grand Theft Auto right, this is basically a cheap rip-off of that.  Kill everything, drive like a maniac, murder cops and civilians alike, destroy half the town.  If you're old enough to be able to shave without carving your face into hamburger, this probably isn't your cup of tea.  If you're 14 years old, then yeah, this is probably just your kind of game.  A little cheap nudity, fast driving in things that look like cars but aren't anything like them, blow stuff up, kill a lot.  A 14-year-old wet dream.

From FIVE-BN GAMES comes Mystic Journey: Tri Peaks Solitaire; a game I saw and knew I immediately needed to download. Released in May 2017, this is still a relatively new game, and already, it’s had a lot of positive feedback, so I knew it was one of the games for me.
I’ve always loved playing online solitaire games, especially when they look as pretty as this in the backgrounds. I saw there were some achievements for it and I launched the game as soon as it had finished downloading.
First of all, the achievements aren’t that challenging. There are one or two that are (going to be) difficult to get, but the majority of them are more than easily achievable.
This game is so relaxing to play. The background music is so lovely, I would love to actually purchase the soundtrack and have it on my phone. The background pictures are so beautiful. A few times I just look at the background rather than just actually playing the level I’m on. The structures that the cards are laid out into are done really well and are quite challenging and complex – it’s not an easy ride at all on some of them.
The only downside to this game, is it runs with a very “Facebook style” theme. You have five lives, lose a round, lose a life, wait a certain amount of time for all your lives to come back again. That’s really the only downside in my opinion. I could play this game all day long if it weren’t for the life mechanism.
Of course, a portion of this game does come down to luck, due to the cards drawn and laid face down, etc. but this is still a really nice game to play. I definitely have fun with it, and I think that this is one of those that people should give a try. I definitely recommend it, and if you love solitaire games, this may just be the one for you.

Get the game only on sale. It's not worth full price.
It's a fun game, that can eat hours of your day.
BUT, devs left it unpolished.
- It's not easy to transition into late game because you can't easily build the base you want. In the beginning you have to conserve resources, making your design out of necessity and not efficiency. And you can't build any other building UNLESS it is connected to a previous building. The most stupid thing they did to the game, and they won't change it.
- Cannot choose what resources go into what storage dome
- Cannot prioritize picking up resources so they don't get ruined by weather.
- Cannot upgrade buildings, so if it's in the middle of your base, you're screwed.
- Cannot dictate build order, so if you don't build slowly, your citizens will build themselves in a corner and die.
- Cannot have multiple people pass through an airlock at once. Which makes it really hard to work around 3 or 4 airlocks at a busy part of your base.
- Cannot carry multiple items, so if you want to trade 50 of your surplus food. 50 trips will have to be made, which means air lock jams and lots of jobs not getting done (until very late game when u have 50 robots).
Do buy the game, but don't buy at full price.

In my opinion, Forged Alliance can only be described as one of the best Real-Time RTS games of its type. Despite its age it still looks modern with high graphics settings and the addition of a 4th race to the game expands the gameplay possibility compared to the original. However the best thing about this game is the loyal community that continue support of the game with new updates and balance changes through the Forged Alliance Forever (FAF) Lobby after support for the game ceased. FAF provides the essential multiplayer this game absolutly thrives on, the game is still very competitive through the multiplayer and therefore I can also recommend Forged Alliance to seasoned veterans of the RTS genre. The game has quite a steep learning curve though and the fact that there can be 1000s of units on the battlefield means that the game can be laggy unless you have a good computer. Despite this, I think it is a brilliant title that is definitly worth your time if you have any interest whatsoever in the genre, especially as this part of the genre has very little competition.

I loved Total Annihilation and if it ever had a successor, this would certainly be it - and a worthy successor it is! If you haven't played Total Annihilation, it was arguably the defining RTS of the late 90's which dethroned the C&C series. It's now recently become available on Steam too FYI :)
SC built on what TA did so well by changing a few of the mechanics (for the better), increasing the map sizes and unit count, along with improving the visuals. SC:FA refines this further by adding more stuff. It's RTS perfection!
Sure there are other RTS's out there that are equally good (or arguably even better - CoH anyone?), but SC has a winning formula that makes it along with its predecessor (TA), unique and most of all - an awful lot of fun!
There's too much to list about why I love this game so much, it really is truly brilliant.
If you're a true RTS gamer, you will almost certainly already own SC / SC:FA or both. If you've never played a "proper" RTS before, this advertises the genre very well indeed!
To sum the game up in one word; EPIC!

Banzai Pecan: TLHFTYC isn't good, but at least it's better than Altered Beast.
Wait....No...It's worse than Altered Beast. Yes I'm going there.
For those who don't remember, Altered Beast is a single-plane beatemup by Sega. You rise from your grave to save the girl. It's a very simple game, and can be beaten in less than 15 minutes. Most of its appeal is its spectacle. There are huge bosses, neat effects, and it doesn't require any effort to play. Doing well is another story entirely, but like any proper Arcade game, eventually players can beat it without continuing, without losing a life, and even without taking damage. Banzai Pecan has more moves, more personality, more characters, more levels, and women in tiny outfits. So why is it worse than Altered Beast?
Close your eyes and imagine huge red letters scrolling by.
M   E   C   H   A   N   I   C   S ! ! ! ! ! ! ! !
Banzai Pecan has terrible mechanics!
Why would anyone make a game and overlook the most important element? WHY WHY WHY WHY WHY?????
I'm bouncing my PC against the wall like its made of rubber trying to figure this out. Mechanics are the order of all things.  Altered Beast, as simple and plain and dull as it is, actually has functional mechanics. It's a 15 minute game, and you can figure out how everything works in less than 30 seconds. You know when to punch or kick, when to duck, when to jump, and when to get out of the way. Everything provides appropriate feedback.
Banzai Pecan, for all of its tools and special abilities, nothing seems to work like it could. It's not enough to just punch a bunny-girl. No you have to jackhammer the attack button to guarantee a full combo. If you let off the button for 1/60th of a second you'll get hit. There's no middle ground, because enemies can't be stunned. Sometimes they get dizzied, but if you hit them once they recover instantly. Banzai has a couple different moves like an uppercut that sets up air combos(doesn't work on bosses or certain enemies). She also has a dodge but it's hard to avoid something when you can never see it coming. Enemies have two animations, standing, and attacking. There's no wind-up, not even an extra frame or two to indicate that they're going to attack. There's a !! warning when a powerful move is about to happen, but by the time you see it, it's already too late.
As amusing as it is to launch bunny-girls into space and pop their tacos, it makes for an incredibly shallow game. But that would be fine for me. I could enjoy a quaint little romp away from the usual...oh...oh right...the boss-fights. Banzai Pecan has a number of multiple-phase bosses. They have three health meters. The first one? Just mash until it empties. The second? They're going to counter-attack almost every time, maybe you'll get lucky and out-damage them. By the third health meter the bosses use their special techniques. The only way to counter this is to be standing in the right spot and hitting the attack button. This is more trial & error than anything.
Bad game design and mechanics have a habit of culminating at specific points. It's usually a bunch of minor issues that you don't pay any notice, until they come together and snap the game in half. The only way to do any significant damage in Banzai Pecan is through the "magic series" (mash the button for an auto-combo. It's in 95% of beatemups). A single punch in this game does next to nothing. So let's pick a boss like uh...Spearmint. Even though I can't tell when she'll strike, I can mash the dodge button to avoid everything, and pick out the few moments she's actually vulnerable. The problems are: Single strikes don't do any damage & she'll break out of any & all combo attempts. There's no way I'm out damaging her so....um...now what?
....No really...What am I supposed to do now? Am I supposed to "git gud"? Did I miss something in the tutorial? Maybe there's a strategy on youtube...hmm...well shoot. I've played through this game before on easy, and even then I won that fight through blind luck(and easy gives you more health and drops bosses down to half). I seriously can't figure this out. I've beaten Ornstein & Smough, some of those absurd final bosses in 2D shooters without dying, the last boss in Shinobi for the Playstation 2, so uh...What's the deal with Spearmint? Either I'm a complete dullard at Banzai Pecan, or it's so poorly-designed and mechanically defunct that something as standard as a mid-game boss-fight is a ridiculously frustrating struggle.
I'm not failing Banzai Pecan for its aesthetics. I'm failing it because it doesn't even achieve a basic level of competency. It has the stylish moves and loads of extras, but where's the structure? I'd rather play some bland arcade game with two buttons, at least I'd be all but guaranteed a properly-designed game. Sure, arcade games might have been designed to eat quarters, but if they were total crap, players would only spend 25-50 cents on them. By the time you've figured out that this game isn't worth it, you're already out $8-10*. When it comes to bad games I find myself asking far too many questions. It's been well over thirty years and we're still seeing videogames that don't grasp the basic fundamentals.
It's depressing.
*Or you received this game via an indie bundle. In that case you're only out time, which IMO is much costlier.

I Have been a backer of this project for over 3 years now and had access to the pre-Alpha, Alpha, and now am playing the early access(beta) on steam.  At the time of writing this I have over 110 hours played in this game. First a little info about my feelings on the previous versions of the game I have played.
PRE-ALPHA:
I got Access to Pre-Alpha about 3 days after it was available. I mostly hung out in the teamspeak talking to the other backers as well as Ethan; just to get as much info on the game and the people as I could. In Pre-Alpha there was terraforming and a few models available for building, but not much more than that. I played around with the terraforming and built a few things, but ultimately didn't play much as there were no real features in game to test or play with other then terraforming.
ALPHA:
Fast forward about a year or so and I'm in alpha. Now we are on an all new game engine with better graphics, and a much more streamlined pipeline for development. Many bug fixes at a pace of about 4 patches a week some times more. Multiple new assets to play with, and now we have the survey tool, and general crafting tool to play with. I walked around the bare world looking for resources, and even crafted myself a set of cloths, a hopper, and one harvester just to check things out. At this time there wasn't many people playing, and the world was so empty I just lost interest after a few hours each day, and would go to another game to get my gaming fix on. A few months later Ethan did the ferrocrete tool stream on youtube, and I joined in to see the new features in game, and all the fixes. I wasn't able to get a tool at the time because I forgot to ask for one xD so after that stream I didn't play much more.
WEEK TO STEAM LAUNCH:
So it's about a week before the steam launch and I logged in to see some improvements to the world and bug fixes yata yata, but really not much had changed; so I waited in anticipation of what the launch would bring. Also at this point we stopped being allowed to log in because they where transitioning the game over to steam preparing for the launch.
STEAM EARLY ACCESS LAUNCH:
I started playing day two after the launch and in the week I had been away from game, let me tell you.
•	COMBAT BABY OH YEAH.
•	Many guns and ammo types
•	the quality of resources you use have a HUGE impact on the quality of the item you make. Meaning more health for you walls, better capacity on your harvesters, bigger rang on your power grids and so on.
•	All human sub species have been made available and working.
•	Synthetics are working and not glitching out at all.
•	Skill trees working(not all, but in Alpha there were none really).
•	The entire world had been revamped and beautified with plants, trees, grass,  a few mobs(glitchy but they were there) and even entire terrain revamps.
•	hundreds of bug fixes.
•	at least a hundred new things to craft.
Needless to say I was excited to test things out.
NOW FOR THE GOOD PART:
It has now been about one week from the launch of Divergence Online Early Access. I have never been more proud to say; that the work done in the last week is above and beyond anyone's expectations.
•	They have added hundreds of new blue prints to the crafting trees and almost all of the artisan skill tree is working.
•	 As well as medic and some parts of marksman and they are working on more as I write this.
•	 They have added 3 new synthetic chassis to the game.
•	Another hundred or so blue prints to make new items.
•	 Finished creating all the differences between the races (although some mechanics aren't in game so really health is the big one you can see right now).
•	At least a hundred or more bug fixes.
•	An average of about 8 patches a day.
•	An entire new area of the game has been added.
•	As well as finishing the rest of the world in terms of adding more resources, trees, rocks, revamped terrain, more mobs(mobs still aren't fully working though), just an all around face lift.
•	resistances have been added to certain things and more are coming fast.
NOW THE BAD:
You can't have a good review without telling the bad stuff too.  This is beta and as such there are certain things that can be exploited and certain things that bug out and glitch on occasion causing you to have to re-log.
•	Personal factories are a great example of something that take extreme skill to use because you have to do things in the right order and perfectly in order to get it to work(re-logging is almost always required).
•	Walls do not have resistances yet, and apart from people not being able to damage them by punching; they do take full damage from bullets. This means it take 12 shots from the best gun to destroy you solid steel wall. This makes it difficult to protect your stuff because if someone gets in your base (Rory) and destroys your hopper EVERYTHING goes with it.
•	Certain commands from Alpha are still in game making it way to easy for people to get around who know about them. This gives an unfair advantage to the people who know about them and are willing to use them. I know them, but choose not to use them because I enjoy exploring to find my resources and not just teleporting to certain areas that have some already.
•	THIS DOES NOT FALL ON THE GAME DEVS PLATE BUT: Certain people in the current community go around destroying hoppers because they find it funny, and also placing hoppers on resources they don't plan on harvesting, but do it just so other people cannot place their own harvesters.
•	No way to reset your spawn point and cloners cannot be made yet so when you die you start back in the "Spawn zone" like everyone else and have to make the walk all the way back to where ever you where. This can be good and bad; bad for you, good when you kill an enemy.
•	The complexity of the game and current lack of tutorials (in game tutorials, there are many on YouTube and the steam forums) make it kind of overwhelming for certain people who don't want to take the hour or so it takes to fully figure everything out.
CONCLUSION:
Yes there are some bugs, and yes there are some a** hats in game that will try to make you life a living h311. My advice, is to solder on and figure the game out before quitting. Move out of the starting zone and focus on gathering the resources you need for a gun, ammo, hopper, and walls. Use these to build a base and protect your♥♥♥♥♥♥ the more walls the better, make them work to get to your hopper. The hoper only takes three damage from the strongest gun, forcing them to punch it for  over 4,700 times to destroy it. So make the ammo cost unreal with your walls, and you will be safe. Don't like being grifed? Make that gun, and kill the griefer! You can fight back in this game; don't just lay down and take it. I have personally formed a small patrolling alliance of neighbors to protect our area, and its working great. You can also subscribe if you want, for $10.00/month giving you access to the ferrocrete tool as well as an additional 2 play slots. This gives you the ability to play three different characters. Find the resources with one, and then bring the others to the area. If you get killed, log in with one of your other guys and finish the fight ;) . Over all, this game Is very fun, very in-depth, and very, VERY addicting. I would recommend anyone who is not a pixel hugger to buy this game immediately, and get a head start on what is sure to be the greatest MMO of this generation. I hope my review has assisted in your consideration of buying this game, and I hope to see you in game very soon.

An honest review.
From the get go this game does not hold your hand or even give you a clue as to how to get started, i'm a veteran player of SWG and even i couldn't leap in and simply "work it all out". However, i simply asked in game if theres any advice someone can give a noob and i received plenty of help from other players and mainly the Dev himself who always seems to be online! (or at least a GM). There is now a player guide here on steam to help get you started and some youtube tutorials, i strongly recommend you give them a quick look before leaping in!
Once you're past the learning curve and come to learn the controls it becomes apparent that this is a world full of potential, you can envisage the NPC's, player built settlements, vehicles, guilds and all the other professions coming into play. But in it's current state Crafting is really the only option open to us, so if you're looking for a MMORPG where you can dance in a cantina for money, or skin animals for hide then check back on this game in a few months and see whats going on. But if you like the Artisan route it's a good laugh mining for resources, building bases and seeing the results of your labours (if you handle the grind), plenty of people always seem up for teaming together to try and build a home of epic proportions.
This leads me to the community of the game, so far from the people i've met and interacted with i've found a solid base here. No doubt you'll always gets "those few" on games that seem like their only purpose in life is to troll but so far everyone seems helpful and reasonably friendly...  PvP is currently on with no opting out!, so at any time you could be shot or punched, which is worrying sometimes!. But so far i've had ZERO firefights, everyone i've met seems to wanna trade or team up to explore the world.
I've had no problems running this at all with 60 fps and the one week i've been playing i've seen plenty of updates fixing bugs, unlocking new items and skills. To watch a game being worked on as you play it is awesome! (in my humble opinion at least)
As with any Alpha game, it's a work in progress!. So if you want a fully polished, bug free, complete game with all the trimmings then please wait until release and never buy any alpha!!. Because it is an Alpha i can be forgiving for the lack of beasts to hunt and wildlife in the world, there are many many features yet to be implemented into Divergence but i have complete faith this project will come to full fruition as i see it being worked on everyday i play, and from an outsiders point of view i see very passionate people behind it who want nothing more than to make a fun game that takes the crafting and complexity of SWG and turning it into something new.
I can't wait to watch this game grow and evolve over time!!

In Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc, you play as Makoto Naegi, a normal high school student who's just transferred to Hope's Peak Academy with several remarkably talented students. On his first day, he faints and wakes up to find that someone has trapped him and the other students inside the school, isolating them from the outside world. Will they be able to unravel the mysteries that surround them?
Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc is a unique visual novel with a emphasis on investigations, relationships, rhythm game elements (¯\_(ツ)_/¯) and dark themes. It is a well constructed but relatively linear experience that will appeal to people looking for unique experiences, mysteries and fans of Spike Chunsoft's other series Zero Escape.
Pros
- Super satisfying overarching story, intrigue, reveals and conclusion.
- Unique mix of ideas and game genres (visual novel, dating sim, mystery/investigation game, rhythm game) into a cohesive whole.
- Great integration of tutorials for a game with many unique gameplay elements.
- Visuals are outrageously stylish.
- Amazing soundtrack by Masafumi Takada (killer7, God Hand, Earth Defense Force, No More Heroes).
Cons
- Frustrating sometimes when the main character acts stupidly to make the story progress.
If you enjoy weird games, visual novels, the Zero Escape series and are not bothered by dark themes such as murder, suicide, etc. then you might enjoy Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc.

This review covers Black Hole, Ripley's Believe It or Not, Tales of the Arabian Nights and Theatre of Magic. I will edit the review if and when I buy and play more tables.
The pinball physics engine is really good for the most part. There are some noticeable ball speed issues where they seem to move at unrealistically fast speeds in comparison to real-life pinball machines. Depending on the table, there are some major differences between the quality of the textures and sounds, but it's usually acceptable. The worst textures are of the flooring and walls, but those can't really be considered as being parts of the tables. It would be nice if the developers actually made an effort to polish every facet of the game though, since the flooring and walls are also part of the gaming experience. At the time of this writing we are waiting on an apparently big DirectX 11 patch, but there's no telling if the overall look and presentation will actually be improved or if more negative aspects will be erroneously added because of the update. Let's hope it's a positive change.
Some tables seem to be plagued by various bugs. I'm not sure if these bugs are also present in the real-life machines, but in Ripley's Believe It or Not, there are some game breaking bugs. Balls will get stuck and the game engine doesn't recognize some key moments, and these bugs will make you stuck. The only way to fix it is to quit the game and go back. I've contacted support about these bugs and they said that they are aware of these bugs and are working on fixes at the time of this writing.
All four tables I played seem to be emulated well, despite the issues I've mentioned earlier. What's great about Pinball Arcade is that all tables available are based on actual real-life machines. You won't find any digital pinball related gimmicks or gameplay mechanics. This game is almost like an unlimited, interactive museum of these classic gaming machines where physics, reflexes, and skills are all that matter. On the other hand, in addition to the lack of overall polish and some bugs, my other complaint is about their pricing model. I understand some people may feel that $30 per pack is reasonable, but I feel that it's a mistake. If the prices were lower and if there were good sales, I'm sure they would sell much more on Steam. It also seems like the Steam/PC platform is not their priority, as they appear to be spending much more time with other platforms. Overall, if you have an interest in playing real-life pinball machines on your PC, this is probably one of the best options available, and new tables are supposed to be added on a monthly basis.

Pac-Man CE DX+ is the remake of the classic arcade game for the modern age & tastes.  While the core mechanics of the game are practically untouched (eat dots, avoid ghosts, ect.), CE DX+ spices things up for dynamic gameplay.  With half of the playfield (the side you're NOT ON) refreshing after eating the fruit on the other side & stages designed to keep you running with the flow, you'll be on the edge of your seat trying to keep one step ahead of the ghosts.  The addition of bombs, serving as your "panic button" helps to prevent an unexpected turn or an accidental misstep from seriously killing your run.
Pac-Man CD DX+ is designed for those who want to quick game, with 5 & 10-minute game modes, you can play a quick game without it turning into a major gaming session (unless you want it to).  With online leaderboards, you can see how you stack up against the world (& your friends) as you strive to tweak out a few more points with each run.
While this is NOT your parents Pac-Man (back in the arcade era), it's one in the series that you'll be playing for quite some time.  Just remember to have a controller handy when you play!

An honest and long review with backstory.
I was looking for a new Tripeaks game I could earn achievements for here on Steam. I was once a long time user of Club Pogo (and a "badge" hungry player) until MyCokeRewards stopped offering Club Pogo memberships and my year long membership expired at the beginning of 2017. I didn't think I would care so much since I hadn't been on there for a while since I had been a member for well over seven years. Well, it's June 2017 and here I am on Steam looking up card games including Tripeaks; which leads me to this game and why I'm telling you all of this.
I saw it said "mostly negative" but I didn't read the reviews. I figured everyone had some gripe with the game and perhaps it was a personal gripe. I don't know. I went a head and downloaded it. Seemed interesting. Nice little introduction at the beginning and finally I got into playing. About six levels in I was doing pretty good. The music was calming, the graphics were nice, and I was stacking up those achievements. Level 7 began my utter downfall. It seemed impossible to get passed with a three star rating. I tried for what seemed a decade and gave up. Moved on to the next level. Had the same issue. Next thing I knew I was out of..lives? Energy? I don't know. Something it wanted me to buy. Buy how I'm not sure as I wasn't that interested. (I'm a cheap gamer. lol)
Look if you want me to outright buy a game put it right on the store page. Don't make me download your game only to find out there's in-app purchases. I really hate "free" games with strings. There's a reason I stay away from 98% of all gaming apps in the iTunes store now. I really wanted to like this game. I really did. And I see there's a timer that counts down and will give you extra lives, but when I'm knee deep in playing these games I don't want to stop and wait for some timer either. Either charge a price to unlock the full game or expect negative reviews.
If I have to compare it and now I will. Go with Pogo's Tripeaks solitare. Yeah, you have to pay a membership to play the website version but you still get a ton more games for your buck. The better version and which I was mainly comparing it to was "Tri-Peaks 2: Quest for the Ruby Ring" - which is awesome. I'll back that up in a heartbeat. The pirate theme is the best! You may not be able to find that on the Pogo site but it's on BFG. Go with the Ruby Ring. Once you pay for it; everything is unlocked and it's a hell of a lot more fun.
Sorry Mystic Journey. I appreciate the effort, but you just didn't come through.

There's little to no skill involved. You dash around a house that you're unfamiliar with while the camera isn't fixed over your character. It sways and swerves, and there's an odd little delay everytime you pick an item up that slows you down a lot. Your family doesn't have the mindfulness to run into the bunker itself, and the bunker has very little stored in it. Most of what you hide with comes from the 60 seconds you're running around to grab stuff. You can't tell your family to grab things either like how in real life, families have emergency plans of what to grab, where to go, who to call, and what to do.
The game doesn't progress either. Everytime you play is the same as the last, so you can't "bank up" items from previous run throughs as a reward for getting so and so far. This is especially annoying with the random events that can destroy your items. There's no way to flood-proof your bunker, secure the vents, or improve the locks. You will inevitably lose your gas mask, lock, map, flashlight, and other items to random events. You also can't store multiple of these, so there's no way to have a backup plan.
Ultimately, the game is just a run of luck, and very repetitive. You occasionally send family members out to grab things, but they sometimes come back hurt. You probably won't have a medpack to help them with either since you already spent it on someone else who got sick while someone was out. There's also no way to recover your members from going crazy. You can prevent it by having more members alive, by having cards and checkers, and by tuning into the radio when you get the chance, but unless you get the chance to talk with crazy members, they'll probably just attack the gas mask, eat rations when they're not supposed to, and run away.
The same thing goes with family members who are tired and need rest. Can you give them a massage? No. Can you find a heating pad to put on their backs? No. Can you sing them a song or give them a hug or a shoulder to cry on? No. These are all very basic things, but none of them are available.
Also, the plot gimmicks are fun for the first playthrough, but after that, they're boring. You just read the same lines over and over and over.
There's no online MP high score list either. This game would be a blast to play with friends like when you go to a casino and sit at a blackjack table together to see who does the best at a given sitting. The game itself is boring, but in a social setting, it has potential.
Honestly, I bought the game on sale for halfprice, and I still believe it's a ripoff.

Not too sure what to write here so heres a recipe for Pancakes instead
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

Just like with Pinball FX2, Pinball Arcade is worth a try since you can play one table for free and you can try out some of the other tables for a short amount of time. There is also the added bonus of "free table of the month" where different tables are available to play in full when you select "play trial version".
I played FX2 before I played this, so I will probably go into some comparisons with that, so this review might be more helpful for those who have played that one are are wondering if this game is also worth it. I'll start out with the pros:
Pros:
-Well done recreations of real life pinball tables.
-Decent virtual pinball physics (but different feeling than FX2, I'll elaborate later).
-Plenty of great, tried and true classic tables to pick from. A few aren't so good but with how many tables there are you will still get your money's worth. I suggest buying them in the packs (and from what I've heard, people are having issues with in game purchases for the Steam version of this game, so you might be best off sticking to the packs).
Cons:
-Textures and lighting definitely need some improvement (improved lighting for the PS4 version, yet we're still left behind here on the PC).
-Though physics are decent, ball can sometimes be a bit too fast and bouncy, sometimes making it all the way up ramps after a bounce that should barely have made it past the ramp entry.
-Terrible UI. The menu system looks like it came from a half-broken game from the mid-90's, and it doesn't feel very responsive. Tables are selected from one long list and can't be sorted in any way.
-The extra features you get for the "pro versions" of the tables are not worth the extra price. I don't see why anyone should have to pay extra just to have access to the operator menu and a few other minor bells and whistles.
Now, a bit more on the physics and the feel of the game. I did a short review for Pinball FX2 a while ago and was perhaps a bit over-zealous calling the physics spot-on. The physics in both these games feel very good, the best I've ever felt in a pinball videogame, but they are both a bit different and reality actually falls right in the middle of the two. If you are used to Pinball FX2 but have never played a real table, I can describe the ball as being a bit "heavy" and it makes flipper catching and gaining control just a bit too easy. In Pinball Arcade, the ball seems to feel a bit "light", sometimes traveling too fast and making some wierd bounces that send it up ramps and into places it normally would never go (yet despite the extra bouncing I almost never see "airballs"). It also makes flipping catching and gaining control a bit more difficult.
If you've never played on a real pinball table (or have only played a few times and it was a long time ago or something similar) then this probably won't bother you. However, if you have at least some experience on any of the real life tables in Pinball Arcade then this can become frustrating at times. Balls will bounce into outlanes more than usual and sometimes you'll be struggling to pull off flipper catches that you know you can repeat over and over again in reality. However, this extra difficulty is balanced a bit in the scoring by the fact that the ball might also bounce into places or make it up ramps that might not actually happen in reality.
Overall I would recommend this game. It's a solid pinball title that does a decent job recreating real life tables. Just don't expect it to be perfect.

If you ever visited arcades in the 70's, 80's, or 90's, this game is a main line to the nostalgia pleasure spot of your brain. With over 50 tables (and counting), you'll likely never be bored. Beyond that, it's pinball! These aren't fantasy tables, these are loving recreations of machines you'd be hard pressed to find in the wild today. Are they perfect? No. Do they play the same as the real thing? Well there's a world of difference between playing something fully mechanical with all the randomness of real world physics, and that of a digital version. That being said, it will improve your pinball IQ, and many times it comes damn close to being just like the real thing.
A note on purchasing. Buy the seasons, as you are paying for 6 tables and getting 10. It's an even better deal for seasons 1 and 2. Yes, that might make the game seem expensive, but look at it more as if you are buying a new Madden every year, only the old seasons work side by side with the new. Seriously, $30 is not bad for a block of tables that will keep you busy for an entire year. Even better if you get 'em on sale!

As a long time pinball fan, and also a fan of keeping the game alive, I have tried many different forms of digital pinball.
Pinball Arcade not only flawlessly recreates classic tables, but keeps the vibe intact with all the sounds, bells, whistles and other etc that make it feel like the closest thing out there to actually having a table in your home.
Plain and simple: If you like pinball, get this game.

Obviously based on the other reviews, you already probably know this game is incredibly excellent.  So instead of reviewing it, I'll just say that the things that blow me away every time I play this is the detail, economy and graphics.  The detail lays in the fact that every class of military unit (air, naval, land) has a factory which produces it, and each of those factories can be upgraded up to three times, and will enable you to produce new units (as well as old) with each upgrade.  This alone, and not even considering the complex and amazing ways these units can interact with each other, sets this game automatically in a league by itself in comparison to most other RTS games where you level up your entire civilization with a click of a single button and the lapsing of a single timer.  In SCFA, if your T3 factories go down and you haven't upgraded your commander, you start right back at the beginning.
Secondly economy.  Two resources.  So simple!  So deceivingly simple.  I have never cursed or praised the accompanying deficit/surplus of a resource before, and the clever surplus resource sharing mechanics with allies is something I have never seen before or since, and can lead to some shocking revelations about the state of your own economy as your ally's base takes a beating by the enemy.
Third, this is a beautiful game.  This seems incredible to say considering it is years old and I have played cutting edge games on my 2014 mid to upper range gaming rig to compare it to.  But despite the huge maps and environments, it contains incredible detail on many of the units (UEF engineers will flip their treads down when going into water, for example) and the textures just look plain beautiful.  Zoom out to see the entire map and the coloured icons representing entire armies, or zoom in so that you are just metres away from the surface to see two units duel to the death, and you will have an equally satisfying eye-candy experience.
Final verdict, best RTS I have ever played, and certainly one of the most impressive video games period.

Pac-Man CE DX+ is the remake of the classic arcade game for the modern age & tastes.  While the core mechanics of the game are practically untouched (eat dots, avoid ghosts, ect.), CE DX+ spices things up for dynamic gameplay.  With half of the playfield (the side you're NOT ON) refreshing after eating the fruit on the other side & stages designed to keep you running with the flow, you'll be on the edge of your seat trying to keep one step ahead of the ghosts.  The addition of bombs, serving as your "panic button" helps to prevent an unexpected turn or an accidental misstep from seriously killing your run.
Pac-Man CD DX+ is designed for those who want to quick game, with 5 & 10-minute game modes, you can play a quick game without it turning into a major gaming session (unless you want it to).  With online leaderboards, you can see how you stack up against the world (& your friends) as you strive to tweak out a few more points with each run.
While this is NOT your parents Pac-Man (back in the arcade era), it's one in the series that you'll be playing for quite some time.  Just remember to have a controller handy when you play!

Fantastic tactical turn-based CRPG. The combat has a "feel" to it that's pretty similar to X-Com, if you're already familiar with that. Crunchy and satisfying - player skill is definitely a major component. There's occasionally some space made (and even sometimes bonus karma - the game's XP equivalent) for non-violent problem solving too, which is appreciated. The non-violent options are almost always dialogue-based, though. Stealth is very rarely an option.
The world-building, characterization, and storytelling are all solid too. The production values are a little labor-of-love at times, though - for instance, there's zero voice-acting, so actually experiencing that world-building, etc. is definitely an "I hope you like text" experience. If you can get past that, however, you're gonna find you got a lot of bang for your buck. The Shadowrun setting is a fascinating cyberpunk-meets-D&D blend, and, as alluded to, the characters are well-drawn and engaging. The shaman who used to be front man for a punk rock band is a good example. The setting - a kind of anarchist polity called the Berlin Flux State - is another one. One last thing I liked - while what happens in the story is definitely very important to you and the region you live in, it's not yet another messianic save-the-world quest. Think more Fallout: New Vegas in terms of the stakes of the story. There are multiple endings based on what you choose at the end (and to a lesser extent earlier in the story) available as well. That said, I would have enjoyed a wrap-up that included more by way of showing the ramifications of your choices, as well as a bit more of a branching narrative based on earlier choices.
Basically, if you want to see what X-Com combat would look like in a story-driven CRPG with a very unique setting, this is going to be a very strong "would recommend" game.

Free-to-play "match-three-in-a-row" game with awesome amount of single-play missions and questionable multiplayer part. I've seen many reviews depicting that game as a mixture of Puzzle Quest and Hearthstone. Well, haven't played either of them, so I'll describe Gems of War a bit more in detail.
As you can see from screenshots, you got table with jewels, which needed to be moved together, and you have some cards on the sides, 4 for you and 4 for your opponent. There are two ways to win the round: first, you collecting skulls - that's a direct attack, second, you collecting some colour jewels to fill "mana" pool of your units, to perform some specials, unique for every card. And since there are more than 120 different cards, you can gather thousands of combinations of them. Some will be better in particular single-player quests, some - for multiplayer battles.
About multiplayer - being a single-play focused type of gamer, I really enjoying that part. But if you are want to actually battle with somebody on "who's better match 3-rows", that's not your game. For you don't actually making PvP there. You accessing cards of other players, and fight with AI, which using another player's stats and card combination.
Nice thing for that type of "multiplayer" casual game is that you don't have any time counter. It is good for mobile games which you are playing while taking some quick-brake. So you can easily stop playing this game, and return to your main tasks (and vise versa), without any delays. Which is good when you driving in heavy traffic, with big jams on your way, for example...
So. You start your game with some basic cards, quite easily gaining more cards, the most of achievements (except of 3, where you need to play alot for making more exp for levels)... If you're wandering how much is that a "pay-to-win", well, like I said, the focus of that game is on the single-play. All of the selling content can be collected without any payments. So you need to pay only if you want to get on some top roaster from the start, and bend everything on your way from the 1st level. But! Even there it is better if you can actually play the game, and not using super-powers. Without paying any money, on my 30th level I win the most of my battles (more than 80%), just being good with matching jewels. And yeah, I've played versus 80th levelled players (more precisely, their decks and stats with AI) and usually I'm winning. I've seen some reviews from pro-players, who spended hundreds of hours there, that "pay-to-win" becoming a problem lately, much more, than it was before. Dunno. Haven't noticed so far (about 75 hours of playtime and 40 levels gained).
The only real problem is that Gems of War is a server-based game, and every your step should be loaded via internet, to move forward. You can't proceed with anything there without net connection, and if the game loosing that connection, it is freezing until you get back on line.
Conclusion. For a free-play game, this one is very solid. The concept is not original, but so far, it is quite properly balanced. If you can play "match 3" games over and over, I easily recommend you that one, for being variable enough, challenging enough, and fair enough. I can conveniently play it as replacement of my precious Windows Minesweeper and Solitaire games. Well, maybe not as replacement, but good addition to that list.
My mark 7/10. I plan to get the 100th level, but it will be after about 150-200 hours of play, so it is not a good game for quick gold on achievements (even with cash invested).

Bit of a cautious review, this one. I'm only ten hours deep into a game that I've heard can take upwards of thirty hours to beat, and my appreciation of it hinges heavily on how the story plays out.
So far, though, I'm very optimistic.
Basic info first. Dragonfall is the expansion for Shadowrun Returns, and this Director's Cut is completely standalone. The game takes place in Berlin, in a cyberpunk future where humans, elves, trolls, and some other races, share roughly equivalent status and co-exist peacefully, at least notionally. Naturally, there are factors - indeed, there are factions - which threaten to destabilise what could potentially grow into a decent world for all, and your merry band of shadowrunners will be at the centre of it all.
Combat is turn based, and during normal play you can only control "your" character, with the other party members following along behind you. It would have been nice to be able to direct them independently, to get a tactical advantage when you know a fight is brewing, but c'est la vie, one can't have it all. You'll use guns, wield knives and swords, cast spells and summon spirits in order to defeat your many and varied foes. To level up you use Karma points, which are earned as they are in every RPG ever: by completing quests. There aren't enough that you can be a jack-of-all-trades, so try to pick a class you enjoy and go with it.
The combat system is robust, with actions playing out on a tile (or hex) based grid, and plenty of cover to make use of, simply by moving next to it. Flanking bonuses are available, and critical hits are possible on exposed enemies (or on your own team, if you fail to take cover), so it's important to find a decent place and use your action points, or AP, judiciously. You don't want to run out of them and end up stranded in the middle of the room, where everyone can take pot-shots at you. Your team can be equipped with items, such as grenades or medpacks, which can be used at an AP cost and could tilt a fight in your favour. Don't think you can just hoard loads of grenades, though, as inventory space is quite limited. Certain characters will also be able to "jack into" computers and fight in virtual reality, which comes with its own set of abilites, but I've not done much of that yet. It's all turn based and on a grid, though, so probably not that different.
One issue I've had with the combat is that it isn't always possible to tell whether moving to a particular space will let you flank an enemy. I've had to chance a move on a couple of occasions, and I wasn't always able to flank even though the situation seemed very similar. I think a visual indicator before you make your move would have been a great help - perhaps as a toggle so more experience players could disable it?
The real meat of this game, though, is the story. Now, as I say, I'm just dipping my toes in really, but so far it has been very impressive. Shortly after the start, there are some jaw-dropping twists which I didn't see coming, and there haven't been any missions so far which felt like filler, or which took place in boring locations or with boring NPCs. The writing is strong, and the beautiful portrait artwork for different characters does a lot more to inspire my imagination that some plastic-faced polygonal goon ever would. There have been quite a few spelling and grammar errors in the script, though. Not enough to ruin the experience, certainly, but enough to stand out and jolt me out of the experience.
With an interesting world, lovely art, very strong writing and some decent, if not particulaly inventive, combat, Shadowrun: Dragonfall is well worth your time. Jack me

What is Defense Grid 2?
A Tower Defence game in the traditional format. Aliens spawn from one or more locations in progressively harder waves, move towards your base, steal power cores, and attempt to escape. The player has to stop them by spending limited resource points to place towers such as lasers and flamethrowers, in specific build locations around the map.
Is it any good?
Absolutely. Tower Defence has become one of my favourite genres, I've had alot of fun with the original Defense Grid (Steam tells me I've played it for 84 hours) and several other games, so I was expecting to enjoy DG2 and it has not let me down.
What pleased me?
•	Level design. There's a nice mixture of narrow paths, wide open plazas where you can build a maze, and multiple paths that force you to split resources.
•	New types of aliens. One can regenerate health when not taking damage, another gives off an EMP that temporarily disables nearby towers when it dies, and there's also a dropship that lands next to your base and spawns a bunch of other aliens.
•	Tower loadouts. There aren't many new towers, but each tower can unlock new special abilities that are equipped pre-mission. For example, lasers can slow down the targeted alien, teslas can disable an alien's stealth ability, and several other towers can automatically prioritise the strongest alien in range.
•	Orbital laser has alternate modes, such as shooting towers to overcharge them and do more damage for a short time, or shooting loose cores to teleport them back to base.
•	All of the above points result in lots of tactical depth and variety.
•	Value for money. There are 20 maps, they all have multiple alternate challenge modes, and 4 difficulty levels. You can potentially spend dozens of hours trying to achieve a gold medal on each one.
•	Your current score is displayed while playing, which is really useful to see how close you are to earning a medal.
•	Stability. I've only suffered 1 crash in 10 hours, and the developers have just released a patch which should fix the most common crash reasons.
What disappointed me?
•	The story is nonsensical gibberish and voice acting is poor. However, I don't think Tower Defence games need to be strong in this area, so its not a big problem.
Overall recommendation
If you like Tower Defence, buy DG2 at full price. If you've never played the genre, DG2 would be a good game to start with. I don't think its essential to play the first game to enjoy the sequel.

Defense Grid is one of the best tower defense games and Defense Grid 2 does not disappoint.
A must have for tower defense players!

Defense Grid 2 is a traditional tower defense game and the sequel to the excellent Defense Grid: The Awakening.
The Great:
- This series is the pinnacle of the tower defense genre, and this game continues that and expands upon it
- Level design is outstanding to provide just the right amount of difficulty and reward
- New elements added including the missile tower are nice improvements and increase the overall satisfaction of the game
- New RPG elements are added to towers to tailor your playstyle
- Multiple different types of alternative challenges are provided so that there is incredibile replayability
- Steam workshop support to increase longevity of the game
The Good:
- The game looks and runs very well
- The game only marginally improves on the first game (but the first game was great)
The Bad:
- The story is more or less standard, but there are too many characters that don't add anything
- The story dialogue bits happen after you complete a level and more often than not you quickly skip to the next level without thinking and miss parts of the story
- The first Defense Grid had a limited amount of clever humor that did not overstay its welcome.  This game tries too hard to make dialogue funny that really isn't
- Some small bugs
Conclusion:
The Defense Grid series remains the definitive tower defense experience, and Defense Grid 2 - while mostly iterative - only extends and enhances that lead.  I highly recommend the game for anyone interested at all in the tower defense genre

A match 3 game with a nice little twist.  You collect troop cards to build on and level up throughout the game, and it's the strength of your team that helps you win each match.  You can join a guild and earn numerous rewards.  There's a LOT of hours of game play in this game!
You have to earn gold to take part in things throughout the game, and I see numerous negative reviews complaining about how they have no gold to do things throughout the game.  I don't understand...even as a casual player, I've earned more than enough gold to do just about anything that I want in the kingdom, and still have a cushion.
The game can be highly addictive, if you like match 3 games.  It's not just a mindless match 3 game, either.  You have to plan out your moves, otherwise you could end up in some serious trouble.
Of course, you have the option to purchase diamonds to buy special chests and other things in-game, but you can also purchase chests with gold and glory that you earn; although they're not as "high class" as the diamond chests, they're pretty good nonetheless.  Anything you need...except for the diamonds, of course...can be earned in numerous different ways throughout the course of the game.
The game play itself is a lot of fun. Depending on what sort of troop you're playing against, the game can go quickly, or it can be an intensive grind match that lasts and lasts.  It's the grind matches that give you a serious sense of accomplishment in the game when you win one, which is something that you really don't find in other match 3 games.
Overall, I think this is an excellent game, and well worth a try for even the most serious match 3 game player!

Initially I was hesitant on purchasing this game after reading some reviews that claimed bugs spoiled good gameplay. However I did so anyway and have to say that I'm very pleased with the product. In fact I suspect some of the 'bugs' were just player's inabilities to manage their base properly and obtain what amounts to a very delicate balance of supplies, oxygen, water and power to keep your personnel alive.
If you aren't a fan of the slow but sure building sims this game isn't for you. I started out landing on the desert planet and started goofing trying to decide on what to build first. By the time I made a decision and where to place the item my crew started dropping like flies due to lack of oxygen. This occurs during the first three minutes or so of the game so start constructing an airlock, oxygen generator and everything else needed to support oxygen production. Having done that I thought I'd now take my time and watched my crew die of starvation because I failed to get buildings and machines to support sleep, food and water up in time. Once you manage to achieve this you move on to other structures/machines that further support your little colony. Failing to watch the balance of all this as well as not having enough or having too litle colonists factors into the equation as well. You also find that shutting down production in some also allows certain stocks to recoup and spreads your work force out to concentrate on other more important tasks. As I said...lotta things to factor in to make the place work and survive.
So I won't bore you with game play. Just know it's long and trying but as long as you can keep everyone happy, working, fed, watered and breathing you're doing fine. Once you reach certain achievements on the planet you're currently colonizing the next planet of four (which becomes harsher and difficult to inhabit with each progression) becomes available for you to colonize.
The best way I can descibe this in similarity is think of "Banished" except in outer space. Players of 'Banished' have found that it too is just as unforgiving as Planetbase can be. Each requires balancing many factors to keep things going smoothly.
Kudos to the developers on this one. I still have something along the lines of 5 achievements on the first planet to complete so there is still plenty more gameplay as far as I'm concerned but I daresay some folks would eventually consider it repetitious. I'm content with just struggling to survive.
